Emblems in 3D · a working edition

The whole Hypnerotomachia, in English

Robert Dallington's Elizabethan English of 1592 stops partway through chapter XVII, at the word Mustulento — facsimile page 193 of 467 — and everything after it has existed in English only under copyright. This edition renders every page of the book: the second half into English for the first time, and the first half afresh beside Dallington's, from the title page and Leonardo Crasso's dedication onward. Each page is set beside the 1499 Italian it came from, so that any sentence can be checked.

463 of 463 pages englished · 153,537 of 153,537 source words (100.0%)

Method. The Italian is the Wikisource transcription of the 1499 Aldine (scanned from the MIT Press facsimile). That transcription is unproofread, so where it looks corrupt we check the facsimile and the 1545 Aldine reprint before translating rather than rendering a scanner error into English. Readings still in doubt are marked [?like this] and explained in the notes; a page is only verified once none remain.

Register. Modern but formal. We do not imitate Dallington — a reader should be able to tell at a glance which English is 1592 and which is ours. The formality comes from vocabulary and sentence shape, not from archaic grammar.

Rights. The 1499 original is public domain, and a faithful transcription of a public-domain work carries no new copyright. Joscelyn Godwin's 1999 translation is in copyright and has not been consulted, quoted, or paraphrased at any point; every English sentence here was made from the Italian in the left-hand column.

The whole book, section by section

A synopsis of all thirty-eight chapters and the closing matter. The first half is Dallington’s 1592 English; from chapter XVII the summaries lead into our own translation — click a chapter number to jump to its parallel text.

Book I — Poliphilo's Dream

Chapters I–XVI · in Robert Dallington's 1592 English

The first half of the dream already exists in English: Robert Dallington's Hypnerotomachia: The Strife of Loue in a Dreame (London, 1592), which runs to facsimile page 193 before breaking off mid-sentence. These summaries orient the reader through Dallington's half; the parallel text below begins where he stopped.

Dallington's 1592 English at Project Gutenberg ↗
IDallington, 1592

Sleepless with longing for his Polia, Poliphilo falls asleep at dawn and the dream begins. He wakes, within the dream, on a wide plain and strays into a dark, trackless wood where neither light nor path survives; terrified, he prays his way out at last to a clear stream and drinks.

IIDallington, 1592

Following a sweet Dorian music across a flowering country, Poliphilo is so overcome by wonder that he falls asleep within the dream, and wakes into a deeper dream-region strewn with the ruins of antiquity.

IIIDallington, 1592

The great antiquities: a colossal stepped pyramid crowned by a needle-obelisk — the vastest structure the imagination can raise — set out with exact measurement, together with a winged horse, elephants of stone, and a bronze colossus he climbs into and through.

IVDallington, 1592

The triumphal portal. Poliphilo studies a monumental gateway to the last inch — its columns and entablature drawn to the Vitruvian rule, its friezes and Egyptian hieroglyphs decoded — the book's first great architectural ekphrasis and, in effect, its architectural manifesto.

VDallington, 1592

The dragon. In the dark vaulted passages beyond the gate a fearsome dragon starts up; Poliphilo flees in blind panic through the labyrinthine dark and breaks out into a bright and pleasant land.

VIDallington, 1592

The five nymphs. Five lovely nymphs — the five senses — find the trembling Poliphilo, put his fear to rest, and invite him to bathe with them.

VIIDallington, 1592

The bath. In a jewelled bath-house the nymphs bathe with him amid teasing, playful eroticism, and spring a trick fountain on him — the book's lightest and most sensuous interlude.

VIIIDallington, 1592

Queen Eleuterylida. The nymphs lead Poliphilo through marvellous gardens to their sovereign, Eleuterylida (Free Will), enthroned in a palace of impossible richness.

IXDallington, 1592

The palace and its gardens. The queen's residence unfolds: its architecture and precious materials, a great obelisk, a topiary garden, and a water-labyrinth figuring the ages and hazards of human life.

XDallington, 1592

The banquet. A feast of unmeasured luxury — gold and gem vessels, perfumed dishes served in order, music and dance — described course by course as a set-piece of the senses.

XIDallington, 1592

The two guides. After the feast the queen shows Poliphilo emblematic marvels and gives him two handmaids to lead him on: Logistica (Reason) and Thelemia (Will, or Desire).

XIIDallington, 1592

The three doors. The guides bring him to three portals, three ways of life: Theodoxia, the glory of God; Cosmodoxia, the glory of the world; and Erototrophos, the mother of Love. He looks behind each in turn.

XIIIDallington, 1592

The choice of Love. Poliphilo chooses the third door, the amorous life; Reason departs from him in sorrow, and a nymph — Polia, though he does not yet know her — takes him in charge.

XIVDallington, 1592

The Triumphs of Jove. The nymph leads him to four triumphal chariots celebrating the loves of Jupiter — Europa, Leda, Danaë, and Semele — carved, gilded, and peopled in the book's most sustained ekphrasis of the antique triumph.

XVDallington, 1592

Vertumnus and Pomona. Further triumphs pass: the seasonal procession of Vertumnus and Pomona, gods of the turning year and the orchard, with rustic sacrifice and song.

XVIDallington, 1592

Toward the temple. The rustic triumphs continue toward the rites, the offerings are prepared — and the narrative approaches the altar of the Seasons where, on facsimile page 193, at the word Mustulento, Dallington's English breaks off.

Book I — Poliphilo's Dream, continued

Chapters XVII–XXIV · newly translated in this edition

From here to the end of the book the only prior English was under copyright. These chapters are translated afresh from the 1499 Aldine; each links into the parallel text below.

XVIIpp. 189–224

The four Seasons and the Temple of Venus. Our translation opens with the four Seasons carved on an altar and the rustic rite of Priapus, then the round Temple of Venus Physizoa ("life-giving Venus") — its vine-cast bronze dome, its self-opening magnet-door inscribed Trahit sua quemque voluptas ("each is drawn by his own pleasure") — where, at the sacred well, Polia at last reveals herself and the lovers are joined.

XVIIIpp. 225–241

The sacrifice and the miraculous rose-bush. Polia, a temple-initiate, burns the incense of Venus and sacrifices the turtledoves; a winged spirit rises from the smoke; the priestess speaks the great prayer to Venus, and from the blood-quenched fire a rose-bush miraculously springs, whose fruit the lovers eat in communion. Then they come out to the ruined Polyandrion, the seaside tomb-temple of those who died of love.

XIXpp. 242–282

The Polyandrion and its epitaphs — the longest chapter. Poliphilo explores the ruined tomb-temple: the obelisk of Caesar with its ant-and-elephant concord-hieroglyph, the crypt with its fire-and-ice Hell-mosaic of lovers, and a great sequence of love-death epitaphs (Nevia, Leontia and Lollius, and Artemisia's Mausoleum). A Rape-of-Proserpina fresco frightens him back to Polia; Cupid then arrives by boat, and the marine gods do him homage as the crossing begins.

XXpp. 283–289

The crossing to Cythera. In Cupid's reversible boat, under the hieroglyph-standard Amor vincit omnia, the six nymphs rest their oars and sing; Polia answers alone in the Lydian mode, and the boat skims to the island — "perseverance alone wears the victor's diadem."

XXIpp. 290–325

The gardens of Cythera. The circular island, ring within ring, is described from its own measured plan: the outer grove, the ring-river with its citrus pergola, the seven-step terraces and their jewelled knot-parterres (planted herb by herb), an aviary of the transformed, and the herb-set inscriptions dedicating the rings to Jupiter.

XXIIpp. 326–357

The triumph of Cupid and the theatre of Venus. The landing, the trophies of the disarmed gods (Quis evadet? — Nemo, "Who escapes? — No one"), the masque of allegorical nymphs, and the serpent-drawn car that bears the lovers, bound in roses, to the great amphitheatre — an obsidian-floored theatre of planted tiers and perfumed pavements, where the lovers are unbound and Psyche restores Cupid's golden arrow.

XXIIIpp. 358–368

The Fountain of Venus. At the theatre's centre stands the most-holy fountain; the curtain before the goddess is torn away, and Venus is revealed in her majesty — the scene the whole island, and the whole 3-D world, is built to walk toward.

XXIVpp. 369–380

The spring of Adonis. Out of the theatre to a sacred spring and the tomb of Adonis, where Venus's yearly rite of mourning for her slain love is told — and Book I closes.

Book II — Polia's Telling

Chapters XXV–XXXVIII · newly translated in this edition

The second book turns the whole story over to Polia, who tells it in her own first person to the nymphs at the fountain — her lineage, her cruelty, her punishment and conversion — before Poliphilo takes up his side. It is among the earliest sustained female first-person narrations in the Italian romance tradition.

XXVpp. 381–386

Book II begins: Polia's lineage. Polia takes up the telling in her own voice — her ancient family, the founding of Treviso from the rivers of the Veneto, and, at her window in the year 1462, Poliphilo's first sight of her.

XXVIpp. 387–397

The plague and the cruelty. Struck by the plague, Polia vows herself to Diana and enters the chaste temple; when Poliphilo declares his love there, she answers with hatred, watches him die at her feet, and flees — the dark centre of her confession.

XXVIIpp. 398–408

The visions of the punished. A whirlwind carries Polia to a wood where she sees Cupid torturing two cruel women; a nightmare of two executioners follows; terror at last begins to break her frozen heart, and her nurse takes her in to give counsel.

XXVIIIpp. 409–416

The nurse's counsel. By myth, and by a cautionary tale of a girl who refused love in her season and was ruined by it, the nurse argues that Love conquers even the gods — "adapt the sweet years to love" — and sends Polia to the priestess of Venus.

XXIXpp. 417–427

The conversion and the revival. The flame at last kindles in Polia; she hastens to the temple, revives the dead Poliphilo with her tears and her embrace, is beaten from Diana's shrine, and — Venus's fire routing Diana's ice in a vision — comes to the priestess and vows herself to love.

XXXpp. 428–431

Poliphilo before the priestess. Called forward, Poliphilo petitions the priestess to make the two hearts one; Polia, overcome by a love she can no longer contain, interrupts to answer him.

XXXIpp. 432–435

Polia's avowal. Polia declares her answering love and seals it with the pledge-kiss; the priestess, seeing them already joined by Love himself, blesses the union.

XXXIIpp. 436–443

Poliphilo's telling begins. Obeying the priestess, Poliphilo praises perseverance and recounts his own side: how he first saw Polia at a festival in Diana's temple and fell instantly in love, and how — unable to speak his heart — he resolved to write.

XXXIIIpp. 444–447

The love-letters. Poliphilo sends two courtly love-letters; Polia, unmoved, receives them "as a marble statue."

XXXIVpp. 448–454

The third letter, and the death. A third letter fails too — his love, he sees, only hardens her to stone; he finds her alone in the temple and, pleading, collapses and dies at her feet: the death-scene now told from his own side.

XXXVpp. 455–460

The vision at Venus's throne. His freed soul is borne to Venus's throne, where he complains against Cupid; the god strikes Polia's image with the golden arrow — her conversion, seen from heaven — and gives her to Poliphilo, and Venus's voice, "which could soften a diamond," sends his soul home.

XXXVIp. 461

The binding. Revived in Polia's arms, Poliphilo prays the priestess to bind the two of them for ever; and Polia brings her long narration to a close.

XXXVIIpp. 462–464

The dream's end. The nymphs return to their dance; the lovers, alone at last, exchange their final avowals — and, at the very height of the embrace, Polia dissolves into fragrant smoke: "Poliphilo, my dear — loving me — farewell."

XXXVIIIp. 465

The awakening. Poliphilo wakes to the nightingale and the risen sun — the dream, and Polia, gone.

The closing matter

Polia's epitaph, and the printer's leaf

Epitaphium Poliaep. 466

Polia's epitaph, and the verse in which Poliphilo speaks — the book's grief made a monument.

Errorip. 467

The 1499 errata leaf, closed by the Aldine colophon: "At Venice, in the month of December 1499, in the house of Aldus Manutius, most accurately."

p. 2confidence: highdrafted

Leonardus Crassus Veronensis Guido Illustrissimo Duci Urbini S. P. D.

CUM semper Dux invictissime ob singulares virtutes et famam tui nominis te colui et observavi, tum maxime ex quo frater meus tuis auspiciis in Bibienae obsidione militavit, quicquid enim tunc per te in eum collatum fuit, id autem multum fuisse saepe memorat benignitatem et humanitatem in se tuam referens, id totum ad Crassos omnes pertinere arbitrati sumus, et quod unus tulit, id omnes tibi acceptum ferimus, nec iam ei concedimus, ut magis tuus sit, quam nos omnes sumus. Sed fratres mei occasionem expectant causa tua non modo sua omnia, sed vitam etiam exponendi. Ego autem, qui pro virili mea, quo nam pacto me tibi aperiam saepe cogito, cogitaboque, donec perfecero, nunc in voti mei spem venio aliquam. Nam, cum sciam tecum non fortunae bonis plus agi posse, quam aquis (ut fertur) cum mari, solasque apud te literas et virtutes posse, literis aditum ad te tanquam vadum tentavi. Venit nuper in manus meas novum quoddam et admirandum Poliphili opus (id enim nomen libro inditum est) quod ne in tenebris diutius lateret, sed mortalibus mature prodesset, sumptibus meis imprimendum et publicandum curavi. Verum ne liber iste parente orbatus veluti pupillus sine tutela, aut patrocinio aliquo esse videretur te patronum praesentem delegimus, in cuius nomen audaculus prodiret, quo, ut ego amoris nunc et observantiae in te meae ministro et nuncio, sic tu ad studia, et multiplicem doctrinam tuam socio saepe utereris. Tanta est enim in eo non modo scientia, sed copia, ut cum hunc videris, non magis omnes veterum libros, quam naturae ipsius occultas res vidisse videaris. Res una in eo miranda est, quod cum nostrati lingua loquatur, non minus ad eum cognoscendum opus sit graeca et romana, quam tusca et vernacula. Cogitavit enim vir sapientissimus, si ita loqueretur, unam esse viam, et rationem, qua nullus, quin aliquid disceret veniam negligentiae suae praetendere posset, sed tamen ita se temperavit, ut nisi, qui doctissimus foret in doctrinae suae sacrarium penetrare non posset, qui vero non doctus accederet non desperaret tamen. Illud accedit, quod si quae res natura sua difficiles essent, amoenitate quadam tamquam reserato omnis generis florum viridario oratione suavi declarantur, et proferuntur figurisque et imaginibus oculis subiectae patent et referuntur. Non hic res sunt vulgo expositae et triviis decantandae, sed quae ex philosophiae penu depromptae, et musarum fontibus haustae quadam dicendi novitate perpolitae ingeniorum omnium gratiam mereantur. Suscipias igitur princeps humanissime Poliphilum nostrum, qua doctos fronte soles, et ita suscipias, ut cum animi grati munusculum sit, tui Leonardi Crassi admonitus libentius legas quod si (ut spero) feceris, et hic nullius censuram

(Leonardo Crasso's dedicatory letter to Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino. Latin. It runs over onto page 3.)

LEONARDO CRASSO OF VERONA SENDS MUCH GREETING TO GUIDO, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS DUKE OF URBINO.

Since I have always honoured and regarded you, most unconquered Duke, for the singular virtues and the fame of your name — and most of all since my brother served under your auspices at the siege of [?Bibbiena] — whatever was then bestowed by you upon him (and he often recalls it was much, reporting your kindness and humanity toward him), all of that we have reckoned to belong to all the Crassi; and what one received, we all count as received by us from you, nor do we now concede to him that he is more yours than we all are. But my brothers await an occasion to expose for your sake not only all they have, but their lives as well.

I myself, who so far as my strength allows think often — and shall go on thinking, until I have done it — by what means I may [?open myself to] you, now come into some hope of my wish. For since I know that with you one can do no more by the goods of fortune than (as the saying goes) by water with the sea, and that letters and virtues alone have power with you, I have tried letters as a ford, for a way of approach to you.

There came lately into my hands a certain new and admirable work of Poliphilo (for that is the name given to the book), which — that it should not lie hidden any longer in darkness, but should profit mortals in good time — I have seen to the printing and publishing of at my own expense. But lest that book, bereft of its parent, should seem to be like a ward without guardian or any patronage, I have chosen you as its present patron, in whose name it might go forth [?a little more boldly]: so that as I now use it as the servant and messenger of my love and regard toward you, so you may often use it as a companion to your studies and your manifold learning.

For there is in it not only such knowledge but such abundance that, when you have seen this book, you will seem to have seen not so much all the books of the ancients as the hidden things of nature herself.

There is one thing in it to marvel at: that although it speaks in our own tongue, one has no less need of Greek and Latin to understand it than of Tuscan and the vernacular. For that most wise man reckoned that, if he spoke so, there was one road and one method by which nobody could plead his own negligence as excuse for learning nothing. Yet he tempered himself so that none but the most learned could penetrate into the sanctuary of his doctrine, while one who came to it unlearned should not despair even so.

Add to this, that if any matters were by their own nature difficult, they are declared and brought out in sweet speech with a certain pleasantness — as though a garden of every kind of flower were unlocked — and they lie open and are set before the eyes in figures and images. These are not things set out for the crowd and to be chanted at the crossroads, but such as, drawn from the storehouse of philosophy and drunk from the fountains of the Muses, polished with a certain novelty of speaking, may deserve the favour of every wit.

Take up then, most humane prince, our Poliphilo, with the brow you are wont to show the learned; and take him up so that, since he is the little gift of a grateful mind, you may read him the more willingly for being reminded of your Leonardo Crasso. And if you do this (as I hope), then he will fear no one's censure, having undergone yours; and he will be read the more often by others, who will be thought to have been read by you; and I shall hope that in some part I have attained what I had wished for.

(The end of Crasso's letter; then Giovanni Battista Scita's poem to him; then the beginning of the anonymous elegy to the reader, which runs over onto page 4. Latin.)

…Farewell, and number your Crassi, with me, among your own.

Notes

A poem of Giovanni Battista Scita to the most distinguished Leonardo Crasso, learned in the liberal arts and in pontifical law.

This wonderful and new little book,
to be set level with the books of our ancient forebears,
in which whatever in the whole world life offers
that is rare and noble is borne and borne again —
it brings you, Crasso, as much thanks
as it brought to Poliphilo its parent.
Poliphilo gave it life; you too
have given it life, and more: you drive off its death.
For when it lay buried in neglect,
already dreading Lethe close at hand,
you give it to all the nations to be read;
nor do you spare your money or your labour,
but, better than its parent, you have lifted
the cast-out child into your lap.
They say Lyaeus was once twice-born.
So has it now befallen this book: and Poliphilo
gives it back a father, and Crasso a Jove.

---

An anonymous elegy to the reader.

Candid reader, listen to Poliphilo
telling his dreams — dreams sent from the highest Pole.
You will not waste your labour, nor will it irk you to have heard these things:
the work abounds in wonders, with matters so various.
If, grave and stern, you despise the erotic, then learn, I beg,
the sequence of its matters, so well disposed.
Do you refuse? Then at least the style, the new tongue and the new
grave speech: wisdom asks that you look at her.
If you decline that too, then look at the geometry; learn the many
ancient things crowded with the marks of the Nile.
Here are pyramids, baths, and enormous colossi,
and the ancient form of obelisks lies open.
Here shines a diversity of bases and columns in their variety,
and their arches, friezes, architraves,
and capitals and beams, and cornices with the quadrant —

(the elegy continues on page 4)

---

Confidence: high. Verse is rendered line for line and plainly, without rhyme or metre: forcing either would put words in the poet's mouth, which is the one thing this edition may not do.

  • What Scita's poem is actually saying, and it is the sharpest thing in the front matter:
  • "They say Lyaeus was once twice-born." Lyaeus is Bacchus, born first of Semele and a second
  • The elegy is a table of contents in verse, and a wonderfully cynical one. It works down a
  • "The marks of the Nile" — niliacis notis, the Egyptian hieroglyphs, which Poliphilo reads
  • "With the quadrant" — cum quadrante, an architectural term for the fillet or quarter-round
  • Giovanni Battista Scita of Verona was a friend of Crasso's. His poem and the anonymous

Here is the two-coloured dance of robbers, and the whole life

Here read what he says of the threefold majesty of the Thunderer,
and what he himself performed at the three gates.
What form Polia had, how adorned; then behold
the four heavenly triumphs of Jove.
Besides these, he tells the various affections of love,
and its works, and how fiercely that God rages.
Here Pomona triumphs together with Vertumnus.
Here too are rites performed to the Lampsacan god.
Here is a huge temple, more perfect than any art,
and the manifold rites of the ancient sacred things.
Soon you will see another temple, spoiled by the teeth of time;
and here very many things pleasing to your mind:
the seats of Tartarus, many epitaphs, and the boat
in which the boy of Venus is carried over the vast straits;
and the highest honours reverently shown to him
by all the gods, as many as the waters hold.
Here see Cythera, marked out with gardens and meadows,
in the middle of which curved theatres lie open.
And here you may behold the triumph of Cupid.
Here is the fountain, and the venerable form of the Paphian Goddess;
and what is celebrated around the tomb of beloved Adonis
yearly by Venus — and you shall read the Naiads' laws.
This is the series of matters contained in the first volume:
these are the new dreams of the divine Poliphilo.
Where she was born, of what stock, of what parents sprung,
is Polia — the book that follows sets out thereafter.
And who first founded the walls of Treviso.
From there it has the whole sequence of a long love.
Lastly the book is furnished with a long appendix,
which I do not think, reader, it will be thankless to read.
There are very many things besides; it wearied me to report them all.
Take what the horn of plenty has generously given.
Behold, the book delights and profits. If you scorn both,
believe the fault is not the book's, but yours.

The end.

Lector si tu desideri intendere brevemente quello che in quest’opera se contiene, sapi che Poliphilo narra havere in somno visto mirande cose, la quale opera ello per vocabulo graeco la chiama pugna d’amor in somno. Ove lui finge havere visto molte cose antiquarie digne di memoria, et tutto quello lui dice havere visto di puncto in puncto et per proprii vocabuli ello descrive cum elegante stilo, Pyramide, Obelisci, Ruine maxime di edificii. La differentia di columne la sua mensura, gli capitelli, base, epistyli, cioè trabi recti, trabi inflexi, zophori, cioè frisii, coronice cum gli sui ornati. Uno magno caballo. Uno maximo elephanto. Uno colosso, una porta magnifica, cum le mensure et li sui ornamenti, uno spavento, li cinque sentimenti in cinque Nymphe uno egregio bagno, fontane, el palatio della regina che è el libero arbitrio. Uno regio pasto et superexcellente. La varietate di zoie overo petre pretiose et la sua natura. Uno gioco de scachi in ballo a tre mensure de soni. Le tre porte in quale lui rimanse Polia come era di habito et habitudine. Polia el conduce a mirare quatro triumphi mirandi di Iove, le amorose deli Dei. Quelle di poeti, l’affecto et effecto d’amore vario. El triumpho di Vertumno cum Pomona. El sacrificio all’antica di Priapo, uno maraveglioso tempio per arte descripto. Ove furon facti sacrificii cum mirabili riti et religione. Come Polia et lui andorono allo littore aspectare Cupidine, ove era uno tempio destructo. Nel quale Polia suade a Poliphilo el vadi intro a mirare le cose antiche. Et quivi vide molti epitaphii, uno inferno depincto di musaico. Como per spavento de qui se partì et vene da Polia. Et quivi stanti vene Cupidine cum la navicula da sei Nymphe remigata. Nella quale ambo intrati, Amor fece vela cum le sue ale. Et quivi dagli Dii marini et Dee, et Nymphe et monstri li fu facto honore a Cupidine, giunseron all’insula Cytherea, la quale Poliphilo distincto in boschetti, prati, horti, et fiumi, et fonti plenamente la descrive, et li presenti fu fatti a Cupidine et lo accepto dalle Nymphe, et come sopra uno carro triumphante andorono ad uno mirando theatro tuto descripto. In mezo del’insula. Nel mezo dil quale è il fonte venereo di sete columne pretiose, et tutto che ivi fu facto, et venendo Marte d’indi se partirono et andorono al fonte, ove era la sepultura di Adone. Et qui narrano le Nymphe lo anniversario che in memoria faceva Venere. Suadeno poscia le Nymphe a Polia che la narri la sua origine et el suo inamorare. Et questo nel primo libro. Nel secondo Polia narra el suo parentato, la aedificatione de Tarviso, la difficultate del suo inamoramento, et lo foelice exito, et compita la historia cum infiniti et dignissimi accessorii et correlarii, al canto dilla philomela se sveglioe. Vale.

(The summary of the whole work, addressed to the reader. Italian — and, unlike everything around it, plain Italian. One unbroken sentence-chain of about five hundred words.)

Reader, if you wish briefly to understand what is contained in this work, know that Poliphilo tells of having seen wondrous things in sleep; which work he calls, by a Greek word, the strife of love in a dream. Wherein he feigns to have seen many antique things worthy of memory, and all that he says he saw he describes point by point and by their proper terms, in an elegant style: pyramids, obelisks, the greatest ruins of buildings; the difference of columns, their measure, the capitals, bases, epistyles — that is, straight beams — bent beams, zophori, that is friezes, cornices with their ornaments. A great horse. A very great elephant. A colossus. A magnificent gate, with its measures and its ornaments. A terror. The five senses in five nymphs. An excellent bath, fountains, the palace of the queen who is Free Will. A royal and most excellent feast. The variety of jewels, or rather precious stones, and their nature. A game of chess danced to three measures of music. Three gardens: one of glass, one of silk, one in a labyrinth which is human life. A brick peristyle, in the middle of which the Trinity was set out in hieroglyphic figures — that is, sacred Egyptian carvings. The three gates, at which he stayed behind with Polia. How she was in habit and in bearing. Polia leads him to look upon four wondrous triumphs of Jove, the loves of the gods, those of the poets, the various affection and effect of love. The triumph of Vertumnus with Pomona. The sacrifice to Priapus in the antique manner. A marvellous temple, described by its art, where sacrifices were made with wonderful rites and religion. How Polia and he went to the shore to await Cupid, where there was a destroyed temple; in which Polia persuades Poliphilo to go in and look upon the antique things. And there he saw many epitaphs, and a hell painted in mosaic. How for terror he departed thence and came to Polia. And as they stood there Cupid came with the little ship rowed by six nymphs, into which both entered, and Love made sail with his wings. And there honour was done to Cupid by the sea-gods and goddesses, and by the nymphs and monsters; and they came to the Cytherean island, which Poliphilo describes fully, laid out in groves, meadows, gardens, rivers and fountains; and the presents that were made to Cupid, and how he was received by the nymphs; and how upon a triumphal car they went to a wondrous theatre, all described, in the middle of the island. In the midst of which is the Venereal fountain of seven precious columns, and all that was done there. And, Mars coming, they departed thence and went to the fountain where was the sepulchre of Adonis. And here the nymphs tell of the anniversary that Venus kept in his memory. Then the nymphs persuade Polia to tell her origin and her falling in love. And this is in the first book. In the second, Polia tells her parentage, the building of Treviso, the difficulty of her falling in love and its happy issue; and, the history being completed with infinite and most worthy accessories and corollaries, at the song of the nightingale he awoke. Farewell.

(An Italian poem in terza rima, addressed to Leonardo Crasso and then to the reader. It is the anonymous Latin elegy of pages 3–4 done over again in the vernacular, for readers who have no Latin — which is itself an argument about who the book was for. It runs over onto page 7.)

Leonardo Crasso, my revered doctor,
prelate accomplished in the liberal arts
and, as I understand it, in every excellent virtue:
he merits the highest and immortal praise
for the expense and the undertaking he has assumed
to furnish us with such a compendium.
Polished reader, then — listen, listen
to the dreams of Poliphilo as he tells them,
sent down from heaven with much sweetness.
You will not waste your time extravagantly;
rather you will rejoice at having heard
the work, exuberant with various things.
If, grim, you scorn the new erotic
invitation, then do not scorn the well-disposed
sequence, with its fine and exquisite style.
If the grave discourse and well-composed learning
should not please you, then look at the figures,
ancient in geometry — which costs little.
The many signs, with their measures,
kept beside the Nile by the Egyptians;
the ancient pyramids, sepulchres,
with the obelisks set upright on top of them;
the therms and baths and statues of colossi,
such that whoever looks on them is left undone.
Here are diverse bases and thick arches,
various columns proportioned to them,
with capitals and beams that can bear them,
and the cornices with their quadrants,
the symmetries, the zophori, epistyles,
which have shown us proud roofs.
There you will see palaces cultivated and fair
of kings and lords, and the nymphal fountains,
and the banquets befitting them.
There you will see diverse chessmen joined
in a game of robbers, and human acts
conjoined in labyrinth and darkness.
Here you will read of threefold and not idle
deeds, and the majesty of the great Thunderer
in the three gates and his sound counsels.
Who Polia was, fair and triumphant,
you will see thereafter; and of Jove the celestial —

(the poem continues on page 7)

ANDREA MARONE OF BRESCIA.

Whose work is it, Muse, say? — It is mine, and the eight sisters'.
Why then was the title given to Poliphilo?
— He earned still more from us, our common foster-child.
But I ask: who is Poliphilo, by his true name?
— We do not wish him to be known. Why? — It is settled to see first
whether rabid envy devours even things divine.
If it spares him, [?what will he be? He will be known]. But if not, we do not
think you worthy of Poliphilo's true name.
O how happy beyond all mortals you alone are,
Polia, who live though dead — and better so.
While Poliphilo lies buried in deep sleep,
you make the man keep watch, through learned lips.

POLIPHILUS POLIAE S. P. D.

MOLTE FIATE POLIA COGITANDO CHE gli antichi Auctori ad gli principi et magnanimi homini, alcuni per pretio, altri per favore, tali per laude, le opere sue aptamente dicavano. Dique per niuna di così facta cagione, se non per la media, questa mia Hypnerotomachia, non trovando a chi più digno principe, che ad te mia alta Imperatrice dicare la offerisco. La cui egregia conditione, et incredibile bellecia, et venerande, et maxime virtute, et costumi praeclarissimi, sopra qualunque Nympha negli nostri saecoli principato tenendo, excessivamente me hano dil tuo insigne Amore infiammato, arso, et comsumpto. Recevi dunque di bellecie diffuso splendore, et di omni venustate decoramento, et di inclyto aspecto conspicua, questo munusculo. Il quale tu industriosamente, nel amoroso core cum dorate sagitte in quello depincto, et cum la tua angelica effigie insignito et fabricato hai, che singularmente Patrona il possedi. Il quale dono sotto poscia al tuo solerte et ingenioso iudicio (lasciando il principiato stilo, et in questo ad tua instantia traducto) io il commetto. Onde si menda appare, et meno dilla tua elegante dignificatione in alcuna parte sterile et ieiuno troverai, incusata sarai tu optima operatrice, et unica clavigera dilla mente et dil core mio. Il praemio dunque di magiore talento et pretio, non altro specialmente aestimo et opto, che il tuo amore gratioso, et ad questo il tuo benigno favore. Vale.

(Poliphilo's dedication of the work to Polia. Italian — and here the book's own voice begins: the Latinate, clause-heaped style that will run for another four hundred and fifty pages.)

POLIPHILO SENDS MUCH GREETING TO POLIA.

MANY TIMES, POLIA, CONSIDERING THAT the ancient authors fittingly dedicated their works to princes and magnanimous men — some for a price, others for favour, some for praise — for none of such causes, then, but for the middle one, I offer this my Hypnerotomachia, finding no worthier prince to whom to dedicate it than to you, my high Empress: whose excellent condition and incredible beauty, and venerable and greatest virtues, and most illustrious manners, holding sovereignty over whatever nymph there is in our centuries, have exceedingly inflamed, burned and consumed me with your signal Love.

Receive then this little gift — you, suffused with the splendour of beauties, and adorned with every comeliness, and conspicuous of glorious aspect. Which gift you yourself have industriously made and fashioned, painted with gilded arrows in my amorous heart and marked with your angelic likeness; so that you possess it singularly as its Patroness.

Which gift I thereafter commit to your diligent and ingenious judgement, leaving the style I began in and translating it into this one at your instance. Whence, if a fault appear, and if in some part you find it barren and meagre, falling short of your elegant worth, then you shall be the one accused — you, best of workwomen, and sole key-bearer of my mind and of my heart.

Therefore I esteem and desire no prize of greater talent or price, especially, than your gracious love; and, for this, your kind favour. Farewell.

Notes

Chapter I

Sleepless with longing for his Polia, Poliphilo falls asleep at dawn and the dream begins. He wakes, within the dream, on a wide plain and strays into a dark, trackless wood where neither light nor path survives; terrified, he prays his way out at last to a clear stream and drinks.

HYPNEROTOMACHIA POLIPHILI.

AURORAE DESCRIPTIO

Phoebo in quel’hora manando, che la fronte di Matuta Leucothea candidava, già fora dalle Oceani unde, le volubile rote sospese non dimonstrava. Ma sedulo cum gli sui volucri caballi. Pyroo primo, & Eoo alquanto apparendo, ad dipingere le lycophe quadrigie della figliola di vermigliante rose, velocissimo insequentila, non dimorava. Et corruscante gia sopra le cerulee & inquiete ondule, le sue irradiante come crispulavano. Dal quale adventicio in quel puncto occidua davase la non cornuta Cynthia, solicitando gli dui caballi del vehiculo suo cum il Mulo, lo uno candido et l’altro fusco, trahenti ad l’ultimo Horizonta discriminante gli Hemisperii pervenuta, et dalla previa stella aricentare el dì, fugata cedeva. In quel tempo quando che gli Rhiphæi monti erano placidi, né cum tanta rigidecia più l’algente e frigorifico Euro cum el laterale flando quassabondo el mandava gli teneri ramuli, et ad inquietare gli mobili scirpi et pontuti iunci et debili Cypiri, et advexare gli plichevoli vimini, et agitare gli lenti salici, et proclinare la fragile abiete sotto gli corni di Tauro lascivianti. Quanta nel hyberno tempo spirare solea. Similmente el iactabondo Orione cessando di persequire lachrymoso, l’ornato humero Taurino delle sete sorore.

In quella medesima hora che gli colorati fiori del veniente figliolo di Hyperione, el calore ancora non temeano nocevole. Ma delle fresche lachryme de Aurora irrorati et fluidi erano et gli virenti prati. Et Halcyone sopra le æquate onde della tranquilla Malacia et flustro mare, ad gli sabuleti litori appariano di nidulare. Dunque alhora che la dolente Hero

POLIPHILO BEGINS HIS HYPNEROTOMACHIA, DESCRIBING THE HOUR AND THE SEASON WHEN IT APPEARED TO HIM IN SLEEP THAT HE FOUND HIMSELF UPON A QUIET AND SILENT SHORE, DESERTED OF ALL CULTIVATION. THEREAFTER, UNAWARES, IN GREAT FEAR HE ENTERED A PATHLESS AND SHADOWED WOOD.

HYPNEROTOMACHIA POLIPHILI

DESCRIPTION OF THE DAWN

At that hour when Phoebus, issuing forth, was whitening the brow of Matuta Leucothea, he did not yet show, risen clear of Ocean's waves, his rolling wheels held aloft. But diligent with his winged horses — Pyrous first, and Eous somewhat appearing — he did not delay in painting the pale-lit four-horse chariot of the daughter of vermilion roses, following after her most swiftly. And already, glittering above the cerulean and restless wavelets, his beams came curling. At which arrival, in that instant, the un-horned Cynthia gave herself over to her setting, urging on the two horses of her vehicle together with the Mule — the one white, the other dusky — drawing her to the last Horizon that divides the Hemispheres; and having come there, the day being kindled by the star that runs before it, she yielded and fled.

In that season when the Riphaean mountains were at peace, and the chill and frost-bearing Eurus no longer shook the tender branches with such rigour in its sidelong blowing, nor troubled the swaying rushes and the pointed reeds and the frail Cyperus, nor harried the pliant withies, nor stirred the slow willows, nor bowed down the brittle fir beneath the horns of the wanton Bull — as much, that is, as it is wont to blow in the season of winter. And likewise the boastful Orion, weeping, left off pursuing the adorned shoulder of the Bull and the seven sisters.

In that very hour when the coloured flowers no longer feared the heat of Hyperion's coming son as a thing that harms them, but were bedewed and flowing with the fresh tears of the Dawn, and the meadows green; and the Halcyons, above the levelled waves of a tranquil calm and a becalmed sea, appeared to be nesting on the sandy shores. Then, therefore, when the grieving Hero

ad gli derosi littori el doloroso et ingrato decessio del natante Leandro caldamente sospirava. Io Poliphilo sopra el lectulo mio iacendo, opportuno amico del corpo lasso, niuno nella conscia camera familiare essendo, se non la mia chara lucubratrice Agrypnia, la quale poscia che meco hebbe facto vario colloquio consolanteme, palese havendoli facta la causa et l’origine degli mei profundi sospiri, pietosamente suadevami al temperamento de tale perturbatione. Et avidutase de l’ora che io già dovesse dormire, dimandò licentia. Diqué negli alti cogitamenti d’amore solo relicto, la longa et taediosa nocte insomne consumando, per la mia sterile fortuna et adversatrice et iniqua stella tutto sconsolato, et sospiroso, per importuno et non prospero amore illachrymando, di puncto in puncto ricogitava, che cosa è inaequale amore. Et come aptamente amare si pole, chi non ama, et cum quale protectione da inusitati et crebri congressi assediata, et circumvenuta da hostile pugna, la fluctuante anima possi tanto inerme resistere, essendo praecipue intestina la seditiosa pugna, et assiduamente irretita di soliciti, instabili et novi pensieri. De cusì facto et tale misero stato, havendome per longo tracto amaramente doluto, et già fessi gli vaghi spiriti de pensare inutilmente, et pabulato d’uno fallace et fincto piacere ma dritamente et sencia fallo d’uno non mortale, ma più praesto divo obiecto di Polia, la cui veneranda Idea in me profundamente impressa, et più intimamente insculpta occupatrice vive. Et già le tremule et micante stelle incohavano de impallidire el suo splendore, che tacendo la lingua, quel nemico desiderato, dal quale procede questo tanto et indesinente certame, impatiente solicitando el core sauciato, et per proficuo et efficace remedio el chiamava indefesso. Il quale altro non era che innovatione del mio tormento, sencia intercalatione, crudele. Cogitabondo et la qualitate degli miselli amatori, per quale conditione per piacere ad altri dolcemente morire optano, et piacendo ad sé malamente vivere. Et el frameo disio pascere, et non altramente, de laboriose et sospirabile imaginatione. Dunque quale homo, che dapò le diuturne fatiche lasso, cusì né più né meno, sedato apena el doloroso pianto exteriore alquanto, et inclaustrato el corso delle irrorante lachryme le guance d’amoroso languore lacunate, desiderava hogimai la naturale et opportuna quiete. Hora li madidi ochii uno pocho tra le rubente palpebre rachiusi, sencia dimorare tra vita acerba, et suave morte. Fue invasa et quella parte occupata et da uno dolce somno oppressa, la quale cum la mente et cum gli amanti et pervigili spiriti non sta unita né participe ad sì alte operatione. O Iupiter altitonante, foelice o mirabile o terrifica, dirò io questa inusitata visione, che in me non sa trova atomo che non tremi et ardi excogitandola. Ad me

warmly sighed, upon the gnawed shores, for the sorrowful and thankless departure of Leander the swimmer: I, Poliphilo, lying upon my little bed, that timely friend of the weary body, with no one in the room that knew my secret save my dear watcher Agrypnia — who, after she had held various converse with me to console me, and I had made plain to her the cause and the origin of my deep sighs, mercifully urged me to temper such a disturbance; and, perceiving the hour at which I ought by now to sleep, asked leave to go. Whereupon, left alone in the high cogitations of love, consuming the long and tedious night without sleep, all unconsoled by my barren fortune and my adverse and unjust star, and weeping for an importunate and unprospering love, I turned over point by point what a thing unequal love is; and how one may fitly love who does not love in return; and with what protection the fluctuating soul, besieged by unaccustomed and repeated assaults and surrounded by hostile battle, may resist at all, being so unarmed — the seditious battle being above all an inward one, and ceaselessly ensnared by anxious, unstable and ever-new thoughts.

Having grieved bitterly and at length over a state so made and so wretched, and the wandering spirits being already worn out with thinking to no purpose, and fed upon a false and feigned pleasure — yet rightly and without fail upon an object not mortal but rather divine, upon Polia, whose venerable Idea lives deeply impressed in me and more inwardly carved still, and holds me. And already the trembling and glittering stars were beginning to pale their splendour, when, the tongue falling silent, that desired enemy from whom proceeds this so great and unceasing contest, impatiently urging the wounded heart, called upon it tirelessly for a profitable and effectual remedy — which was nothing other than the renewal of my torment, without interval, cruel.

Musing too upon the quality of wretched lovers, by what condition they choose sweetly to die in order to please another, and, pleasing themselves, to live ill; and to feed a spear-like desire upon laborious and sigh-laden imagining, and upon nothing else. Then, like a man weary after long labours, just so and no otherwise, the sorrowful outward weeping being scarcely at all abated, and the course of the streaming tears shut in, my cheeks hollowed with the languor of love, I now desired the natural and timely quiet. Now, my wet eyes a little closed within their reddened lids, without lingering between bitter life and gentle death, that part was invaded and possessed and pressed down by a sweet sleep which is not united with the mind, nor with the loving and wakeful spirits, nor shares in operations so high.

O high-thundering Jupiter! Happy, or wonderful, or terrifying shall I call this unaccustomed vision, which leaves in me no atom that does not tremble and burn to think upon it. To me

parve de essere in una spatiosa planitie, la quale tutta virente, et di multiplici fiori variamente dipincta, molto adornata se repraesentava. Et cum benigne aure ivi era uno certo silentio. Né ancora alle promptissime orechie de audire, strepito né alcuna formata voce perveniva. Ma cum gratiosi radii del Sole passava el temperato tempo.

Nel quale loco io cum timida admiratione discolo, da me ad me diceva. Quivi alcuna humanitate al desideroso intuito non già apparisce, né ancora silvatica, né silvicola, né silvia, né domestica fera. Né casa rurestra alcuna, né alcuno tugurio campestro, né pastorali tecti, né Magar né Magalia se vide. Né similmente ad gli herbidi lochi non videva Opilione alcuno, né Epolo, né Busequa, né Equisio, né vago grege et armento, cum le sue bifore Syringe rurale, né cum le sue cortice Tibie sonanti. Ma freto per la quieta plagia, et per la benignitate del loco, et quasi facto securo procedendo, riguardava quindi et indi, le tenere fronde immote riposare, niuna altra opera cernendo. Et cusì dirrimpecto d’una folta silva ridrizai el mio ignorato viagio. Nella quale alquanto intrato non mi avidi che io cusì incauto lassasse (non so per qual modo) el proprio calle. Diqué al suspeso core di subito invase uno repente timore, per le pallide membre diffundentise, cum solicitato battimento, le gene del suo colore exangue divenute. Conciosia cosa che ad gli ochii mei quivi non si concedeva vestigio alcuno di videre, né diverticulo. Ma nella dumosa silva appariano si non densi virgulti, pongence vepretto, el Silvano Fraxino ingrato alle vipere, Ulmi ruvidi, alle foecunde vite grati, corticosi Subderi apto additamento muliebre, duri Cerri, forti roburi, et glandulose Querce et Ilice, et di rami abondante, che al roscido solo non permettevano, gli radii del gratioso Sole integramente pervenire. Ma come da camurato culmo di densante fronde coperto, non penetrava l’alma luce. Et in questo modo me ritrovai nella fresca umbra, humido aire, et fusco Nemorale.

it seemed that I was in a spacious plain, which showed itself all green and much adorned, painted variously with manifold flowers. And with kindly airs there was there a certain silence. Nor yet did any noise, nor any formed voice, come to ears most ready to hear. But with the gracious rays of the Sun the temperate season passed.

In which place I, wandering with timid wonder, said within myself: here no humanity appears to the desiring gaze, nor yet any wild thing of the woods, nor forest-dweller, nor creature of the glade, nor any tame beast. No country house, no cottage of the fields, no shepherd's roof, no hut nor shieling is to be seen. Nor likewise, in these grassy places, did I see any keeper of sheep, nor goatherd, nor oxherd, nor groom, nor any straying flock and herd, with their rustic two-mouthed Syrinx, nor with their sounding pipes of bark. But confident, because of the quiet shore and the kindliness of the place, and going forward almost made secure, I looked this way and that, and saw the tender leaves resting unmoved, discerning no other work.

And so, straight before me, I turned my unknowing journey towards a thick wood. Into which, having entered somewhat, I did not perceive that I had thus incautiously left — I know not in what manner — the path itself. Whereupon a sudden fear at once invaded my suspended heart, spreading itself through my pale limbs with a quickened beating, my cheeks become bloodless of their colour. Seeing that to my eyes no trace whatever was granted to be seen, nor any turning aside. But in that thorny wood there appeared only close thickets, pricking brakes, the woodland Ash that is hateful to vipers, rough Elms grateful to the fruitful vine, the corky Cork-oak fit for a woman's adding, hard Turkey-oaks, strong oaks, and acorn-bearing Oaks and Holm-oaks, and so abounding in branches that they did not permit the rays of the gracious Sun to reach the dewy ground entire. But, as beneath a vaulted roof covered over with thickening leaves, the kindly light did not penetrate. And in this manner I found myself in the cool shade, the humid air, and the dusky wood.

Per la quale cosa, principiai poscia ragionevolmente suspicare et credere pervenuto nella vastissima Hercynia silva. Et quivi altro non essere che latibuli de nocente fere, et cavernicole de noxii animali et de seviente belve. Et perciò cum maximo terriculo dubitava, di essere sencia alcuna defensa, et sencia avederme dilaniato da setoso et dentato Apro, quale Charidemo, overo da furente, et famato Uro, overo da sibillante serpe et da fremendi lupi incursanti miseramente dimembrabondo lurcare vedesse le carne mie. Diciò dubitando ispagurito, ivi proposi (damnata qualunque pigredine) più non dimorare, et de trovare exito et evadere gli occorrenti pericoli, et de solicitare gli già sospesi et disordinati passi, spesse fiate negli radiconi da terra scoperti cespitando, de qui, et de lì pervagabondo errante, hora ad lato dextro et mo al sinistro, tal hora retrogrado et tal fiata antigrado, inscio et ove non sapendo meare, pervenuto in Salto et dumeto et senticoso loco tutto granfiato dalle frasche, et da spinosi prunuli, et dal intractabile fructo la facia offensa. Et per gli mucronati cardeti, et altri spini lacerata la toga et ritinuta impediva pigritando la tentata fuga. Oltra questo non vedendo delle amaestrevole pedate indicio alcuno, né tritulo di semita, non mediocremente diffiso et dubioso, più solicitamente accelerava. Sì che per gli celeri passi, sì per el meridionale aesto quale per el moto corporale facto calido, tutto de sudore humefacto el

For which cause I began thereafter, and with reason, to suspect and to believe that I had come into the vastest Hercynian forest; and that there was nothing there but the lairs of harmful beasts, and the caves of noxious animals and of raging brutes. And therefore, with the greatest terror, I feared that, being without any defence, I should be torn without warning by some bristled and tusked Boar, as Charidemus was; or by a raging and starved wild Ox; or by a hissing serpent; or that I should see my flesh miserably dismembered and gulped down by wolves rushing upon me and howling.

Fearing this, and terrified, I resolved there — all sloth being condemned — to linger no longer, but to find a way out and escape the perils that offered, and to urge on my steps, already halting and disordered; stumbling often on the roots laid bare from the earth, wandering here and there astray, now to the right hand and now to the left, at one time going backwards and at another forwards, ignorant, and not knowing where to pass; having come into a woodland glade and a thicket and a place full of briars, all scratched by the branches, and my face injured by the thorny sloes and by their intractable fruit. And by the sharp-pointed thistles and other thorns my gown was torn, and, held back, it hindered and made sluggish my attempted flight.

Beyond this, seeing no sign of instructive footprints, nor the worn line of any path, in no small measure mistrustful and doubting, I hastened the more anxiously. So that, what with my swift steps and what with the midday heat, made hot also by the motion of my body, all moistened with sweat the

Et cusì alla fine, alle mie sospirante voce Sola Echo della voce aemula novissima offerivase risponsiva. Disperdando gli risonanti sospiri, cum il cicicare dell’amante rauco della roscida Aurora, et cum gli striduli Grylli. Finalmente in questo scabroso et invio bosco. Solamente della Pietosa Ariadne cretea desiderava el soccorso. Quando che essa per occidere el fratello monstro conscia, el maestrevole et ductrice filo ad lo inganevole Theseo porgette, per fora uscire del discolo labyrintho. Et io el simigliante per uscire della obscura Silva.

POLIPHILO TEMENDO EL PERICULO DEL SCURO BOSCO AL DIESPITER FECE ORATIONE, USCITTE FORA ANXIOSO ET SITIBONDO, ET VOLENDO DI AQUA RISTORARSE, ODE UNO SUAVE CANTARE. EL QUALE LUI SEQUENDO, REFUTATE L’AQUE, IN MAGIORE ANXIETATE PERVENE.

OFFUSCARE GIÀ PRINCIPIATO havendo el mio intellecto, de non potere cognoscere, et nubilare gli sentimenti, quale optione eligere dovesse, over la odibile morte oppetere, overo nell’ombrifero et opaco luco nutante sperare salute. Indi et quindi discorrendo, dava intenta opera ad tutte mie forcie et conati de uscire. Nel quale quanto più che pervagando penetrava, tanto più obscuriva. Et già de grande pavore invalido devenuto, solamente d’alcuna parte dubitando expectava, che qualche saevissima fera impetente incominciasse a devorarme. Overo inpremeditatamente cespitando caecuciente, cadere in abyssosa fossura et scrobe, overo in qualche vasto hiato di terra praecipitare. Et hogi mai la fastidiosa vita de terminare simile ad Amphiarao et Curtio absorpto dalla voragine mephitica terrestre, et cadere da magiore altitudine, che non fece el vecorde Pyreneo. Per questo modo quasi sencia sperancia la mente d’ogni parte conturbava, pur sencia lege vagante et devio exito tentando. Onde più tremulo, che nel mustulento Autumno le mobile foglie ad gli furenti Aquili sencia il virore et sencia el suchioso pondo del suo humore, tra me cusì orante diceva. O Diespiter Maximo, Optimo, et Omnipotente, et Opitulo. Si dalli divini suffragii la

cold breast. Not knowing any longer what to do, I held my mind bound and intent upon terrible thoughts alone. And so at last, to my sighing voice, Echo alone, rival of the voice, offered herself newly in answer; scattering my resounding sighs, together with the hoarse chirping of the lover of the dewy Dawn, and with the shrill Crickets. At last, in this rough and pathless wood, I desired only the succour of the merciful Cretan Ariadne — who, being privy to the killing of her monstrous brother, held out to the deceiving Theseus the masterly and guiding thread, that he might come forth out of the wayward labyrinth. And I the like, that I might come out of the dark Wood.

POLIPHILO, FEARING THE PERIL OF THE DARK WOOD, MADE PRAYER TO DIESPITER; HE CAME FORTH ANXIOUS AND THIRSTING; AND, WISHING TO RESTORE HIMSELF WITH WATER, HE HEARD A SWEET SINGING, WHICH, FOLLOWING AND REFUSING THE WATERS, HE CAME INTO GREATER ANXIETY STILL.

MY UNDERSTANDING HAVING NOW BEGUN to be darkened, so that it could not discern, and my senses to be clouded as to which choice I ought to take — whether to meet hateful death, or to hope for safety wavering in that shadowy and dark grove — running this way and that, I bent all my strength and striving to get out. Into which, the further I penetrated in my wandering, the darker it grew. And being already made feeble by great terror, I only waited, fearing it from some quarter or other, for some most savage beast to fall upon me and begin to devour me; or else, stumbling blindly and without forethought, to fall into some abysmal pit and trench, or to be thrown headlong into some vast gape of the earth; and by now to end this wearisome life like Amphiaraus, or like Curtius swallowed by the mephitic gulf of the earth, and to fall from a greater height than the witless Pyreneus did.

In this manner, almost without hope, my mind was troubled on every side, yet still attempting, lawlessly wandering, some way out. Whereupon, trembling more than the moving leaves in the must-scented Autumn under the raging North winds, stripped of their green and of the juicy weight of their moisture, I said within myself, praying thus: O Diespiter, Greatest, Best, Almighty and Helping, if by the divine suffrages the

Chapter II

Following a sweet Dorian music across a flowering country, Poliphilo is so overcome by wonder that he falls asleep within the dream, and wakes into a deeper dream-region strewn with the ruins of antiquity.

Al praesente di qualunque fragile offensa dolente, te supplice invoco summo patre degli superi, Medioximi, et inferi aeterno rectore, che de questi mei mortali pericoli et praesente horrore, me ad la tua immensa Deitate piaqui liberare, et finire questa mia dubiosa vita per altro megliore fine. Et quivi quale Achemenide horridulo dal horrifico Cyclope exorava cum solicite et precarie voce Aenea, più praesto desiderando da gli homini inimici morire che per cusì horrendo interito. Cusì né per altro modo io precante orai. A pena le divote oratione sinceramente fusse, cum el core unito orante, contrito et exagitato, de lachryme perfuso hebbi terminate, fermamente tenendo, che gli Dii ad la bona mente occorreno, che sencia mora fora dell’angusto, aspero, et imbricoso nemore inadvertente me ritrovai. Et quasi ad novo dì, da l’humida nocte fora pervenuto. Gli ochii obumbrati, per alquanto non pativano l’amabile luce. Tutto lurido et moesto, et anxioso. Non manco niente al desiderato lume ad me parve de essere giunto. Che de uno caeco carcere chi fora advenisse diloricato delle gravose et molestante cathene, et uscito de caliginose tenebre. Tutto sitibondo lacerato, et la facia et le mane cruentate, et da morsicante Urtica pustulate sentendome exanimo, ad la gratiosa luce pur niuna cosa obiecta istimando. In tanto era sitiente, che delle fresche aure non poteva refrigerarme, né ancora acconciamente al sicco core satisfare. Avidissimo d’inglutire la vana Saliva che in me era assucta. Ma poi che alquanto io fui rasicurato, et in me rivocato uno pauculo de animo, el pecto arefacto per crebri sospiri et per anxietate di spirito, et per corporale faticha, deliberai per ogni modo di extinguere l’arida sete, diqué per quella plagia curiosamente explorando de trovare qualche aqua, onde molto lasso inquirendo, opportunamente, ad me uno iocundissimo fonte se offeritte cum grossa vena de aqua freschamente resurgente. Il loco del quale gli palustri Achori et la barba Silvana mi discoperse, et la fiorita Lisimachia, et la muscariata Imperatoria. Dal quale nasceva uno chiarissimo fluento, che cum discursivi rivuli per medio della deserta silva cum discolo et flexuoso alveo influente, incremento da molti altri liquenti canali tollendo dilatavase. Et per gli impedienti Saxi et ruinati trunchi insurgevano le corrente et sonante unde. Et poscia da impetuosi et undisoni torrenti dalle risolute neve dagli alpestri et rigidi monti lapse cadendo, gli quali non tropo lontano distare apariano candidati nel algente monstro de Pana, grande augumento riceveva. Al quale molte fiate nella mia timorosa fuga pervenuto. Io trovava alquanto de fusca luce, per gli excelsi arbori uno poco

prayer that deserves it by just petition ought to be heard: now, grieving under every fragile injury, I call upon thee as suppliant, highest father of the gods above, the middle and the below, eternal ruler, that it may please thy immense Deity to free me from these my mortal perils and this present horror, and to end this doubtful life of mine by some better end. And there, like the bristling Achaemenides pleading with Aeneas in anxious and beseeching words to be saved from the horrifying Cyclops — desiring rather to die at the hands of enemy men than by so horrid a destruction — so, and in no other way, did I pray.

Scarcely had I finished those devout prayers, sincerely made, with the heart united in prayer, contrite and shaken, and bathed in tears — holding firmly that the gods come to the aid of a good mind — when without delay I found myself, unawares, outside that narrow, harsh and overshadowing wood. And as if come forth into a new day out of the humid night, my shadowed eyes could not for a while endure the lovely light. All wan and mournful and anxious, it seemed to me nonetheless that I had come to the light I had longed for, as one might come out of a blind prison, stripped of heavy and troubling chains, and issue from murky darkness.

All thirsting, torn, my face and hands bloodied and blistered by the biting Nettle, feeling myself half dead, I counted nothing else as anything against the gracious light. So thirsty was I that the fresh airs could not cool me, nor fitly satisfy my dry heart; most greedy to swallow the empty saliva that had dried within me. But when I had somewhat reassured myself, and recalled a little spirit into me — my breast parched with repeated sighs and with anxiety of spirit and with bodily labour — I resolved by every means to quench that arid thirst. And therefore, searching carefully over that shore to find some water, and seeking long and very wearily, there offered itself to me most timely a most joyful spring, with a great vein of water freshly rising up. The place of it the marsh Acorus and the Silvan's beard disclosed to me, and the flowering Loosestrife, and the musky Masterwort.

From it there was born a most limpid stream, which, running off in little rills through the middle of the deserted wood in a wayward and winding channel, widened as it took increase from many other flowing channels. And against the hindering Rocks and fallen trunks the currents rose up in sounding waves. And thereafter it received great increase from impetuous and wave-sounding torrents fallen from the melted snows of the alpine and rigid mountains, which appeared to stand not too far off, made white in the freezing monster of Pan. To which, having come many times in my fearful flight, I found there a little dusky light, where the lofty trees were somewhat

nelle cime discuneati, sopra el limoso fiume, ove vedeva el coelo lacerato per gli impedienti rami frondosi, et tali sicchi, horrido loco a homo solo ritrovarse Sencia traiecto alcuno. Ancora cum le ultranee rive più che le citime obscure et intricabile apparendo. Quivi era el mio spavento sentire de lì alcuna fiata sibilante ruina d’arbori, et uno fragore de rami, et sfindere crepitante de ligne, cum geminato et horrisono strepito, per longo tracto nella densitate degli arbori et incluso aire riservato. Volendo dunque io Poliphilo territo et afflicto evaso tanto horrore, le optate aque sopra le verdose rive exhaurire, cum gli popliti consternato, et in clausura le dette reducendo, et la vola lacunata, feci vaso da bevere gratissimo. La quale infusa nel fonte et di aqua impleta per offerire alla rabida et hanelante bucca, et refrigerare la siccitudine del aestuante pecto. Più grate alhora ad me, che ad gli Indi Hypane et Gange, Tigride et Euphrate ad gli Armenii, né ancora è cusì grato alle gente Aethiopice el Nilo. Et ad gli Aegyptii el suo inundare imbibendo la tosta gleba. Né Eridano ancora alli populi Liguri, quanto mi se offerivano le acceptissime et fresche rive. Né cusì peracceptissimo fue a Libero Patre el fonte dimonstrato dal fugiente Ariete. Acadette che non cusì praesto le expectate et appetibile aque claustrale, nella caveata mano ad la bucca aperta era per approximarle, che in quello instante audivi uno Dorio cantare, che non mi suado, che Thamiras Thratio el trovasse, per le mie caverniculate orechie penetrante, et ad lo inquieto core tanto suave dolce et concino traiectato. Cum voce non terrestre, cum tanta armonia, cum tanta incredibile sonoritate cum tanta insueta proportione. Umè quanto mai si potrebbe imaginare. Perché sencia dubio questa cosa excede ultra la potentia di narratione. La dolcecia della quale et delectatione, molto più de oblectamento che la potiuncula offerentise mi se praestava. Intanto che l’aqua hausta intra la clausura dell’intervalli degli denti, insenso quasi et già obstupefacto lo intellecto, et sopito l’appetito, niuna virtute contradicendo reserati gli nodi se sparse ad humida terra.

wedged apart at their tops above the muddy river, and where I saw the sky torn by the hindering leafy branches — some of them dry — a place of horror for a man to find himself in alone, with no crossing anywhere; the farther banks appearing still darker and more tangled than the nearer.

There was my terror to hear from that quarter, now and again, the hissing ruin of trees, and a crash of branches, and the crackling splitting of wood, with a doubled and horrid-sounding din, held long in the density of the trees and the enclosed air.

Wishing therefore, I Poliphilo, terrified and afflicted, having escaped so much horror, to drink up the longed-for waters upon those green banks, I lowered myself upon my knees; and drawing my hands together into an enclosure, with the palm hollowed, I made of them a most welcome drinking vessel. Which, dipped in the spring and filled with water, I made ready to offer to my raging and panting mouth, and to cool the dryness of my burning breast. More welcome then to me than the Hypanis and the Ganges to the Indians, than the Tigris and Euphrates to the Armenians; nor is the Nile so welcome to the Ethiopian peoples, nor to the Egyptians its flooding that drinks into the baked soil; nor yet Eridanus to the Ligurian peoples, as those most acceptable and fresh banks offered themselves to me. Nor was the spring shown by the fleeing Ram so exceedingly welcome to Father Liber.

It happened that no sooner was I about to bring the awaited and desirable waters, enclosed in my hollowed hand, to my open mouth, than in that instant I heard a Dorian singing — which I cannot persuade myself Thamyras the Thracian ever found — penetrating through the little caverns of my ears, and passing through to my restless heart so sweet, so soft and so harmonious. With a voice not of earth, with such harmony, with such incredible sonority, with such unaccustomed proportion. Alas, how could it ever be imagined? For without doubt this thing exceeds the power of telling.

The sweetness of it and the delight offered me far more pleasure than the little draught that was offering itself. So much so that the water drawn up, held within the enclosure of the intervals of my teeth — my understanding as it were senseless and already stupefied, and my appetite laid to sleep, no faculty gainsaying it — the knots being loosed, was spilt upon the moist earth.

Now, like an animal that for the sweet bait does not weigh the hidden trap, setting aside my natural need, I went without delay, hastening vehemently on the way, after that more-than-human strain. And when I reasonably judged that I had come to it, I heard it in another quarter; and when I had hurried to that place, it appeared to have settled somewhere else. And so, as it changed its places, so likewise it changed to a voice more sweet and more delightful, with heavenly harmonies.

Therefore, by this empty labour, and having run so far with troublesome thirst, I so weakened myself that I could scarcely sustain my weary body. And my panting spirits being no longer able to bear up the body, gravely wearied as it was — what with the terror now past, what with the urgent thirst, what with the long wandering search, and also with my heavy anxieties and with the hot hour — I was left defenceless and abandoned by my own powers, desiring and craving nothing whatever save quiet rest for my weakened limbs.

Wondering at the chance that had befallen, stupefied by that mellifluous voice, and much more at finding myself in a region unknown and uncultivated, though a country pleasant enough. Beyond this it grieved me sorely that the flowing spring, found with such labour and sought out with such care, had been taken away and lost from my eyes. For all which things I stood with my mind entangled in ambiguity, and much perplexed. At last, seized by so great a weariness, my whole body

Sopra el sinistro lato cessabondo, iacente, atraheva cum gli attenuati spiriti le fresche aure, più assiduamente cum le crespe labra, che el stanco Cervo fugato et ad fianchi dagli mordaci et feroci cani morsicato, et nel pecto cum la sagitta vulnerato, apodiata cum le ramose corne alle debole tergore la ponderosa testa, ultimamente consistere non valendo, sopra gli volubili genochii moribondo se prosterne lasso. Onde in questa simigliante angonia iacendo scrupulosamente nell’animo discorreva, degli litii intricatissimi della inferma fortuna, et gli incanti della malefica Cyrce, si a caso per gli sui versi innodato fusse, overo contra me usato el Rhombo. Ad questi tali et tanti accessorii spaventi. Umè dunche, ove potrei io quivi tra sì diverse herbe ritrovare la Mercuriale Moly, cum la nigra radice per aiuto, et mio medicamento? and languid. Beneath a rough and most ancient oak, abounding in its cupped or tufted fruit, despised by fertile Chaonia, in the midst of a spacious and grassy meadow — an oak leafy with knotted and spreading branches, making a cool shade, its trunk gaping — I laid myself down upon the dewy herbs. Resting upon my left side, lying there, I drew in the fresh airs with my thinned spirits, more constantly with my parted lips than the weary Stag that has been driven and bitten in the flanks by biting and fierce hounds, and wounded in the breast by the arrow, and that at the last, propping his heavy head with its branching horns upon his weakened back and no longer able to stand, sinks down dying and weary upon his buckling knees.

Whence, lying in this like agony, I ran over anxiously in my mind the most tangled quarrels of infirm fortune, and the enchantments of the maleficent Circe — whether by chance I had been knotted into her verses, or the magic wheel had been used against me. To these and so many attendant terrors: alas then, where could I find here, among herbs so various, the Mercurial Moly with its black root, for my help and my medicine? Then I said: this is not that; but what is it, if not a malign deferring of the death I long for?

Standing thus in these pernicious agitations, my powers dwindled little by little, and I could think of no other Safety than to draw in and receive frequently and diligently the fresh airs, and, having warmed them in my breast where a little vital heat still gathered and beat, to breathe them out again through my parched throat. Finding myself therefore in no other way than half alive, for a last refreshment I took the moist dew-laden leaves kept beneath the leafy oak, and offered them to my pale and harsh lips, sucking them dry with the greediest avidity, licking at them ravenously, and cooling a little my thirsty palate. Desiring then that Hypsipyle might show me too the spring of Langia, as she did to the Greeks. For I anxiously suspected that perhaps in the vast wood I had been bitten unawares by the serpent Dipsas, so unbearable was my thirst.

At last, renouncing and proscribing this wearisome life, whatever might come of it, astonished and estranged by the gravest cogitations, and reeling as though in madness, once again beneath this oaken shade, wanton with the spreading darkness of its branches, I was overcome by an overpowering sleep; and the sweet drowsiness being spread through my limbs, it seemed to me that I slept again.

Chapter III

The great antiquities: a colossal stepped pyramid crowned by a needle-obelisk — the vastest structure the imagination can raise — set out with exact measurement, together with a winged horse, elephants of stone, and a bronze colossus he climbs into and through.

POLIPHILO HERE RELATES THAT IT SEEMED TO HIM THAT HE SLEPT AGAIN, AND THAT ELSEWHERE, IN SLEEP, HE FOUND HIMSELF IN A VALLEY WHICH AT ITS END WAS CLOSED BY A MARVELLOUS BARRIER WITH A PORTENTOUS PYRAMID, WORTHY OF ADMIRATION, AND A LOFTY OBELISK ABOVE IT; WHICH WITH DILIGENCE AND PLEASURE HE CONSIDERED SUBTLY.

THE FEARFUL WOOD AND THE CROWDED grove being escaped, and those first other places left behind through the sweet sleep that had spread itself over my broken and prostrate limbs, I found myself anew in a place far more delightful than the one before. It was not girdled about with horrid mountains and sheer crags, nor scythed with knotted ridges, but was composed of pleasant little hills of no great height; wooded with young oaklings, with oaks, ashes and Hornbeams, and with leafy Italian oaks and Holm-oaks, and with tender Hazels, and Alders, and Limes, and Maples, and with barren wild Olives, disposed according to the aspect of those tree-bearing Hills. And down on the level there were pleasant little woods of other woodland

Behold, then, a famished and flesh-eating wolf appeared to me on the right hand, with its mouth full.

At the sight of which my hairs at once stood up on end, and, wishing to cry out at it, I had no voice. And it immediately fled. And I, then somewhat returned to myself, lifting my eyes towards that quarter where the wooded hills appeared to join, saw far off, in a deep recess, an incredible height in the figure of a tower, or of a most lofty watch-tower; and near it a great building appearing still unfinished, yet a work and structure of antiquity.

Where, towards this building, I saw the gracious little hills of the valley rising ever higher, which I saw joined to the aforesaid edifice; and it was a closure between the one mountain and the other, and made an enclosed valley. Judging this thing shrewdly to be most worthy of beholding, I turned my already hastened journey eagerly towards it without delay. And the nearer I came to it as I went, the more I discovered a work huge and magnificent, and the desire to look upon it multiplied. For it no longer appeared a lofty watch-tower, but rather a high Obelisk, founded upon a vast heap of stones.

The height of which incomparably exceeded the summits of the mountains on either side, however famous a mountain I might reckon Olympus, or Caucasus, or Cyllene, to be. Having come eagerly even to this deserted place, surrounded with a pleasure beyond imagining at beholding freely so great an insolence of the builder's art, and a structure so immense, and an eminence so stupendous, I halted quietly.

Looking upon and considering the whole mass and thickness of this fragmented and half-ruined structure of white Parian marble: the squared and four-angled blocks fitted together without the glue of cement, and equally set and placed, so polished and so exquisitely reddened at their edges as could ever be done — so much so that between the one edge and the other, that is at the joints, no thinness whatever, however sharpened, could have resisted being thrust in and yet have penetrated in the least.

Here, then, I found so noble a colonnade, of every figuration, lineament and material as any man could ever suppose: part broken down, part still in its place, and part preserved unhurt, with their Architraves and with capitals excellent in device and in rough carving; Cornices, Zophori or Friezes, arched Beams. Great fractures of statues, many of their bronzed and finished members struck off. Basins, and Shells, and vases, of Numidian stone and of Porphyry and of various marble and ornament. Great washing-basins. Aqueducts, and almost infinite other fragments of noble sculpture, wholly deprived of any knowing what they had been when whole, and reduced as it were to their first rough beginning; fallen and cast down to the earth here and there. Onde si io el suo excesso, oltra el credere, inopinabile cosa meritamente de essa essere el speculare arbitrava, la quale imperoché mirando non mediocremente la potentia visiva affatichava, et gli altri spirituali sensi attenuando, quanto più affare? Per tanto a ciò che in alcuna parte, quanto ad me se praestarà el capto del mio intellecto, per questo modo ad hora io brevemente el descrivo.

Great fragments in many parts of plane rounding, and of Ophite and of Porphyry, and of a Coralline colour, and of many other pleasing colourings. Fragments of various storied work in high relief and half relief, in finished and in half-finished carving; declaring its excellence, which unfailingly accuses our own times, and shows that of such an art the perfection is fallen asleep.

Having come therefore near the middle front of that great and illustrious work, I saw an entire portal, wonderful and conspicuous, and proportioned to the whole building. Which fabric I saw continuous, set between the one and the other of the mountains with their sheared-off slopes, so that I could reasonably conjecture its dimension to be twenty paces and six stadia. The joining of these mountains was made level perpendicularly from the summit right down to the floor.

For which cause I stood pondering within myself with what iron instruments, and with how much wearing of men's hands, and what numbers of them, so great an artifice had been forcibly brought to pass — so incredibly laborious, and with so great a grinding away of time. Here, then, with the one mountain and the other, this admirable structure joined itself in knowing adhesion. By which joining, as is said above, the valley was fortified with a closure, so that no one could go out from there, or turn back, or enter, save through this open gate.

Now above this so huge work of building — whose height from the topmost cornices to the footing and base could easily be conjectured at a fifth of a stadium — there was founded an adamantinely pinnacled and most portentous Pyramid. Whereupon I reasonably judged that not without inestimable expense, and time, and the greatest multitude of mortals, could such an incredible artifice ever have been devised and set up. And if I rightly judged its excess, beyond belief, to be a thing unimaginable to look upon — which in the beholding wearied the visual power not a little, and thinned the other spiritual senses — how much more to make it? Therefore, so far as the grasp of my understanding will grant it me, in this manner I now briefly describe it.
