Ciascuna facia dilla quadratura della meta, sotta all’initio della gradatione de questa admiranda Pyramide, sopralocata al praefato aedificamento, in extensione longitudinale, era stadii sei. Multiplicati per quatro in ambito, la dicta nel pedamento aequilatero occupava comprehendendo, quatro et vinti stadii. In altitudine daposcia da qualunque angulo levando le linee, cum mensura, quanto la ima linea è del plintho, tutte quatro al summo mediano inseme conveniente concurrendo la figura Pyramydale perfecta constituivano. Il perpendicolo mediano sopra el centro degli dyagonii del Plyntho incruciati, delle sei partitione una meno constava delle ascendente linee.

La quale immensa et terribile Pyramide cum miranda et exquisita Symmetria gradatamente Adamantale salendo, continiva dece, et quatro cento et mille gradi, overo scalini decrustati. Dempti gradi dece opportuni ad terminare el gracilamento. Nel loco di quali era apposito et suffecto uno stupendo Cubo solido et fermo, et della crassitudine monstruoso, offerentise sencia credito di subvectura in quella summitate deputato. De quella medesima petra Paria, che erano le gradatione. El dicto quadrato fue per basa et substentaculo supposto dell’obelisco, che se hae da dire. Questo ingentissimo saxo, che tale non fue chermadio levato da Titide, havea uno prolapso in ambito, de sei parte, due in descenso, et una nella cacuminata planicie, ristava nel supremo plano lato per diametro passi quatro. Nella coaequatura del quale, eminevano quatro pedi de Harpyia de metallo cum gli pilaci et branchie ungiute fusile, nella maxima petra verso gli anguli, sopra le linee dyagonie, infixi et fermamente implumbati. De crassitudine proportionata, et de altecia di dui passi. Le quale inseme bellissime innodantise, ambiendo ligavano lo infimo Socco di uno grande Obelisco. Conflati in mirabile folgiature, et fructi, et fiori di conveniente granditate. Sopra gli quali premeva lo Obelisco firmissime supraposito. La latitudine del quale de passi bini, et sette, tanto in altecia, artificiosamente acuentise, de petra Pyropecila Thebaicha. Nelle facie del quale erano Hieroglyphi aegyptici egregiamente insculpti, lisso, et quale speculo illustramente terso.

Nel supremo fastigio dil quale, summa cum diligentia et arte sopraposito resideva una stabilita basa di auricalco. Inella quale ancora era una versatile machina, overo uno petaso, in uno stabile perone, overo pollo superinfixa. El quale retinia una imagine de Nympha elegante opera della recitata materia. Da convertire in stupore chi acuratissimo, et cum obstinato intuito la considerava. Cum tale et cusì fata proportione, che la se concedeva alla communa statura nel aire perfectamente giù di vedere. Each face of the squared base of the mass, below the beginning of the stepping of this admirable Pyramid set above the aforesaid building, was in length six stadia. Multiplied by four in circumference, the said equilateral footing took up, all told, four and twenty stadia. Then in height, raising the lines from each angle by measure — as far as the lowest line of the plinth extends — all four running together and meeting at the middle of the summit constituted the perfect Pyramidal figure. The middle perpendicular, above the centre where the diagonals of the Plinth cross, was one part less in six than the ascending lines.

Which immense and terrible Pyramid, rising by steps adamantine with wonderful and exquisite Symmetry, contained one thousand four hundred and ten steps, or stairs, wrought in relief — apart from ten steps needed to finish the tapering. In place of these was set and substituted a stupendous Cube, solid and firm and monstrous in its thickness, offering itself beyond belief as a thing carried up and appointed to that summit; of that same Parian stone of which the steps were made.

The said square was set beneath as the base and support of the obelisk that is to be spoken of. This most huge stone — such as was never the block quarried by Titis — had a falling-away in its circumference of six parts, two in the descent and one in the pointed level; and it remained on the topmost plane four paces broad by diameter. In the levelling of which there rose four Harpy's feet of metal, with their pads and clawed talons cast, fixed into the great stone towards the angles, along the diagonal lines, and firmly leaded in; of proportioned thickness, and of the height of two paces. Which, knotting themselves most beautifully together, encircled and bound the lowest Socle of a great Obelisk, cast in wonderful foliage, and fruits, and flowers of fitting greatness. Upon which the Obelisk pressed, most firmly set above them. Its breadth two paces, and seven times as much in height, artificially sharpening itself, of Theban fire-flecked stone. On the faces of which were Egyptian Hieroglyphs excellently carved, smooth, and brightly polished like a mirror.

On the topmost pinnacle of it, set above with the utmost diligence and art, rested a settled base of brass. In which there was besides a turning engine, or broad-brimmed cap, fixed upon a stable pivot or pole. Which held up an image of a Nymph, an elegant work of the material already named — enough to turn to stupefaction anyone who considered it most carefully and with fixed gaze. Of such and so made a proportion that she allowed herself to be seen perfectly from below, in the air, at the common stature. And

Which most lofty Obelisk allows me still not the least belief that another showed any conformity to it, or any likeness. Not the Vatican one. Not the Alexandrian. Not the Babylonian. It held in itself such a heaping-up of wonder that I stood senseless with stupefaction at the considering of it. And far more still, the immensity of the work, and the excess of the subtlety of that opulent and most acute genius, and the great care and exquisite diligence of the Architect.

With what daring invention of art, then; with what power and human strength, and order, and incredible expense, was so great a weight carried up and set so high in the air, in emulation of the heavens? With what Windlass, and with what wheeled Pulleys, and with what Crabs, or Block-and-tackle, and other hauling Engines, and framed Scaffoldings? Let every other incredible and greatest structure keep silence here.

Which, excavated with a straight passage, its top vaulted, penetrating as far as the centre — or as far as the middle perpendicular central line of the topmost Cap of that portent-bearing Pyramid — made a most ample entrance and approach.

To which opening of the mouth one ascended by way of her twisted hairs, expressed with an inconceivable subtlety of understanding, and art, and studied thought of the craftsman; with such rule and reduction that they aptly made climbing steps up to the open mouth. And in place of curling tresses I gazed astonished at vipers and twisted serpents, in living and huge coils, wrapping themselves confusedly about the monstrous head with the swiftest turnings. In the eyes of which were most conveniently enclosed the brightest little stones — so much so that, had I not been certain the material was marble, I should not have dared approach so easily.

The above-named passage, carved within the solid rock, led to where the stairs were, with a winding course, in the centre, by spiral turnings; by which one climbed to the highest summit of that Pyramid, onto the surface of the square Cap. Upon which was founded the eminent Obelisk.

The greater part on foot, fighting confusedly with darts and bucklers. Some in corslets and helmets, marked with varied crests; and others naked, showing that they attacked with a lively heart, intent upon death. Some breastplated, adorned with various and most noble military ornaments. Many with the fearful look of men crying out; some with the semblance of obstinacy and fury.

Those who were about to die, with a thread rivalling nature, expressed the effect; and others dead, with hateful and manifold engines of war and slaughter. They showed the robust limbs and the swelling muscles, and gave the eyes to see the office of the bones, and the hollows where the hard sinews drew. Which conflict and duel appeared so fearful and horrible that you would say it was bloody and arms-mighty Mars himself about to fight in single combat with Porphyrion and Alcyoneus; and the flight they had at the braying of the ass came into my memory to see.

All these images exceeded the natural tallness and stature, and the carving was in deep relief of most illustrious and polishable marble, the flat space between introduced of the blackest stone for the comeliness and grace of the white stone and for the setting-off of the statuary work; and they stood out perfectly. Here, then, were infinite tall bodies, last strivings, intent acts, breastplated habits, and various death, with doubtful victory. Alas, my wearied spirits, and my understanding confused by such continual variety, and my disordered senses, cannot fitly bear not only to tell the whole, but they are not able to express even a part, with completeness, of so polished a stone-carving.

And whence then was born so great a boasting, and so burning a lust, to heap up stones by joining them into so great a mass, a pile, a pinnacle? And with what Waggon? with what Bearers? and Dray? with what Rollers was so great and such a vastness of stones forced along? And upon what propping were they joined and confederated? And upon what mound of cemented rough-work? And of so great an immensity, the loftiest Obelisk, and the immense Pyramid? Chapter IV

The triumphal portal. Poliphilo studies a monumental gateway to the last inch — its columns and entablature drawn to the Vitruvian rule, its friezes and Egyptian hieroglyphs decoded — the book's first great architectural ekphrasis and, in effect, its architectural manifesto.

Per la quale discursione ragionevolmente iudicai, overo che tutto solido et massiccio ristato del monte fusse subdito, overo l’una compacta congerie de glutinato cemento et glarea et di rude petratura. Per cusì facta animadversione io explorai per l’ampia porta. Et vidi che nel intimo era densa obscuritate et concavitate. La quale porta inseme cum el mirando, et superbo aedificamento (cose digne di aeterno monumento) cusì nel sequente como era egregiamente disposita, sarae alquantulo descripta.

POLIPHILO POSCIA CHE EGLI HAE NARRATO PARTE DELLA IMMENSA STRUCTURA, ET LA VASTISSIMA PYRAMIDE, CUM EL MIRANDO OBELISCO NEL SEQUENTE CAPITULO DESCRIVE MAGNE ET MIRAVEGLIOSE OPERE, ET PRAECIPUAMENTE DE UNO CABALLO, DE UNO IACENTE COLOSSO, DE UNO ELEPHANTO, MA PRAECIPUAMENTE DE UNA ELEGANTISSIMA PORTA.

IUSTISSIMAMENTE SE POTREBBE CONcedermi licentemente de dire, che nel universo mundo unque fusseron altre simigliante magnificentissime opere, né excogitate, né ancora da humano intuito vise. Che quasi diciò liberamente arbitrarei, che da humano sapere et summa et virtuosa potentia, non aptamente simile insolentia di aedificatura et artificii potersi excitare, né di invento diffinire. Diqué tanto erano a questo intento et obstinato conspecto, captivati cum excesso piacere inseme, et cum stupore, gli sentimenti mei, che altro nella rapace memoria solatioso, et periocundo non mi occurreva. Se non quandonque io applicato mirava, et curiosamente tutte le parte al venusto

matter of his loftiest conceit of Mount Athos. For this most ample structure without fail exceeds the Egyptian insolence. It surpasses the marvellous labyrinths. Let Lemnos be quiet. Let the Theatres fall dumb. The dignified Mausoleum is not its equal. For this was certainly not known to him who wrote of the seven miracles, or spectacles, of the world. Nor in any age was such a thing ever seen or conceived — passing over in silence even the wonderful sepulchre of Ninus.

At the last I considered discreetly what opposed and obstinate resistance of vaults could ever sustain or support beneath it, and what Hexagonal and four-square Piers, and what smallness of columning could firmly, set beneath, endure so great a heaviness and intolerable weighing. By which reasoning I judged rightly that either the whole remained solid and massive, the mountain being subject beneath it, or else it was one compacted heap of glued cement and gravel and rough stonework. By such consideration I explored through the ample gate. And I saw that within there was thick darkness and hollowness. Which gate, together with the wonderful and proud building — things worthy of an eternal monument — will be somewhat described in what follows, as it was excellently disposed.

POLIPHILO, AFTER HE HAS TOLD PART OF THE IMMENSE STRUCTURE, AND THE VASTEST PYRAMID WITH ITS WONDERFUL OBELISK, DESCRIBES IN THE FOLLOWING CHAPTER GREAT AND MARVELLOUS WORKS, AND CHIEFLY A HORSE, A LYING COLOSSUS, AN ELEPHANT, BUT ABOVE ALL A MOST ELEGANT GATE.

MOST JUSTLY MIGHT IT BE FREELY granted me to say that in the universal world there were never other like most magnificent works, neither conceived nor yet seen by human gaze. So that I would almost freely judge that from human knowledge and the highest and most virtuous power no like insolence of building and of artifice could fitly be raised up, nor defined by invention. Whereupon my senses were so captivated at this intent and obstinate sight, together with excess of pleasure and with stupefaction, that nothing else came into my ravished memory that was solacing and most joyful, except when I looked applying myself, and curiously all the parts to the comely

composito conveniente, examinando di quelle excellente et eximie statue lapidee, di virginale factura, che di subito excitato caldamente singultando sospirava.

In tanto che risonavano gli mei amorosi et sonori suspiri in questo loco solitario et desertato, et di aere crassitato commemorantimi della mia Diva et exmensuratamente peroptata Polia. Omè paucula intermissione se praestava, che quella amorosa et coeleste Idea, non fusse simulacrata nella mente, et sedula comite al mio tale et cusì incognito itinerario. Nella quale fermamente nidulata l’alma mia contentamente cubiculava, quale in tutissimo praesidio, et intemerato Asylo secura. Dunque essendo per questo modo ad tale loco pervenuto, ove erano dalla copiosa et eximia operatione antiquaria gli ochii mei ad tale spectatione furati et occupati. Mirai sopra tutto una bellissima porta tanto stupenda, et d’incredibile artificio, et di qualunque liniamento elegante, quanto mai fabrefare et depolire se potria. Che sencia fallo non sento tanto in me di sapere, che perfectamente la potesse et assai discrivere. Praecipuamente che nella nostra aetate gli vernacoli, proprii, et patrii vocabuli, et di l’arte aedificatoria peculiari, sono cum gli veri homini, sepulti, et extincti. O execrabile et sacrilega barbarie, come hai exspoliabonda invaso, la più nobile parte dil pretioso thesoro et sacrario latino, et l’arte tanto dignificata, al praesente infuscata da maledicta ignorantia perditamente offensa. La quale associata inseme cum la fremente, inexplebile, et perfida avaritia, ha occaecato quella tanto summa et excellente parte, che Roma fece et sublime et vagabonda Imperatrice.

Dinanti ad questa egregia porta (primo questo dire censendo) in subdivale relicto era una platea Tetragona passi per il suo diametro trenta. Cum spectabile silicato di quadrature marmoree, distincte uno pede, intersito, di tessellatura in varii intricamenti et colligatura et coloramenti. In molte parte per la ruina di petre disrupto et arbusculato. Et nelle extremitate dilla dicta platea, dilla dextera et dilla leva, verso gli monti, erano ad libella dui ordini de columnatione cum exquisito intervallo dil Areostylo interiecto, secundo la exigentia opportuna d’una columna all’altra. Ove il primo corso, overo ordine d’ambe due le parte, initiavano equali al limbo, overo extremo termine dil silicato nel metopa, overo fronte dilla magna porta. Et tra una et l’altra columnatione, era spatio di passi .xv. Dille quale columne alcune et la magiore parte overo numero integre se vedevano. fitting composition, examining those excellent and choice stone statues of maidenly making, so that, stirred at once, I sighed warmly and sobbing.

So that my loving and sounding sighs echoed in this solitary and deserted place, in air made thick, recalling to me my Goddess and immeasurably longed-for Polia. Alas, scarcely a little pause was granted in which that loving and heavenly Idea was not figured in my mind, and a diligent companion of my strange and unknown journeying. In which, firmly nested, my soul lay contentedly, as in the safest garrison and an inviolate Asylum, secure.

Being therefore come in this manner to such a place, where my eyes were stolen and taken up with such a sight by the copious and choice work of antiquity, above all I beheld a most beautiful gate, so stupendous and of such incredible artifice, and so elegant in every lineament, as could ever be wrought and polished. Which without fail I do not feel that I have knowledge enough in me to describe perfectly, or even sufficiently. Chiefly because in our age the vernacular, proper and native words, and those peculiar to the art of building, are buried and extinguished together with the true men.

O execrable and sacrilegious barbarism, how despoilingly have you invaded the noblest part of the precious treasure and sanctuary of Latin, and that art so dignified, at present darkened and ruinously injured by accursed ignorance! Which, associated together with raging, insatiable and perfidious avarice, has blinded that most high and excellent part which made Rome both sublime and a wandering Empress.

Before this excellent gate — judging this the first thing to say — there was left open to the sky a four-square courtyard, thirty paces by its diameter. With a notable pavement of marble squares, divided by one foot, set between with tessellation in various interlacings and bindings and colourings. In many parts broken up by the fall of stones, and grown over with shrubs.

And at the extremities of the said courtyard, on the right and on the left, towards the mountains, there were two orders of columns set to the level, with the exquisite interval of the wide-spaced manner set between, according to the fitting requirement from one column to another. Where the first run, or order, on both the one side and the other, began level with the edge, or outermost bound, of the pavement at the front of the great gate. And between the one colonnade and the other was a space of fifteen paces.

Of which columns some, and the greater part in number, were seen whole; with their Doric, or cushioned, capitals, with the bark-like, or spiral, volutes outside the ringed echinus, with the astragals beneath, hanging here and there, exceeding by a third part its own base — that is, of the capital, which was of a thickness equal to the half-diameter of the column set beneath it. Upon which lay the Architrave, or straight beam,

The hoof of which occupied, upon the level of the base, in the outermost line of the rounding of one shoe, five feet. And from this outermost circuit of the hoof up to beneath the breast I found it, by due reckoning, nine feet high.

With its head loose and unbridled, with two little ears, the one thrust forward and the other drawn back. With waving and flowing mane hanging down over the right of the neck. Whereupon some were falling, some stood on the point of falling headlong. Some on their backs, and some thrown over backwards, and others were climbing up leaning on it; some, tumbled over, held vainly to the long hairs caught in their gripping hands. There were some fallen, and then in the act of rising, slipped beneath the body of the shaker-off.

Stupefacto dunque non poco, ruminando, et cum summo dilecto curioso riguardando tale ingente machina conflata in animale da humano ingenio, dignissimo imaginato. Che in omni membro indefectamente participasse la egregia harmonia et compaginatione. Onde nella retinente memoria mi soccorse il sfortunevole cavallo Seiano.

Da poscia allucinato di tale artificioso mysterio offerentise non meno mirando spectaculo ad gli ochii mei uno maximo Elephanto, cum summa voluptate di properare ad quello. Ma echo che io in un’altra parte sento uno aegritudinale gemito humano. Et d’indi al capo cum horrore inspectabondo venendo, coniecturai che l’aura intromessa per le patorate piante, cum divino invento, il gemito moderatamente expresso causava. Il quale taceva decumbendo supino di metallo mirabile artificio conflato, di media aetate, sublevato alquanto sopra uno pulvino tenendo il capo. Cum sembiante di aegro, cum la bucca di suspirare et gemere indicante. Hiante, di proceritate passi .60. Not a little stupefied, therefore, turning it over and looking with the greatest curious delight upon that huge machine cast into an animal by human genius, most worthily imagined — so that in every member it shared unfailingly the excellent harmony and joining — there came into my retaining memory the ill-fated horse of Seianus.

Then, dazzled by such an artificial mystery, there offered itself to my eyes a spectacle no less wonderful, a very great Elephant, and with it the greatest desire to hasten towards it. But behold, I hear from another quarter a human groan as of sickness. I stood at once, my hair rising, and without further deliberation, hurrying towards the groan, I climbed a heap of ruins of great fractures and marble cuttings. And having gone forward fitly from there — behold, I see a most Vast and wonderful colossus, with the feet hollowed out and without soles, and all the Shin-bones open and empty.

And coming from there to the head, gazing with horror, I conjectured that the air let in through the gaping soles, by a divine invention, caused the groan to be moderately expressed. Which lay silent, reclining on its back, cast of metal by a wonderful artifice, of middle age, holding its head raised a little upon a cushion. With the semblance of a sick man, with the mouth showing that it sighed and groaned. Gaping, of a tallness of sixty paces. And by the hairs one could climb up over the breast, and by the matted and tormented hairs of the thick beard, to the lamenting mouth. Which by passages was all void and empty. Through that, then, driven by the stimulus of curious searching, without other counsel, into the throat by little steps

Et ad qualunque mirai inscalpto in tre idiomati, Chaldeo, Graeco, et Latino, di quella parte la sua appellatione, che in ciascuno naturale corpo vedesse intestini, nervi, et ossa, vene, musculi, et pulpamento. Et quale morbo in quella si genera et la causa, et la cura, et rimedio. Diché per tutte le inglomate viscere, era aditiculo et commoda aditio. Cum respiracoli diversamente distributi per il corpo ad gli opportuni lochi illuminanti. Nulla parte meno che nel naturale consiste. Et quando al core applicai, vidi legendo come d’amore si genera li sospiritti, et dove amore gravemente offende. Et quivi tutto commoto, dal profundo dil mio core subtraxi uno mugente suspiro, Polia invocando. In tanto che tuta la erea machina risonare cum non poco horrore sentiti. An art invented above every exquisite thing, that a man should make himself without an excelling anatomy.

O illustrious wits of the past! O truly golden age, when virtue kept concert with fortune! To this age alone you left ignorance and rival avarice as an inheritance.

Where also, not too far distant from the great horse, there offered itself at the level a very great Elephant of blackening stone, more than Obsidian, sparkling with gold and with silvery flecks copiously scattered like a fine dust, and glittering through the stone. And this fittingly, because on the summit of its most ample back it had a marvellous Bronze saddle-cloth, with two tight Girths carried round the monstrous bulk. For being hollow within, it is not solid, nor lasting.

Which quadrangular part was beautifully lined on each of its three faces with Egyptian characters. In the flat of which — surrounded with waving foliage — I saw certain Ionic and Arabic letters.

Now its voracious trunk did not keep to the level of the base, but raised and hanging it stood, turned somewhat towards the front, with the furrowed ears very widely let down, or barred. Which image in its vastness showed itself not one whit less than the natural. And in the oblong circuit of the base were carved hieroglyphs, or Egyptian characters. Decently polished, with the due base-course, with the block, gorge, torus and roundel, with their Astragals or little bindings, with the reversed Cyma at the footing. And above no less, with the projecting Cyma turned back, and the collar of the scotia and the dentils with the Astragals; excellently Symmetried according as the thickness required. The length, breadth and height: twelve paces, five, and three. The extremities of which were formed in a half-circle.

In the hinder half-round part of the base just described, I found a stepped ascent of seven steps carved for climbing upon the flat surface. By which, eager for novelty, I mounted. And towards the reserved quadrangle, set beneath the perpendicular of the saddle-cloth, I saw a little door hollowed out. A thing of great admiration, that in so stubborn a material so apt a hollow was afforded; so that by certain posts of metal fixed after the manner of a ladder, by which was a convenient ascent, one

For which cause, greatly stirred by curious eagerness, I entered and climbed. Where I found the greatest and most prodigious monster all hollow and void, and made a cavern — save that the same solid mass was left within, which stood beneath as the ballast. And it had as much passage, both towards the head and towards the hinder part, as a natural man could make his way through.

And there, hung in the vault of the back, there burned with brazen chains an inextinguishable lamp, with a prison's lighting. By which, in this hinder part, I beheld an ancient sepulchre granted to the stone itself, with a perfect image of a man, naked, of the common natural size, crowned, of the Stone, most black. With the teeth, eyes and nails covered in shining silver. Standing above the arched sepulchral cover, clothed in scale-work and other exquisite lineaments. It showed the forepart with a gilded sceptre of bronze, the arm stretched out. And in the left hand it held a keel-shaped shield, its form taken exactly from the skull-bone of a horse, inscribed in three tongues with little letters — Hebrew, Attic and Latin — to this sense:

I should be naked, had not the beast covered me. Seek, and you shall find. Let me be.

At which unaccustomed thing I stood not a little stupefied, and with some horror. Whereupon, without delaying too long, turning to go back, I saw likewise another lamp burning and shining, as is said before. And crossing over the opening by which one climbs, there towards the head of the animal, in this side too I found a like making of a most ancient burial. And the

Di tanta novitate digna di relato mirabondo, et degli aenigmati praelegendoli saepicule, dil tutto io restai ignaro, et dilla interpretatione et sophismo significato molto ambiguo. Non era auso perciò alcuna cosa pertentare. Ma quasi incusso da timore in questo loco tetro et illumino, quantunque gli fusse il lucernale lume, niente di manco il solicito desiderio di contemplare la triumphante porta stimulante, più legitima causa fue che quivi non dimorasse, che altro. Diqué sencia altro fare, cum pensiero et proposito per omni modo dapò la contemplatione di essa porta mirabile, un’altra fiata quivi ritornare, et più tranquillamente speculare tale magnificentia de invento dagli humani ingegni, citissimo all’apertura perveni. Et descendando uscivi fora dil exviscerato monstro. Inventione inexcogitabile, et sencia existimatione, excesso di faticha, et temerario auso humano, quale Trepano terebrare tanta durecia et contumacia di petra, et evacuare tanta duritudine di materia, overo altre fabrile machine poteron? Concordemente conveniendo il cavato introrso cum la forma exteriore. Finalmente sopra la piacia ritornato, vidi in questo

statue standing above the whole, like the other, save that this one was a queen; which, having raised the right arm, pointed with the forefinger to the part behind her shoulders, and with the other held a tablet, held fast with its cover and with her hand undivided. On which likewise was inscribed this epigram in three tongues:

Whoever you are, take as much of this treasure as you please. But I warn you: take away the head. Do not touch the body.

At so great a novelty, worthy of the telling, and reading over the riddles again and again, I remained wholly ignorant, both of the interpretation and of the sophistical meaning, which was very ambiguous. Nor did I dare therefore to attempt anything. But being struck as it were with fear in this dark and unlighted place — for all that there was the lamp's light there — nevertheless the anxious desire to contemplate the triumphal gate, urging me on, was a more lawful cause for my not lingering there than any other.

Whereupon, without doing anything else, with the thought and purpose of returning there once more by every means after the contemplation of that wonderful gate, and of considering more tranquilly such a magnificence of invention from human wits, I came most swiftly to the opening. And going down I came out of the disembowelled monster.

An invention unimaginable and beyond estimation, an excess of labour and of rash human daring: what Auger could bore through so great a hardness and stubbornness of stone, and hollow out so great a hardness of material, or what other builder's engines could do it? The hollowing within agreeing harmoniously with the outward form. At last, having returned onto the courtyard, I saw in this

Daposcia uno Malluvio, et uno vaso Gutturnio, sequendo uno glomo di filo, infixo in uno Pyrono, et uno Antiquario vaso cum l’orificio obturato. Una Solea cum uno ochio, cum due fronde intransversate, l’una di oliva et l’altra di palma politamente lorate. Una ancora, et uno ansere. Una Antiquaria lucerna, cum una mano tenente. Uno Temone antico, cum uno ramo di fructigera Olea circunfasciato. Poscia dui Harpaguli. Uno Delphino, et ultimo una Arca reclusa. Erano questi hieraglyphi optima scalptura in questi graphiamenti.

Le quale vetustissime et sacre scripture pensiculante, cusì io le interpretai.

Which most ancient and sacred writings, considering them, I interpreted thus:

From your labour sacrifice liberally to the god of nature; little by little you will bring back a mind made subject to god. He will hold a firm guard over your life, governing it mercifully, and will keep it unharmed.

Relicta questa praecellentissima et mysteriosa et inexcogitabile factura iterum ritornai a riguardare il prodigioso Caballo. Il quale havea il capo osseo, et macro, et proportionatamente picolo, optimo figmento apparea dil stare inconstante, et di mora impatiente, vedevasi quasi il tremulare degli sui pulpamenti, et più vivo che fincto. Cum una parola graeca excavata nel fronte. GENEA. Daposcia molti altri grandi frusti, et fragmenti di qualunque liniamenti, tra maximi acervi di ruina confragosi. Et di tutte solamente intacte lo edace et volabile tempo havea ad queste quatro stupende cose, Porta, Caballo, colosso, et Elephanto benignamente perdonato. O sancti patri antiqui artifici, quale immanitate invase tanta vostra virtute, che con vui nella sepultura, portasti di tante divitie la exhaereditatione nostra?

Pervenuto dunque ad questa veterrima porta di opera molto spectabile, et cum exquisite regulatione et arte, et praeclari ornati di scalptura, et di vario liniamento maravegliosamente consttucta. Per le quale tutte cose essendo io studioso et di voluptate infiammato di intendere il fetoso intellecto, et la pervestigatione acre dil perspicace Architecto, dilla sua dimensione, et circa il liniamento et la prattica perscrutandola subtilmente cusì io feci.

Uno quadrato collocato soto le columne, bine per lato diligentemente mensurai. Dalla quale mensuratione facilmente tuta la symmetria compresi dilla praelibata porta. La quale explanando transcorrerò brevemente. Una tetragona figura .A.B.C.D. divisa per tre linee recte et tre transversarie aequidistante, sarano sedeci quadrati. Addendo poscia alla figura quanto è la sua medietate, et cum quelle medesime partitione dividendo l’adiuncto, trovasi .xxiiii. quadrati. Questa figura di cordicelle quanto si praesta utile et opportuna ad reportare al curto, in segmento, overo in lepturgia et in pictura in prompto se offerisce. Trahendo iterum nella prima figura A.B.C.D. dui diagonii. Et ancora in quella segnando due linee, recta, et transversaria mutuamente intersecte, quatro quadrati se faceano. Item in quella vacua sopra le isopleure facti quatro mediani puncti, et da uno ad l’altro deducte le linee si constituisce il Rhombo.

Conscripte per tale via le praedicte figure, io acconciamente considerava, quale ragione hano li caecutienti moderni da sé existimantise nell’arte aedificatoria non sapendo che cosa si sia? Tanto enorme ancora nelle sue false aedicule cusì sacre come prophane publice et private regulano, dehonestando le parte dal medio procedente, negligenti di quella che la natura indicando insegnia. Essendo aureo et coeleste dicto et documento, che la virtute in quello consiste et beatitudine canta il poeta, il quale deserto et neglecto necessario conviene disordinato reuscire, et omni cosa .

Leaving this most excellent and mysterious and unimaginable making, I returned again to look upon the prodigious Horse. Which had a bony head, and lean, and proportionately small; it appeared an excellent figuring of standing unquiet and impatient of delay, and one saw almost the trembling of its flesh, and it was more alive than feigned. With a Greek word hollowed in its brow: GENEA.

Then many other great pieces and fragments of every lineament, among the greatest broken heaps of ruin. And of all of them, devouring and flying time had kindly spared these four stupendous things only, untouched: the Gate, the Horse, the colossus, and the Elephant. O holy fathers, ancient craftsmen, what savagery invaded so great a virtue of yours, that you carried with you into the sepulchre the disinheriting of us from such riches?

Having come, then, to this most ancient gate, of work most notable, and marvellously constructed with exquisite rule and art, and with illustrious ornaments of carving and of various lineament — for all which things, being studious and inflamed with the desire to understand the fertile understanding and the keen searching-out of that perspicacious Architect, both his dimension and his lineament and his practice — I set about examining it subtly, and did thus.

I diligently measured a square set beneath the columns, two to a side. From which measuring I easily grasped the whole symmetry of the aforesaid gate. Which, explaining, I shall run over briefly. A four-sided figure A.B.C.D., divided by three straight lines and three cross lines equally distant, will be sixteen squares. Then, adding to the figure as much as its half, and dividing the addition by those same partitions, there are found twenty-four squares. This figure of little cords offers itself ready to hand, and how useful and fitting it is for reducing to a smaller scale, in cutting, or in fine work and in painting.

Drawing again in the first figure A.B.C.D. two diagonals; and marking in it besides two lines, a straight and a cross one, mutually intersecting, four squares were made. Likewise in that empty space above the equal sides, four middle points being made, and lines drawn from one to the other, the Rhombus is constituted.

The aforesaid figures being described in such a way, I considered fitly: what reason have the blind moderns, who esteem themselves in the art of building, not knowing what the thing is? So enormously still they order their false little buildings, sacred as well as profane, public and private, dishonouring the parts that proceed from the middle, neglectful of that which nature teaches by showing. It being a golden and heavenly saying and lesson that in that consists virtue — and the poet sings of blessedness — which, being deserted and neglected, must needs come out disordered, and everything with it.

Perché turpe è qualunque parte al suo principe non congruente. Remoto però l’ordine, et la norma, che cosa commoda, overo grata, overo dignificabile si poté praestare? Adunque la causa di tale disconveniente errore nasce da ignorantia negativa et ha l’origine dalla illitteratura. Niente dimeno quantunque che la perfectione dilla dignissima arte non devia da la rectitudine, tamen il solerte Architecto, et industrioso, ad gratificare lo obiecto cum lo obtuto, pole licentemente cum adiectione et detractione, depolire l’opera sua. Sopra tutto il solido integro conservando, et cum l’universo conciliato. Il quale solido chiamo tutto il corpo della fabrica che è il principale intento, et inventione et praecogitato, et Symmetria dil Architecto, sencia gli accessorii bene examinato et conducto, indica (si non me fallo) la praestantia dil suo ingiegnio, perché lo adornare poscia è cosa facile. Advegnia che etiam importa il suo distributo, et non locare la corona alli pedi ma alla testa, et cusì lo ovolato, et denticulato, et gli altri, al loco congruente se debeno destinare. Lo ordinare dunque, et la praecipua inventione è participata ad gli rari, et ad gli molti ancora vulgari, overo idiote commune ad lavore se praestano gli ornamenti. Et però gli manuali artifici sono dill’architecto ministri. Il quale architecto per modo niuno alla maledicta, et perfida avaritia succumba. Et oltra la doctrina sia bono non loquace, benigno, benivolo, mansueto, patiente, faceto, copioso, indagatore curioso universale, et tardo. Tardo pertanto io dico, per non essere poscia festino alla menda, di questo sia assai.

Reducendo finalmente le postreme tre figure dimonstrate in una, adiuncta la seconda da gli .xvi. quadrati in essa contenti, produrassi questa figura. Dalla quale removendo poscia il rhombo, et gli diagonii. Lasciando le tre pendicule, et le tre recte, excepto la mediana. La quale inclusive tra le perpendicule truncata finisce. Et per questa regula, trovase dui perfecti quadri, l’uno supero, et l’altro infero, continenti in sé ciascuno quatro quadrati. Nel imo quadro facendo il diagonio, il quale ridriciato in perpendiculo verso la linea recta .A.B. habilemente si trovarà per il suo defecto a giungere, essere tanto la crassitudine dill’archo, et dille Ante. Dunque la linea .A.B. serà il debito loco dil Trabe extenso, overo recto. Il puncto mediano dilla linea truncata .E.F. sarà il ponto da inflectere l’arcotrabe in hemicyclo. Il quale debi havere tanto additamento agli inversi corni quanto è il semidiametro dilla sua crassitudine. Altramente essendo tale defecto, perfecto non il chiamo. Ma questo dagli optimi et periti veteri fue bellissimo exquisito, et diligentemente observato negli sui arcuati, per dar all’arco elegantia, et conveniente resistentia, et per vitare lo occupamento delle proiecture degli Abachi.

For any part that does not agree with its chief is base. The order and the norm being removed, however, what convenient, or pleasing, or worthy thing could be afforded? The cause, then, of such unfitting error is born of negative ignorance, and has its origin in want of letters.

Nevertheless, although the perfection of that most worthy art does not stray from rightness, yet the shrewd and industrious Architect, to make the object gratify the gaze, may lawfully polish his work with addition and subtraction. Above all preserving the whole solid entire, and reconciled with the universal. Which solid I call the whole body of the fabric, that being the principal intent and invention and forethought and Symmetry of the Architect; which, well examined and carried through without the accessories, shows (if I do not deceive myself) the excellence of his genius — because the adorning afterwards is an easy thing.

Granted that its distribution also matters, and that one should not set the cornice at the feet but at the head; and so the ovolo, and the dentil, and the rest, must be destined to their fitting place. The ordering, then, and the chief invention are shared among the few; the ornaments offer themselves to be worked by the many, and the common or unlearned sort. And therefore the handworking craftsmen are the architect's ministers.

Which architect must in no manner succumb to accursed and perfidious avarice. And beyond his learning let him be good, not talkative, kindly, well-wishing, gentle, patient, pleasant, copious, a curious and universal searcher-out, and slow. Slow, I say, so as not to be hasty afterwards in mending. Of this let it be enough.

Reducing finally the last three figures shown into one, and adding the second from the sixteen squares contained in it, this figure will be produced. From which, then, removing the rhombus and the diagonals, and leaving the three perpendiculars and the three straight lines, except the middle one — which, cut off, ends inclusively between the perpendiculars — and by this rule two perfect squares are found, the one above and the other below, each containing in itself four squares.

In the lower square, making the diagonal, which set upright in a perpendicular towards the straight line A.B. will readily be found, by what it falls short of reaching, to be exactly the thickness of the arch and of the Antae. So then the line A.B. will be the due place of the extended, or straight, Beam. The middle point of the truncated line E.F. will be the point from which to bend the arch-beam into a half-circle. Which must have as much addition at its turned-back horns as is the half-diameter of its thickness. Otherwise, such a falling-short being there, I do not call it perfect. But this was most beautifully and exquisitely and diligently observed by the best and most skilled of the ancients in their arches, to give the arch elegance and fitting resistance, and to avoid the encroachment of the projections of the Abaci.

Finalmente il frontispicio cum exquisita correspondentia participando il liniamento dilla elegante coronice, nel suo primo ordine usurpava poscia il piano dil proiecto quadrato, ultimo, una parte di coronice denticulata, intra la quale si continiva la planitie angulare.

La praedicta porta fue diligentissimamente adfabrefacta in una politura aequata di lapideo tabulato secto, conformantise le undulate figure nel cohaeso dille tabule. Cum vaga convenientia dille inserte opere, et la materia luculea, et gratiosa. Da uno lato et l’altro dal contento dilla porta separate dui passi, extavano ancora immote due magne et superbe columne fina alla sua crepidine di scabricie di ruina sepulte. Dalle quale io al potere il ruinamento rimovendo, le base aenee denudai discoprendole, et tali di materia erano gli Capitelli, egregiamente conflati. Et per piacere mesurando la crassitudine di una Base, et duplicantila, exprimeva il diametro integro dilla ima crassitudine dilla columna. Per la quale mensuratione trovai la proceritate sua più che duidetriginta cubiti. Le due vicine alla porta, di finissimo Porphyrite, et di gratioso Ophites, l’altre due cariatice, overo striate, overo canaliculate, et optimamente prompte. Ultra queste poscia alla leva et dextra parte ordinariamente cum sotiale binato altre cum modesta Enthesi petra durissima laconica astavano.

Il semidiametro de l’ima circuitione dilla columna facea la crassitudine dilla Base, la quale di Thori, di orbiculo, overo Scotia, overo Trochilo, et Plintho constava. Quel semidiviso per tertio, per sé uno usurpava il Plintho, la sua latitudine uno diametro et semi. Partito ancora le due partitione in quatro, una tolleva il summo Thoro. Distribuite le tre in parte gemine una apprehendeva il Thoro imo, et l’altra se praestava all’excavato Trochilo. Cum gli lymbi tolta una septima parte sua. Tale mensuratione trovai dagli periti artifici elegantemente observata. Sopra gli regulati capitelli dille antedicte columne, se extendeva una egregia Trabe, overo Epistylio cum la ima fascia ornata di rotundati verticoli, overo bacce, et la secunda cum associatione in longo di fusi truncati, intercalati tra l’uno et l’altro dui spondili soppressi in filatura. La tertia cum venustate aprovata era investita di Simate auricule in nobile foliatura cauliculata di expresso probatissimo. Superassideva a questo il Zophoro di sinuose fronde, nelle spire, overo vertigini grandi et diversi scapi et fiori cum vaga pampinulatura profundamente interscalpti, negli quali molte volucre nidulavano. Sopra poscia sequiva uno ordine di exquisiti Mutuli, cum

the cut of the lateral extension of the cornice, where the fitting slope appeared. The edges of which, or extremities, coupled themselves justly with the Cymatia of the projection of the crowning.

Finally the frontispiece, with exquisite correspondence sharing the lineament of the elegant cornice, in its first order then usurped the flat of the projected square; and last, a part of dentilled cornice, within which was contained the angular flat.

The aforesaid gate was most diligently wrought in a levelled polish of cut stone panelling, the waving figures conforming themselves in the joining of the panels. With a pleasing fitness of the inserted works, and the material bright and gracious.

On the one side and the other, separated by two paces from the compass of the gate, there stood still unmoved two great and proud columns, buried up to their footing in the roughness of the ruin. From which, removing the ruin as far as I could, I laid bare the bronze bases, uncovering them; and of like material were the Capitals, excellently cast. And measuring for pleasure the thickness of one Base and doubling it, it expressed the entire diameter of the lowest thickness of the column. By which measuring I found its height more than eight-and-twenty cubits.

The two near the gate were of finest Porphyry and of gracious Ophite; the other two channelled, or fluted, or grooved, and most excellently ready. Beyond these, then, on the left and the right hand, stood others in orderly fashion, paired in company, with modest swelling, of hardest Laconian stone.

The half-diameter of the lowest circuit of the column made the thickness of the Base, which consisted of Tori, of a roundel, or Scotia, or Trochilus, and a Plinth. That half being divided by three, the Plinth usurped one for itself, its breadth one diameter and a half. The two partitions being divided again into four, one took the topmost Torus. The three being distributed into twin parts, one took the lowest Torus, and the other was afforded to the hollowed Trochilus, with the edges taking a seventh part of it. Such measurement I found elegantly observed by the skilled craftsmen.

Above the ruled capitals of the aforesaid columns there extended an excellent Beam, or Architrave, with the lowest band adorned with rounded whorls, or berries; and the second with an association lengthwise of truncated spindles, with two whorls pressed down in a row set between the one and the other. The third, with approved comeliness, was clothed with Cymas turned like little ears, in noble foliage with stalk-work of most approved expression.

Above this sat the Zophorus of winding fronds, deeply carved among the spirals, or great turnings, and various stalks and flowers with pleasing vine-work, in which many birds were nesting. Then above there followed an order of exquisite Modillions, with

Malamente indicando quale si fusse lo aedificio definito et perfecto. Sotto la praelibata trabe derivava la cima, overo il fastigiato culmo dil frontispicio dilla praeservata porta. Cum hirsute barbe et fronti laureati, cum indole digna et maiestale.

Nella quadrata proiectura dil Zophoro sopra le antescripte columne in fronte, era tale caelatura. Le gracile extremitate dil quale de qui et de lì invinculate di varicante Cymose suspese erano tenute, di exactura quasi pervia.

spacing between. Above which began the reversed stepping of a copious cornice. Beyond this broken crowning, then, the greater part was seen demolished and shattered, with the trace, or imitation, of paired and great windows, widowed of their ornaments — ill showing what the building had been when defined and perfect.

Beneath the aforesaid beam ran down the top, or pinnacled summit, of the frontispiece of the preserved gate. Where, between its slope and the lining of the beam, that space imitated the figure of a stairway, which shows a triangle of unequal sides, or ribs.

Beneath the beam, in the space between the columns, there was sustained upon marvellous modillions, with an artificial hollow between — in this figure described, as much as could embrace the greater space — two roundels hollowed out, in imitation of a dish bound about at the lips with waving-work, gullets and scotias; where in the topmost stepping, in the middle of the lineaments drawn about it, there swelled a Torus, nobly clothed in oaken foliage, joined one beneath another, bound about with grooved thongs, with fruits scattered.

Within which resided two venerable images, freed from the vase, that is to say from the hollow, from the midriff upward. The breast part covered with a mantle over the left shoulder in an antique knot. With shaggy beards and laurelled brows, with a bearing worthy and majestic.

In the square projection of the Zophorus above the columns written of, in front, was this carving. An Eagle with wings spread, with clawed talons, rested upon a swelling little bundle of fronds and fruits hanging in the middle. The slender extremities of which, on this side and on that, were held suspended, bound about with straggling tendrils, of a working almost pierced through.

Therefore the conspicuous Gate, standing free in the flat of the levelling between the columns, of marble jointly panelled, was situated with the highest approbation. For which cause, the required showing of the more principal members of the said magnificent gate being somewhat fitted, it seems to me opportune in what follows to explain its pleasing and most comely ornaments. Because for the architect the being presents itself as harder than the being well. That is to say, that first it belongs to him above all to dispose the solid, and to define in his mind (as I said above) the universal fabric, rather than the ornaments, which are accessory to the principal.

Therefore to the first, the fertile skill of one alone is required. But to the second many handworkers, or unlearned operatives — called by the Greeks Ergatai — necessarily come together. Who, as has been said, are the instruments of the Architect.

Chapter V

The dragon. In the dark vaulted passages beyond the gate a fearsome dragon starts up; Poliphilo flees in blind panic through the labyrinthine dark and breaks out into a bright and pleasant land.

POLIPHILO ASSAI SUFFICIENTE HAVENDO FACTA LA DIMONSTRATIONE ET LA SYMMETRIA DILLA MAGNA PORTA, SEQUITA OPTIMAMENTE DESCRIVENDO IL PERPOLITO ET FABERRIMO SUO ORNATO, ET QUANTO MIRABILMENTE COMPOSITA ERA.

ALLA NOBILE TURBA CHE AL PIACEvole amore assiduamente dano opera, non gli rencresca (oro) perché io hebi alquanto dimoratomi, nel superiore narrato. Il quale per aventura a quelli non è unquantulo gratioso, cupidi di quella cosa intendere tractabondo (che quantunque in sé acerba sia) cum patiente animo il suo core festivo in quella collocanti se nutriscono. Diqué l’affecto humano naturalmente variabile essendo, per tale causatione non sia per questo da essi insimulato, il pane grato al palato illaeso, si alcuna fiata al pravato è displicebile, ma più praesto da cui gustando gli piace benignamente gratificato. Perché in alcuna parte havendo facto moto del fine debito all’architectare, che è la praestante inventione, di acquistare modulatamente dil aedificio il solido corpo. Poscia licentemente quello invento, lo Architecto per minute divisione el reduce, né più, né meno quale il Musico havendo invento la intonatione et il mensurato tempo in una maxima quello da poi proportionando in minute Chromatice concinnamente sopra il solido lui el riporta. Per tale similitudine dapò la inventione la principale regula peculiare al Architecto è la quadratura. Et questa distribuentila in parvissime, la harmonia se gli offerisce dil aedificio et commodulatione, et al suo principale gli convenienti correlarii. Per la quale cosa questa porta per la sua admiranda compositione et invento per excellentia essendo bellissima, et alla quale essendo adiecta tanta praecipua elegantia, et cum tanta emendata distributione, che parte in minimo recisamento castigabonda non se accusava. Digno pertanto hora io existimo il perfecto suo compimento descrivere.

Alla dextera primo se repraesenta uno stilypodio, overo columnipedio sotto le base dille columne. Dal quale modificatamente exacta di sopra una coronicetta, et cum le sue moderate inundature nel imo dal perfecto quadrato, rimania per regulatione più lata che alta cioè quadrangula. Vulgatissime prolatione, et non vernacule mi convene usare, perché degenerati siamo et scemati da tale thesoro, che dritamente explicare

POLIPHILO, HAVING MADE SUFFICIENT DEMONSTRATION OF THE SYMMETRY OF THE GREAT GATE, GOES ON TO DESCRIBE EXCELLENTLY ITS MOST POLISHED AND MOST SKILFULLY WROUGHT ORNAMENT, AND HOW MARVELLOUSLY IT WAS COMPOSED.

LET IT NOT VEX THAT NOBLE COMPANY who give themselves continually to pleasing love, that I have lingered somewhat in what is narrated above — which perhaps to them is not in the least gracious, being desirous, as they treat of it, to understand that thing in which (however bitter it be in itself) they nourish themselves with a patient mind, placing their festive heart in it.

Whereupon, human affection being naturally variable, let it not for this cause be laid to their charge: bread grateful to an unhurt palate is sometimes displeasing to a depraved one, but is rather kindly welcomed by him to whose taste it is pleasing. For, having in some part made mention of the due end of building — which is that excellent invention, to acquire by measure the solid body of the edifice — thereafter, that being freely invented, the Architect reduces it by minute divisions; neither more nor less than the Musician, having invented the intonation and the measured time in one greatest note, then, proportioning it in minute Chromatics, neatly carries it back upon the solid.

By such likeness, after the invention, the chief rule peculiar to the Architect is the squaring. And distributing this into the smallest parts, there is offered to him the harmony of the building and its measured proportion, and to his principal the fitting corollaries.

For which cause, this gate being for excellence most beautiful by its admirable composition and invention, and there being added to it so much especial elegance and with so amended a distribution that no part accused itself as needing correction in the least cutting-back — I therefore now think it worthy to describe its perfect completion.

On the right first there presents itself a pedestal, or column-foot, beneath the bases of the columns. From which, a little cornice being drawn out above in due measure, and with its moderate swellings at the base of the perfect square, it remained by rule broader than high — that is, four-cornered. Most common expressions, and not native ones, I must use, because we are degenerate and cut off from that treasure, so as rightly to set out

p. 48confidence: unstatedverified

tutte le particularitate di tale operamento. Ma cum quelli che di tale factione sono rudi reservati ratiocineramo.

Dunque in questa (come cusì dico) Ara, profundata cum gulature, intecte di foglie, cum modesta gradulatione di subtile incisure. Tra le quale di transparente petra Alabastrite, rimaste immune le proportionate fascie, per l’extremitate dilla quadrangula fronte, aequilata ambiente. Summa cum diligentia era inscalpto uno homo di aetate appresso la virilitate excedente, di rusticitate rubesto, cum la barba folta di pilatura da durecia irriciati al mento, per lo exito suo malamente dalla dura pelle.

Sedeva sopra uno saxo fincto, cum una pelle hircina. La quale cum le posteriore parte excoriata in nodulo la havea d’antorno sopra gli sui fianchi cincta. Et la parte dil collo cum la pilatura verso ad sé, tra le sue varicose tibie pendeva. Dinanti a llui in medio le tumide Sure era uno Acmone, overo incude, in uno toroso frusto di arbore truncato infixo. Sopra dil quale egli intento fabricava uno paro di candente allette, il malleo levato tenendo il suo artificio percotendo. Et quivi ananti a llui se stava una nobilissima Matrona, che alle sue delicate spalle erano inserte due ale di plumatile penne. La quale teniva uno infante suo figliuolo nudo, sedente sopra cum le clunule la polposa coxa genitricia alquanto la Dea Matre levata tenentila, cum il pedi nudato sopra posito ad uno saxo, ritenuto inseme cum il sedile dil malleante fabro, simulato in lapideo monticulo. Cum una fornacula in una cavernicula in cui ardeva il carbunculato foco. Et la Matrona havea le sue trece compositamente riportate sopra dilla sua dilatata fronte, circumornando la copiosa testa, tanto expressa delicatamente, che io non so per quale ragione quelle astante statue in lei non fusseron incitate, le quale parimente sa ritrovavano all’opera fabrile. Ancora poscia ivi era uno armigero di sembiante fremebondo induto di antiquaria torace aegide, cum il spaventoso capo di Medusa nel pecto, et cum altri nobili exquisiti toracali. Cum il baltheo transversale per l’amplo pecto, et teniva cum il musculoso brachio una hasta alquanto levato. Et cum Apice cristata galea munito il capo, l’altro brachio non apparendo, dalle anteriore figure impedito. Apparea etiam uno giovene et vedevasi dal pecto in suso, vestito di tenue panno, oltra lo inclinato capo dil dicto fabro.

La praedicta historia l’artifice sopra uno piano di coralicea petra di colore, havea diligentemente riportata, et introducta nel termine undulato dilla Ara. Il quale coloramento per la translucida petra ridundava, solamente supposita la colorata ad gli nudi corpi et membri, et nel intervacuo conterminato ambiente alle figure. Quale rosa incarnate

all the particularities of such a working. But with those who are unskilled in such craft we shall keep our reckonings in reserve.

Therefore in this (as I so call it) Altar, deepened with gorge-mouldings covered with leaves, with a modest stepping of fine cuttings — among which, of transparent Alabaster stone, the proportioned bands remained untouched, going round by the extremity of the four-cornered front, equal-sided — there was carved with the greatest diligence a man of an age passing beyond manhood, robust with rusticity, with a thick beard of hair curled by hardness at the chin, its growth coming ill through the hard skin.

He sat upon a feigned rock, with a goat's skin, which, flayed at the hinder parts, he had girt about him in a knot over his flanks; and the part of the neck, with the hair turned towards him, hung between his knotted shins. Before him, in the middle of his swelling calves, was an Anvil, fixed in a brawny piece of a truncated tree. Upon which, intent, he was forging a pair of glowing little wings, holding the hammer raised and striking his work.

And there before him stood a most noble Matron, at whose delicate shoulders were set two wings of feathered plumage. Who held a child, her son, naked, sitting with his little haunches upon the fleshy thigh of his mother — the Mother Goddess holding him somewhat raised, with her bared foot set upon a rock, held together with the seat of the hammering smith, feigned in a little hill of stone; with a little furnace in a small cavern in which the coal-red fire burned.

And the Matron had her tresses composedly carried back over her broad brow, adorning her copious head round about, so delicately expressed that I do not know by what reason those standing statues were not stirred to her, who were likewise found at the smith's work.

There was moreover there an armed man of raging semblance, clothed in an antique aegis-breastplate, with the fearful head of Medusa on the breast, and with other noble and exquisite breast-pieces; with the baldric across the ample breast, and he held with his muscular arm a spear somewhat raised. And with a crested helmet with its peak he had his head defended; the other arm not appearing, hindered by the figures in front. There appeared also a young man, seen from the breast upward, clothed in thin cloth, beyond the bowed head of the said smith.

The aforesaid history the craftsman had diligently carried upon a flat of coral-coloured stone, and introduced within the waved bound of the Altar. Which colouring flooded through the translucent stone, the coloured part being set only beneath the naked bodies and limbs, and in the hollow bounded round about the figures. Like a rose, flesh-tinted,

Ancora simelmente, nel sinistro subcolumnio. Uno homo nudo di aetate virile, era inscalpto, nello aspecto benignio, nel quale esso indicava summa velocitate. Sedeva et esso sopra d’una quadrata sede, ornata di veterrima caelatura. Di coturni calciato, dal perna enverso le sure disuti. D’indi prosilivano dui petasi singulo per pede. Ove et quella medesima Matrona cum divo effigiato nuda. Nel pecto angusto dilla quale due mamillule pululavano, immote dilla sua duritudine et dilla sua rotundatione. Cum ampli fianchi, tanto cum l’altra conforme expressa, che sigillate mentivano in medesima forma, quello proprio figliolo puello ad questo homo disciplinabondo offeriva. Il quale al puerulo già allato, sopra gli sui petioli ananti a llui stante inclinatose. Tre sagitte accortamente gli monstrava. Per tale acto, che facilmente si coniecturava amaestrarlo per quale arte lui le dovesse usando adoperare. Et la diva matre la pharetra teniva inane et cusì l’arco distento. Ad gli pedi di questo maestro, giacea uno viperato caduceo. Quivi similmente ritrovavase l’armigero et una femina galeata, la quale sopra di una hasta gestava uno Trophaeo d’una veterrima toraca appensa, et nella cima una sphaera, cum due ale, et tra una et l’altra dille ale, inscripto cusì stava. NIHIL FIRMUM. Vestita di volante subucula, cum ostensione dal suo pecto sopra.

Le due prompte Porphyrice columne Dorice di septe diametri, sopra qualunque di questi cusì explicati quadrati premevano di puniceo colore fusco cum gli sui orbiculetti più chiari, confusamente diseminati, lucido et terso. Canaliculate, cum .xxiiii. Strie per una, tra gli iustissimi Nextruli overo cordelle. Ma dille tre parte una era rudentata la inferiore. La cagione perché cusì erano caelate, di cavatura et cum il tertio rudentato, cogitai perciò, che questa superexcellente fabrica, overo tempio, ad uno sexo et l’altro doveva essere ritualmente dedicato. Questo è a Dio, et a Dea. Overo ad matre et a figlio, overo ad patre et mogliere, overo ad patre et a figliola et simiglianti. Et però gli periti antiqui patri al sexo femineo, maiore parte di cavatura attribuivano, che al mascolo il rudentato perché quella lubrica natura, excede la virile in lascivia.

La causa di tutte le striate fu per il tempio d’una Dea, per le strie indicando il vestimento rugato femineo. Sopra le quale poseno lo capitello cum le praependente Volute, ad indicio dilla retorta capillatura et ornato muliebre. Quelle cariatice che per el capitello hano una testa muliebre Cincinata, furono expresse nel tempio di quello ribellante populo. Il quale poscia iterum resubiugato ad ostentatione de inconstantia quale femine, in significato

every lineament of this column-foot was seen equally in the other, differing only in its history.

Likewise also, in the left column-foot, a naked man of manly age was carved, kindly in aspect, in which he showed the greatest swiftness. He too sat upon a squared seat, adorned with most ancient carving; shod with buskins, unfastened from the heel towards the calves. Thence sprang two winged caps, one to each foot.

Where also that same Matron, naked, figured as a goddess — in whose narrow breast two little paps budded, unmoved in their hardness and their roundness, with ample flanks, so conformably expressed with the other that, sealed, they counterfeited one and the same form — offered that same boy, her son, to this teaching man. Who, the little boy being already beside him, standing before him upon his little feet, bent himself down and shrewdly showed him three arrows. By which act one easily conjectured that he taught him by what art he should use them in his working. And the divine mother held the quiver empty, and the bow likewise unstrung. At the feet of this master lay a viperous caduceus.

Here likewise was found the armed man, and a helmeted woman, who bore upon a spear a Trophy of a most ancient breastplate hung up, and at the top a sphere with two wings; and between the one wing and the other stood written thus: NOTHING IS FIRM. Clothed in a flying shift, with a showing of her breast above.

The two ready Doric columns of Porphyry, of seven diameters, pressed upon each of these squares thus explained; of a dark crimson colour with their little roundels lighter, confusedly scattered, shining and polished. Channelled, with twenty-four Flutes apiece, between the most exact little cords. But of the three parts, the lowest one was cabled.

The reason why they were so carved, hollowed and with the third cabled, I judged to be this: that this most excellent fabric, or temple, must have been ritually dedicated to the one sex and the other — that is, to a God and a Goddess; or to a mother and a son; or to a father and a wife; or to a father and a daughter, and the like. And therefore the skilled ancient fathers attributed to the female sex the greater part of hollowing, and to the male the cabling, because that slippery nature exceeds the manly in wantonness.

The cause of all the fluted ones was for the temple of a Goddess, the flutes showing the wrinkled womanly garment. Upon which they set the capital with the volutes hanging before, in token of the twisted hair and womanly ornament. Those caryatids which have for capital a woman's head with curled locks were expressed in the temple of that rebelling people; which, being afterwards subjugated again, in token of inconstancy like women's, in the meaning

p. 50confidence: unstatedverified

dille columne ad perpetua memoria cusì extructe.

Queste eximie et expedite columne sopradicte, le sofrente base di aeramento subigevano, cum gli Thori overo Cymbie di quercivole fronde, cum gli expressi fructi, strictamente di volubile ligatura circuncincti sopraconquiescente al subiecto Plintho. Gli superappositi capituli dilla materia delle base, di opera ad tutta la harmonia conveniente, et requisita. Che tali Callimacho Catategnos dal Calatho sopra la sepulta virgine Corinthia non vide il germinato Acantho ad exprimere il suo venusto ornato non fece. Contecti dagli sinuati Abaci, overo operculi inflexi cum il lilio nel medio decorati. Il vaso degli quali investito egregiamente di dui ordini di octo foglie di Acantho al modo Romano et Corinthio. Fora dille dicte foglie uscivano le minore Elices, obviantise nel medio dil vaso, producevano il lilio appacto bellissimamente nel sinuato dil Abaco. Dille quale poscia gli cauliculi sotto il protenso dil Abaco se invertiginavano. Quali approbatamente pose Agrippa dil Pronao dil mirando Pantheon, attribuito per sua altecia uno integro diametro dil imo dilla columna, cum observabile Symmetria di qualunque sua parte et accessorio.

Il limite hora dicendo dilla porta, una ingente petra praxina il faceva digenerata cum seminario di macole albente nigre, et lutee, et di altri varii, et imperfecti maculamenti durissima. Superextavano ad questo, le recte Ante, del interstitio aspecto expedite et illustre, quanto la latitudine dil supposito limite uno passo tanto late extavano, ma la facia forinsica notabilmente fureno scalpate. Sencia signo di cardini nel limite né ancora nel sublime. Né ancora appariano indicii degli ferrei capti degli harpiconi, retinenti gli semicapituli dilla sua petra. D’indi poscia inarcuendo l’arcotrabe, overo hemicyclo, cum gli requisiti liniamenti et mensurate fascie dil trabe. Cioè piluli, overo bacce, et cum decimati fusuli, come insuti in una filatura coaequati, et auricole canine, et cum undulante decumbatura antiquariamente sinuate, overo laciniate, cum gli cauliculi. La spina dil quale, overo fibula, overo Cuneo, digno di admiratione, et di una subtile et temeraria fictione, et elegante politura tale se obiectava spectatissima.

Mirai attonito dunque in una pugnace et nigerrima petra una Aquila paulo meno che tutta evulsa dal solido cum le ale aperte. La quale havea amorosamente rapto uno ingenuo et delicatissimo Puello per gli sui panniculi. Tanto accorta che le pontute et adunche ungule la mollicula carne invertentise non offendevano. Et cusì per il brancare per le lacinule trahendo gl’inserati pedi sui verso il tumido et carinato

of the columns were so built for perpetual memory.

These choice and ready columns aforesaid the sustaining bases of bronze subdued, with the Tori, or mouldings, of oaken fronds with the fruits expressed, closely girt about with a winding binding, resting above upon the Plinth set beneath. The capitals set above, of the material of the bases, of work fitting and requisite to all the harmony — such as Callimachus the Cunning Craftsman did not see in the sprouted Acanthus from the Basket upon the buried Corinthian maiden, nor made to express his comely ornament.

Covered by the curved Abaci, or bent lids, decorated with the lily in the middle. The vase of which was excellently clothed with two orders of eight Acanthus leaves in the Roman and Corinthian manner. Out of the said leaves came the lesser Helices, meeting in the middle of the vase, and produced the lily most beautifully fitted into the curve of the Abacus. From which then the little stalks twisted themselves beneath the projection of the Abacus. Such as Agrippa approvedly set in the Porch of the wonderful Pantheon, attributed for its height one entire diameter of the base of the column, with observable Symmetry in each of its parts and accessories.

Speaking now of the threshold of the gate: a huge green stone made it, degenerate with a seed-bed of whitening, black and yellow markings, and of other various and imperfect mottlings, most hard. Above this stood the straight Antae, free and shining in the aspect of the space between; as broad as the breadth of the threshold set beneath, one pace, so broadly they stood; but the outward face was notably carved. Without sign of hinges in the threshold, nor yet in the lintel; nor did there appear any trace of the iron catches of the cramps holding the half-capitals of its stone.

Thence, then, arching the arch-beam, or half-circle, with the requisite lineaments and measured bands of the beam — that is, little balls or berries, and with tenth-part spindles, as though threaded in a row made equal, and dog's-ear mouldings, and with waving down-lying work antiquely curved, or jagged, with the little stalks. The keystone of which, or clasp, or Wedge, worthy of admiration, and of a subtle and daring feigning, and of elegant polish, offered itself thus most notable.

I gazed astonished, then, upon a stubborn and most black stone, at an Eagle almost wholly torn out of the solid, with wings spread. Which had lovingly seized a noble and most delicate Boy by his little garments. So shrewdly that the pointed and hooked talons, turning themselves aside, did not hurt the soft flesh. And so, by gripping and drawing at the little folds, its clenched feet towards the swelling and keeled

Aperti dunque gli ambidui brachioli cum le tuberule mane all’osso remigale strictamente prehenso se havea commesso dille ale spanse, questo è al remigio, che è quello osso il quale connexo cum il corpo mobilemente adhaerisce. Per il quale exquisitissimo expresso isteti stupefacto excogitando. Como lo elegante artifice cusì perspicacemente se imaginoe di applicare aptissimamente quella petra ad tale officio et proposito. Sì che io ragionevolmente coniecturai per le pinne alquanto circa al rostro irriciate, et il rostro semiaperto cum la ludibunda lingua apparendo che lei apertamente se accusava tutta di essere intenta et in libidine resoluta. Imitava cum il suo dorso il voluto dilla clausula, et cum essa conducea similmente et il dorso dil puerulo pandante.

Lo Arcotrabe residuo poscia nel suffito disposito in quadrati cubiculi egregiamente liniati, dentro pendevano aspramente gli exacti rosacii, quanto era il contento dille Ante, dallo illigamento degli capitelli sopra il quale illigamento oltra le ante protendeva sotto lo inito dil flexo dil fornice dil adito, overo laxamento dilla porta.

Negli triangoli che l’arco causava, era una Pastophora per una nobilissima scalptura, di artificio quale nomina il vulgo Chameo. Cum gli panni imitanti il virgineo corpusculo volabili cedendo parte alle belle sure pecto et lacerti, cum gli capigli soluti et discalciate, verso il cuneo porrigevano il victoriale Trophaeo. Le quale perpolitamente occupavano tutto il piano trigonale di petra nigerrima, da indicare la veritate degli metalli, et le Nymphe lactee et candidissime. Di sopra il Trabe assideva il Zophoro, nella medietate dil quale era una Tabella harpata di metallo aureato, cum uno epigramma di egregie maiuscule graece di copellato argento infixe che cusì dicevano.

it left the little hanging child bared from the navel down. Where the tender little buttocks came down between the feathered thighs of the winged one. This most shapely little boy, worthy of him who had carried him off for himself, gave sign in his little face of dreading his case.

Both his little arms being opened, then, with his knobbed hands he had gripped himself tightly to the rowing bone of the spread wings — that is to say, to the rowing part, which is that bone which, connected with the body, adheres so as to move. That little boy was exactly and artificially made of the white vein of the Agate, or Onyx; and the winged one of the Sard, which is the other vein coming together with it. At which most exquisite expression I stood stupefied, considering how the elegant craftsman so perspicaciously imagined to apply that stone most aptly to such an office and purpose.

In the triangles which the arch made, there was a shrine-bearing figure in each, of a most noble carving, of that artifice which the common sort call Cameo. Which most smoothly took up the whole triangular flat of most black stone, to show the truth of the metals, and the Nymphs milky and most white. Behind the columning was seen the white panelling of the best marble, fitted on.

Above the Beam sat the Zophorus, in the middle of which was a curved Tablet of gilded metal, with an epigram of excellent Greek capitals of refined silver set into it, which said thus:
