Diis Veneri et filio amori, Bacchus, et Ceres de propriis (scilicet substantiis) Matri pientissimae. Da l’uno et l’altro extremo dilla Tabella aenea erano dui retinenti fanciulli, overo spirituli alati, perfectamente formati, per sì facto modo, che il diligente statuario degli celebri fanciulli geruli dilla Ravennata Cochlea tale exemplare non vide. Giuncte le tumidule mano ad essa, promptamente la tenivano nudi dil dicto metallo. Sopra di uno piano di petra Cyanea aptamente reportati, più ad gratia dil suo colorato, che quella che in pastilli compacta, constricta è alla vomitione dil perfecto azuro, et di lustro vitreo perluceva.

Nel fronte dil Zophoro sopra le porphyritice columne porrecto, erano Spolie di Thorace, Lorice de trilitiati anuli inodate, Clypei, Galee, Fasce, Secure, Face, Pharetre, Iacoli et molte altre bellice machine, non meno Aerie, che maritime, et terrestre dignissima factura, et cusì alle Anche sue, indicavano sencia dubie le victorie, potentia, et triumphi, che l’altitono Iove feceron personare, et perire in dolcecia gli mortali.

Ordinatamente da poscia seguiva la facinorosa Coronice, di tali liniamenti, quali ad tanta elegantia di opera decentemente concorreno. Perché altramente cusì quale nel humano corpo una qualitate da l’altra discorde, la aegritudine accede, perché la convenientia non se ritrova in amicitia dil composito. Et gli accidenti al loco dovuto non essendo concinnamente distributi sequita deformitate. Cusì né più né meno dissona è quella fabrica et inferma, ove non si trova debita harmonia et commodulato ordine. La quale cosa gli moderni Idiote confundeno ignorando la locabile distributione. Imperò il sapientissimo maestro nostro al bene participatamente proportionato, et decoramente vestito corpo humano assimiglia lo aedificio.

Oltra questa corona cum inversa gradatione quatro quadrature praesidevano, due stante sopra l’ordine dille striate, overo Cariatice Columne, et due contracte. Nella mediana divisione dille memorate due, assideva una Nympha dil suo anaglypho excellente di auricalcho, cum due facole, una extincta tenendo alla grave terra rivoltata, et una accensa verso il Sole. L’ardente nella dextera, et l’altra nella sinistra mano.

Alla parte dextra dunque nella quadratura vidi la zelotypa Clymene, che li

To the gods Venus and her son Love: Bacchus and Ceres, out of their own substance, to the most tender Mother.

At the one and the other extremity of the bronze Tablet were two boys holding it, or winged little spirits, perfectly formed, in such a manner that the diligent statuary of the famous burden-bearing boys of the Ravenna Snail-stair never saw such an exemplar. Joining their swelling little hands to it, they held it readily, naked, of the said metal. Aptly carried upon a flat of Cyanean stone, more to the grace of its colouring than that which, compacted in little cakes, is forced to the vomiting-out of the perfect azure; and it shone with a glassy lustre.

In the front of the Zophorus stretched above the porphyry columns were Spoils of Breastplates, Corslets knotted of triple-threaded rings, Bucklers, Helmets, Bundles, Axes, Torches, Quivers, Darts and many other engines of war — no less Airy than maritime and terrestrial — of most worthy making; and thus at their Haunches they showed without doubt the victories, the power and the triumphs which made high-thundering Jove resound, and mortals perish in sweetness.

Then in due order followed the wickedly fine Cornice, of such lineaments as decently concur with so great an elegance of work. For otherwise, just as in the human body one quality discordant from another brings on sickness — because fitness is not found in the friendship of the composition — and, the accidents not being neatly distributed to their due place, deformity follows: so, neither more nor less, is that fabric dissonant and infirm where due harmony and measured order are not found. Which thing the modern unlearned confound, being ignorant of the placing distribution. Wherefore our most wise master likens the building to a human body well proportioned in its sharing and decently clothed.

Beyond this cornice, with reversed stepping, four squarings presided: two standing above the order of the fluted, or Caryatid, Columns, and two drawn in. In the middle division of the two remembered, there sat a Nymph of excellent relief of brass, holding two torches: one quenched, turned towards the heavy earth, and one lit, towards the Sun. The burning one in the right, and the other in the left hand.

On the right side, then, in the squaring, I saw the jealous Clymene, who

immobile fronde convertiva. Et Phoebo rigibondo indignatose, lachrymabonda insequente, et egli più perfugo gli quatro velocissimi cursori dille volucre quadrige solicitante. Né più né meno che chi da mortale nemico persequitato gli passi sui celero festina.

I’nel quadrato sopra l’ordine dille columne sinistro, de invisitata scalptura se continea historiato come il sconsolato Cyparisso all’aere li tenelli membri rectitava excelsi, per la sagittata Cerva. Et Apolline diciò duramente illachrymare.

Il tertio quadrato, a quello che collocato stava sopra le resistente columne vicinato tale coelatura bellissima offeriva. Leuchotoe dal proprio patre impiamente occisa, in tenere cortice, et mobile fronde, et proclinabonde virge, le candide, et puellare carne mutava.

Nella quadratura quarta si monstrava la dispiacevola Daphne ad gli ardenti disii dil comoso Delio unquantulo arendevola le virginee carne, verso gli caldi coeli in aeterna virentia dolorosamente transformava.

Hora cum successivo ordine sopra il Cimasio (che di qualunque liniamento la suprema linea se chiama) di queste descripte historie extensa superemineva una corona denticulata, et ovolata interiecti gli fulmini, overo straletti, tra lo hiato di uno, et dil altro ovolo, et foliature, et gli imbrici, cum gli verticuli, et Nicoli et altri Sigilli, et altre eximie operature expresse, et mutuli cum li Astragali, sencia defecto alcuno, et postremo la Sima di Acantho cum perpolito intercalamine infoliata. Dille quale cose tanto praestante scalptura se praestava, che delle aspramente excavate opere, minimo stigma dil rosicante Trepano non appareva.

Al frontispicio, overo fastigio debitamente ritornando, nella dispositione dil quale (como io ho antedicto) si replica in esso tutte le subiecte coronice ad tutte le parte delle operature, ad gli perpendicoli correspondendo sequestrato il stillicidio dilla suprema coronice, denegato ad questo membro.

Al praesente occorre di expedire la planitie trigonale dilla dicta parte templada in la quale non sencia admiranda contemplatione sa ripraesenta ad considerare, quanto continere poteano gli extremi di questa intersita figura, tanto fue appacta una corona di diverse fronde, et fructi, et scapi implicata, et diligentemente explicita di verdissima petra, in quatro parte stricta, in noduli de lori per li fasciculi implicati. Retinuta da due Scylle semihumane, et la inferna parte piscea, le quale cum il brachio di supra et l’altro di sotto aptamente l’amplexavano. Dall’una et l’altra parte degli iacenti anguli sopra il cimasio dilla coronice, extendevano le pistricie code, impedite da prompte vertigine, et verso lo extremo dilla squammea coda

was turning into unmoving fronds. And Phoebus, grown stiff, indignant at it, weeping and pursuing; and he, more fugitive, urging on the four swiftest runners of his winged four-horse chariot. Neither more nor less than one pursued by a deadly enemy hastens his swift steps.

In the square above the order of the columns on the left, of unaccustomed carving, was contained the history of how the disconsolate Cyparissus lifted his tender limbs high into the air, for the Hind struck by his arrow; and how Apollo wept hard for it.

The third square, that which stood placed next above the resisting columns, offered such a most beautiful carving: Leucothoe, impiously slain by her own father, changed her white and maidenly flesh into tender bark and moving fronds and drooping twigs.

In the fourth squaring was shown the unwilling Daphne, in no way yielding her virgin flesh to the burning desires of the long-haired Delian, sorrowfully transforming herself towards the warm heavens into eternal greenness.

Now, in successive order, above the Cymatium — which of any lineament is called the topmost line — of these histories described, there rose extended a dentilled cornice, and one of ovolos with the thunderbolts, or little darts, set between the gape of one ovolo and another; and foliage, and the tiles, with the whorls and Nicolo-stones and other Seals, and other choice workings expressed; and modillions with the Astragals, without any defect; and last the Cyma foliated with Acanthus with a most polished spacing between. Of which things so excellent a carving was afforded that, of works sharply hollowed out, not the least mark of the gnawing Auger appeared.

Returning duly to the frontispiece, or pinnacle, in the disposition of which (as I have said before) there are repeated in it all the cornices set beneath, in all the parts of the workings, answering to the perpendiculars — the drip of the topmost cornice being set aside, denied to this member.

At present it falls to me to dispatch the triangular flat of the said temple-like part, in which, not without admiring contemplation, there presents itself to be considered: as much as the extremities of this inserted figure could contain, so much was fitted in it a crown of divers fronds and fruits and stalks entwined, and diligently unfolded, of most green stone, drawn tight in four parts, in knots of thongs plaited through the little bundles. Held by two Scyllas, half human and the lower part fish-like, which with the arm above and the other below aptly embraced it. From the one and the other of the lying angles above the cymatium of the cornice, they stretched out their sea-beast tails, hampered by ready coils; and towards the end of the scaly tail

Dal interscapilio poscia le harpyiatice ale uscivano expanse, et verso gli vertigini dilla involuta cauda extente. Et ad gli monstruosi fianchi circuivano gli phocei remigii. In nel contento dilla corona mirai una hirta et foeta capra, che uno puerulo lactava. Il quale sotto a llei sedeva, cum le polpose Tibiette l’una porrecta, et una alquanto verso ad sé ritracta. Cum gli lacertuli alle pendente et ruvide lane sé tenendo, et cum il volto alle tumide ubere intento le asuchiava. Et l’altra dille Nymphe poscia blandiente inclinatase sublevato tenia uno pede dilla capra cum la sinistra. Et cum l’altra gli porrigieva le distente et grave ubere al suchiante osculo di lactabondo infante, sotto la quale si legea AMALTHEA. Et una Nympha alla testa dilla bestia stante, cum uno brachio il collo officiosamente ambiva, et cum l’altra mano accortamente per le corne la frenava.

Una tertia ancora in medio stava, cum frondature in una, et nell’altra mano uno veterrimo Cymbio tenendo, cum exquisite ansule. Ad gli pedi di questa era inscripto. MELISSA. Due Nymphe poscia tra una et l’altra dille tre antedescripte, cum strumenti Corymbantei agile saltante chorigiavano, ciascuna cum Nymphei habiti imitanti expressamente la moventia dilla agitata forma. O quanto artificiosamente adimpivano il mysterio suo di praeclara factura. Toreumata sencia fallo, non di lithoglypho Policleto, né di Phidia, né di Lysippo, et alla pia Artemisia ancora Regina di Caria, di tale praestante magisterio di celti se praestorono Anaglypti Scaphes, Briaxe, Timotheo, et Leocare et Theon. Finalmente nel templario fastigio, overo frontispicio, sotto l’ordine dilla superiore coronice in esso nel pianato perfecte maiuscule Atthice appariano in scalptura queste due parole ΔΙΟΣ ΑΙΓΙΟΧΟΙΟ. Di questa conspicua et spectatissima porta tale mirabile composito et excellente dispositione se speculava. the fish-like fins. With maidenly faces, with their tresses partly twisted above the brow and the rest womanishly dressed about the head, and part hanging in ringlets over the flat temples. And another of the Nymphs then, coaxing, bending down, held raised one foot of the goat with her left hand; and with the other she held out to him the distended and heavy udders, to the sucking kiss of the milk-drinking infant. Two Nymphs then, between the one and the other of the three described above, danced nimbly leaping with Corybantic instruments, each in Nymph-like habits expressly imitating the movement of the agitated form. O how artificially they fulfilled their mystery of illustrious making! Chased work without fail not of the stone-carver Polyclitus, nor of Phidias, nor of Lysippus; and to the pious Artemisia, Queen of Caria besides, there were afforded, of such excellent mastery of the chisel, the relief-workers Scopas, Bryaxis, Timotheus and Leochares and Theon. For this was most skilfully made beyond human genius and any relief-work whatever.

Finally in the temple-like pinnacle, or frontispiece, beneath the order of the upper cornice, in the flat of it there appeared in carving these two words in perfect Attic capitals: Of aegis-bearing Zeus.

Of this conspicuous and most notable gate such a wonderful composition and excellent disposition was to be seen. Of which, if its every measured proportion has not been particularly explained, the blame must be laid upon regard for prolixity, and upon the lack of the proper words of description. And because gnawing time had left this one alone untouched, therefore I did not approve of passing on without having said and treated something especially of it.

Manifesto è, che il residuo dilla antedicta clausura, et da una et da l’altra parte, era magno ostentamento, di stupendo fabricato, et questo chiaramente si comprehendeva per essere alcune operature indi et quindi intacte praeservate. Come nelle inferiore parte alcune Nane columne designate allo importabile pondo resistente. Altre Corinthie cum ignorata Enthesi, cum tanta moderata politura pregne, et così come requireva la Symmetria, et come voleva la exigentia dilla gravecia, et lo ornato, quasi dalla humana similitudine exacta, et solertemente acquistata l’artificiosa ragione, quale homo, che il grave pondo ad sustentamento gli convene le large piante sotto le robuste gambe havere, cusì nella modulata fabrica al gravamento le Nane, et poscia alla ornatione, columne Corinthie et Ionice gracile se attribuisce. Et secundo la requisitione dilla harmonia di lo aedificamento, cusì tutte le parte cum approbata elegantia constavano. Cum decente partiario dil coloramento degli marmori et vaga discriminatione, cum participamento allo obiecto gratioso, di Porphyrite, di Ophite, Numidice, Alabastritie, Pyropecile, Lacedaemonice, et candido di marmore varicosamente undulate, et Andracine digenerate cum bianchissime macule. Altre di multiplice coloramento confusamente commixto. Et dalla circunferentia trovato il suo salire per altra regula dal diametro dilla crassitudine inferiore.

Trovai et una rara forma di base Pulvinate. Le quale sopra il Plintho havevano dui trochili, separati per una interpositione di Hypotrachelii et Astragali, cum il supremo Thoro. Et in diverse parte era occultatione per la pendente et folta edera, da terra in suso serpendo, il ligno cui poculato divide Bacco da Thetide, cum gli sparsi Corymbi foecundi dille nigre bacce, et cum virente lanugine, et de qui et de lì occupando molti lochi dillo aedificio antiquario inseme cum molti altri arbusculi murali. Et nelle crepature accresceva il vivabile digitello, et altronde praependeva il Cotylidone, et Erogenneto, a cui porta il nome suo grato, demisso pendeva negli suggrundii. Et in altre rupture la Parietaria, et Alsine diuretica, et Polipodio, et Adianto, et il fimbriato Citracho cum il riverso erugineo, et la geniculata lunaria minore, et altri Aizoi amanti la vetustate murale, et di saxi, et il Polytrico, et la virente Oliveta cultrice di ruine. Diqué molti digni lavorieri erano di tale et molte altre virdure investiti et contecti.

Et dille magne et turbinate columne una sopra l’altra inextimabile collapsione, che non di columne, ma lignale acervo confuso et ad terra dirupto appariano. Tra il ruinamento similmente di statue reliquie conspicue, cum multiplici acti, multe nude, alcune cum gli indumenti rugosi

It is manifest that the remainder of the aforesaid closure, on the one side and the other, was a great display of stupendous building; and this was clearly understood from certain workings preserved untouched here and there. As in the lower parts certain Dwarf columns designed to resist the unbearable weight; others Corinthian with unnoticed swelling, pregnant with so moderate a polish, and just as Symmetry required, and as the exigency of the heaviness and of the ornament wished — the artificial reasoning being drawn as it were from human likeness, and shrewdly gained. As a man to whom it belongs to sustain a heavy weight must have broad soles beneath robust legs, so in the measured fabric the Dwarf columns are attributed to the weight-bearing, and thereafter, for the adorning, the slender Corinthian and Ionic.

And according to the requirement of the harmony of the building, so all the parts stood with approved elegance. With a decent sharing of the colouring of the marbles and a pleasing distinction, with a gracious sharing towards the object: of Porphyry, of Ophite, Numidian, Alabaster, fire-flecked, Laconian, and of white marble waved with veins, and dark-red degenerate with whitest markings. Others of manifold colouring confusedly mixed. And from the circumference its rising was found by another rule than from the diameter of the lower thickness.

I found also a rare form of Cushioned base, which above the Plinth had two trochili, separated by an interposition of little necks and Astragals, with the topmost Torus.

And in divers parts there was a hiding by the hanging and thick ivy, creeping from the ground upward — the wood whose cup divides Bacchus from Thetis — with its scattered fruitful Clusters of black berries, and with green down, taking up here and there many places of the ancient building, together with many other wall-shrubs. And in the cracks grew the lively little finger-fern; and elsewhere hung the Navelwort, and Houseleek, to which its pleasing name belongs, hanging low in the eaves. And in other breakages the Pellitory, and diuretic Chickweed, and Polypody, and Maidenhair, and the fringed Spleenwort with its rusty back, and the jointed lesser Moonwort, and other House-leeks that love the antiquity of walls and of stones, and the Hair-moss, and the green Olive-grove that dwells in ruins. Whereupon many worthy works were clothed and covered with this and much other greenery.

And of the great and turned columns, one upon another, there was an inestimable collapse, so that they appeared not columns but a confused heap of timber cast down to the ground. Among the ruin likewise conspicuous relics of statues, with manifold acts: many naked, some with the garments wrinkled

Distributo il pede in sexta parte dill’altecia, overo cubiti quatro. Alcune ancora integre sopra la sua Arula stante, et tale negli Solii cum modesta promptitudine assidevano. Vidi innumeri Trophaei, manubie spolie, et infiniti ornamenti. Et capi di bovi et equini cum debito intervallo dispositi. Et dagli corni reste di fronde cum pomi scapi, et teche, et altri fructi nella corpulentia pandante, cum pueruli equitanti ludibondi. Per le quale tutte cose rectamente se iudicava, quanto copioso praestavasi il cogitamento dil multiscio Architecto, di cura, di studio, et de industria. Et di quanta vigilantia il foecundo intellecto se manifestava. Et cum quanta voluptate lo effecto dil suo proposito havea operosamente exposto. Et quanto era la Eurythmia propalando la subtilitate dill’arte lapicidaria, et quanta arte nelle petre monstrava la scalptura, certamente cum tanta facilitate, che non di marmoro quantunque duro, ma si molle creta et argilla havessese praestata la materia. Et cum quanta conclausura le petre coagmentate et composite, a norma regula et libella.

Questa fue la vera arte, che discopre la nostra confisa ignorantia, et detestabile praesumptione et publico et damnosissimo errore. Questo è quello chiaro lume che dolcemente ne invita alla sua contemplatione per illuminare gli nostri obscurati ochii. Imperoché niuno si non chi reluctando essa refuge caeco rimane cum gli aperti ochii. Questa è quella che accusa la nephanda avaritia, rapace et consumptrice di omni virtute, vermo rosicante il core continuamente di chi è suo captivo, maledicto obstaculo et obice ad gli dispositi ingegni, nemica mortale dilla bona architectura. Idolo execrando dil praesente saeculo, tanto indigno et damnosamente venerato. Veneno exitiale, che misero fai che da te è laeso, quante magnifice opere sono ruinate et parte interdicte? Per la quale cosa rapto et prehenso de dilecto et inexcogitabile solatio essendo, et dalla sancta et veneranda antiquitate, cum tanta gratia et admiratione, ch’io me ritrovai cum indeterminati instabili, et impasti riguardi. Indi et quindi volentiera mirando, et di admiratione stipato, et nella mente circunfulto examinava discorrendo, quello che le caelate historie significavano, cum ultroneo piacere quello fixamente speculando. Cum gli labri aperti intento per longo protracto, niente dimanco non poteasi satisfare gli avidi ochii, et inexplebile appetito di mirare et remirare, le excellente et veterrime operature. Spogliato dunque et sequestrato di omni altra pensiculatione, solamente la mia philesia Polia spesse fiate nella viscida memoria servabile et gratissima succurrea. Ma per tutto questo, cum uno sonante

or folded, clinging over the naked figure and repeating the covered limbs. Some resting upon the left foot, and some upon the other, holding the heavy head perpendicular above the centre of the heel, and then holding the other free and loosed of all weight, stretched forward. The foot distributed as a sixth part of the height, that is, four cubits. Some still whole, standing upon their little Altar, and some sitting in Thrones with modest readiness.

I saw innumerable Trophies, spoils of war, and infinite ornaments; and heads of oxen and of horses disposed at due interval, and from their horns ropes of fronds with fruits, stalks and pods, and other fruits hanging in their bulk, with little boys riding upon them in play.

For all which things it was rightly judged how copious the thought of that many-knowing Architect showed itself, in care, in study and in industry. And with how much vigilance his fertile understanding declared itself. And with how much pleasure he had laboriously set forth the effect of his purpose. And how great was the Eurythmy, publishing the subtlety of the stone-cutter's art; and how much art the carving showed in the stones — certainly with such facility that it seemed the material afforded had been not marble, however hard, but soft clay and potter's earth. And with how great a closing the stones were joined and composed, to the norm, the rule and the level.

This was the true art, which discovers our confident ignorance, and detestable presumption, and public and most damaging error. This is that clear light which sweetly invites us to its contemplation, to illuminate our darkened eyes. For no one, save he who struggling flees from it, remains blind with open eyes. This is that which accuses wicked avarice, the ravening consumer of every virtue, the worm continually gnawing the heart of him who is its captive; accursed obstacle and barrier to well-disposed wits, mortal enemy of good architecture; execrable idol of the present age, so unworthily and damagingly venerated. Deadly poison, that makes wretched whoever is hurt by you — how many magnificent works are ruined and in part forbidden?

For which cause, being seized and taken with delight and unimaginable solace, and by that holy and venerable antiquity, with such grace and admiration, I found myself with undetermined, unstable and unfed gazings. Looking gladly here and there, and crowded with admiration, and encircled in my mind, I examined, running over what the carved histories signified, gazing fixedly at it with a willing pleasure. Intent with parted lips for a long stretch, none the less my greedy eyes and insatiable appetite could not be satisfied with looking and looking again at those excellent and most ancient workings.

Stripped therefore and sequestered of every other thought, only my beloved Polia came often to my sticky memory, kept and most welcome. But for all this, with a sounding

INTRATO ALQUANTO POLIPHILO NELLA DESCRIPTA PORTA, CUM GRANDE APIACERE ANCORA VEDEVA EL MIRO ORNATO DIL SUO INGRESSO. ET VOLENDO POSCIA RETRO RITORNARE, VIDE EL MONSTRIFERO DRACONE, ET ELLO OLTRA EL CREDERE PERTERREFACTO PER LOCHI SUBTERRANEI PREHENDE FUGA. ALLA FINE EXPECTATISSIMO EXITO RETROVANDO PERVENE IN UNO LOCO AMENO.

MAGNA ET LAUDABILE COSA SENCIA fallo sarebbe il potere facilmente narrare, et ad puncto disertare la incredibile factura, et inopinabile componimento dilla vastissima structura, et la granditudine di tanto aedificamento, et dilla spectatissima porta in loco aedito et conspicuo commodamente situata. Diqué il dilecto dil contemplare excedeva la grande mia admiratione, perché me Iove arbitrava ad gli superi ardua non essere qualunque factura, sospicando quasi che da niuno artifice, et da humano sapere, non poterse componere tanta vastitate et tali amplissimi concepti exprimere, et tanta novitate excogitare, et cum tanta elegantia ornare, et disponere cum tanta singulare symmetria, sencia supplemento et correctione perfectamente definire, dilla praefata structura la sua praeclara et inexcogitabile ostentatione.

Per tale ragione non dubitarei unquantulo che si il naturale historico mirato questo o inteso havesse, che spreta l’Aegypto, et la industria et lo ingegnio degli artifici sui mirando. I quali in distincte et diverse officine distributi, da essi statuarii electa una parte scalpenda et consignata la proceritate. Et cum tanta Symmetria perfectamente poscia tutte cum il suo frusto consentivano et alla compositione di uno ingente colosso tanto definitamente, quanto si da uno solo artifice depolito fusse. Et la sagace solertia di Satyro architecto et de gli altri famosi. Et praecipuamente ad Simandro l’opera mirifica dil praestante Memnone di tre magne statue dil summo Iove in uno solido saxo exscalpte. Dille quale una sedendo li pedi overo la pianta septeni cubiti excedeva. Harebbe cum ragione parvifacto. Harebbe et simigliantemente ceduto quivi il stupendo miraculo dilla statua dilla magnanima Semirami nel monte Bagistano di stadii .x. et .vii. inscalpta. Et tacendo ancora dilla insolente

I laid her somewhat ill aside. I persevered therefore in wonder at those most welcome antiquities.

POLIPHILO, HAVING ENTERED SOMEWHAT INTO THE DESCRIBED GATE, WITH GREAT PLEASURE STILL BEHELD THE WONDERFUL ORNAMENT OF ITS ENTRANCE. AND WISHING AFTERWARDS TO TURN BACK, HE SAW THE MONSTROUS DRAGON; AND HE, TERRIFIED BEYOND BELIEF, TOOK FLIGHT THROUGH UNDERGROUND PLACES. AT LAST, FINDING A MOST LONGED-FOR WAY OUT, HE CAME INTO A PLEASANT PLACE.

A GREAT AND PRAISEWORTHY THING WITHOUT fail it would be to be able easily to narrate, and to set out point by point, the incredible making and unimaginable composition of that vastest structure, and the greatness of so much building, and of that most notable gate, conveniently situated in a high and conspicuous place.

Whereupon the delight of contemplating exceeded my great admiration; for I judged that to Jove among the gods no making whatever is hard, suspecting almost that by no craftsman and by no human knowledge could so great a vastness be composed, and such most ample conceits expressed, and so much novelty devised, and adorned with such elegance, and disposed with such singular symmetry, and perfectly defined without supplement and correction — the illustrious and unimaginable display of that aforesaid structure.

For which reason I should not doubt in the least that, if the natural historian had beheld or understood this, he would have scorned Egypt, and the industry and genius of its craftsmen at which he wondered — those who, distributed in distinct and various workshops, chose a part to be carved and were assigned its length; and then with so much Symmetry all agreed with their own piece, and to the composition of a huge colossus, as exactly as if it had been polished by one craftsman alone. And the sagacious shrewdness of Satyrus the architect and of the other famous ones. And chiefly, for Simandius, the wonderful work of the excellent Memnon, of three great statues of highest Jove carved in one solid rock, of which one, seated, its feet or sole exceeded seven cubits. He would with reason have made little of them.

He would likewise have given way here, that stupendous miracle of the statue of the magnanimous Semiramis carved on Mount Bagistan, of seventeen stadia. And the writers, keeping silence too on the insolence

Il quale (simile all’altro per opposito) era di petra nigerrima, al duro ferro contentibile di nitore speculabile. Insatiably, then, considering now one and now another most beautiful and massive work, I said silently: if the fragments of holy antiquity, and its breakages and ruin, and in a manner its very Chippings, lead us into stupendous admiration and to so much delight in looking at them, what would its completeness do?

And so I thought too within myself, reasonably: perhaps in the inner shrines is the venerable Altar of the mysterious sacrifices and sacred flames, or else the statue of the Divine Venus, or her most holy Aphrodisium, and that of her bow-bearing and arrow-shooting little son. And with devout veneration, the right foot set upon the sacred threshold, there ran before me a fleeing and white Mouse.

At once, without other curious thought, with searching eyes I entered somewhat into the open space and the lighted entry, and things worthy of eternal regard presented themselves to me. Here on the right and left side the panelled wall was of most polished marbles. In the middle part of which levelling was fitted a great roundness, enclosed in the circuit of a leafy jewel with excellent company of carving. Which (like the other opposite it) was of the blackest stone, contemptuous of hard iron, of a mirroring brightness.

Between which, passing (unaware of them), I was invaded by a sudden fear at my own image. Nevertheless I was tempered again by an unlooked-for pleasure. Because in them there was clearly offered the judgment of the histories notably painted in mosaic work. And on both the lower parts, beneath the shining mirrors, were lengthwise seats of stone. The pavement clean and free of dust, worked in new and gracious pottery-work. And so too the coloured soffit was free of the wicked Spider's weaving, because there breathed there continually a most fresh air; the panelled walls joined beneath the binding. Which binding, of most subtle conceit, extended from the capitals of the most upright antae as far as the extremity of the said entry. As long as

Nel contento spatio di questi, mirai tale antiqua historia depicta.

Europa adulescentula natante in Creta sopra il praestigiato bove. Et ad gli sui filioli lo edicto di Re Agenore, a Cadmo, Fenice, et Cilice. Che la vitiata sorore insequenti di ritrovare. Et non la ritrovando, al surgente fonte il squammoso Dracone strenuamente occiseron. Et dapò consultati, da Apolline determinorono cum gli comiti di aedificare la citade, ove la mugiente Iuvenca se affermasse. Diqué quella patria fin hogi dì aeternalmente serva el nome dil Boato mugire. Aedificava dunque Cadmo Athene. L’altro fratello Fenicia. Il tertio Cilicia. Optimamente disposita, et cum tirato ordine expedita, di fictione, di depicti di naturali colori come exigeva, gli acti, gli lochi, et dilla historia la opportuna expressione, era questa museaca pictura.

by perspective I judged twelve paces.

Above which most polished binding the soffit began to arch, its vaulted bend conforming to that of the gate. Of such a fertile and delightful conceit it offered itself, with such excellent carving, neatly full of little water-monsters in the feigned water, and among the moderate wavelets half-men and women, with spiralling little fish-tails. Upon these, near the back, some sat fitly; some of them naked, embracing the monsters with mutual entwining. Some pipers, others with fantastical instruments. Some drawn along, sitting in strange Chariots. Crowned by the ever-swimming Dolphins with the cold flower of the water-lily; some clothed in its own leafage.

Some with manifold vessels of copious fruits, and with crowded horns of plenty. Others with little bundles of sweet-flag, and of flowers of the Silvan's beard, struck at one another. Some were girt with reeds. The other part, riding upon hippopotami, wrestled. And other divers and hateful beasts, with tortoise-shell for shield. And here they gave themselves to wantonness, and here to various games and feasts, with lively strivings and movements excellently carved and expressed. Completely, from the one end and the other, they adorned it.

In the turning of the vault I saw a most diligent worm-like work of exquisite little glass tesserae, with a gilded surface and of every most pleasing colouring. And first there presented itself a frieze two feet broad, which, going about, adorned the enclosed extremities of all the vaulted space, from the bindings recited upward, and along the length of the vault's pinnacle, with a companionable joining, existing in lively colourings. Nor otherwise than as if they had been composed just then: with natural foliage of emerald greenness, with the reverses of a Punic colour, with flowers of Cyan and of Phoenician and of adulterate hue, with gracious entwinings and knottings.

In the space contained by these, I beheld this ancient history painted.

The young Europa swimming to Crete upon the counterfeited bull. And to her sons the edict of King Agenor: to Cadmus, Phoenix and Cilix, that pursuing they should find their violated sister. And not finding her, at the rising spring they strenuously slew the scaly Dragon. And thereafter, having taken counsel, they determined by Apollo, with their companions, to build a city where the lowing Heifer should stop. Whereupon that country to this day eternally keeps the name of the Lowing bellow. Cadmus therefore built Athens; the other brother Phoenicia; the third Cilicia. Most excellently disposed, and carried out in a drawn-out order, of feigning, of painting in natural colours as it required — the acts, the places, and the fitting expression of the history — was this mosaic picture.

On the part opposite, in this same manner, I beheld the wanton Pasiphaë, kindled with infamous love, and lying hid in the wooden engine

and closed up; and the robust Bull wantoning upon the coupling he did not know. And then the Minotaur of monstrous shape, shut up and imprisoned in the laborious and pathless labyrinth. Lastly the sagacious Daedalus, fleeing from the prison-cloister, ingeniously making Wings for himself and for Icarus. It happened that I gazed with parted lips most intently (my unstable and most swift eyelids not moving), with my mind ravished, attending only to those most beautiful and so well disposed and perfectly ordered and artificially painted and elegantly expressed histories, left inviolate by any breakage — so tenacious was the seizing glue that the glass tesserae, pressed down page-wise and perpetually cohering, stood to this hour unhurt, and not one removed from its placing. For that excellent craftsman had gathered every absolute diligence to this excellent making.

And there, carrying myself foot before foot, pertinaciously examining with what direction of the painter's art he had observed to place with pondered distribution the readiest figures upon their just planes. And how the lines of the fabrics drew towards the object. And how from the eyes certain places were as it were lost. And things imperfect brought little by little to the perfect, and so on the contrary, granting his judgment to the eyes. With the exquisite by-works: waters, springs, mountains, hills, little woods, animals. The colouring impaired with distance, and with the light opposed, and with the neat reflections in the folds of the garments and in the other workings, not with little emulation of shrewd nature. So wondering and absorbed that I was almost not present in myself.

In this manner I had come to the end of the entry, where the gracious histories ended, because beyond was a most thick darkness that I did not dare to enter. But turning myself therefore to go back — behold, without pause I heard through the broken ruins as it were a crashing of bones and of crackling branches. I stood still, my so sweet solace suddenly interrupted and cut off.

And thereafter I heard still more plainly as it were a dragging, as of a great dead ox, through the warty place and over the heaped and uneven ruins, always coming towards the gate with a nearer and more consonant din; and I heard a very great hissing of an excessive serpent. I was stupefied. And my voice being forbidden and my hair raised, I did not make myself safe by fleeing, and in that darkness to rush on.

O unhappy me, and sad of fortune! Behold, of a sudden I see plainly, coming to the threshold of the gate — not, as to Androcles, the limping lion in the cave, but a fearful and horrendous Dragon, its three-forked

Where I firmly held that I had come into the inextricable fabric of the sagacious Daedalus, or of Porsena, containing so many inexplicable goings and returnings with frequent doors to cheat the exit, and to come back into those same errors; or into the chambered cave of the terrifying Cyclops, and into the foul Cavern of thieving Cacus. But with my arms stretched out before my face, so as not to run butting into some pillar, I went, those doing the office of my darkened eyes. As the Snail, bearer of its own governance, putting forth its soft little horns and drawing them back, and feeling out the way and contracting them at obstacles. And I likewise, groping, so as not to strike against those greatest supports of the mountain and Pyramid. And turning towards the gate to see whether the cruel and fearful dragon came behind me, the light was wholly spent.

I found myself, then, in the blind bowels and pathless passages of those shadowy caverns, and in greater terror and mortal trouble than Mercury making himself an Ibis, and Apollo in Thrace, and Diana in Chlomone a little bird, and Pan in his twofold shaping; and in greater than those of Oedipus, of Cyrus, of Croesus and of Perseus; and in greater fright and destruction than the bear-shaped robber Thrasyleon; and in greater straits than Psyche, and in more laborious perils than Lucius made an ass — and when he heard the robbers' counsel of his own destruction, without any choice to be counselled, truly ignorant and desperate.

At that point, made most fearful and anxious above all the fears, terrors and frights named, there came besides the frequent flight of light-shunning owls about my head, to redouble the fearful straitness. And sometimes, at their screech, without delay I believed myself to be among the pointed teeth of the venomous Dragon, and held fast between its gripping jaws like a toothed saw. Without delay there followed upon this a redoubling both of my perilous and grave terror and of the truth of my heart's grief: there came into my mind the wolf I had seen, whether by chance it had been a pernicious portent to me and a messenger of my wretched outcome.

Wandering and running here and there, like the corn-gathering ant that loses the scent of its track and strays, with wakeful ears to perceive whether the horrendous monster had come upon me, sorrowful, with the peril of its Lernaean and strong venom and its horrible sword and most foul devouring. And therefore everything that offered itself to me in that first approach I suspected to be that very thing.

And there, finding myself naked and deprived of every refuge in so mortal a strait and dissolute grief — although naturally hateful death is in no way welcome, yet in this hour I esteemed it gracious. The

Where are those eyes so barren, sucked and drained and deprived of moisture, that they did not all melt into thickest falling tears? But behold me dying, for I feel it at my shoulders. Who ever saw turned upon himself a more atrocious and deformed savagery of fortune?

Behold unhappy and insolent death, and the supreme hour and accursed moment at hand, in this dark gloom; and that my body and my human flesh should be the sating of this terrible beast! What ferocity? What rage? What more monstrous misery could mortals suffer — that the sweet and friendly light should be taken from the living, and the earth denied to the dead? O how much more ghastly a calamity and enormous misery, so sorrowfully and so importunately desired, in abandoning my most welcome and most perfect Polia. Farewell, farewell then, excellent light of virtue and of every true and real beauty, farewell.

I gave urgent effort to escaping the peril to be dreaded, and to saving my brief and scant contaminated life — or else, by this violence without any remedy, sorrowfully gasping to die, and without further delay; for I did not know, most confused, what to do with myself, wandering, fugitive and wayward through uncertain places and pathless byways. And my legs now weakened and numb, and every bodily power shattered and languishing, half dead, and altogether bewildered and as it were ghost-ridden.

Brought nevertheless to this tearful pass, having suppliantly invoked (my last refuge) the gods above and almighty, and my good Genius, with a guiltless mind — they having perhaps in this miserable case, by their perennial pity, some fortunate care of me — behold, I began to discover a little light coming. Towards which, alas, with what alacrity swiftly making my way, I saw a hanging lamp burning eternally before a devout Altar. Which, so far as I could then discern in a moment, was five feet high and twice as broad, with three golden images sitting.

Here, disappointed by the condition of the light, I was struck with no little religious horror at those venerable darknesses, in which little was seen, however much the illuminating lamp burned — because light is an enemy to thick and bad air. And always with intent ears, and never empty of my familiar terror; but somewhat the blackened statues appeared, and round about there offered themselves the vast and uncertain openings and fearful Passages underground, or under the mountain, supported here and there, and distributed in infinite places: many greatest four-square and six-square piers, and in other places eight-sided props, scarcely discerned by the weak light, aptly set beneath in proportion to bearing the excessive vastness of the pressing Pyramid above.

Here, praying a little while, without delay I made above all things towards unknown flight. Whereupon, thus half dead, no sooner had I run past the most holy Altar than there appeared to me besides a little of the desired light, which shone faintly as through a most subtle breathing-hole seen as a funnel. O with what feasting and with what gladness of my exhilarated heart I beheld it! And hastening merrily towards it without other thought — perhaps with greater nimbleness than Canistius and Philonides — no sooner did I see it with such unbridled gladness and longing than I called back most gladly my repudiation of that thankless and troublesome life; successively clearing my disturbed mind and fluctuating spirit, and somewhat refreshed and as it were reassured; and my emptied heart, drained of love, somewhat recalled, quickened again with resprouting love, and altogether filled; and every lost and exiled thought fitted itself again to its former work. And now more fixed upon my lovable Polia, binding me with renewed entanglements more closely,

it persuaded me with firm and flattering hope to obtain lovingly and gloriously in the future that which, dying untimely, I judged I should sorrowfully lose. O how extremely it tormented me. Yet I did not refuse any boiling and new-come accessory of love that should freshen itself, festering anew in my long-suffering and occupied heart. Being therefore somewhat consoled by the kindly light, and the spirits I had lost and renounced being taken back into me, and my prostrate strength gently restored, my suspended and pathless journey and flight urged me, striving straight on. For as I drew nearer to it I discerned it multiplying. To which at last, the heavenly will accompanying me, and most beloved Polia vigorously reigning in my loving breast, I came anxiously.

Where, blessing the gods undeservedly, and obsequious fortune, and my golden-haired Polia, I found a wide way out; and thence hastily going forth, and urgently fleeing, waiting not at all. And my arms, already stretched out to avoid striking against the thickest pillars, now most fittingly adapted themselves as oars for flight. And thence, striving, Safe, I came into a most pleasant Site and region.

In which, still terrified by that horrible monster, I doubted of the wished-for sitting down and settling myself, having it so impressed upon my mind that continually and without interval I thought I felt it at my shoulders. And for such cause I could not so quickly dissolve or displace so great a terror from there. Whereupon I justly judged, doubting, that it still pursued me. And I was moved also by manifold persuasions to enter and go forward. First by the pleasantness of that most beautiful place; then by my disordered mind urging me to flee at once. And chiefly, being always desirous to see and find things perhaps not customary among mortals.

Equally such considerations provoked me by every means to enter, and to go on as far beyond as I could, and to remove myself from the way out; where I might quietly calm myself in some place and clear my mind, and put in oblivion the terror now past — there coming not unwelcome into my retaining memory the appearance of the white Mouse in the entry of the gate. And this came as a very exhortative awakening to hearten me, because it was always welcome in the auspices, and a propitious and good Omen.

Therefore it persuaded me opportunely to give effort to keeping myself for the kindness of fortune, which sometimes may be to me a bountiful and long-haired minister of prosperous and favourable things. Et realmente viva et non ficta quella immane bellua era, et tanto spaventevola, raramente tale viduta dagli mortali Heu me quale non vide Regulo. Et di lei reminiscente, gli demissi capigli di novo salivano, et io il grado pernice accelerava. Poscia in momento in me ritornando diceva. Quivi sencia dubio (sì come accortamente arbitro per la benignitate dil praesente sito) habitare non debino si non gente humana. Ma più praesto forsi divi spiriti et heroi sono quivi tutelarii, et diversorio di Nymphe, et degli antichi Dei. Pertanto l’appetito suasivo agevolemente il frenato grado provocando exhortava al incepto viagio. Là onde io come captivato dagli perseveranti stimoli, cum feroce animo proposi di sequire dovunque la ludibonda fortuna cadesse, ancora tabescente.

Considerando adunque la bella et amoena patria et gli feraci agri et fertili campi et il dilecto di quelli coniecturando summamente laudai tale invitatorio, et ad spalle reiecta qualunque trepidante refrenatione moesto pavore alquanto intrai. Ma prima la divina luce invocata, et gli prosperi Genii, che ad questo mio ingresso guidando se praestasseron praesenti, et alla mia erratica Proselytia Comiti, et dil suo sancto ducato largitori.

weakened legs, I made my way. But still trembling decently at not coming into such a place where my entering by chance, and my hasty arrival in an unknown country, would not have been lawful, but a wicked daring and presumption, much more than the entrance of the magnificent gate.

And so, with my breast continually beating and with a long-suffering mind, I said within myself: what now persuades me to turn back? Is not fleeing and free escape easier here? And much better, I think, to expose my doubted life in this light beneath the open sky, than cruelly to perish in the blind darkness? Nor indeed should I know how to return to that opening and way out.

And in a moment, drawing from the depth of my sad heart groaning sighs, I turned over in my tenacious remembrance how much pleasure and delight my senses had lost in an instant; for that working was full of marvel and of stupefaction. Thinking again in what manner I was so ill deprived of it. Imagining to myself the bronze Lions of the temple of that most wise Jew, which by frightening brought men into oblivion.

Therefore, by such a likeness, I almost doubted that the dragon had done the same to me: that so many elegant and marvellous makings and stupendous conceits, showing themselves not human, most worthy of the telling, which I had diligently beheld, I must now let lightly flee from my dried memory; and that by such an event I should not know how to narrate them in order.

I said: certainly this is not so, nor do I feel in myself any lethargic affliction. But I hold it all placed most freshly in my understanding and my memory, kept safe, and painted indelibly. And truly that huge beast was alive and not feigned, and so fearful, rarely seen such by mortals — alas, such as Regulus did not see. And remembering it, my fallen hair rose again, and I hastened my nimble step.

Then, returning to myself in a moment, I said: here without doubt (as I shrewdly judge from the kindness of the present site) there must dwell none but human folk. But rather perhaps divine spirits and heroes are guardians here, and a lodging of Nymphs and of the ancient Gods. Therefore persuasive appetite easily provoked my reined-in step, exhorting me to the journey begun. Whereupon I, as though captured by persevering goads, with a fierce mind resolved to follow wherever playful fortune might fall, though still wasting away.

Considering therefore that beautiful and pleasant country, and the fruitful fields and fertile plains, and conjecturing the delight of them, I praised such an invitation most highly; and casting behind me every trembling restraint of mournful fear, I entered somewhat. But first I invoked the divine light, and the prospering Genii, that they should be present to guide me at this my entering, and be Companions to my wandering Pilgrimage, and bestowers of their holy guidance.

Chapter VII

The bath. In a jewelled bath-house the nymphs bathe with him amid teasing, playful eroticism, and spring a trick fountain on him — the book's lightest and most sensuous interlude.

POLIPHILO TELLS OF THE KINDNESS OF THE COUNTRY HE HAD FOUND AND ENTERED, IN WHICH, WANDERING, HE FOUND AN EXQUISITE AND MOST NOTABLE FOUNTAIN; AND HOW HE SAW FIVE GRACEFUL DAMSELS COMING TOWARDS HIM, AND HOW THEY, MUCH MARVELLING AT HIS COMING THERE, MERCIFULLY REASSURED HIM AND INVITED HIM TO SHARE THEIR PLEASURES.

HAVING COME OUT OF THAT HORRENDOUS pit, and from those inner darknesses and that place almost of the dead (for all that the holy and consecrated Aphrodisium was there), into the most desired light and friendly air, and being come into this most welcome place, I turned back to look at where my going-out had been. And where my life — a life I had never valued — I saw at that point troubled and in peril.

I looked upon a mountain of no great size with a moderate slope, all wooded with greenest and pliant fronds: with acorn-bearing Oaks, Beeches, Ilexes, Turkey-oaks, Italian oaks, Cork-oaks, and the two Holm-oaks — the one Smilax, or Holly, or Acilon. Then, towards the level, it was thick with cornel-trees, with hazels, with sweet-smelling and flower-bearing privets, and with a fragrant whitening flower; two-coloured Naxian, reddening in the north aspect and whitening in the south; Hornbeams and Ashes, and the like in such aspect, with sprouting saplings.

Wrapped in greening and climbing Honeysuckle and in winding hops, they gave a cool and shadowy shade. Beneath which was the Cyclamen, harmful to Lucina, and the jagged Polypody, and the Trientale Hart's-tongue, or Spleenwort; and both the Hellebores named from the shepherd; and the three-leaved tora, or triangularis; and the Groundsel, and many other shade-loving herbs, and Woodland trees, some without and some with flowering — a place none the less broken and rough, and closely shut about with trees.

The opening, then, by which I came out of those most hidden lairs, was somewhat high in the mountain, all overgrown with shrubs. And so far as I could conjecture, it was built over against the other mentioned before; and I understood that this too had been a wonderful working, a postern, and that one ancient. But envious and rivalling antiquity, and the narrowness of the approach, and above all the wall-shrubs of ivy and other branches, had made it a thicket — so that one scarcely discerned that there was any way out or gape. A place only for going out, but showing the utmost difficulty for returning. Then to me so much

Which hieroglyphs — the branches excepted, for I did not know whether they were of fir, or pine, or larch, or juniper, or the like — I interpreted thus.

On the other side I beheld this elegant carving: a circle; an anchor, about whose shank a dolphin wound itself. And these I interpreted most excellently thus: Always make haste slowly.

Beneath which ancient, solid and excellent bridge there gushed a broad vein of most limpid living water, which, dividing itself, made two running streamlets, one to the right and the other to the left. They ran through their fretted and gnawed channels, and between banks washed and cut, murmuring most cold; the stony and shaded banks covered with trees. In which banks the straggling roots appeared uncovered, and in them hung the Maidenhair, and the Adiantum, and the Ivy-leaved Toadflax, and the tresses of other little woodland herbs that love the river banks.

Which wooded and cool grove was pleasant to look upon and desirable for its spaciousness, and joyful with fronds, full of little woodland and mountain birds. Beyond the bridge it stretched somewhat further towards a pleasant plain, everywhere sounding with sweet chattering. There leapt the restless Squirrels and the sleepy Dormice, and it was inhabited by other harmless little animals.

In this manner, then, was shown this wooded district, shut about by the tree-bearing mountain, much to be gazed at by the eyes; and the plain covered everywhere with a variety of herbs. And the most limpid little rivers flowed murmuring down through the feet of the sloping mountains into the valley. Adorned with the flowering and bitter Oleander, and with Periwinkles, and Coltsfoot, and Loosestrife; shaded by tall black and white Poplars, and the riverside Alder and Manna-ash. And upon the mountains I saw the tall single-stemmed Fir, and the weeping Larches, and Silver-firs, and other noble kinds of like foliage.

For which cause, considering the place so pleasant, and a most convenient station and welcome retreat for shepherds — a place certainly inviting one to sing bucolic songs — I stood not a little stupefied, and suspended in mind, seeing a country so kindly yet deserted of people and uncultivated.

And then directing my eyes to the adorned plain, anxiously passing by the aforesaid place, I beheld a marble building appearing among the trees, and above the tender tree-tops its pinnacle. Whereupon, made all cheerful, judging that I had at last found a habitation and some refuge, I came to it joyfully without delay.

I found an eight-sided building with a wonderful and excellent fountain. Which also offered itself not in vain as a sweet invitation to my thirst, so long held back and not till then satisfied and quenched.

This fabric, pinnacled with an eight-sided roof and covered with lead, had at one front a stone as much higher as was one half of its square, of white and shining marble. Which most beautiful Nymph lay sleeping comfortably upon an outspread cloth. And beneath her head it was beautifully stuffed and folded into a cushioned mound. And a part of the said cloth was then most aptly brought to cover that which fittingly ought to stay hidden. Lying upon her right side, the arm beneath drawn back, with the loosed hand she idly propped her head beneath the cheek. And the other arm, free and without office, stretched itself over the left loin, coming down open to the middle of the fleshy thigh.

From the little buds — as of young girls — of her breasts there gushed a thread of most fresh water from the right; and from the left it rose hot. The fall of both fell into a porphyry vessel, with two receivers joined together in one solid piece, set six feet apart and distant from the Nymph, before this fountain, upon a stone pavement fitly placed.

Between the one receiver and the other was a little channel set in, in which the waters met, their edges cut in the middle of the one and the other receiver, where the waters made their meeting. Which waters, mingled then, flowed away fallen into a water-furrow, or little rill. Whereupon the one being tempered by the other, they made every greenness sprout; the hot one leaping so high that it did not hurtfully hinder the other for him who set his lips to the right breast to suck and to drink, nor at the crossing.

Now this most notable statue the craftsman expressed so exactly that I should truly doubt whether Praxiteles had carved such a Venus — for which Nicomedes, king of the Cnidians, offered (so fame flies) all the substance of his people. And so comelily beautiful did he express her that men, burning in sacrilegious longing for her, violated the image. But so far as I could rightly value it, I judged that such an image was never so perfectly feigned by chisel or graver; so that I almost reasonably suspected that in this place she had been turned to stone from the living, and so petrified.

Behold, I hear suddenly behind me a great crashing and din, like the shaking of the bony wings of the dragon; and behind me, alas, I heard a sounding of a Trumpet. At once, wretched and gasping, I turned myself about, and I see on one side many trees of Egyptian Carob, with their ripened, very long fruits hanging and shaking, which by the wind had somewhat struck one against another. Whereupon, coming swiftly to myself, and falling into laughter at a case so befallen, I moved on.

For which cause I then religiously invoked the kindly gods Jugatinus, the goddess Collatina, and Vallonia, that as I journeyed through their consecrated places they might show themselves propitious to me. Seeing that I had almost feared a warlike army because of the trumpet's sound; but, considering, I judged it to be of shepherds' trumpets of bark, whereupon I rather reassured myself than mistrusted otherwise.

But after this there was no long delay before I hear coming, singing, a company (by their voices of tender and flowering age) of damsels graceful (as I judged) and beautiful, sporting and taking their solace among the flowering herbs and in the gracious cool shades, free of any retarding suspicion, and journeying with great applause among the comely flowers. The incredible sweetness of their modulated voice, carried by the temperate and dew-bearing airs, spread itself through that delightful place, and was brought back with the sweetest sound of an accompanying lyre.

At which novelty, searching about and bending down beneath the low branches, I saw them coming towards me with a gesturing step. With their maidenly heads gathered in most notable fillets of threads of gold, wrapped and above bound and garlanded with flowering Myrtle and with manifold flowers. And over their snowy brows the yellow and trembling forelocks curled like vine-tendrils. And then down over their most white and comely shoulders flowed the long tresses, composed with nymph-like neatness and elegant art.

Clothed in a Carpathian habit of silk most adorned, and of various colouring and texture. There were three tunics, the one shorter than the other and distinct. The lowest of shellfish purple; above followed the silken one of most green colour woven through with gold. The topmost of finest cotton, saffroned and crimped, girt with a golden collar beneath the bound of their round little breasts.

Their outstretched arms were clothed by the last tunic, and copiously covered by the cotton one, which granted with the highest grace the colour beneath. And near their swelling little hands they were fitly bound with little cords of fine silk, with little golden loops, of a pleasurable artifice. And some of them had their little feet excellently laced with double soles, with manifold binding of threads of gold and of purpling silk. Some shod then over stretched hose of scarlet and greening cloth, and some over the naked, of soft and gracious shining leather, and others of chamois dyed in most beautiful colourings, without accusing the toes.

At last, having taken counsel with myself to make the venture and to risk whatever might follow — it persuading me all the while that by no conjecture could there be found in these any inhumanity or savagery, and above all that the innocent carries his protection with him — I stirred up my lukewarm spirit, still reined in by a numbing shame, knowing myself to have come unworthily into this perhaps holy place, and solacing assembly of most delicate and divine Nymphs.

And still it did not persuade me with a sincere and tranquil mind that I had entered and come there, rashly perhaps into forbidden places and a prohibited country, and with wicked daring. Turning over therefore such thoughts within myself — behold, one of these, more confident and bold, said: "Who are you, then?"

Then, all confounded between my familiar fear and sudden shame, I did not know what to say nor what to answer; and, my voice together with my spirit being forbidden me, I remained half alive, and like a statue. But those virtuous girls, perceiving that in me was a real and human shape, but terrified and fearful, all drew near, saying: "O young man, whoever you are here, our looks and presences should never make you afraid here; therefore do not doubt in the least. For here no savagery whatever is used, nor will you find displeasure in any way. Who are you, then? Speak, do not fear."

At this request, having somewhat taken back my voice, stirred by those alluring and nymph-like looks and recalled by their sweet speaking, answering I said to them: "Divine Nymphs, I am the most graceless and unhappy lover that ever could be found in the world. I love; and she whom I so ardently love and heartily desire, I know not where she or I may be. And by the greatest and most mortal peril that I could ever express, I have been led and come here."

And the piteous tears being already called to my eyes, and bowing to the earth and casting myself at their maidenly feet, sighing I cried out, beseeching pity by the most high God. At once, all shaken in their soft hearts with compassion and piteous sweetness, and moved almost likewise to little tears, dutifully and striving with one another to draw me by the arms from the ground, they raised me up; and with sweetest and most coaxing speech they said to me pleasantly:

"We think, poor little one — indeed it is so — that by the way you have entered here, wretch, few can escape. But above all things praise highly the divine power and the kindness of your star, for you have now escaped an extreme peril. But at present there is nothing more to fear that is disturbing, nor any troublesome assault; for by this way you might perhaps easily find yourself blessed. Settle yourself therefore, and be tranquil again, and comfort your mind. For here, as you plainly see, is a place of pleasure and delight, and not of grief nor of any terror. Because the age is uniform, the site secure and unchanging, time does not run, the joyful convenience, the gracious and companionable living

Questa sacra plagia excede la ubertate dilla Hyperborea insula nel Oceano Indico iacente, né cusì sono gli Lusitani. Né Talge in Caspio monte. Di continuo la quarta cum più fervore affirmando diceva. Vana è la abundantia aegyptica in comparatione dilla nostra, quantunque chiamasi Oreo publico dil mundo. Novissimamente una nel aspecto ad omni praecipitio illectiva cum elegante pronunciatione adiunse. In questa alma patria non si trovarebbe occupamento di effusissimi paludi lacessenti cum il molesto aire. Né di abrutissimi monti inclusiva, ma di ornatissime colline. Et dalla parte exclusiva munitamente circumvallata di asperi et invii praecipitii. Et cusì per questo modo eliminata omni tristitia, quivi è omni cosa che pole conferire dilecto, et confugio degli dei, cum beata sicuritate di animo. Ultra di tutte queste dicte cose, assecle siamo de una inclyta et insigne regina, munificentissima et di effusissima largitate. Chiamata Eleuterilyda, di mira clementia pientissima. La quale quivi cum summo et valido sapere governa, et cum amplissimo imperio rege, et fausta et foelice cum cumulata gloria impera. Et grato gli sarae grandemente, quando che alla sua veneranda praesentia et maiestale conspecto te conduceremo. Et si a caso l’altre nostre di lei conserve et aulice il presentiscono, quivi catervate correreberon, ad riguardare quello che di raro quivi si vide, dunque da te fuga et excludi qualunque affligente tristitia et componi l’animo tuo festivamente consolabondo cum nui, et dà opera ad solacio et a piacere, depulsa omni trepidatione.

POLIPHILO, HAVING BEEN MADE AT HOME AND MADE SAFE BY THE FIVE NYMPHS, WENT WITH THEM TO THE BATHS, WHERE THERE WAS MUCH LAUGHTER AT THE JEST OF THE FOUNTAIN, AND ALSO AT THE ANOINTING. BEING AFTERWARDS LED TO THE QUEEN

ELEUTERILYDA CONDUCTO, VIDE PER LA VIA, ET AL PALLATIO COSE EGREGIE ET UNA EXIMIA OPERA DI FONTANA.

RECEPTO AFFABILMENTE ET DALLE pietose Nymphe summamente assicurato, et tutto dalle blandivole puelle confortato, et gli infugati spiriti non mediocre recentati, al tutto che esse coniecturare valeva grato et piacersi, volentera prompto exhibendome, licentemente familiare et deditissimo me exposi. Et perché haveano alabastri diapasmatici, et vasculi smigmatici d’oro et di petre fine, et lucenti speculi, et aurei discerniculi nelle sue delicate mano, et candidi velamini di seta plicati, et balneare interule offerentime portitore, recusabonde mi disseron. Che il suo accesso ad questo loco era perché venivano al bagno. Et immediate subiunxeron. Volemo che cum nui tu vengni. Il quale costì dinanti è, ove funde una fontana, non tu quella vedesti? Io riverentemente risposi, venustissime Nymphe. Si in me mille et varie lingue si ritrovasseron, io acconciamente non saperei rendere le demerite gratie, et rengratiare tanta domestica benignitate, imperoché opportunissimamente vivificato me havete. Dunque non acceptare tale gratioso et Nymphale invitatorio, rustica viltate si reputarebe. Et per tanto cum vui più praesto me foelice aexistimeria essendo servo, che altronde dominare. Il perché quanto coniecturare posso inquiline et contubernale siate di omni dilecto et vero bene. Dovete sapere ch’io vidi la miravegliosa fontana et cum solerte senso speculata, più praeclara opera che ad gli ochii mei unque se repraesentasse confesso et affermo. Et tanto l’animo mio solerte occupai illecto circa di quella intentamente riguardantila, et ingluviamente bevendo, la grave et diurna mia sete salubremente extinguendo, che più oltra expiare non andai.

Respose una lepidula placidamente dicendo. Dami la mano. Hora si tu sospite et il bene venuto. Nui al praesente siamo cinque sociale comite come il vedi, et io me chiamo Aphea. Et questa che porta li buxuli et gli bianchissimi linteamini, è nominata Osfressia. Et quest’altra che dil splendente speculo (delitie nostre) è gerula, Orassia è il suo nome. Costei che tene la sonora lyra, è dicta Achoé. Questa ultima, che questo vaso di pretiosissimo liquore baiula, ha nome Geussia. Et andiamo compare ad queste temperate Therme, ad oblectamento et dilecto. Diqué brevemente ancora tu (poi che la propitia fortuna tua quivi è caduta) venirai cum nui

ELEUTERYLIDA, HE SAW ALONG THE WAY, AND AT THE PALACE, EXCELLENT THINGS, AND A CHOICE WORK OF A FOUNTAIN.

BEING AFFABLY RECEIVED AND HIGHLY reassured by those merciful Nymphs, and altogether comforted by those coaxing girls, and my fled spirits not a little refreshed — showing myself readily willing in everything that I could judge welcome and pleasing to them — I set myself freely familiar and most devoted.

And because they had alabaster boxes of perfumed powder, and little cleansing vessels of gold and of fine stones, and shining mirrors, and golden hair-partings in their delicate hands, and white folded veils of silk, and bathing shifts, and offered me to be their carrier, they told me, refusing, that their coming to this place was because they came to the bath. And immediately they added: "We wish you to come with us. It is there before you, where a fountain pours. Did you not see it?"

I answered reverently: "Most comely Nymphs, if a thousand and various tongues were found in me, I should not fitly know how to render the thanks I owe, and to thank so homely a kindness — for you have most opportunely brought me to life again. Therefore not to accept such a gracious and Nymph-like invitation would be reckoned rustic baseness. And for so much I should esteem myself happier being a servant with you than ruling elsewhere; because, so far as I can conjecture, you are the dwellers and companions of every delight and true good.

"You must know that I saw the marvellous fountain, and considered it with a shrewd sense; and I confess and affirm it a work more illustrious than ever presented itself to my eyes. And I so occupied my shrewd mind, allured, intently gazing upon it and drinking greedily, wholesomely quenching my heavy and day-long thirst, that I went no further to explore."

One of them answered, saying placidly: "Give me your hand. Now you are safe and welcome. We are at present five companions together, as you see; and I am called Aphea. And this one, who carries the little boxes and the whitest linens, is named Osfressia. And this other, who is the bearer of the shining mirror — our delight — Orassia is her name. This one who holds the sounding lyre is called Achoë. This last, who bears this vessel of most precious liquor, has the name Geussia. And let us go together to these temperate Baths, for pleasure and delight. Whereupon shortly you too (since your propitious fortune has fallen here) will come with us

p. 80confidence: unstatedverified

Daposcia ritornaremo tutti inseme laetificati al pallatio magno dilla insigne Regina nostra.

La quale tutta clementissima, et di larga liberalitate summamente munifica, ad gli tui intensi amori, et ardenti desiderii, et alti concepti habilissimamente suggerendo disponerai, prehendi animo et conforto. Andiamo.

Cum voluptici acti, cum virginali gesti, cum suasivi sembianti, cum caricie puellare, cum lascive riguardature, cum suave paroline illo solaciabonde blandicule me condusseron. Di omni cosa praesente contento. Si non che la Chrysocoma Polia mia, non era ad supplemento dilla suprema foelicitate, et sexta essere cum queste ad constituire il numero perfecto. Da l’altra parte discontento me trovai, che l’habito mio conforme non era infra questo delicioso consortio, ma alquanto domesticatome incominciai cum esse affabilmente tripudiare. Et elle dolcemente rideano, et io parimente cum esse, agiungessimo finalmente al loco.

Quivi mirai uno mirifico aedificio di therme octogono. Et in omni singulo angulo exteriore, erano geminate dui pili, ad libramento di l’area initiavano gli subiecti areobati circuncincti. Poscia seguivano uno tertio dilla sua crassitudine exacto dal solido le pilli. Cum capitelli subditi alla trabe recta. Cum uno phrygio di sopra, sotto una coronice integramente ambienti. El quale phrygio era deornato di eximia scalptura. Cum aliquanti puppi nudi, egregio expresso, aequalmente distanti. Cum le mano intricate di laquei retinenti fasciculi turgidi, di frondenti ramusculi inseme strophiati, concincti di lori. Sopra la quale dicta coronice, poscia saliva (cum elegante fornicato) una octogona Cumula, ad imitatione dil subiecto. La quale tra angulo ad angulo, era transpertusata di myrifica operatione per via, di mille nobili excogitati, et riturati di lamicule di puro crystallo, che da lontano plumbo iudicai.

El Pterygio adnixo era sopra uno acuminato, la forma octogonale dilla Cupula Sectario, alquanto eminente, et quivi immediate super apposito era uno Trigone, nel supremo centro del quale infixo, ascendeva uno firmatissimo stylo nel quale instobato era immisso uno altro instabile et gyrabile stylo libero ludibondo al quale appacta era una ala, che da qualunque flabile vento impulsa, seco vertiva il fistulato stylo, et una pila nella cima per il tertio dilla infernate. Sopra questa uno puello nudo cum il perna dextro calcante assideva, l’altra gamba pensile tenendo. Lo occipitio del quale fina alla bucca era tutto lacunato, in forma de infundibulo, cum lo orificio terebrato fina alla bucca, alla quale ferruminata, adiuncta era una tuba, tenuta cum una mano dal puello proxima alla ferruminatione, et l’altra porrecta verso lo extremo dilla tuba, a linea libellata dilla ala. Ogni

Afterwards we shall all return together, made glad, to the great palace of our distinguished Queen. Who, most clement in all things and most munificent of a wide liberality, will most ably suggest and dispose your intense loves and burning desires and lofty conceits. Take heart and comfort. Let us go."

With pleasurable acts, with maidenly gestures, with persuasive semblances, with girlish caresses, with wanton glances, with sweet little words, they led me there, solacing and coaxing. Content with everything present — save that my golden-haired Polia was not there for the fulfilment of the highest happiness, and to be a sixth with these and make up the perfect number.

On the other hand I found myself discontented, that my habit was not conformable amid this delicious company; but having made myself somewhat at home, I began affably to dance with them. And they laughed sweetly, and I likewise with them; and at last we came to the place.

There I beheld a wonderful eight-sided building of baths. And at every single outer angle two piers were paired; level with the floor began the base-courses girt about beneath them. Then the piers followed, a third of their thickness drawn from the solid, with capitals set beneath the straight beam; with a frieze above, going entirely round beneath a cornice. Which frieze was adorned with choice carving: with several naked boys, excellently expressed, equally distant, with their hands entangled in nooses holding swelling little bundles of leafy twigs bound together, girt with thongs.

Above the said cornice there then rose (with an elegant vaulting) an eight-sided little Dome, in imitation of what was beneath. Which, from angle to angle, was pierced through with a marvellous working by way of a thousand noble conceits, and stopped with little plates of pure crystal, which from afar I judged to be lead.

The little wing was fixed above a pointed thing, the eight-sided form of the Dome being sectioned, somewhat eminent; and there, immediately set above, was a Triangle, in whose topmost centre, fixed, there rose a most firm shaft, into which was let another shaft, unstable and turning, free and playing; to which was fitted a vane, which, driven by whatever wind blew, turned the tubed shaft with it, and a ball at the top of a third of the one below.

Upon this a naked boy sat, treading with his right heel, holding the other leg hanging. The back of whose head, as far as the mouth, was all hollowed in the form of a funnel, with the orifice bored through to the mouth; to which, soldered, was joined a trumpet, held with one hand by the boy near the soldering, and the other stretched towards the end of the trumpet, levelled in a line with the vane. Every

cosa enea tenuissima conflata perfectamente, et fulgentissimamente deaurata. La quale Ala, et la Pila, et el Puello, cum il figmento o vulto in acto di sonare, cum il vacuato occipitio, verso el flato ventale, facilmente violentava, ove intro spirabile la tuba, tubava.
