Per la quale cosa cogitai ridendo, che a homo in loco incognito solo ritrovantise et expaventato, che facilmente per omni strepitulo se terricula.

Modo nella facia di ricontro alla bellissima Nympha in fonte, vidi l’introito. Cum una porta expolitissima. Tutto artificio dil praestante Lithoglypho, che la Nympha dormiente havea caelato pensai, nel phrisio dila quale vidi tale titulo in caractere graeco, ASAMINTHOS Dunque tale therme non suppedita l’amplitudine di Tacio.

Dentro circundavano sedili in quatro gradi lapidei cum perpetuo coniugio concincti, tutti minutamente di diaspro segmentati et Calcedonii di omni coloratione. Dui degli gradi la tepida aqua copriva, fina allo margine, overo superficie dil tertio. Negli angoli per ciascuno extava una expedita et ritondata columnella Corinthia, di vario coloramento. Cum varicose undule di diaspro tanto più grato, quanto più fare suole la artificiosa natura. Cum decente base. Et gli capitelli optimamente compositi sotto d’uno trabe, oltra il quale iaceva il Zophoro di nudi pueruli nelle aque ludenti, cum aquatici monstruli, cum palaestra et contrasti infantili, cum apti conati di promptitudine alla aetate conveniente, et vivace moventie et ioci, circuncingeva bellissime cum una corona superapposita. Di sopra l’ordine et proiectura dille columnelle ad perpendiculo tendeva da ciascuna in la summitate dilla cupula, uno

thing of thinnest bronze cast perfectly, and most brightly gilded. Which Vane, and the Ball, and the Boy — with the figure or face in the act of sounding, with the hollowed back of the head towards the blowing of the wind — easily forced it; where, the air being breathable within, the trumpet trumpeted.

And therefore, the Egyptian carobs being shaken by the wind, likewise there too the wind made the trumpet sound. For which cause I thought, laughing, that a man finding himself alone in an unknown place and frightened is easily terrified by every little noise.

Now, in the face opposite the most beautiful Nymph of the fountain, I saw the entrance, with a most polished door. All the artifice of that excellent Stone-carver who, I thought, had carved the sleeping Nymph; in the frieze of which I saw this title in Greek characters: ASAMINTHOS. Such baths, then, the amplitude of Tatius does not surpass.

Within, seats went round in four stone steps, girt with a continuous joining, all minutely inlaid with jasper and Chalcedonies of every colouring. Two of the steps the tepid water covered, up to the margin, or surface, of the third. In the angles there stood at each a free and rounded little Corinthian column, of various colouring, with straggling waves of jasper — the more welcome, the more the artful nature is wont to make it — with a decent base. And the capitals most excellently composed beneath a beam; beyond which lay the Zophorus of naked little boys playing in the waters, with little water-monsters, with wrestling and infant contests, with apt strivings of a readiness fitting to their age, and lively movements and games; and it girt it round most beautifully with a crown set above.

Above the order and projection of the little columns there tended perpendicularly from each, to the summit of the dome, a

toro cum moderata tuberatione di fronde quercinee, una sopra l’altra paginatamente compresse fimbriate et sinuate di verdissimo diaspro, et di deaurate faseole circumramentate, le quale ascendendo derivavano nel convexo coelo dilla cupula ad una rotundatione copulantise, intro la quale una testa occupava de leone cum arriciate iube. Teniva mordico nelle fauce uno annulo. Al quale erano commendati gli laquei di auricalcho pendenti et egregiamente innexi. Li quali retinivano uno politissimo vaso, cum lata apertura et poco lacunato dilla dicta materia lucentissima. Alto da l’aqua dui cubiti suspenso. El residuo del convexo internate, dalle obturatione del crystallo exempto, era tutto di coloratione Cyanea de Litharmeno contecto, disseminatamente glandulato di bulle inaurate eximie prenitente.

Non molto distante era nella terra una fissura, la quale continuamente vomeva ignita materia, tolta di questa et farcita la concha dil vaso superposeno alcuni gummi et ligni odorati feceron uno inextimabile suffumigio di fragrantia quale di optimi passalli. Poscia conclause le gemine valve terebrate di metallo, et di crystallo lucidissimo impedite rendevano periocundo et multiphariam colorato lume. Per questa medesima terebratione di pervii nodamenti, chiaramente illuminavano le odorante therme, et interdicto rimania la fragrantia et il calore fora non exalava.

Il pariete aequato interposito poscia tra l’una et l’altra columna monstrava petra nigerrima di durecia respuente il metallo et illustre. Inclaustrata di una ambiente fascia di latitudine quadrante, di diaspro coraliceo, ornata de liniamento di duplici gurguli, o veramente verticuli. Nel mediano di questo tale pariete, tra una et l’altra columna, pausando assideva una elegante Nympha nuda cum distincto pausare et officio, di petra Gallatite di nitore eburneo. Sopra locate fermamente alle conveniente arule. Le quale di liniamento rotonde compositamente colligavano in circinao cum le base dille columne. O quanto exquisitamente sculpte mirava le dicte imagine, che più delle fiate, gli ochii mei dalle vere et reale deviare concedeva et riportarli ad le fincte.

La pavitata areola sotto l’aqua di varia emblematura di petre dure tessellate, in meravegliosi graphidi per diversi coloramenti vedevasi. Perché la limpidissima aqua non sulphurea, ma odorosa et temperatamente calida sencia Hypocausto et praefurnio, et purgatissima oltra omni credito, non era medio impediente tra lo obiecto et il senso visivo. Imperoché gli varii pisciculi negli fronti degli sedili et dil fondo, artificiosamente di museaco scobamente expressi ad aemulatione dilla natura, vivi natanti appariano. Trigle, overo mulli, mustelle, o vero lampetre et multiplici altri, non considerata la

torus with a moderate swelling of oaken fronds, one pressed above another page-wise, fringed and curved, of greenest jasper, and branched about with gilded little beans; which, ascending, ran into the vaulted heaven of the dome, coupling themselves into a rounding, within which a lion's head took its place, with curled mane. It held biting in its jaws a ring, to which were commended hanging chains of brass, excellently knotted, which held up a most polished vessel with a wide opening and little hollowed, of the said most shining material, hung two cubits above the water.

The rest of the inner vault, apart from the stoppings of crystal, was all covered with a Cyanean colouring of litharge, scattered and studded with gilded bosses, choicely shining.

Not far off there was in the earth a fissure, which continually vomited fiery matter; and taking of this and stuffing the hollow of the vessel above, they laid on certain gums and scented woods, and made an inestimable fumigation of a fragrance like the best perfumes. Then the twin leaves being closed, pierced with metal and stopped with most limpid crystal, they gave a most joyful and manifoldly coloured light. By this same piercing of open knots they clearly lit the fragrant baths, and the fragrance was kept in, and the heat did not breathe out.

The levelled wall set between the one column and the other then showed a most black stone, of a hardness rejecting metal, and shining. Enclosed by a surrounding band a quarter broad, of coral-like jasper, adorned with a lineament of double gorges, or whorls. In the middle of such a wall, between the one column and the other, resting there sat an elegant naked Nymph, with distinct resting and office, of Gallatite stone of ivory brightness; firmly placed above upon fitting little altars, which, of round lineament, composedly bound themselves in a circle with the bases of the columns. O how exquisitely carved I beheld the said images, so that more than once my eyes allowed themselves to stray from the true and real ones and to carry themselves to the feigned.

The paved little floor beneath the water was seen of various inlay of hard stones tessellated, in marvellous drawings of divers colourings. Because the most limpid water — not sulphurous, but sweet-smelling and temperately warm, without furnace or stoke-hole, and purged beyond all belief — was no hindering medium between the object and the sense of sight. For the various little fishes, on the fronts of the seats and of the floor, artificially expressed in mosaic in emulation of nature, appeared to swim alive. Red mullets, or mullets; lampreys, and manifold others — the

natura, ma la venustate dilla pictura. Le petre nigerrime dil pariete erano intercise, et diligentemente rimesse una spectatissima compositione di illaqueatione, overo ligature di antiquarie foglie, et di fiori, di lucente Conchule Cytheriace, tanto ad gli ochii acceptissimo, quanto mai explanare valesse. Sopra la porta interstitio di petra Gallactite, vidi uno delphino repando tra le placide unde, et uno adolescente sopra sedeva et cum una lyra sonante. All’incontro sopra il geloeasto fonte simelmente un altro delphino natante cum Posidonio sopra aequitante, et cum la sua fusina acuminata. Queste historiette exacte erano da li contermini del medesimo saxo, et riportate in nigerrimo plano. Quivi meritamente laudai il praeclaro architecto, et non meno il statuario. Da l’altra parte extolleva la venusta dignitate dille formose et piacevole fanciulle. Imperoché io non sapea comparare tra il spavento praeterito, et tra questo inexcogitato et casuale solacio il suo excesso, ma senza dubio me ritrovai in extremo dilecto et piacere. Et quivi iocundissimamente intrati in tanta redolentia quale mai in Arabia potrebbese germinare. Sopra li lapidei sedili in loco di Apodytorio expoliantise, li sericii vestimenti exponevano, invilupate bellissime le bionde trece sotto le reticulate Vette di fili d’oro tesute, et innextrulate dignissime. Et senza rispecto alcuno la formosa et delicata persona tutta nudata liberamente videre, et peculiarmente cernere concedevano, la honestate riservata, carne senza fallo delicate rosee et di matura neve perfuse. Heu me il core agitato io el sentiva resultante aprirsene et di voluptica laetitia tuto occuparsi. Di che foelice alhora me existimai, solamente tante delicie speculando. Perché pertinacissimamente non poteva obstare ad gli ardentissimi incendii noxiamente insultanti nel infornaceo core molestantime. Et per questo alcuna fiata per mio megliore suffugio mirare non audeva tanto le incentrice bellecie cumulatissime in quegli divi corpusculi. Et esse animadvertendo rideano degli mei simpliculi gesti prehendendo puellare spasso. Et io per questo stava cum l’animo sincero et contento, per essergli im piacere et gratia. Et residendo in medio di tanto ardore, non mediocre patientia sustineva. Ma però cum tolerantia pudibondo et sufferente me stava, conoscendomi impare de sì bello et tale consortio. Et io ancora invitato, quantunque reluctando excusatome havendo, niente di manco intrai nel bagnio. Quale cornice tra candide columbine, per tale cagione io stava da parte erubescente, cum gli ochii inconstanti de cusì praestanti obiecti illecti scrutaticii. Et quivi Osfressia molto faceta facondula mi disse. Dimi giovane che nome è il tuo? Et io riverentemente li risposi. Poliphilo Hera. Piacemi assai mi disse si l’effecto al nome corresponde. Et senza inducie subiunse. Et come chiamase la tua chara amorosa? Io morigeratamente resposi Polia. Et ella dixe. Ohe io arbitrava che il tuo nome indicasse molto amante, ma quello che al praesente io sento, vole dire, Amico di Polia. E subito dixe. Si quivi sa

nature not considered, but the comeliness of the painting.

The most black stones of the wall were cut through and diligently set again with a most notable composition of interlacing, or bindings, of antique leaves and flowers, of shining Cytherean little Shells, as most acceptable to the eyes as ever one could set forth.

Above the door, in a space of Gallactite stone, I saw a dolphin bending among the calm waves, and a youth sitting upon it and sounding a lyre. Opposite, above the laughter-making fountain, likewise another dolphin swimming, with Poseidon riding upon it and with his pointed trident. These little histories were made exactly from the bounds of the same stone, and carried upon a most black flat. Here I deservedly praised that illustrious architect, and no less the statuary.

On the other hand, the comely dignity of those shapely and pleasing girls exalted itself. For I did not know how to compare, between the terror now past and this unthought-of and chance solace, the excess of it; but without doubt I found myself in extreme delight and pleasure.

And there, having most joyfully entered into such a fragrance as could never sprout in Arabia, they stripped upon the stone seats in place of a dressing-room, and laid aside their silken garments, their blond tresses most beautifully wrapped beneath netted Fillets woven of threads of gold, and most worthily bound. And without any regard they allowed their shapely and delicate persons, all naked, to be seen freely and particularly discerned — honesty reserved — flesh without fail delicate, rosy, and suffused with ripe snow.

Alas, I felt my stirred heart leaping to open itself and to be wholly taken up with a pleasurable gladness; whereupon I esteemed myself happy then, only in beholding such delights. Because most pertinaciously I could not withstand the most burning fires hurtfully assaulting and troubling me in my furnace-like heart. And for this, sometimes for my better refuge, I did not dare to look so much at those enkindling beauties heaped up in those divine little bodies.

And they, perceiving it, laughed at my simple gestures, taking girlish sport. And I for this stood with a sincere and contented mind, at being pleasing and welcome to them. And sitting in the midst of such burning, I bore no ordinary patience. But yet with tolerance I stood, bashful and forbearing, knowing myself unequal to so fair and such a company. And being invited also, although struggling and having excused myself, none the less I entered into the bath — like a crow among white doves; for which cause I stood apart, blushing, with my eyes unsteady, searchingly allured by objects so excellent.

And there Osfressia, very witty and eloquent, said to me: "Tell me, young man, what is your name?" And I answered her reverently: "Poliphilo, Lady." "It pleases me well," she said, "if the effect answers to the name." And without delay she added: "And what is your dear beloved called?" I answered modestly: "Polia." And she said: "Ah, I judged that your name signified 'much loving'; but what I now hear means 'the friend of Polia'." And at once she said: "If here

ritrovasse praesente, che ne faresti? Quello hera mia resposi che alla sua pudicitia si convene, et ad vostre dive praesentie digno fusse. Dimi Poliphilo gli porti tu grande amore? Sopra la vita mia Heumè suspirando dissi. Oltra tutte le delicie et sopra tutte le divitie di qualunque thesoro dil mondo pretiosissimo, io porto quello nello incandente et cremato core servabile transfixo. Et ella. Dove l’ai tu (tanto cosa dilecta) abandonata? Io non intendo, et dove io ancora me sia non so. Disse surridendo, et si alcuno ti la trovasse che indicina gli daresti? Ma sta cum laeto animo et dà opera a piacere, che la tua dilecta Polia la ritroverai. Et cum queste gratissime et simigliante parolette, le placidissime et lepidule puelle, cum molti solatii se lavorno et io. Ad opposito interstitio dilla conspicua fontana di fora dilla dormiente Nympha intro il bagno era un’altra di statue di optimo metallo artificiosamente facta, cum nitore aureo speculabile. Le quale erano infixe sopra uno marmoro in quadratura excavato, et in frontespicio reducto, cum due semicolumnule cioè emicycle. Una per lato, cum il trabetto, zophorulo, et coronicetta, nel solido della unica petra inscalpte. Questo composito praeclaro offerivase quale di tutta l’opera el risiduo tutto, cum eximia arte et invento myrificamente absoluta. Nel cavo intersectio, overo nel intervacuato della dicta petra due perfecte Nymphe astavano, poco che ’l naturale meno grande, fino sopra le crure devestite, ove cedeva la divisione de la superinduta interula, alquanto volante per el moto del suo officio. Et gli brachii similmente nudati, dal cubito ad le spalle excepto. Et sopra el bracio che el puerulo susteniva, era lo habito sublevato reiecto. Li pediculi del quale infantulo. Uno in la mano dela una, et l’altro de l’altra mano de la Nympha calcavano de tutti tre li vulti ridibondi et cum l’altra mano le Nymphe dimovando le lacinule del puellulo fina al suo cingiere overo umbilico discoprivano. Et el fanciullo cum tutte due le mano el membrulo suo teniva. Il quale dentro alle calde aque mingeva (tepidantile) aqua freschissima. In questo delitioso et excellentissimo loco io era per tale conditione tuto soluto in gaudio et contento, ma interrotto el praecipuo piacere degli sentimenti, solamente perché tra esse contentibile et tra tanta albescentia, et rore concreto in pruina, quasi aegyptino et melancochro me vedeva. Una de queste dunque nominata Achoé, affabilmente mi disse surridendo. Poliphile nostro, togli quello vaso de crystallo, et portami quivi poco di quella aqua recente. Sencia morula affectando, et senza altro pensiculare, si non che gratificandome, et non solum promptamente obsequioso exhibendome, ma etiam lixabondo per compiacerli, praesto io andai. Né più praesto uno pede posui sopra uno grado per farme all’aqua cadente, che il mengore levoe il priapulo, et nella calda facia trassemi l’aqua frigidissima, che quasi in quello instanti me congenulai indrieto. Per la quale cosa tanto riso acuto et foeminile sotto la obtusa cupula risonava, che ancora io incominciai (in me ritornato) fortemente di ridere che me sentiva morire. Daposcia io conobbi la deceptione dil artificio peritissimamente

your Polia were found present, what would you do?" "That," I answered, "which befits her modesty, and which should be worthy of your divine presences." "Tell me, Poliphilo, do you bear her a great love?" "Above my own life," I said, sighing. "Beyond all delights and above all the riches of whatever treasure most precious in the world, I bear that love pierced through and kept in my burning and consumed heart." And she: "Where have you abandoned so beloved a thing?" "I do not understand it, and where I myself now am I do not know." She said, smiling: "And if someone were to find her for you, what finder's fee would you give? But be of glad heart, and give yourself to pleasure, for you shall find your beloved Polia again." And with these most welcome and like little words, the most placid and charming girls bathed themselves with much solace, and I with them.

At the space opposite the notable fountain of the sleeping Nymph outside, within the bath there was another of statues, artfully made of the best metal, with a golden and mirroring brightness. These were fixed above a marble hollowed in a square and drawn forward into a frontispiece, with two little half-columns — that is, in a half-circle, one to each side — with the little beam, the little frieze and the little cornice carved in the solid of the single stone. This excellent composition offered itself as the residue of the whole work, wonderfully accomplished with choice art and invention.

In the cut hollow, or in the emptied space of the said stone, two perfect Nymphs stood, a little less than the natural size, unclothed as far as their thighs, where the parting of the shift they wore over gave way, somewhat flying with the movement of their office; and their arms likewise bared, save from the elbow to the shoulders. And above the arm that held up the little boy the garment was raised and thrown back. The little feet of which infant — the one in the hand of the one Nymph, the other in the other's hand — they pressed; the faces of all three laughing. And with the other hand the Nymphs, moving aside the little boy's fringes as far as his girdle or navel, uncovered him. And the child held his little member with both his hands. Which, within the warm waters, made water of the freshest, cooling them.

In this delicious and most excellent place I was, by such conditions, wholly dissolved in gladness and content; but the chief pleasure of my senses was interrupted, only because among these contented ones, and among such whiteness and dew condensed into hoar-frost, I saw myself as it were Egyptian and of a swarthy hue.

One of these, then, named Achoe, affably said to me, smiling: "Our Poliphilo, take that vessel of crystal and bring me here a little of that fresh water." Without delay and without further weighing of it — save that I was gratifying her, and showing myself not only promptly obedient but even eager to please her — I went at once. And no sooner had I set one foot upon a step to get to the falling water than the little water-maker lifted his spout and drew across my hot face the coldest water, so that almost in that instant I fell back upon my knees. At which so shrill and womanish a laughter rang beneath the blunt dome that I too began (having come to myself) to laugh so hard that I felt myself dying of it.

Afterwards I understood the deception of the artifice, most skilfully

p. 85confidence: unstatedverified

excogitato, che ponendo sopra el grado imo instabile, pondo alcuno, in giù el se moveva, et in su traheva lo instrumento puerile. Onde cum subtile examine investigato la machina et curioso artificio, mi fue molto gratissimo. Et però nel Zophorulo era inscripto elegante di Atthice formule questo titulo. GELOIASTOS. Doppo molto iocoso riso balneati, et lavatone tutti, cum mille et dolce amorose et piacevole parolette, et virginali scherci et blandimenti. Fora delle thermate aque uscissimo, saliendo sopra li assucti gradi cum grande tripudio et festa ove se unxeno cum gli fragranti odoramenti diaspasmatici, et cum myristico liquore oblite, ad me ancora offeriteno una bussula et unxime. Di che assai

devised: that setting any weight upon the lowest and unstable step, it moved downward, and drew upward the childish instrument. Whereupon, the machine and its curious artifice being investigated with careful examination, it pleased me greatly. And therefore in the little frieze this title was elegantly inscribed in Attic characters: GELOIASTOS.

After much merry laughter, having bathed and all of us washed, with a thousand sweet, loving and pleasant little words, and maidenly jests and caresses, we went out of the heated waters, climbing up upon the dry steps with great dancing and festivity; where they anointed themselves with fragrant perfumed unguents and were smeared with an ointment of nutmeg, and offered me too a little box, and anointed me. Of which

p. 86confidence: unstatedverified

opportuno mi fue questa tale lenitiva unctione et salubre lotura. Perché oltra la mirabile suavitate, praecipuamente proficuo alle prosternate membre se praestoe nella mia praeterita et tanto periculosa fuga. Daposcia tutti induti, et elle alquanto di longiuscula mora nella Nymphale politura, strisso, et ornamento detente, cum grande feste alacre, domesticamente aperseron gli vasi de gli delicatissimi confecti, consolabonde gustorono et io, sequendo poi il pretioso poto. Dunque sufficientemente refecte, et reiterabonde ad gli speculi cum scrupuloso examine del decoramento delle dive praesentie, et della luculente fronte ombrata di globuli, degli flavi crinuli antependuli. Et cum limpico tegmine gli madidi crini obvoluti, finalmente laetabonde mi disseron. Poliphile hora alla nostra inclyta et sublime Regina Eleuterilida cum laeto animo andiamo, ove maiore oblectamento sentirai, ridibonde suggiungendo. Heus l’aqua pure te percosse nel viso. Et rinovavano il dolce riso, sencia alcuna misura, alacremente di me solaciantise, l’una cum l’altra innuentise cum lascivo nictare di ochii, et cum Hirqueo intuito, overo transverso. Et d’indi facendo gratioso discesso in medio delle festevole fanciulle andando, dolcemente incominciorono di cantilare in phrygio tono rithmiticamente, una faceta metamorphosi. Conciosia cosa che volendose uno inamorato cum unctione in avicula tramutarse, il bussolo fallite, et transformosi in rude asino. Concludendo che alcuni credono essere le uncture ad uno effecto, et daposcia è ad uno altro. Per questo io suspicai quasi che in me si risolvesse il motivo, per gli sembianti sui verso me ridiculosi convertiti, ma io diciò alhora non feci altro pensiero. Arbitrando dunque accortamente che quella unguentatione a solevamento degli membri fessi stata mi fusse. Ecco che io repente incomincio tanto in lasciva prurigine et in stimulosa libidine incitarme, che tutto me rivolvea torquentime. Et quelle versute licentemente rideano, sapendo il mio tale accidente. In tanto vegetavase, che io me sentiva in grande irritamento ognhora più extimulare. Onde io non so quale morso, overo pastomo me cohibisceron, che in esse quale rabida et affamata aquila tra una turma di perdice rapace et perpete sé dil aire praecipita, non invadesse raptore. Così né più, né manco era fortemente istimulato alla violentia. Et tanto incitamento omni hora incrementare sentendo, salace et pruriente me cruciava. Et tanto più oltra mensura di venerea libidine prono flagrava, quanto che sì opportuni et accommodati obiecti violentissimi se offerivano, incremento di una quasi perniciosissima peste et di inexperta urigine percito. Una dunque di queste flammigere Nymphe di nome Aphea ludibonda mi disse. Poliphile che hai tu? Ad hora laeto scherciavi, et hora io te vedo alterato et mutitato. Io li dissi. Perdonatime che me contorqueo più che

such a soothing anointing and wholesome washing was very timely for me. Because, beyond its marvellous sweetness, it proved chiefly profitable to my limbs, laid low in my past and so perilous a flight.

Afterwards, all being clothed — and they detained a good while longer in their nymphlike trimming, combing and adorning — with great cheerful festivity they familiarly opened the vessels of the most delicate confections, and comfortably tasted them, and I with them, the precious drink following after. Then, sufficiently refreshed, and turning again to the mirrors with a scrupulous examination of the adornment of their divine presences, and of the bright forehead shadowed with the little globes of their hanging golden curls — and their damp hair wrapped in a clear covering — at last they said to me joyfully:

"Poliphilo, let us go now with glad heart to our renowned and lofty Queen Eleuterylida, where you shall feel a greater delight." And laughing they added: "Ha! the water did indeed strike you in the face." And they renewed their sweet laughter without any measure, cheerfully making sport of me, nodding to one another with a wanton blinking of the eyes and a sidelong, goatish look.

And thence, making a graceful departure and going in the midst of the festive girls, they began sweetly to sing, rhythmically in the Phrygian mode, a droll metamorphosis. Namely, how a lover, wishing to change himself by an ointment into a little bird, mistook the box, and was transformed into a rough ass; concluding that some believe unguents to be for one effect, and afterwards they are for another. By this I suspected that the point of it was aimed at me, from their looks turned mockingly towards me; but at the time I thought nothing further of it.

Judging then, shrewdly, that that anointing had been for the relief of my weary limbs — behold, of a sudden I began to be so stirred by a wanton itching and a goading desire, that I turned and twisted wholly about. And those cunning ones laughed freely, knowing what had befallen me. So much did it quicken that I felt myself every hour more sharply pricked. Whence I know not what bit, or what halter, restrained me from falling upon them like a ravening and famished eagle that hurls itself out of the air, rapacious and constant, upon a flock of partridges. Neither more nor less was I strongly goaded to violence. And feeling so great an incitement grow every hour, it tormented me; and the more I burned, bent beyond measure with desire, the more such fit and convenient objects offered themselves most violently, stirred as I was by the increase of an almost deadly plague and of an unknown heat.

One, then, of these flaming Nymphs, Aphea by name, said to me in sport: "Poliphilo, what ails you? A moment since you were jesting merrily, and now I see you altered and changed." I said to her: "Forgive me, for I writhe more than

p. 87confidence: unstatedverified

una salicea strophia, io me perdo (date venia) di ardore lascivo, ad questo commoventise tutte in effrenato riso. Ad me disseron. Ohe, et se la tua peroptata Polia quivi ella fusse, che ne faresti tu hen? Heu me diss’io. Per quella divinitate a cui succumbendo servite, ve supplico, non agiungete face et non accumulate teda et resina al mio incredibile incendio, non picate più il mio arsibile core, non me fate ischiantare ve prego. Imperoché non mediocremente me perdo et totalmente me strugo. Ad questo mio lamentabile et moerente risponsorio, incontinente cum le coralicee buccule piene di ridenti clamori fortemente excitate, deveneron ad tanto excesso, che esse, né io, valevemo hogi mai per multiplicabile riso caminare. Ma sopra gli odoriferi fiori et sopra il solo herbido corruendose et involventise, da insolente riso se suffocavano, onde opportuno fue il suo stricto succintulo transverso, alquanto ralentare, et laxare, et per questo modo semianime iacendo sotto per le umbrigere et foliose arbore, et per la patula opacitate degli rami pausavansi. Quivi dunque cum domesticata fiducia gli dissi. O foemine ignibonde et di me malefice, cusì mi fate vui? Ecco che modo licita occasione di irrumpere et opprimere, et di vui fare violentia excusabile mi se praesta. Et verso quelle nuto facendo di volerle prehendere, fingendo audaculo di fare quello che per niuno modo audeva, ma cum più novo riso, invocando l’una da l’altra adiuto, relicti et indi et quindi gli aurei soccoli et velamini fugendo, asportate dalle fresche aure le tenie. Et tra gli fiori neglecti gli vasculi currevano. Et io drieto correndo. Tanto che veramente non so che non spasemasseron, et io aequalmente, prosternate le virtute, et tutto in proluvio de libidine ruente per nimietate del nervico rigore impatiente. Dunque alquanto havendo durato questa solatiosa ludificatione, et questo ludibrioso spasso, et pienamente satisfacto del mio cusì facto agitamento. Recollecti gli soccoli et l’altre cose sparse. Appresso gli verdegianti et madenti rivi d’uno corrente fluviolo, temperato il suave riso, di me tenerrime miserate quivi ad gli ornati rivi di humili et flexuli iunci, et saliuncula, et cum natante Vitrice, et avicino copiosi di vivaci et aquabuli simplici, una di queste morigera Geusia chiamata inclinatose, extirpoe la Heraclea Nymphea, et una radice di Aron, et Amella, le quale in poca distantia l’una da l’altra germinavano mi offerite ridendo, quale ad me di queste piacesse eligere devesse, et ad mia liberatione gustarle. Per la quale cosa io ricusai la Nymphea. Damnai il Draconculo per il suo caustico, acceptai Amella. Et questa mundificata suaseme di gustare. Onde non fue longo intervallo di tempo, che migrante il venereo lubrico et incentivo stimolo, la intemperantia libidinosa se extinse. Dunque per questo modo le illecebre carnale obfrenato,

a withy band; I am undone — give me pardon — with a wanton ardour." At this they were all moved to unbridled laughter, and said to me: "Ho! and if your longed-for Polia were here, what would you do then?" "Alas," said I, "by that divinity to whom you submit and serve, I beseech you, add no more torches, heap no more brands and resin upon my incredible burning, prick no further my kindled heart, do not make me burst asunder, I pray you. For I am undone in no ordinary measure, and am utterly consumed."

At this lamentable and mournful response of mine, straightway, their coral-red little mouths full of laughing clamours strongly stirred, they came to such an excess that neither they nor I were able any longer to walk for multiplying laughter. But falling down and rolling among the fragrant flowers and upon the grassy ground, they were choked with unruly laughter; whence it was needful to slacken and loosen a little the tight girdle across them. And lying thus half dead beneath the shady and leafy trees, and in the spreading shade of the branches, they rested.

There, then, with a familiar boldness, I said to them: "O women full of fire, and mischievous to me, is it thus you use me? See how a lawful occasion is offered me of breaking in and overwhelming you and of doing you an excusable violence." And nodding towards them as though I would seize them, feigning a boldness in doing what by no means I dared — they with fresh laughter called one another to help, and fled, leaving their golden slippers and veils here and there, their fillets carried off by the cool breezes; and their little vessels ran among the neglected flowers. And I running after. So much so that truly I do not know that they did not swoon with it, and I as well, my powers laid low.

When, then, this comfortable make-game and this mocking sport had lasted a while, and my agitation thus raised was fully satisfied, and the slippers and the other scattered things gathered up — near the green and dewy banks of a running little stream, the sweet laughter being tempered and they most tenderly pitying me, there by the trimmed banks of low and bending rushes and little willow, with the osier swimming, and nearby plentiful in living water-simples, one of these, a well-mannered one called Geusia, bending down, plucked up the Herculean water-lily, and a root of Arum, and Amella, which were sprouting a little apart one from another; and laughing offered them to me, that I should choose which of these pleased me and taste it for my deliverance. For which cause I refused the water-lily; I condemned the little dragon-plant for its burning; I accepted the Amella. And this, being cleaned, she persuaded me to taste. Whereupon it was no long space of time before, the slippery goad departing, the intemperance was extinguished. Thus in this manner the carnal enticements being bridled,

p. 88confidence: unstatedverified

solaciantise le festigiante damigelle, faconde et facete, pervenissimo sencia avedersene in uno celebre loco, summamente amoeno. Quivi cum decente ordine et distantia era una percupressata via de driti et excelsi cupressi, cum gli sui angulosi et rimati Coni, densi di frondatura quanto essere per sua natura poteano, et compositamente collocati. Et il coaequato solo per omni parte di verdissima vincapervinca contecto, abondante degli sui flosculi azurini. La quale ornata via di debito laxamento lata, ad una verdegiante clausura directamente tendeva, et alla apertione di quella, ad libella gli cupressi distributi, di longitudine di stadii quatro. Al quale claustro pervenuti laetamente, trovai quello aequilatero, di tre alamenti, alla simigliancia di drito muro, alto quanto gli sublimi Cupressi della via. Il quale era tutto di spectatissimi Citri, di Naranci, et di Limoni, cum gratissima foliatura compressamente congesti, et cum artificiosa cohaesione innexi, et di pedi sei iudicai la sua crassitudine. Cum una porta nel mediano inflexa del proprio arborario, cum diligente industria del artifice compositamente conducto, quanto meglio dire si potrebbe né fare. Di sopra al conveniente loco, erano ordinate fenestre. Diqué nella superficie ligno overo stipite alcuno se pandeva, ma solamente delle florulente fronde la periucunda et grata virdura. Tra le belle, folte, et vivace foglie era del candido fiore cumulatissimamente ornato, odore naranceo spirante suavissimo et ad gli desiderosi ochii, maturi fructi et imperfecti summamente delectabili copiosi se offerivano. Poscia nella interstitia crassitudine, mirai gli rami (non sencia miraveglia) per tale magisterio Compacti, che per quegli commodamente se saliva per tutta la capace compositione. Onde per la fultura degli nexi rami gli salienti non apparevano. Intrando dunque nui in questa verdosa et quam gratissima clausura ad gli ochii summamente spectabile, et ad lo intellecto dignia di aestimatione, vidi che l’era uno elegante claustro in fronte ad uno mirando pallatio et amplissimo, et di symmetriata architectura eximio et molto magnifico. Il quale della frondifera conclusione rendeva il quarto alamento, di longitudine passi sexanta. Et era questo ambito uno Hypaethrio quadrato subdiale. Nella parte mediana di questa spectatissima area, vidi uno eximio fonte di limpidissime aque, scaturiente in alto fina alla sublimitate quasi della viridante clausura per angustissime fistulette, et giù in una larga concha cadevano, la quale era di finissimo amethysto il cui diametro tre passi continiva, di crassitudine quadrante verso gli labri in uncia demigrante, di excellentissima fusura, circuncirca apparendo di anaglypho dignissimi expressi di monstri aquatuli. Di quanti mai gli antiquarii inventori in

the festive damsels solacing me, eloquent and witty, we came without noticing it into a famous place, exceedingly pleasant.

Here, in fitting order and distance, was a way set with cypresses, straight and lofty, with their angled and cracked cones, as thick with foliage as by their nature they could be, and composedly placed. And the levelled ground covered on every side with the greenest periwinkle, abounding in its little azure flowers. Which adorned way, broad with a due spaciousness, tended straight towards a green enclosure; and to the opening of that the cypresses were distributed by the line, for a length of four stadia.

Coming joyfully to that cloister, I found it equal-sided, of three walls, in the likeness of a straight wall, as high as the lofty cypresses of the way. Which was all of choice citrons, oranges and lemons, thickly heaped together with a most welcome foliage and knit with an artful cohesion; and I judged its thickness to be six feet. With a door bent in the middle out of the tree-work itself, composedly carried through with the diligent industry of the maker, as well as one could say or make it. Above, in a fitting place, windows were set in order. So that on the surface no wood or stem whatever showed itself, but only the pleasant and welcome green of the flowering fronds.

Among the fair, thick and living leaves it was most abundantly adorned with white blossom, breathing a sweet orange scent; and to the desirous eyes ripe fruits and unripe offered themselves plentifully, in the highest degree delectable. Then within the thickness I looked at the branches (not without wonder), so compacted by such mastery that by them one climbed easily through the whole capacious composition. Whence, by the propping of the knitted branches, those who climbed did not appear.

Entering, then, into this green and most welcome enclosure — to the eyes exceedingly worth looking at, and to the understanding worthy of esteem — I saw that it was an elegant cloister facing a wonderful and most ample palace, excellent in its symmetried architecture and very magnificent. Which rendered the fourth wall of the leafy enclosure, of a length of sixty paces. And this circuit was a square open court beneath the sky.

In the middle part of this most notable area I saw an excellent fountain of the clearest waters, spouting on high almost to the top of the green enclosure through the narrowest little pipes, and falling down into a wide basin, which was of the finest amethyst, its diameter containing three paces, of a thickness of a quarter, dwindling towards the lips to an inch, of most excellent casting; and all round about there appeared, in relief, most worthily expressed, water-monsters — as many as the inventors of antiquity

duritudine fingere prestantemente valseno. Opera daedalea et di admiratione conspicua. Né tale se iacti Pausania havere statuito il suo cratere aeneo ad Hippari. La quale habilmente fondata era sopra uno egregio stylo di diaspro, di varicose mixture, la una per l’altra venustamente adulterantese, intersecantese il diaphano calcedonio, di colore di marina aqua turbida, riduto in nobilissima factura. Excitato di vasi gutturii, uno sopra all’altro, cum separatione di eximia nodatura. Il quale erecto stava infixo nel centro di uno plyntho rotondato di verdigiante Ophites. Il quale rotondo, era levato dal aequato pavimento, quincuncio cum il circundante Porphyro, che era cum perpolite undule curiosamente liniato. Circuncirca al stylo subiecte alla concha quatro Harpyie d’oro cum gli unguicosi pedi et rapaci, sopra la planicie del Ophites posite adstavano. Le quale cum le parte posteriore verso al stylo, l’una opposita directamente all’altra, et cum suesplicate ale sotto resistevano al ianthino labro, overo concha, cum virginei volti. Crinite giù per le spalle dalla cervice deflui gli capillamenti. Et cum la testa non giungendo sotto la concha. Cum le caude anguinee inglobantese, et in extremo in antiquaria frondatura se demigrante. Facevano all’infimo vaso gutturnio del stylo, non ingrata, ma amicale illaqueatura et coniugio. Intro nel mediano umbilico del vaso sopra l’ordine del subiecto stylo, era proportionatamente sublevato del proprio vaso Amethystio, uno oblongo calice inverso, tanto più sublato, quanto era exfossato il vaso, il suo medio, dagli ambienti labii della concha. Sopra il quale excitata era una artificiosa Arula, supposita alle tre Gratie nude. Di finissimo oro, alla proceritate communa, l’una cum l’altra adhaerentise. Dalle papille delle tate delle quale, l’aqua surgente stillava subtile, quale virgule apparendo di cinerato argento terso et strissato. Et quale si extilata si fusse per il candidissimo pumice di Taracona. Et ciascuna di esse nella mano dextera teniva una omnifera copia, la quale sopra del suo capo alquanto excedeva. Et daposcia tutte tre le aperture, elegantemente convenivano in una rotondatione et hiato parimente inseme coeunte. Cum fructi et fronde varii pendenti fora degli oruli, overo labii degli intorquati corni abondantemente referti. Tra gli fructi et fogliature alquanto prominevano dispositamente sei Sipunculi effluendo, dagli quali l’aqua per filatissimo exito saliva. Daposcia il solertissimo artifice fusore per non impedire uno cubito cum l’altro, cum signo di pudicitia le statue cum la leva mano occultavano la parte digna di copertura. Sopra gli labii dilla hiante concha (dilla quale la circuitione più ambiva uno pedi del subiacente Ophites) cum il capo levato sopra gli sui pedi viperei stando, cum decentissimo intercalato f

were ever excellently able to feign in hard stone. A work of Daedalus, and notable for admiration. Nor let Pausanias boast of having set up his bronze bowl at Hipparis.

It was aptly founded upon a distinguished shaft of jasper, of straggling mixtures, the one beautifully adulterating the other, and cut across by translucent chalcedony of the colour of troubled sea-water, brought to a most noble making. Raised of ewer-like vessels, one above another, with the parting of a choice knot-work. Which stood upright, fixed in the centre of a rounded plinth of green ophite. Which round was raised from the level pavement by a fifth part, with the surrounding porphyry, which was curiously lined with well-polished little waves.

Round about the shaft, set beneath the basin, four harpies of gold with clawed and rapacious feet stood upon the flat of the ophite. Which, with their hinder parts towards the shaft, the one directly opposite the other, and with unfolded wings, held up beneath the violet lip, or basin, with maidenly faces. Their locks flowing loose down over their shoulders from the neck. And with their heads not reaching under the basin. With their serpent tails coiling into a globe, and passing at the end into antique foliage. They made with the lowest ewer-vessel of the shaft a not ungrateful but a friendly knotting and joining.

Within, at the middle navel of the vessel, above the order of the shaft beneath, there was raised proportionately out of the amethyst vessel itself an oblong chalice turned upside down, lifted as much as the vessel was hollowed, its middle standing clear of the surrounding lips of the basin. Above which was raised an artful little altar, set beneath the three naked Graces. Of the finest gold, of a common tallness, the one cleaving to the other. From the nipples of whose breasts the rising water dripped finely, appearing like little rods of burnished and streaked silvered ash. And as though it had been distilled through the whitest pumice of Tarragona.

And each of them held in her right hand an all-bearing horn of plenty, which rose somewhat above her head. And then all three openings came elegantly together in one rounding, their mouths meeting equally together. With fruits and various fronds hanging out of the rims, or lips, of the twisted horns, abundantly filled.

Among the fruits and foliage six little pipes projected a little, set in order and flowing, from which the water rose in the finest thread. And then the most skilful founder, so as not to hinder one elbow with the other, had the statues hide with the left hand, as a sign of modesty, the part worthy of covering.

Upon the lips of the gaping basin (whose circuit went about one foot wider than the ophite beneath it), standing with heads raised above their viper feet, with a most seemly spacing

La quale cadeva poscia ultra la rotundatione dil Ophites, et tra una rotunditate porphyrica, le quale erano aequalmente più eminente della aequatura de l’area, overo subdivale pavimento, quanto sopra è dicto. Ove interiecto ambiva uno canaliculo tra lo Ophites et essa porphyrica rotundatione lato in apertione di pede uno et semi, et duo integri profundato. Il quale Porphyrico, era tripedale nella plana superficie, cum eximia undiculatione, verso il pavimento. Sencia occupatione deforme, del lacunato della pretiosa concha. Io giamai subcincte et di lucidissimamente explicare non saperei, et meno idoneo il tutto descrivere. Factura non di humano ingegno. there sat six scaly little dragons of shining gold. By such a devised art that the water flowing from the breasts fell directly into the emptied and open crown of the head of the said little dragons, which, with wings spread wide and biting, likewise each of them threw back, or rather vomited out, that water through a little pipe. Which then fell beyond the rounding of the ophite, and between a rounding of porphyry, which stood equally more raised above the level of the area, or open pavement, than is said above. Where, set between, there ran a little channel between the ophite and that porphyry rounding, wide at its opening one foot and a half, and two whole feet deep. Which porphyry was three feet in its flat surface, with a choice waving towards the pavement.

The remainder of the little dragons crept along the moderate hollowing of the basin, until they all came together, their tail-ends transformed into antique foliage and into a most pleasant binding with the little altar set beneath the three images, or rather their footstool, at a proportioned height. Without any deforming encroachment upon the hollow of the precious basin.

So that, by the green meeting of the orange cloister, and by the shining of the bright material, and by the purest waters, there was rendered a most welcome colouring, like a rainbow among hollowed clouds, within the noble, proud and elegant vessel.

Then, in the swelling body of the basin, between the one little dragon and the other at an even space, there stood out of that excellent casting heads of maned lions, with exquisite exactness, which, vomiting, scattered through a devouring pipe the water dripping from the six little conduits set in the most beautiful horns of plenty. Which water rose with so bridled a force that its fall came down among the little dragons into the wide and sounding basin, with a most welcome ringing of the wide-open vessel from the high fall of the said waters.

Of this most rare workmanship, then, chiefly built with so sharp a wit — such as was that uncommon vessel, and the four most perfect harpies, and of what choice dignity was the little altar, where I saw the three figures of most shining gold sitting, and with what artifice and polish it was ordered — I should never know how to speak briefly and clearly, and still less am I fit to describe the whole. A making not of human wit. But I may lawfully testify (calling the gods to witness) that never in our own age was such a chased work, nor anything near its equal, devised more welcome or more worth beholding.

And thus astonished I considered besides those stubbornly hard stones of the support of the great basin — that is, the shaft of ewer-vessels set one above another. With what ready ease, neither more nor less than if the material had been of soft wax, were those drawn threadings made, and so

Quale marmori, quale scalpture, ove mirai le virtute Herculane in petra luculea Semidivulse mirabilmente exscalpte. Exuvie, Statue, Tituli, et Trophoei, mirificamente coelati. Quale Propyleo, o vero vestibulo, quale regio portico. Ad questo debitamente ceda Tito Caesare cum le sue petre phoenicie speculabile, et terse, tale et tanto che exile qualunque foetoso ingegno se damnarebbe volendolo narrare, accede ancora la dignitate della fenestratione et della conspicua porta, et del nobilissimo Podio, lo egregio expresso dill’arte aedificatoria. Non meno excellente vedevasi il miraveglioso soffito bellissime lacunato, cum lacunule tra la undiculatione intecta di fogliatura, quadrate et rotunde insepte. Cum exquisiti liniamenti decorati, di puro oro, et Cyaneo coloramento deaurati, et elegante depicturati. Perdase quivi qualunque altro mirando aedificamento. Essendo hogi mai all’apertione della spectabile porta pervenuti. Ecco che l’era serata la Itione di una iocunda et mirabile cortina intercalare extenta, tutta di filatura d’oro, et di seta ritramata et contexta, cum due imagine dignissime. L’altra di esse, cum omni instrumento apto ad operare circundata. Et una cum il virgineo volto sublevato, il coelo intentamente considerava. La formositate delle quale non immerito me dehortava che cum peniculo (quantunque del praeclaro Apelle) si potesse agiungere. Quivi le faconde et pervenuste et lepidissime comite, ciascuna la sua dextra giunseron benignamente cum la mia volendome introdure et acceptantime dicendo, Poliphile questo è l’ordine servabile, per el quale intrare si convene alla veneranda praesentia, et sublime maiestate della Regina nostra. Questa praecipua et primaria cortina non si concede d’intrare a niuno, sencia recepto di una simplice et vigilante damigella ianitrice, Cinosia chiamata, et questa sentendo il nostro advenire subito se appraesentoe, et urbanamente dimovete la cortina. Et nui intrassimo. Quivi era uno spatio intercluso, et per un’altra velatura diviso, di artificio et compositione nobilissima, et di omni tinctura variata. Nella quale erano signi, Formature, piante, et animali di singulare ritramatura. In questo loco al nostro adventare, una similmente curiosa donna se fece immediate ad nui, Indalomena nominata. Et ingenuamente il suo Sipario reserato, fussemo introducti. Ancora et quivi era uno aequale intervallo, tra la seconda et una tertia cortina, molto eximiamente, cum discorso et ragione, mirabilmente contexta, et de infinite ligature, et retinaculi, et di instrumenti veterrimi di harpagare et mordacemente retinere vermiculatamente f iii

let not the Praenestine way exalt itself for the Gordian building. And to this excellent colonnade let its two hundred columns yield — Numidian, Claudian, Simiadic and Thistian, divided in equal number. What marbles, what carvings, where I beheld the labours of Hercules in shining stone, marvellously cut half free of the ground. Spoils, statues, inscriptions and trophies, wonderfully chased. What gate-house, or vestibule; what royal portico. To this let Titus Caesar duly yield with his mirroring and burnished Phoenician stones — such and so great that any feeble and mouldering wit would condemn itself in wishing to tell of it.

There comes besides the dignity of the windows and of the notable door, and of the most noble podium, the distinguished expression of the builder's art. No less excellent to see was the marvellous ceiling, most beautifully coffered, with little coffers between the wavings, covered with foliage, set in square and round. Adorned with exquisite lineaments, gilded of pure gold and of a dark blue colouring, and elegantly painted. Let every other wonderful building be lost here.

Being now come to the opening of the notable door — behold, the way in was closed by a joyful and marvellous curtain stretched across, all of golden thread, and rewoven and inwoven with silk, with two most worthy images. The one of them was surrounded with every instrument fit for working; and one, with her maidenly face raised, considered the heavens intently. The beauty of which not undeservedly warned me off from thinking that any pencil (even the famous Apelles's) could reach it.

Here the eloquent and most beautiful and charming companions each joined her right hand kindly with mine, wishing to lead me in, and receiving me they said: "Poliphilo, this is the order to be kept, by which one must enter into the venerable presence and lofty majesty of our Queen. This chief and first curtain it is granted to no one to enter without the receiving of a plain and watchful damsel doorkeeper, called Cynosia." And she, hearing our coming, at once presented herself and courteously drew aside the curtain. And we entered.

Here was an enclosed space, divided by another veiling of most noble artifice and composition, and varied with every tincture. In which were signs, shapes, plants and animals of a singular reweaving. In this place, at our coming, a woman likewise careful came immediately to us, named Indalomena. And, frankly unfastening her curtain, we were led in.

Here too there was an equal space between the second and a third curtain, most excellently woven with discourse and reason, and painted in fine work with endless bindings and holdfasts and with the most ancient instruments for grappling and holding fast

asperamente interscalpti, et sencia contumacia rosicante del durissimo smirilio, tali Triglyphi così egregiamente expressi. Ma cum opportuni celti et scalpelli de sì facta temperatura, quale ignora gli nostri moderni artifici, cum praecipua nitella splendescenti. Tutta la intervallata area dunque (in medio della quale excitato era di questo spectatissimo artificio della celebre et sumptuosa fontana) havea il pavimento lapideo di quadrature di fini marmori di vario colore et deformatura. Nelle quale meno del suo capto erano intro appacti bellissimamente rotundi di gratioso diaspro cum summa aequabilitate amussi, dissentanei del coloramento. Et gli relicti angoli cum volubile fronde et lilii venustamente satisfacti erano. Daposcia le large liste, overo fascie, tra le quadrature mirai di optimo tessellato di gratissime petre di colore, cum minuta incisura. In foglie verdacie cum punicei fiori Cyanei, Phoenicei et Glauci, tanto meglio confederatamente coagmentati cum obstinata cohaesione, quanto meno io il saperia exprimere, di artificiosa compositione, et di eximia collustratione nitidissimo, di diligente xesturgia, nobile deformatura. Più vago di coloratione, che non dimonstra il crystallo di varia tinctura dagli solarii radii repercosso. Perché gli colori circunducti, cum lepidissimo congresso in esse terse petre reflectevano niuno grado accusatose negli sectilii Tesseri, Scutuli, Trigoni, Quadrati, ma cum planissima directione, coaequissimi. Per le quale tutte cose, quasi io rimansi degli sensi allucinato et stupido fra me solertemente examinando l’opera summamente insigne, quale di videre non fui assueto. Et volentieri io harei voluto di alquanto pausarme, et tale dignitate di operatura sarebbe stato necessario cum più protracta mora investigare, et alquanto cum più diligentia contemplare, ma io non potea, perché convenevole se offeriva le comite faconde et mie ductrice sedulo sequire. L’aspecto dunque di questo sumptuoso, magnifico, et superbo Pallatio et la sua approbata situatione, o vero collocatione, et la Symmetria della miravegliosa compositione, nel primo congresso mi conciliava ad una praecipua hilaritate et venusta gratia, per la dignitate della quale factura, al progresso di oltra più contemplare fui provocato. Per la quale cosa meritamente arbitrava, che il peritissimo aedificatore sopra qualunque altro, che mai fabricasse fusse praestante, quale dunque contignatione trabeata et di canterii, quale distributa dispositione di conclavi, et penetrali, et caviedii? quali parieti di pretioso coassamento intecti, et incrustati, quale miro ordine di ornato, quale perenne coloratione pigmentaria degli alamenti, quale regula di columnatione et intervallo, et quivi per questo

roughly carved between, and without the gnawing obstinacy of the hardest emery, such triglyphs so excellently expressed. But with fit chisels and gravers of such a tempering as our modern craftsmen know nothing of, shining with a choice brightness.

The whole space of the area, then, in the middle of which was raised this most notable artifice of the famous and sumptuous fountain, had a stone pavement of squares of fine marbles of various colour and shaping. In which, less than their measure, there were most beautifully fitted rounds of gracious jasper, levelled with the utmost evenness, differing in their colouring. And the remaining corners were beautifully satisfied with winding fronds and lilies.

Then the broad bands, or fillets, between the squares I beheld to be of the best tessellation of most welcome coloured stones, with a minute cutting. In green leaves with crimson flowers, dark blue, purple and grey-green, so much the better joined in a confederate way with an obstinate cohesion, the less I should know how to express it — of an artful composition, and most bright with a choice shining, of diligent polishing, a noble shaping. More lovely in colour than crystal of various tincture struck back by the rays of the sun. Because the colours led about, with a most charming meeting, were reflected in those burnished stones; no step betraying itself in the cut tesserae, lozenges, triangles and squares, but with a most level directness, wholly equal.

By all which things I remained as it were dazzled in my senses and stupid, examining carefully within myself the work, exceedingly notable, such as I was not used to seeing. And willingly I should have wished to pause a little, and such dignity of workmanship would have needed a longer stay to investigate, and to contemplate somewhat more diligently; but I could not, because it was fitting to follow closely my eloquent companions and guides.

The aspect, then, of this sumptuous, magnificent and proud palace, and its approved situation or placing, and the symmetry of its marvellous composition, at the first meeting won me to a chief cheerfulness and comely grace; by the dignity of which making I was provoked to go on and contemplate further. For which cause I deservedly judged that its most skilful builder was excellent above any other that ever built. What framing, then, of beams and of rafters; what distributed disposition of chambers and inner rooms and courts; what walls covered and crusted with precious panelling; what wonderful order of ornament; what unfading colouring of pigment upon the walls; what rule of columns and of spacing — and there, by this

Questa similmente, introvocati nui, donoe libero adito. Ultimamente quivi le comite mie, me praesentorono dinanti alla venerabonda maiestate della Regina Eleuteryllida.

QUANTA INSIGNE MAIESTATE FUE QUELLA DELLA REGINA, ET LA CONDITIONE DELLA SUA RESIDENTIA, ET ADMIRANDO APPARATO POLIPHILO AL SUO POTERE IL NARRA. ET LA BENIGNA ET AFFABILE SUSCEPTIONE. ET ELLA MIRAVEGLIATOSE DI LUI. ET QUANTO MIRABILE ET SPLENDIDO FUE IL CONVITO, SOPRA IL CAPTO DELLA HUMANA NOTITIA EXCEDENTE, ET IL LOCO OVE FUE FATO (DI COMPARATIONE PRIVO) ALQUANTO DESCRIVE.

AD LA PRIMA IANITRICE VENUTI essendo, non sencia stupore me vide, et decentemente salutatola et debitamente reverita. Et factomi da lei domestico invito del ingresso, et humano sospitato, et pari modo le sequente cortinarie custode, io vidi uno excelso portico longo quanto il contento del Pallatio. Il testudinato aureo del quale depicto era di verdigiante fogliatura, cum distincti fiori et implicate fronde et volitante avicule eximiamente imphrygiato di opera museaca. Il mundissimo silicato, quale di fora nella septa corte. Gli parieti di petre sumptuose artificiosamente dispositi factura vermiculata incrustati. All’ultima cortina, quella Matrona Mnemosyna molto affectuosamente mi suase, di non dubitare alcuna cosa, ma che al regio suaso et salubre consiglio della Regina sectario strenuo me exponesse, et perseverante executore, perché poscia lo exito senza fallo uscirà piacevole. Et conceduto peculiarmente l’introito. Ecco che agli ochii mei sa repraesentorono più praesto divine cose, che humane. Uno ambitiosissimo apparato in una stupenda et spatiosa corte, ultra el pallatio contigua, ad opposito dell’altra, di quadrato perfecta. Il lepidissimo et pretioso pavimento tra una ambiente tessellatura interiecto vidi uno spatio di .64. quadrati, di pedi tre il diametro di ciascuno. Degli quali l’uno lustrava di diaspro di colore coraliceo, et l’altro verdissimo guttato di sanguinee gutte, cum imperceptibile quasi cohaesione del composito, quale uno

with a bite. Without delay there placidly offered herself to us in this place a third matron, our hostess and receiving us graciously. Whose name was Mnemosyne. She likewise, when we had been called in, gave us free entry. And at last here my companions presented me before the venerable majesty of Queen Eleuterylida.

How great and notable was the majesty of the Queen, and the condition of her dwelling and its wonderful furnishing, Poliphilo tells as best he can. And the kind and affable receiving of him. And how she marvelled at him. And how wonderful and splendid was the banquet, exceeding the reach of human knowledge, and the place where it was held (without comparison), he somewhat describes.

Being come to the first doorkeeper, she saw me not without astonishment; and having greeted her seemly and duly reverenced her, and being given by her a familiar invitation to enter and a courteous welcome — and in like manner by the following curtain-keepers — I saw a lofty portico, as long as the compass of the palace. Whose golden vaulting was painted with green foliage, with distinct flowers and entwined fronds and flying birds, choicely embroidered in mosaic work. The cleanest paving, like that outside in the enclosed court. The walls crusted with sumptuous stones artfully set in fine work.

At the last curtain that matron Mnemosyne very affectionately urged me to doubt of nothing, but to show myself a strenuous follower of the Queen's royal urging and wholesome counsel, and a persevering doer of it, because then the outcome would come out pleasant without fail. And entry being particularly granted — behold, there presented themselves to my eyes things rather divine than human. A most ambitious furnishing in a stupendous and spacious court, beyond the palace and adjoining it, opposite the other, perfect in its square.

The most charming and precious pavement I saw set between a surrounding tessellation: a space of sixty-four squares, of three feet the diameter of each. Of which the one shone with jasper of a coral colour, and the other of the greenest, dropped with bloody drops, with an almost imperceptible cohesion of the composition, like a

Circuncincte di lori, cum le extremitate inundante, circa la gioia perfectamente ornavano. Cum decorata disseminatione di multiplice et inextimabile gemme mirificamente vidi cum ornato. Al sinistro alamento, o vero pariete plasticato similmente era. game of chess. The circuit then of an excellent embroidered border and enclosure, one whole pace its breadth, of subtle devisings of stone cutwork, excellently compacted in the smallest shapes, like a lovely painting of fine stones, cut evenly and framed to rule. The joinings not appearing; most burnished and mirroring, and of so just a levelling by line and square that a round and spherical body set upon it would have shown itself unsteady.

Beyond this, then, there ended a marvellous making of three paces of most noble knot-work of jaspers, prasines, chalcedonies, agates and of other notable manners and kinds of fine stones. Along the walls of the aforesaid area I considered certain most worthy seats of sandalwood, red and citron, most diligently made, and covered over with the greenest velvet. Stuffed, or cushioned, with a moderate downy convexity, or of a soft material that yielded most comfortably to the sitter; and the said silken pile fixed along the rims of the benches with little golden nails with studded heads, upon a silver and stretched braid, or flat little cord.

The splendid facing of the enclosing walls I beheld, all clothed with plates of purest and shining gold, with chasings answering to it, and most fitting to that precious material. In the levelled and most burnished flat, then, of the said plates — divided by certain little pilasters, or squares, of a most fitting measure and correspondence — there appeared in the middle of each, clearly, round jewels fitted in, moderately swelling in the form of the torus of a base, of a thickness suited to the capacity of the space, covered over with fringed leaves pressed one against another. Girt about with thongs, with the ends flowing, they perfectly adorned the jewel round about. Where there came in, most aptly among the foliage in a fitting distribution, a fruitage of shining and various jewels, notably shaped to various expressed lineaments.

In the remaining space, then, walled round with these swelling jewels, painted perfectly with beauty in encaustic work, I beheld with great pleasure the seven planets with their inborn properties. The remaining level, outside the roundness of the jewels, was wrought fiercely in endless and elegant expressions of silversmith's work. With an adorned scattering of manifold and inestimable gems I saw it wonderfully with its ornament.

At the left wall, or moulded partition, it was likewise. And with the spaces and jewels of the same form of ornament and of the same number as the aforesaid — that is, in seven roundings — I contemplated seven triumphs of those subject to the ruling planets, most skilfully made in the said painting. And on the right side I saw likewise seven harmonies of them, and the passage of the soul, with its qualitative receiving of the degrees of the circles, with an incredible history of the celestial operations that come with it.

Il quarto alamento faceva il pallatio, cum distributione parimente quale negli insinuati, la porta dempta occupatrice del mediano intervallo. Gli altri sei cum regulata correspondentia et harmonia degli reliqui, nelle gioie (ad opposito degli pianeti, et Symmetriato congresso) le virtuose operatione subinclinate a quelli, expresse in forma di elegante Nymphe cum gli tituli et signi del suo effecto. La septima mediana nel frontespicio, o vero fastigiato della porta era collocata di directo in obvio della septima gioia, continente il Planeta Sole. La quale era più de l’altre sublevata per la locatione del throno della Regina. Per la quale cosa omni parte accuratissimamente di materia, di numero, di forma ad linea, et qualunque minima parte et locatione aequatissimamente, et a llibella correspondeva, et cusì mutuamente la parte dextra cum la sinistra et de qui et de lì cum exquisitissimo congresso convenivano. Del quale superexcellente loco ciascuno alamento extenso era di passi vintiocto. Per tale elegante dispositione era aequabile questa subdivale corte circumcirca tutta di perfectissimo oro ritecta, opera miranda et ineffabile. Gli pilastrelli, o vero semiquadrangule cum discrepantia di quatro passi l’una da l’altra cum iusta partitione septenaria (numero alla natura gratissimo) erano di finissimo et orientale lapislazuli, cum iocundissima impletione del suo coloramento, cum lepidissima disseminatione di minute scintule d’oro decorate. Il fronte delle quale tra le concludente undiculatione erano mirabilmente interscalpto candelabri, cum spectatissima sociatione di fronde, copie, monstriculi, capi capillati di fogliatura, pupi cum le extremitate in scyle, avicule, et copie, et vasculi ballaustici, cum egregie inventione et cogitati, dall’ima crepidine al summo scapo di anaglypho quasi divulso dal suo plano fundo. The fourth wall the palace made, with a distribution equal to those hinted at, save that the door took up the middle space. burning gems and of marvellous making — such as was never that seat in the temple of Hercules at Tyre, made of the stone Eusebes — the Queen herself dwelt, sitting with a venerable and imperial majesty. Ad tanto dunque imperiale et sublime conspecto venerabondi, et ad terra geniculati, sencia inducia le cubicularie et cortale donne tutte dal quieto sedere se levorono, da tale novitate et spectaculo provocate, che io in tale loco pervenuto fusse, summamente miravegliantise. At so imperial and lofty a sight, then, worshipping and kneeling to the ground — without delay the chamber-women and the ladies of the court all rose from their quiet sitting, provoked by such a novelty and spectacle, marvelling exceedingly that I should have come to such a place. But much more did I feel my sad heart open itself restlessly, anxiously thinking over things past and things present, beset and full of a deep astonishment. Wholly suffused with a reverent fear and an honest bashfulness.

At which novelty the seated ladies called my companions to their ears, curious. And asking under their breath who I might be, and my strange and unlooked-for case besides. And for this the drawn eyes of all were fixed and directed intently upon me.

Finding myself, then, most humble before this most excellent and such a presence, I remained wholly astounded, and as it were without breath and abashed. And being asked by her the course and manner of my coming, and my entry into that place by my companions, they readily set the whole out and fully recited it. but attend and tell me: how have you come in here safe? And how have you escaped the deadly and horrible dragon? And how did you find a way out of those hateful shadows and blind caverns? And thereafter with what laborious difficulty, hurrying, I came to this most acceptable place. At which she marvelled greatly, and with her likewise the venerable ladies. And how besides the five companions had found me terrified and wandering.

So to such distinguished magnificence I bent my mind eagerly with the utmost pleasure. And therefore, my Poliphilo, without any hesitation set yourself there to sit comfortably. For you will most gladly see part of our most splendid ordering, and the plentiful diversity of my more than royal delights, and the chief adornment of the elegant service, and the household splendour, and the inestimable preciousness of my most ample riches, and the wide effect of my beneficence."

Whereupon, at this sincere and holy command, her eloquent and kindly speech being finished, I humbly made myself her bowing servant, and with a small boldness and slight daring, obeying at once, I set myself to sit upon those delicious benches on the right side — still in my woollen gown, which yet held the burrs, or little burdocks, stuck in it, and some clinging husks of goose-grass — in the midst of the five companions, placed second, between Osfressia and Achoe, after the Queen.
