sopra di ciascuna di quelle porte, el suo titulo et indice annotato et inscripto vederai, accuratamente legilo, ma ad la opportunitate del tuo guberno et munimine, io ti darò di tante mie facete et herile pedisseque due, le quale exercite illo tutissimo conducerano, et individue commiterano, cum laeto animo perciò va et cum foelice successo. Et incontanente cum regia largitate educto uno annulo aureo dill’annulare digito, cum una petra Anchite, tolli questo dicendo, et teco in memoria della mia amicabile munificentia laeto il portarai. Ad questa exhortatione et pretioso dono, io quasi Amphasiatico divenuto, non sapea per certo cosa alcuna aequivalente che dire, né regratiare. Ma ella benignamente avidutase matronalmente, et cum una genuina praestantia, et cum gravitate maiestale, ad due praeclare et insigne puelle, se voltoe, al suo Imperiale throno propinque assistrice, ad una che al dextro lato sedeva imperitante dixe. Logistica sarai tu altra che andarai cum il nostro hospite Poliphilo. Et cum sancto religioso et venerabile acto, se voltoe poscia ad lato sinistro dicendo. Thelemia et tu parimente andarai una cum esso, et ambe due datigli ad intendere et chiara notitia in quale porta el debi lui ristare. Dunque Poliphile ad un’altra Regina molto splendida et venerabonda te appraesenterano. La quale si ad te benigna et frugale se praestarae, beato sarai, si al contrario, discontento sarai. Niente di manco nel suo volto la pole comprehendere niuno, perché alcuna fiata cum patricia et genuina urbanitate et cum lepidissima iucunditate, essa se dimonstra, tale volta suapte tetra maligna, et aspernabile, cum instabile incursione. Quella è che termina el tutto. Et per cusì facta obscura conditione, non immerito Regina denominata è Telosia, la quale in tanta fasta et opulentissima mansione non dimora, quale hora manifestamente me vedi inhabitare. Voglio però che tu sapi, che il summo Opifice, né la ordinata natura non ti poteano praestare maiore thesoro, che pervenire ad questo mio divo conspecto et larga munificentia, diqué l’artificiosa natura, non valeria di accumulare maiore divitie, che obtenire, et la mia benigna gratia consequire, et participe essere di tanto bene. Onde cusì come exquisitamente te lice existimare, che unque al mondo tanto thesoro trovare se potrebbe, ad comparatione di quello che in me veracemente se trova, talento coeleste obtento dagli mortali. Ma la Regina Telosia mane in nubilante loco di latebra, et il suo domicilio ha gli aspiramenti obstrusi, perché quella cernere per niuna licentia consente, quanta et quale sia la bellecia sua ad gli homini, perché non lice, né permesso è ad gli ochii corporali diva formositate debbi apparere, et per cusì facta ragione caeco persta lo effecto del successo suo. Ma cum mira observantia se transforma versipelle et moltiforme, non desiderata volendo propalarse.

you will see, above each of those doors, its title and index noted and inscribed. Read it carefully; but for the convenience of your guiding and defence I shall give you two of my witty and mistress-like attendants, who, being practised in it, will lead you there most safely and will keep close by you. Go therefore with glad heart, and with a happy outcome."

And at once, with royal largeness, drawing a golden ring from her ring-finger, with a stone anchitis: "Take this," she said, "and you shall carry it gladly with you in memory of my friendly munificence."

At this exhortation and precious gift, being become as it were speechless, I certainly knew nothing equivalent to say, nor how to give thanks. But she, kindly perceiving it, in a matronly way, and with a native excellence and majestic gravity, turned to two distinguished and notable maidens, sitting near her imperial throne; and to the one who sat commanding at the right side she said:

"Logistica, you shall be one of the two who go with our guest Poliphilo." And with a holy, religious and venerable act she turned then to the left side, saying: "Thelemia, and you likewise shall go together with him, and both give him to understand and to know clearly at which door he ought to stay. Then, Poliphilo, they will present you to another Queen, very splendid and venerable. Who, if she shows herself kind and bountiful to you, you shall be blessed; if the contrary, you shall be discontented. Nevertheless in her face no one can grasp it, because sometimes she shows herself with a noble and native courtesy and with a most charming pleasantness, and at other times of herself gloomy, malignant and to be scorned, with an unsteady onset. She it is who ends everything. And for such a dark condition she is not undeservedly named Queen Telosia; who dwells not in so proud and opulent a mansion as you now plainly see me inhabit.

"I would have you know, however, that the highest Maker, nor ordered nature, could not give you a greater treasure than to come to this my divine presence and wide munificence; wherefore artful nature could not heap up greater riches than to obtain, and to win, my kindly favour, and to be a sharer in so great a good. Whence, as you may exquisitely judge, no such treasure could ever be found in the world in comparison with that which truly is found in me, a heavenly gift obtained by mortals.

"But Queen Telosia stays in a clouded place of hiding, and her dwelling has its approaches shut, since she consents by no leave that men should discern how great and of what kind her beauty is; for it is not lawful, nor permitted, that a divine beauty should appear to bodily eyes; and for such a reason the effect of her outcome stands blind. But with a wonderful observance she transforms herself, changing her skin and of many forms, unwilling to reveal herself unasked.

Et quando le veterrime porte ti serano reserate, in ciascuna dinanti agli ochii tui futura sa ppraesentarà, et tamen non la cognoscerai, se non alquanto la moderatrice prudentia aenigmatice, et cum recto et sincero iudicio la vide, et più praesto la considera, perché di habito et di aspecto ambiguo se tramuta. Et per questa ancipite animadversione, l’homo saepicule dell’expectato remane sencia emendatione decepto. Quello dunque Poliphile che queste mie due consignate, et credite fanciulle suggerendo ti suaderano, et in quale porta doverai intrare, et remanere, et quale di quelle più te piacerà intendere et auscultare potrai per el mio excellentissimo et gratuito dono et praestata licentia liberamente assentire, perché queste di quella alquanta notitia tengono, et poi dicto fece nuto alle due, Logistica et Thelemia, le quale sencia praestolare se feceron humilmente serve. Et io allhora in acto, che parlare, non audeva né non sapea ad tanta sublimitate di praesentia, la regratiai del suo grande munificio. Le due comite delegate, me festivamente cum domestica promptitudine et gesti virginei prehenseron, l’una per la mano dextra, et l’altra per la sinistra, et praecipuamente dalla Regina primo, et poscia da tutte riverentemente obtenta la licentia. Fora per li medesimi Siparii et porta egressi, avido ancora io et inexplebile me rivoltai alla spectatissima porta per speculare integramente l’artificioso pallatio, admirabile di arte aedificatoria et perfinito, la subtilitate della quale opera imitare per niuno valido excogitato degli mortali poté niuno. Imperoché suspicava decentemente essa sagace natura, quivi ad admiratione tante delitie del suo imperceptibile opificio havere singularmente ficto, ad commoditate, ad uso, et ad gratia et adoria aptissimo, et ad la perennitate fermo et constante, et duraturo existente. Per la quale cosa excessivamente volentiera alquanto di morula harei affermatome, ma sectario le ductrice destinate, et mie consorte, io non potei, vero che in uno ocyssimo furare di ochio, nel phrygio, o vero Zophoro di essa porta vidi annotato tale inscriptione. HO TES PHYSEOS OLBOS. Et quanto che cum gli praestissimi sensi poti trahere, tanto praegratissimamente acceptai in esso transito extremo dilecto sumendo, quanto che a dire è incredibile. O foelice dunque chi in tale loco sempre concesso gli fusse essere patritio, o vero inquilino. Essendo nella conclusa Area del Naranceo septo pervenuti, Thelemia cum singulare affabilitate mi dice. Oltra le praeexcellentissime et miravegliose cose, che tu hai Poliphile mirate, ancora quatro admirande ti resta di vedere, et al sinistro lato del incomparabile pallatio in uno spectatissimo viridario me condusseron di maximo excogitato de impendio, di h ii

"And when the most ancient doors are opened to you, in each of them she will present herself before your eyes as one to come; and yet you will not know her, unless moderating prudence somewhat sees her in a riddle, and with an upright and sincere judgement, and rather considers her — because in habit and in aspect she changes herself ambiguously. And by this two-headed watching, man is very often deceived without remedy of what he expected.

"That, then, Poliphilo, which these two girls of mine, entrusted and committed to you, shall counsel you by their suggesting — and at which door you ought to enter and to stay, and which of them shall most please you — you may hear and listen to, and freely assent to it, by my most excellent and gratuitous gift and the leave I grant, because these have some knowledge of that." And this said, she made a sign to the two, Logistica and Thelemia, who without waiting made themselves humbly her servants. And I then, in the act of speaking — not daring, nor knowing how, before so lofty a presence — gave her thanks for her great munificence.

The two appointed companions took me festively with a homely readiness and maidenly gestures, the one by the right hand and the other by the left; and leave being reverently obtained first chiefly from the Queen, and then from all. Going out by the same curtains and door, still eager and unsatisfied, I turned back to the notable door to gaze wholly at the artful palace, admirable in the builder's art and finished, the subtlety of which work no valid devising of mortals could imitate. For I fittingly thought that sagacious nature herself had here singularly feigned, for admiration, so many delights of her imperceptible workmanship — most apt for convenience, for use, and for grace and glory, and firm and constant for perpetuity, and lasting.

For which cause I should exceedingly gladly have stayed a little while; but a follower of the appointed guides and my companions, I could not; true it is that in a swiftest stealing of a glance, in the border, or frieze, of that door, I saw noted this inscription: HO TES PHYSEOS OLBOS. And as much as I could draw with my readiest senses, so much most gratefully I received, taking in that passage an extreme delight, as much as is incredible to say. O happy, then, whoever should be granted to be always in such a place a citizen, or a dweller.

Having come into the enclosed area of the orange hedge, Thelemia says to me with a singular affability: "Beyond the most excellent and marvellous things that you have beheld, Poliphilo, four more wonderful things remain for you to see." And on the left side of the incomparable palace they led me into a most notable garden of the greatest devising, of cost, of

tempo, et di subtilissimo artificio. Il quale di ambito et continentia tanto quanto era quello, ove stava la maiestale residentia, circuncirca cohaerente ad gli alamenti protendevano accommodate capsule hortense, in le quale in loco di virentia, omni pianta era di purgatissimo vitro, egregiamente (oltra quello che se pole imaginare et credere) intopiati buxi, cum gli stirpi d’oro tale materia conducta. Tra l’uno et l’altro degli quali alternava uno cupresso, dui passi non excedendo la sua altitudine, et degli Bussi uno. Referte poscia di mirabile fincto di moltiformi simplici, cum elegantissima secta dilla natura, et cum iocundissime devariate forme di fiori cum distincto coloramine et praegratissimo. La pianatura labiale dello hiato quadrante delle quale capselle, o vero altane, o vero de l’apertione era subcoroniceata di oro cum subtilissimi liniamenti perpolite et ornate, le facie dille quale di plaste vitrine nel intimo deaurate, et cum myrifica graphiatura di curiosissimo historiato, bellissime extavano, circuncluse di alveoli aurei mordicamente quelle continivano cum lo imo soccolo levato sextante. Il septo ambiente dil viridario cum disquisita distantia, era cum columne ventriculate della dicta materia, investite di florigeri convolvoli, di tutto expresso, et de qui et de lì extavano quadrangule d’oro striate, et da una all’altra inarchuava, cum requisite trabe, et Zophoro, et coronice, cum debita proiectura sopra il capitello vitrino della rotonda. Il solido della quale subiecto ad gli volubili, era fincto diaspro cum multiplice coloratione coeunte et illustre. Gli quali volubili dal sodo proportionatamente alquanto erano sublevati et evulsi, le fauce degli archi erano obstipate di Rombi vitrini purgatissimi, uno Triente il suo diametro, tra binati canaleoli simigliantemente inclaustrati et circunsepti cum diversa enchaustica picturatione ad gli sensi peracceptissima. La area ancora tutta era strata di rotundatione vitrinule, et altre convenientissime figuratione, ad suprema gratia, cum mutuo consenso, et stabile cohaesione, cum praecipuo collustramento gemmale, sencia supposita adulteratione di fogliatura. Sopra gli fiori spirava una praecipua fragrantia da uno illimento, peruncti et rosulati. Peritissimamente quivi la dulciloqua Logistica fece alquanta narratione, physiculabonda laudava la praestante factione, et la nobilitate della materia et arte et invento. (Quale non se trovarebbe in Muriano) et vituperando la sua natura, et dixe, Poliphile, ascendamo questa excellentissima specula, propinqua al giardino. Et rimanendo giù Thelemia, per cochleata scansione, nella superna parte coaequata alacramente salissemo. time, and of the subtlest artifice. Which in its circuit and compass was as great as that where the majestic residence stood; round about, cleaving to the walls, there stretched fitted garden-boxes, in which, in place of greenery, every plant was of the purest glass — box-trees clipped (beyond what one can imagine and believe) distinguishedly, with their stems of gold, such material being brought thither. Between the one and the other of which there alternated a cypress, its height not exceeding two paces, and of the box one. Filled then with a marvellous feigning of many-shaped simples, with a most elegant following of nature, and with the most joyful and varied forms of flowers, with a distinct and most welcome colouring.

The flat lip of the square opening of these little boxes, or raised beds, was corniced with gold, with the subtlest lineaments, well polished and adorned; the faces of which, of glass plates gilded within, and with a wonderful graving of a most curious history, stood out most beautifully, enclosed within golden channels which held them bitingly, with the lowest socle raised a sixth of a foot.

The hedge going round the garden, at a nice distance, was with bellied columns of the said material, clothed with flower-bearing bindweed, all in relief; and here and there there stood fluted squares of gold, and from one to the other it arched, with the required beam, and frieze, and cornice, with a due projection above the glass capital of the round column. The solid part of which beneath the arches was feigned jasper with a manifold colouring, meeting and bright. Which arches were somewhat raised and drawn up from the solid in proportion; the throats of the arches were stopped with rhombs of the purest glass, a third of a foot their diameter, between twinned little channels likewise enclosed and hedged about with a various encaustic painting most acceptable to the senses.

The whole area besides was strewn with little glass roundings and other most fitting figurings, to the utmost grace, with a mutual consent and a steady cohesion, with a chief gemlike shining, without any adulterating of foliage set beneath. Above the flowers there breathed a chief fragrance from an anointing, they being smeared and made rosy.

Most skilfully here the sweet-spoken Logistica made some little narration, and, discoursing of nature, praised the excellent making, and the nobility of the material and the art and the invention (such as would not be found at Murano), and blaming its nature, she said: "Poliphilo, let us climb this most excellent watch-tower, near the garden." And Thelemia remaining below, by a winding stair we climbed cheerfully to the levelled upper part. Where she showed me, with a divine eloquence, a garden of a very wide circuit, drawn out in the form of a various intricate labyrinth, and its circling passages not to be walked,

ma navigabili. Imperoché in loco delle gressibile strate, correvano rivuli d’aque. Il quale mysterioso loco era de sé agro salubre et di glebe foelice amoeno ferace, vario di omni copia di suavi fructi referto, et di exuberantia di fonti ornato, et di omni florulenta virentia iocundo, di omni solacio diffuso et di maximo oblectamento. Et dixe. Pensiculo io Poliphile che di questo mirando sito non intendi la sorte conditionata sua. Attendi. Chi entra, non pole retrocedere. Ma come manifesto vedi quelle specule et indi et quindi distribute, sette circuitione una da l’altra distano, et il danno extremo che sortiscono gli introeunti questo è che in quella specula centrica nel patore hiato del suo ingresso uno mortifero draco voracissimo et invisibile dimora. Et questo è dannosissimo in una parte, et nell’altra quiete, non lo potere videre, et extremo terribile non lo poter vitare. Il quale et nel ingresso et nel progresso dove lui a caso et statuito vole, devora gli introgressi. Et si tra una specula et l’altra non gli occide, passano securi tutta la septenaria circuitione fina alla specula propinqua. Dunque quelli che quivi entrano per quella prima Turre. (Mira il titulo di graeca annotatione scripto et accuratissimo pensicula. DOXA KOSMIKE HOS POMPHOLYS) vano cum la navicula cum alveo secondo, et sencia cura alcuna et fatica, gli fructi et fiori cadeno nel scaphidio, et cum summo piacere et gioco per le sette rivolutione discorreno, fina alla seconda specula. Et considera Poliphile quanta chiarecia è di aere in questo exordio, fina alla mediana specula accrescendo, et d’indi paulatinamente circa il centro decrescente se infusca tetro et illumino. In quella primaria torre, praesidente habita aeternalmente una pientissima matrona, et benigna largitora, dinanti alla quale stabilissimo sta una veterrima et sortitia et promptuaria urna, ornata di sette littere graece come vedi cusì. THESPION stipata di fatali melli, et ad gli introeunti a ciascuno lepidissima et munifica uno di quelli dona, sencia rispecto di conditione, ma secondo che occorre la eventicia dispositione. Questi recepti fora venendo incominciano a navichare nel labyrintho, sepiti gli meati di rose et arbori fructigeri. Transacta dunque la prima longa circuitione delle sette revolutione di Ariete ad la extrema cauda pissatile pervenendo alla seconda specula trovano innumere puelle di diversa conditione, le quale a tutti gli domandano la ostensione degli sui melli, et monstratolo ad quelle. Esse peritissime cognoscono il propriato et disposito mello, et quello amplexantilo hospite l’acceptano, et seco l’envitano, le altre sette circuitione pervagare, et secondo la sua inclinata promptecia, et cum diverso exercitio individue gli conducono fina alla tertia specula. In questo loco chi vole perseverare cum la sua comite, quella nunque ello abandona né lassa. Perché quivi altre più voluptuose damigelle trovano, et molti repudiano le h iii

but to be sailed. For in place of walkable roads there ran little streams of water. Which mysterious place was of itself a wholesome and pleasant field, of happy soil and fruitful, various and filled with every plenty of sweet fruits, and adorned with an overflowing of springs, and joyful with every flowering greenness, poured out with every solace and with the greatest delight. And she said:

"I think, Poliphilo, that of this wondrous site you do not understand its appointed lot. Attend. He who enters cannot go back. But, as you plainly see, those watch-towers set here and there stand seven circuits apart one from another; and the extreme harm that falls to those who enter is this: that in that central tower, in the open gap of its entry, a deadly dragon dwells, most devouring and invisible. And this is most harmful on the one hand, and on the other quiet: not to be able to see it, and utterly terrible not to be able to shun it. Which, both at the entry and in the going forward, wherever it chances and is appointed to wish, devours those who have entered. And if between one tower and another it does not kill them, they pass safely through the whole sevenfold circuit as far as the next tower.

"Those, then, who enter here by that first tower (look at the title written in Greek noting, and think most carefully upon it: DOXA KOSMIKE HOS POMPHOLYX) go with the little boat with the current, and without any care or labour the fruits and flowers fall into the skiff, and with the utmost pleasure and sport they run through the seven windings as far as the second tower. And consider, Poliphilo, how great the brightness of the air is in this beginning, growing to the middle tower, and thence little by little, about the centre, darkening and growing gloomy and lightless.

"In that first tower there dwells eternally, presiding, a most pious matron and kindly giver, before whom there stands most steadily a most ancient urn of lots and of dispensing, adorned with seven Greek letters as you see thus: THESPION, packed with fated tokens; and to each of those who enter, most charmingly and munificently she gives one of those, without respect of condition, but according as the chance disposition falls out. These, being received, coming forth they begin to sail in the labyrinth, the passages hedged with roses and fruit-bearing trees.

"The first long circuit of the seven windings being passed, from the Ram to the last fishy tail, coming to the second tower, they find countless girls of divers condition, who ask of all the showing of their tokens; and it being shown to them, they, most skilled, know the proper and disposed token, and embracing him they receive him as a guest, and invite him with them to wander through the other seven circuits; and according to his bent readiness, and with divers exercise, inseparably they lead them as far as the third tower. In this place whoever will persevere with his companion, she never abandons nor leaves him. Because there they find other more voluptuous damsels, and many cast off the

Adventati alla tertia et giunti, et de qui facendo discesso verso la quarta, trovano l’aqua più contrastare, quantunque in questi sette obliqui corsi, si veda grande et variabile et incostante dilecto. Pervenuti alla quarta specula, altre giovenette trovano athlete et pugnatrice, et queste examinati gli primi melli, traheno gli amicali al suo exercitio. Et quelli che non hano la sua consimilitudine, meare permeteno cum le sue. Et in queste circuitione l’aqua ancora trovano più obstante, ove bisogna maiore studio et erumnale fatica di remigare. Alla quinta specula applicati, la trovano speculabile, nella quale contemplano, quanto è bello il suo simigliante, et cum questo periocundo et optatissimo oblectamento, nella mente servabondi cum più laborioso successo passano. In questo loco si discute enucleatamente quello motivo et aureo dicto. Medium tenuere beati. Non liniale, non locale, ma temporale di questo passo et termine, ove cum sincero examine il medio si discerne cum chi se ha coniugato la foelicitate, o beatitudine d’ingegno, o vero di copia. La quale non seco havendola, negli sequenti meno quasi valeno aquistare. Facendo de qui commeato, l’aque per gli amfracti circulari tendere alquanto incominciano il pernice corso verso il medio finale, et cum poco, o vero senza remigatione sono deducti alla sexta. Quivi trovano elegante Matrone, cum coelibi et pudichi aspecti, intente al divino culto, per l’aspecto divo delle quale gli hospiti capti nel suo amore, il pristino damnando et convertendo in nausea, cum queste fano quieto commercio, et pacato transito le sette rivolutione. Transacte queste per le sequente, cum fuscitate di aere, cum molti incommodi et erumnoso viagio, molto curriculo perpendono il traiecto. Perché più che la rivolutione degli meati se approxima nella figura al centro, tanto sono più brevicule. Et tanto più si discorre lapsi cum inefficace celeritate, et cum lubrice ambage, nel voragine della centrea specula, et cum suprema afflictione d’animo per reminiscentia degli belli lochi et societate relicta, et tanto più che cognoscono non potere ritornare nel voltare la prora della sua carina, perché continuamente alla puppa, sono le prore degli altri navanti. Accedendo a maiore pena il titulo spaventoso sopra lo ingresso della mediana specula, cum tale attico expresso. THEON LYKOS DYSALGETOS. Et quivi considerando il displicibile titulo, sono moerenti quasi di essere intrati in tale labyrinthoso pomerio, advegnia che in sé tante delitie compraehenda, et ad tanta miserrima et inevitabile necessitate subiace. Surridendo poscia Logistica, theophorita subiunxe, Poliphile, in questo vorace hiato sede una severa spectatrice stateraria, et degli intranti diiudicatrice, cum aequa lance, libra et scrupulosamente compondera la actione. Per la quale altronde meglio, o vero pegio

"first and cleave to these. So that, departing from that second tower to come to the third, they find the waters somewhat contrary, and it takes the service of rowing. Having come and arrived at the third, and thence making their departure towards the fourth, they find the water resisting more — however much in these seven slanting courses a great and variable and inconstant delight is seen.

"Come to the fourth tower, they find other young women, wrestlers and fighters, and these, having examined the first tokens, draw those friendly to their exercise. And those who have not their like they let pass on with their own. And in these circuits they find the water still more against them, where there is need of greater study and toilsome labour of rowing.

"Landing at the fifth tower, they find it mirroring, in which they contemplate how fair is their like; and with this most joyful and most longed-for delight, keeping it in mind, they pass on with a more laborious course. In this place is plainly discussed that saying, and golden: the blessed have held to the middle. Not of line, not of place, but of time is this passage and bound, where with a sincere examination the middle is discerned, and with whom happiness is coupled, or the blessedness of wit, or of plenty. Which, not having with them, in what follows they are the less able to gain it.

"Taking leave from here, the waters through the circling windings begin to draw somewhat their swift course towards the middle end, and with little rowing, or none, they are carried to the sixth. Here they find elegant matrons, with unwedded and chaste looks, intent upon the divine worship; by the divine aspect of whom the guests, taken with love of them, condemning the former and turning to a loathing of it, hold with these a quiet commerce and a peaceful passage through the seven windings.

"These being passed, through those that follow, with a darkening of the air, with many discomforts and a toilsome voyage, they weigh the crossing by much running. Because the more the winding of the passages draws near in the figure to the centre, the shorter they are. And so much the more one runs, fallen, with an ineffectual swiftness, and with slippery wanderings, into the whirlpool of the central tower; and with the utmost affliction of soul for the remembrance of the fair places and the fellowship left behind, and the more that they know they cannot return by turning the prow of their keel, because continually at their stern are the prows of the others sailing. There comes to a greater pain the frightful title above the entrance of the middle tower, in this Attic expression: THEON LYKOS DYSALGETOS.

"And here, considering the displeasing title, they grieve at having entered such a labyrinthine orchard, seeing that it holds in itself so many delights and yet lies under so wretched and unavoidable a necessity." Then Logistica, smiling, inspired, added: "Poliphilo, in this devouring gap there sits a severe beholder holding the scales, and a judge of those who enter, who with an even balance weighs and scrupulously ponders their action. By which they might fare better, or worse,

Discendamo alla nostra consorte Thelemia, la quale dimandando della nostra mora, Logistica li rispose, non era sufficiente solamente al nostro curioso Poliphilo di vedere, ma ancora ch’io li desse comperto di quello, che la materia non potendo ire, cum il mio interpretato almeno intendando, el possi cognoscere, et dicto questo, Thelemia dice. Andiamo a spasso all’altro giardino, non meno delectoso, et di delitie conferto, che il vitrino contiguo allo alamento dextro del superbo magno et regio pallatio, et quivi introgressi, io rimansi tutto allucinato et excessivamente mirabondo di videre operatura difficile, non tanto di fede, ma di narratione, il quale aequicapace era al vitriculato, cum simigliante dispositione di altane, cum ornati labri di coronatione et aureo socco, excluso lo operamento degli obvallanti parieti et materia, imperoché di seta tutto era artificiato excellentissime, gli buxi et cupressi sericei, stipiti et rami d’oro, non sencia interseminatione aptissima di gemme, et le bustuarie altane confertissime di simplici della matre invidi, cum iocundissima florulentia et desideratissima, cum omni exquisito coloramento, Olidi, et similmente quali gli altri vitrini, ma gli ambienti parieti di mirando opificio et d’incredibile impensa, erano tutti di operimento margaritale, questo è, che tute le facie vidi coperte di lucidissime perle, in uno congeste et coacervate, et cum densa cohaesione, di mediocre crassitudine inseme copulate, et di sopra bellissimamente, germinando fora delle capse varicante et verdissima hedera cum la fogliatura alquanto dalle perle sublevata et pensile, cum gli stipiti d’oro artificiosissimamente serpenti, cum exigue radicule per le margarite errante, cum summa et exquisitissima politura. Et Bacce di gioielli, innexe ad gli Corymbi, cum praestante divisione, per le quadrangule auree capitulate, cum maiestrevole et requisita sequentia di Trabe, Zophoro, et corona d’oro. Le facie delle buste ritramate cum ponto di razzo di historiette d’amore et venatione, in fili d’oro, et argentei, et seta, cum tanta acommodissima picturatione fincte, che niente aequabile. Il solo della aequatissima Area, vedevase gratissimo di seta verdigiante villoso, quale spectatissimo prato, et in medio dell’area una rotunda clausula extava, cum una levata cupula di virgule d’oro, cum multiplici et florigeri rosarii ricoperto egregiamente del dicto operamento. Quasi ch’io direi, molto più praeacceptatissimo questa factura ad gli sensi che la verace. Sotto il quale tecto alla forma ambiente, erano sedili di rubicondo diaspro, et tutta la intersticia area, d’una solida rotunditate quanto il capace ambito di diaspro giallo, di mixture discole confusamente conveniendo et in uno coeunte lepidissimamente adulterato. "elsewhere. And because it would be long to tell all, let what is told be enough for now. Let us go down to our companion Thelemia." Who, asking of our delay, Logistica answered her that it was not enough only for our curious Poliphilo to see, but that I should also give him a knowledge of that which, since the matter could not go further, he might at least understand and know by my interpretation. And this said, Thelemia says:

"Let us go for a walk to the other garden, no less delightful and filled with delights: the glass one adjoining the right wall of the proud, great and royal palace." And having entered there, I remained wholly dazzled and exceedingly full of wonder to see a workmanship hard not so much of belief as of telling. Which was of equal compass with the glass one, with a like disposition of raised beds, with adorned lips of cornice-work and a golden socle, save for the workmanship and material of the enclosing walls — for it was all made most excellently of silk: the box-trees and cypresses of silk, their stems and branches of gold, not without a most apt sowing among them of gems; and the standing beds most thickly filled with the simples that the mother of them envies, with a most joyful and most longed-for flowering, with every exquisite colouring, fragrant, and like the other glass ones.

But the surrounding walls, of a wondrous workmanship and of incredible cost, were all of a covering of pearl — that is, I saw all the faces covered with the brightest pearls, heaped and gathered into one, and with a thick cohesion, joined together of a middling thickness; and above them most beautifully, sprouting out of the boxes, a straggling and greenest ivy with its foliage somewhat raised from the pearls and hanging, with its stems of gold most artfully creeping, with slender little roots wandering among the pearls, with the utmost and most exquisite polish. And berries of jewels, knit to the clusters, with an excellent division, headed by the golden squares, with a masterly and required following of beam, frieze, and cornice of gold.

The faces of the beds rewoven in tapestry stitch with little histories of love and of hunting, in threads of gold and silver and silk, feigned with so most fitting a painting that nothing could equal it. The ground of the most level area was seen most welcome, of green silk pile, like a most notable meadow; and in the middle of the area there stood a round enclosure, with a raised dome of little rods of gold, distinguishedly covered with manifold flower-bearing rose-trees of the said workmanship.

So that I should almost say this making far more acceptable to the senses than the true one. Beneath which roof, in the going-round form, were seats of ruddy jasper; and all the space between of a solid rounding, as far as the ample circuit went, of yellow jasper, of various mixtures confusedly agreeing and most charmingly adulterated in one. With

Diqué altro al praesente desideratissimo non harei unquantulo appretiato. Voglio che tu sapi, essere di maiore oblectamento allo intellecto le cose obiective, che ad gli sensi tanto. Per questo, intramo quivi a satisfare alle due receptibile operatione. La quale cum praeclarissimo comitato vicino ad questo viridario introdussime in uno altro, ove mirai uno arcuato areostylo, dal Area fina al supremo inflexo, passi cinque alti, et tre in hiato, tutto lateritio, cum Symmetriato displuvio, o vero laxamento, in gyro continuo, tutto bellissimamente investito di verdigiante edera et contecto, non apparendo minimo vestigio murale, et erano cento Archi, concludevano uno Pomerio floridante. Per singulo dunque degli Archi, era situata una Ara di rubente Porphyro optimamente liniata. Et in qualunque superassideva una statua aurea di Nympha cum divo effigiato, cum habito variante, et lo ornato del capo, et di acto, ciascuna riverente verso il mediano centro di questo viridario. In questo medio centrico mysteriosamente era fundata una basi di diaphano Calcedonio in forma cubica. Et sopra questo nel quadratile contento stava collocato una rotundatione, dui pedi alta, et di diametro passo uno et semi, di rubicundissimo diaspro. Superassideva poscia ad questo uno Triangulo, per il capto della subiecta figura, di altitudine passo uno et semi, di nigerrima petra. Gli anguli del quale Trigono, extendevano al limbo del subiacente Plyntho. Nella perpolita et expedita fronte di ciascuna, appacta era una spectatissima imagine nell’aspecto diva, grave, et veneranda, cum gli pedi sopra lo immune della figura Trigonia del suppresso rotundo, di procera statura, quanto la nigerrima petra, alla quale cum il dorso adhaerivano, cum gli brachii extensi levorso et dextrorso ad gli anguli, contenivano una copia stipata negli hebetati, o vero decacuminati anguli affixa la mutilatione degli diti aequata uno pede et sextante, di oro purissimo. Le copie, lori, et statue praefulgevano, cum le mane invilupate degli vaganti et varicosi lori. Per la planitie della petra volanti. Et cum habito Nympheo, non humana, ma diva operatura. Et per tanto

so great a shining that they rivalled every object set before them.

Sitting solaced here beneath it a while, the most witty Thelemia took the lyre that she carried with her, and with a heavenly melody and unheard-of sweetness of sweet speech began to sing the origin of so many delights and the rule of her Queen, and with what adornment her companion Logistica's sweet fellowship was — I marvelling that Apollo did not come there to listen, so excessive was the harmony she uttered. So that nothing else at present, however longed for, would I have valued at all.

The divine poem being said, at once the god-loving Logistica, taking me by the hand, led me forth from that place, saying: "Poliphilo, I would have you know that things of the understanding are of a greater delight to the intellect than things of sense are to the senses. For this, let us enter here, to satisfy both the receiving faculties."

Who, with a most distinguished company, led me in near this garden to another, where I beheld an arched colonnade of widely spaced arches, from the floor to the topmost bend five paces high and three in the opening, all of brick, with a symmetried slope, or spread, in a continuous ring, all most beautifully clothed and covered with green ivy, no least trace of the wall appearing; and there were a hundred arches, and they closed in a flowering orchard.

Beneath each one of the arches, then, was set an altar of ruddy porphyry, excellently lined. And upon each there sat a golden statue of a Nymph with a divine likeness, with varying dress, and the ornament of the head, and of gesture, each of them reverent towards the middle centre of this garden.

In this middle centre there was mysteriously founded a base of translucent chalcedony in a cubic form. And above this, within the square compass, there was placed a rounding two feet high, and of a diameter of a pace and a half, of the ruddiest jasper. Above this then sat a triangle, by the measure of the figure beneath, of a height of a pace and a half, of the blackest stone. The corners of which triangle stretched to the edge of the plinth below it.

On the well-polished and free front of each there was fitted a most notable image, in aspect divine, grave and venerable, with their feet upon the untouched part of the triangular figure of the rounding pressed beneath, of a tall stature, as tall as the blackest stone, to which they clung with their backs, with their arms stretched to the left and to the right towards the corners; they held a horn of plenty packed full, fixed at the blunted, or cut-off, corners, the shortening of their fingers made even, a foot and a sixth, of purest gold. The horns, thongs and statues shone forth, with their hands wrapped in the wandering and straggling thongs. Flying along the flat of the stone. And in nymphlike dress, a workmanship not human but divine. And therefore

DYS A LO TOS. Nella circulare mirai tre charactere hieraglyphice perpendiculare sotto gli pedi di ciascuna imagine. Et primo era impressa la forma del Sole. Poscia sotto l’altra uno antiquario Temone. Ultimo appareva una platina, cum una fiamma intro.

Sopra il porrecto degli anguli della obscura petra, rimando vidi uno monstro aegyptio aureo, iacente quadrupedo. L’uno degli quali havea la facia tutta humana. L’altro semihumana, et semibellua. La tertia tutta belluale. Cum una vitta el fronte ambiente, cum dui lemnisci contegendo l’orechie dependuli, et al collo et pecto similmente perlambenti. Et uno per el dorso descendente, cum il corpo di Leena, cum il volto al protenso. Dunque sopra el tergo di ciascuno, praemeva una massicia Pyra aurea triangulare, fina al suo supremo propilato, linee cinque del faciale imo, o vero del suo diametro. In qualunque fronte era inscalpto uno circulo tanto, et di sopra il circulo una litera graeca. OMICRON Ne l’altra facia uno circulo, et sopra una littera. OMEGA. Nella tertia planitie uno circulo, et sopra sé una litera NY. Incomincioe quivi la Theophrasta Logistica praeconizare et a dire. Per queste figure la coeleste harmonia consiste. Et advertisci Poliphile, che queste figure cum perpetua affinitate et coniunctione, sono praeclarissimi monumenti antiquarii, et aegyptii hieraglyphi, gli quali insinuare volendo ti dicono. let the tomb of Tarina, queen of the Sacae, yield here.

In the lowest figure, on each square side, in the flat face, were carved Greek letters — three, one, two, and three, in this order: DYS A LO TOS. In the round one I beheld three hieroglyphic characters, perpendicular, beneath the feet of each image. And first was stamped the form of the Sun. Then, beneath the next, an antique rudder. Last there appeared a dish, with a flame within it.

Above the outstretched corners of the dark stone, looking, I saw an Egyptian monster of gold, lying four-footed. One of which had a wholly human face. The other half human and half beast. The third wholly beastly. With a fillet going round the brow, with two ribbons covering the ears, hanging down, and likewise licking along the neck and breast. And one descending down the back; with the body of a lioness, the face turned forward.

Upon the back of each, then, there pressed a massive golden triangular pyramid, up to its topmost cover five lines of the lowest face, or of its diameter. On each front there was carved a circle of that measure, and above the circle a Greek letter, OMICRON. On the next face a circle, and above it a letter, OMEGA. On the third flat a circle, and above it a letter, NY.

Here Logistica, well taught, began to proclaim and to say: "By these figures the celestial harmony stands. And take heed, Poliphilo, that these figures, with a perpetual affinity and conjunction, are most distinguished antique monuments and Egyptian hieroglyphs, which, wishing to hint at it, say to you: To the divine and infinite Trinity of one essence. The lowest figure is consecrated to the divinity, because from unity it is

p. 130confidence: unstatedverified

producta, et per omni lato è una, et di qualunque figura è primario stabilimento, et in omni basi constante et permansura. La circulare superapposita è immune di principio, et di finimento. Nella planitie circunferita dilla quale, quelli tre liniamenti sono contenti, all’aspecto directe di ciascuna imagine, secondo la sua proprietate attributo. Il Sole cum iocundissima luce, poté omni cosa, et la natura sua ad dio se attribuisse. La secunda è il Temone, che il provido governo exprime del universo, cum infinita sapientia. Il tertio è il vaso igneo, sento diciò una partecipatione d’amore. Et benché distincte siano le tre imagine, tamen è una cosa inseme complexa, et singularmente amplexada et sempiternalmente in uno connexe, benignamente il suo bene communicabile, come poi rimare per le copie ad gli cubiti della figura existente. Et continuando la fatiloquia Logistica consequente dixe. Alla imagine del Sole, nota questa parola graeca, ADIEGETOS Ad quella del Temone, specula quello notato graeco, ADIACHORISTOS. Ad quella del foco inscalpto era, ADIEREUNES. Dunque per tali effecti, subsidendo subiecti sono poscia quelli tre animali al Obelisco aureo sopra incubante, che sono di tale figure tre maxime et celebre opinione. Et cusì come la humana effigie praesta efficacemente all’altre, cusì né più né meno l’opinato. In la Pyra sono tre lati plani liniati di tre circuli uno per singulo tempo significanti. Praeterito, praesente, et futuro. Intendi che niuna altra figura poté continere quelli tre circuii, se non in quella invariabili. Et niuno degli mortali cernere poté perfectamente né videre inseme dui lati della dicta figura, salvo uno integramente, che è il praesente. Et però sapientissimamente furono quelli tre charactere impresse, OON Per la quale cosa Poliphile, non me accusando prolixa, ma expeditissima di rectarte in tale narrato. Sapi che la prima basiale figura è solo ad sé cognita, et ad uno tanto humano et diaphana, ma ad nui non total chiarecia. Poscia colui che di ingegno è dotato, ascende sopra, et solertemente considera della figura il suo coloramento. Indagando più alla tertia figura ascendeno, la quale di sua coloratione è obscura et obstrusa in quelle tre imagine d’oro, et circumvallata. Ultimo più sopra scandendo, considerano una figura in trino aspecto, et d’indi quanto più al praeacuto gracilamento contemplabondi saliscono, et quivi quantunque instructissimi, non hano però altro acquisito, che el se vide, che questo è, ma che cosa sia, restano inscii, invalidi, et imbecilli. Havendo quivi Logistica praestantemente gli probatissimi praecepti cum absolutissima cognitione deprompti, cum sagace solertia, dal effusissimo gremio della natura divina decerpti. Io incominciai

"brought forth, and on every side it is one, and of every figure it is the first steadying, and in every base constant and abiding. The round one set above it is free of beginning and of ending. In the encompassed flat of which those three lineaments are held, set directly before the face of each image, attributed according to its property.

"The Sun, with a most joyful light, can do all things, and its nature is attributed to God. The second is the rudder, which expresses the provident government of the universe, with infinite wisdom. The third is the fiery vessel, and I feel of it a sharing of love. And though the three images are distinct, yet they are one thing folded together, and singularly embraced, and everlastingly knit in one, kindly communicating its good — as one may see by the horns of plenty at the elbows of the figure."

And continuing her fate-telling, Logistica said further: "At the image of the Sun, mark this Greek word: ADIEGETOS. At that of the rudder, look at that Greek noting: ADIACHORISTOS. At that of the fire was carved: ADIEREUNETOS. By such effects, then, those three animals are set below, subject to the golden obelisk lying above them, which are three great and famous opinions of such figures. And as the human likeness effectually surpasses the others, so, neither more nor less, does the opinion.

"On the pyramid are three flat sides lined with three circles, each one signifying a time: past, present, and to come. Understand that no other figure could hold those three circles unchanging save that one. And none of mortals could perfectly discern nor see two sides of the said figure together, save one wholly, which is the present. And therefore most wisely were those three characters stamped: OON.

"For which cause, Poliphilo — not accusing me of being long-winded, but most ready to set you right in such a telling — know that the first base figure is known only to itself, and to one so far as human and translucent; but to us not in full clearness. Then he who is gifted with wit climbs above and skilfully considers the colouring of the figure. Searching further, they climb to the third figure, which by its colouring is dark and shut up in those three images of gold, and walled about.

"Last, climbing higher still, they consider a figure in a threefold aspect; and thence, the more they climb contemplating towards the sharpest narrowing, and there, however well instructed, they have nevertheless gained nothing else than that one sees that it is; but what it may be, they remain ignorant, unavailing, and feeble."

Logistica having here excellently set out the most approved precepts with a most complete knowledge, with a sagacious skill, plucked from the most abundant lap of divine nature, I began

sencia haesitamento persentire dellectatione maiore, che qualunque altra mirabile opera, cum gli ochii mei gratiosamente conspecta, pensitante lo obelisco di tanto mysterio, cum ineffabile aequalitate statario, et ad firmitudine et perpetuitate integro, solido, et aeterno, cum aequatione di parilitate infriabile, et incorruptibile perseverante. Ove spirava spirito gratissimo del coelo, cum aure invariabile, in questo prato circumflorido di largo et circulare spatio permanente fundato, cum fruteti curvescenti di omni fructo, di suavitate gustabile, et di omni salute stipato, cum perpetua virentia, cum directione di regulato ordine ad venustate, et lepiditate, et decoramento dispositi, et consiti, cum praecipuo studio della natura alla perfectione mirificamente producti, et dal pretiosissimo oro indesinente collustrati. Silendo dunque Logistica, ambe per le mane tenentime, per lo hiato, o vero apertione di uno degli archi, festivamente uscissimo, fora la praecinctione della haederale convallatura, et progressi d’indi, medio di esse contento meante, loetissimamente dicendo Thelemia, andiamo hogi mai alle ordinate porte. Diqué per la amoena plaga, et patria, cum prompto et parato progresso procedenti, Mirava il coelo ripurgato da omni fuscante nube, cum suavi, faceti, et peculiari ragionamenti. Io che d’intendere il tutto delle inextimabile divitie, inconsiderabile delitie, et inaequabile thesoro (Al quale ceda Osyri degli dui templi d’oro fabricatore, uno ad Iove coeleste, et l’altro al regio) della Regina Sacratissima inexplebile, gli feci tale questiuncula. Ditimi beate adolescentule, si grato hora vi sia la mia curiosa petitione. Tra tutti gli praetiosi lapilli, che io ho potuto chiaramente videre, di grande talento et praetio imo incomparabile et sencia aestimatione pretiosissimo iudicai. Molto et assai più non fue il Iaspide, che la effigie impresa havea di Nerone toracata. Né tale ancora fue il coruscante Topacio della statua di Arsinoe Regina Araba. without hesitation to feel a greater delight than in any other marvellous work graciously beheld with my eyes — thinking upon the obelisk of so great a mystery, standing with an unspeakable evenness, and whole in its firmness and perpetuity, solid and eternal, with an equality of likeness not to be crumbled, and enduring incorruptible.

Where there breathed a most welcome breath of heaven, with unchanging airs, in this meadow flowering round about, founded and abiding in a wide and circling space, with bending shrubs of every fruit, sweet to the taste, and packed with every health, with a perpetual greenness, with the ordering of a ruled arrangement for comeliness and charm and adornment, disposed and planted, brought wonderfully to perfection by the chief study of nature, and unceasingly lit by the most precious gold.

Logistica being silent, then, both of them holding me by the hands, we went out festively through the gap, or opening, of one of the arches, outside the girdle of the ivied enclosure; and going on from there through the middle of that compass, Thelemia saying most joyfully: "Let us go now to the appointed doors." So that, going forward through the pleasant region and country with a ready and prepared advance, I beheld the sky purged of every darkening cloud, with sweet, witty and particular discoursings.

I, being unsatisfied in understanding the whole of the inestimable riches, unconsiderable delights, and unmatchable treasure (to which let Osiris yield, the builder of the two temples of gold, one to heavenly Jove and the other to the royal) of the most sacred Queen, put to them this little question:

"Tell me, blessed young women, if my curious asking be welcome to you now. Among all the precious little stones that I have been able to see clearly, I judged one of great worth and price — nay, incomparable and most precious beyond esteeming. Much and far more was it than the jasper that had stamped upon it the likeness of Nero in his breastplate. Nor such either was the flashing topaz of the statue of Arsinoe, the Arabian queen. Nor was so great a cost laid out for the gem for which Nonius the senator was proscribed, as for that shining and incomparable diamond, of so unseen a beauty and thickness, that hung from the richest necklace above the snowy breast of our divine Queen. What carving was that? For so great was its flashing, and being besides at a distance, I could not perfectly discern it. So that this only remains, which holds me anxious and my mind in suspense to know."

Logistica, taking note of my honest question, answered at once, saying: "Know, Poliphilo, that in the gem is carved the image of the highest Jove sitting crowned upon his throne. And beneath his majestic and holy footstool are the ruined giants, who wished to climb up to his most high seat, level with the height of his most ample sceptre. And he struck them with lightning. In his left hand he holds a

"little flame of fire. In the right a horn of plenty stuffed full of good, and he stands with his arms spread. This is the whole of what is held in the most precious jewel."

Then I said: "What do those two very unsuited things mean that he holds in his divine hands?" Thelemia, witty, answered: "By his infinite goodness the immortal Jupiter makes a show to earth-born men that they may have at their wish that of the two hands which pleases them, freely to choose."

And without delay I added: "Since our pleasant talking has fallen here, most welcome companions — my kindled desire to understand not being yet wholly fulfilled, and since my boldness did not displease you — tell me this, I pray you. Before my horrible fright I saw, of a daring greatness and art, a stone monster, which is an elephant. Entering, then, into its empty belly, I found two tombs, with writings of an ambiguous meaning, about finding treasure: that I should scorn the body and carry away the head."

Logistica, without any other thinking, expounding it, answered cheerfully: "Poliphilo, I know fully what you ask; I would however have you know that not without a great admiration of human wit, and with an ardent study and incredible diligence, was that huge engine made, with a perplexity of the intellect to understand its divine conceit. Take heed that above its front there hangs the ornament with that double-headed writing, which in the mother and common tongue says: labour and industry. For in the world, whoever living would have treasure, let him leave rotting idleness, signified by the great body, and take the adorned head, which is that writing — and you shall have treasure by toiling with industry."

No sooner were her soothing and effectual words ended than, being perfectly taught the whole, I gave thanks for her affable kindness; yet, being still most eager to search out all that I had before imperfectly grasped, and having made myself familiar with them, I made a third request: "Most wise Nymph, in my coming out of the underground caverns I found an antique and elegant bridge. Which, on both its parapets, in porphyry stone on the one side, and on the other of ophite, I saw certain hieroglyphs carved. And of both I was the interpreter; but I remained ignorant only of the branches, not knowing them, which were bound to the horns, and then why in porphyry stone, and not in the like of the other side."

At once, without other pondering, she kindly answered me: "Of the branches, the one is

And thus, with honest and most approved discourse, we came most festively to a most charming river. Upon the banks of which I saw a gracious plane-grove, besides other greenest little trees, and water shoots excellently set and placed, with lotuses set between. Where there crossed a proud stone bridge of three arches, with its ends upon the banks above the firmest foundations, with the piers keeled at their two fronts to hold the structure most firm, and with most noble parapets.

In which, at the middle curve of the wedge beneath the arch, here and there, there stood out, raised and well polished, a porphyry square with a gable, holding a sunk carving of hieroglyphs. On the right at our crossing I saw a matron bound with a serpent, sitting upon one haunch only, and with the other leg in the act of rising; with the hand on the side she sat on she held a pair of wings, and in the other, on the rising side, a tortoise. Opposite there was a circle, the centre of which two little spirits held, turning their backs with their little breasts to the circumference.

Logistica etiam quivi me dixe. Poliphile, questi hieraglyphi io so che tu non l’intendi. Ma fano molto al proposito, a cui tende alle tre porte. Et però in monumento delli transeunti opportunissime sono collocati. El circulo dice. Medium tenuere beati. L’altro. Velocitatem sedendo, tarditatem tempera surgendo. Hora nella mente tua discussamente rumina. El quale ponte poscia era cum moderato prono, dimostrante la solerte disquisitione, et l’arte et lo ingegno del perspicacissimo artifice et inventore, collaudava in esso la aeterna soliditate, la quale non è cognita dagli caecucienti moderni, et pseudoarchitecti, sencia litteratura, mensura et arte, fucando, et di picture, et di liniamenti operiendo exta per omni modo il fabricato inconcinno et difforme. Il quale era tuto di marmoro Hymetio venustissimo. Havendo nui el ponte transacto, ambulavamo sotto per le fresche umbre, di vario garrito di avicule suavemente celebrate. Ad uno saxoso et cotico loco, ove gli excelsi et ardui monti se attollevano, pervenissimo. Et d’indi poscia contiguo ad una abrupta et invia, et salebrosa montagna, tuta derosa et piena di hernia scabricie. Alta fino nel aere, a ppendice fina delumbata, et nuda de omni virentia, et monti adryi circunquaque. Et quivi erano interscalpte le tre randuscule porte, rudemente excavate nel vivo saxo, opera antiquaria, et oltra il credere veterrima in magna asperugine di sito. * * * * * *

Logistica said to me here too: "Poliphilo, these hieroglyphs I know you do not understand. But they are much to the purpose for one who goes to the three doors. And therefore they are most fitly set here as a monument for those passing by. The circle says: the blessed have held to the middle. The other: temper swiftness by sitting, and slowness by rising. Now turn it over discussingly in your mind."

Which bridge was then of a moderate slope, showing the skilful inquiry, and the art and wit of its most clear-sighted maker and inventor; and I praised in it the eternal solidity, which is not known to the purblind moderns and false architects, without letters, measure or art, who paint it over, and covering it with pictures and lineaments the building stands in every way ill-joined and misshapen. Which was all of most comely Hymettian marble.

Having passed the bridge, we walked beneath through the cool shades, sweetly kept by the various chattering of small birds. We came to a stony and rocky place, where lofty and steep mountains rose up. And thence next to a broken and pathless and rugged mountain, all gnawed away and full of a bursting roughness. High into the air, worn down to a spur, and bare of all greenness, and dry mountains round about. And there were carved the three rough doors, rudely hollowed in the living rock, an antique work, and beyond belief most ancient, in a great harshness of site.

Et seco havea sei contubernale et individue vernule ministrante, assai deiectamente vestite et obese. Delle quale una nominavasi Parthenia. La seconda Edosia, et una Hypocolinia. La quarta Pinotidia. Et ad presso egli era Tapinosa, la ultima Ptochina. La quale veneranda matrona cum il dextro brachio nudo, l’alto Olympo monstrava. Habitava all’ingresso di una strata scrupea, di progresso difficile, di spini et sente impedita. Il loco apparendo scabroso et dispiacevole, cum il coelo pluvio et turbato, et cum nubila caligine infuscata, et arctissimo calle. And behold, there presented herself to us a woman far on in years, of an unwedded aspect, who came out of a wattled little cottage with a smoky roof and smoked walls, by its small door (which had noted above it PYLURANIA), coming with a modest matronliness; her little chapel set in a solitary place, and in a shady cliff, crumbling with bare and friable stone; torn, squalid, lean, poor, with her eyes fixed upon the ground; Theude her name.

And with her she had six companions and inseparable serving maids, meanly enough clothed and heavy. Of whom one was named Parthenia. The second Edosia, and one Hypocolinia. The fourth Pinotidia. And next was Tapinosa, and the last Ptochina. Which venerable matron, with her right arm bare, pointed to high Olympus.

She dwelt at the entrance of a stony road, difficult to go along, hindered with thorns and briars. The place appearing rough and displeasing, with the sky rainy and troubled, and darkened with a cloudy gloom, and a most narrow path.

So that Logistica, taking note that at the first sight I shrank from such a thing, said to me, almost sadly: "Poliphilo, this path is not known until the end." And thus of this venerable and holy woman Thelemia, sharp-witted, quickly said to me: "O Poliphilo, the love of such a laborious woman is not for you now." I, nodding shrewdly to Thelemia, we came forth from there. And the door being closed again, they knocked at the left-hand one.

I consenting, we went out from this one too; and the brazen valves being bolted, Thelemia struck at the third and middle door, and the bar being removed, without delay it was opened. And being let in, there came to meet us a notable lady, whose name was Philtronia. With wanton and unsteady glances, her most joyful look at the first sight forced me to love her and drew me to it.

A dweller in a voluptuous place, its ground green with soft grass and clothed with flowers, abounding in solace and pleasant idleness, flowing with springs of the clearest fountains and little streams, running with a sounding gush, watered to the greatest pleasure; sunny fields, and the shades of the leafy trees cool and fresh.

She likewise had with her six mistress-like and most shapely girls of her own age, and most charming in their look, with a most welcome elegance and amorous ornaments, trapped out, seemly with an ambitious beauty; of whom the name of the first was Rastonelia, the next was named Chortasina, the third Idonesa, and the fourth was called Tryphelea. And the fifth was called Etiania; the last Adia.

Such and so made presences showed themselves exceedingly welcome and delightful to my intent eyes. For this the sincere Logistica, seeing me readily disposing myself and already abruptly bent to the love of her, and addicted in a servile manner, said with a sorrowful voice:

"O Poliphilo, the painted and feigned beauty of this woman is lying, insipid and savourless; for if you would look discussingly upon her back you would grasp, with loathing, how much unseemliness lies beneath, and how despicable and stomach-turning and abominable they are with their foulness, standing high upon a great heap of filth. For that which flees is fleeting and vanishing, and the pleasure passes, and shame with repentance, with vain hopes, with the briefest cheerfulness, with perpetual weeping and anxious sighs, the toilsome life remains behind.

An elegant Nymph comes to meet him in this place, where he was left alone and deserted by the wanton girls. Poliphilo lovingly describes her beauty and her dress.

My tender heart being excessively struck with amorous prickings, I do not know whether I raved, that I stayed thus astonished at the manner in which so suddenly the most welcome company vanished and disappeared from my eyes. This sun-born Nymph, then, clothed her maidenly and divine little body in a most fine cloth of green silk woven with a warp of gold (that most joyful colouring of the little feathers of a duck's neck) mingled, over a white and crimped shift of cotton, covering her cleanest and most delicate flesh and milky skin, such as the inventress Pamphila, daughter of Plates, first knew how to weave in the island of Cos. Then this raised and tucked-up garment was fastened at the first golden cord with the sacred girdle of holy Cytherea. Sometimes, by the tempered blowing of the little winds, the light garment being driven, it betrayed her modest and neat shape, which made a ready scorn of it. And from beneath the little fillet there came out in an ordered way her vine-tendrilled hair, part of it quivering and shadowing her fair temples, not hiding her smallest ears, more beautiful than were ever dedicated to Memory.

And of this the whole ill beginning of so troubling and contentious a commotion were my unsated and most troublesome eyes, which I felt sowing and stirring up so great and such a harmful quarrel in my sad and wounded heart. By the stubbornness of which I then lost it altogether; and none the less without them I could in nothing at all satisfy them. The raging appetite then extolled her most delicious breast without equal. The eyes, consenting with delight, said: if only we could uncover it all. Such shavings of fir, always deserving to be in vine-curled circles.

Ad l’ultimo pensiculatamente nel archano del mio infocato core ad cogitare incominciai, che sencia fallire la praesente et continua mia poena adaequare potev’io ad quella de lo improbo Tantalo che all’arida et sitiente bucca le gelide et purgatissime aque gustabile et iocunde se offeriscono, et al fremente appetito gli suavi fructi fina alla hiante bucca gratissimamente se appraesentano, rimane finalmente impasto et abstemio del uno et del altro. O me che non per altro modo una venustissima Nympha insigne di forma, di fiorente aetate, più che dire si poté decorata de angelici costumi et de praecipua honestate celebre, nel conspecto degli ochii mei eximiamente benigna praesentata, la visitatione dela quale omni exquisito et delectabile contento humano excedeva, et io allato suo, piena di omni cosa, che solatiosamente vale ad amare et appetire provocabonda, et da qualunque altra operatione lo intellecto astrahendo solo in sé cumulantilo, non succureva perciò ad lo anhelante et voluptabondo desio. Hora per tale via non extinguendo le ardente concupiscentie, quanto io valeva aquetava el languescente core oltra modo inflammato, cum ralentarlo de amorosa et solativa sperancia. Et cum tale discorso che mai si trova carbo tanto extincto, che allo ignito propinquo non parimente per la conveniente dispositione non se accenda, ma gli ochii effrenati più d’omni hora quello di qualunque potere immunito et inerme, di più insolente desiderio le sue praecipue et dive bellecie lo inflammavano. Sempre più bella, più elegante, più venusta, più appetibile, et extremamente apta et praestabile d’amare, cum mirabile incremento de dolce piacere evidentemente monstrantise. Poscia sinceramente pensitava, si per aventura gli summi Dii persentiscono me desiderare et nephariamente appetere et praesumere gli devetati dilecti, forsi in questo sancto loco, et de tale persona ragionevolmente prohibiti, nonne come prophano ad me facilmente potrebbe advenire si como ad molti altri che hanno offeso impudentemente, le frede et infracte ire iustamente usate ad Isione audace et confidentissimo? soiled gown. Which still held the hooks of the biting burrs fixed in it from the wood; and as the peacock, looking again at its foul and vilest feet, lays down its rounded tail, so, neither more nor less, I put down the goadings of every pleasure, breaking off my stubborn desires and vain thoughts, considering how unsuited they were to so divine an object.

For this cause I was strongly disposed with all my strength to conquer and shut in my loose and wandering appetite, and my wavering mind, and to overcome my immodest will, judging by now that it could not be otherwise than so.

At last, thinking upon it in the secret of my kindled heart, I began to think that without fail I could match my present and continual pain to that of wicked Tantalus, to whose dry and thirsting mouth the cold and purest waters offer themselves, tasteable and joyful, and to whose raging appetite the sweet fruits present themselves most welcomely up to his gaping mouth — and he remains at last unfed and fasting of the one and of the other.

Alas for me: in no other manner was a most comely Nymph, notable in form, of a flowering age, adorned more than can be said with angelic manners and famous for a chief honesty, presented most kindly before my eyes — the sight of whom exceeded every exquisite and delightful human content; and I at her side, she full of everything that avails solacingly to love and provokes to longing, and drawing the intellect away from every other working, heaping it in herself alone — and yet it did not succour my panting and delighting desire.

Now, since by such a way the burning longings were not put out, as much as I could I quieted my languishing heart, inflamed beyond measure, by slackening it with an amorous and solacing hope. And with this reasoning: that no coal is ever found so far quenched that, being near a kindled one, it does not likewise, by the fitting disposition, take fire. But my unbridled eyes, more than at any hour, inflamed that heart, defenceless and unarmed against any power, with a more uncommon desire for her chief and divine beauties. Ever more beautiful, more elegant, more comely, more to be longed for, and extremely apt and excellent to love, showing herself plainly with a marvellous increase of sweet pleasure.

Then I thought sincerely: if by chance the highest gods perceive that I desire and wickedly long for and presume upon forbidden delights — perhaps in this holy place, and of such a person, reasonably forbidden — might it not easily befall me, as a profane man, as it did to many others who have shamelessly offended: the cold and unbroken angers justly used upon bold and most confident Ixion? And in like manner

Chapter XIII

The choice of Love. Poliphilo chooses the third door, the amorous life; Reason departs from him in sorrow, and a nymph — Polia, though he does not yet know her — takes him in charge.

Weighing such a reason in good time, then, I thought that those who lightly make themselves secure also lightly perish, and that for such men deceit and failure are not hard to come by. And that among the bold (as it is wont to be said) all deceiving and mocking Fortune does not stand. And besides this, it is hard to search out another's heart. For which cause, as Callisto, feeling with shame her swollen belly grow heavy, withdrew herself from the presence of chaste Diana, so, stirred by shame, I drew myself back from such an impulse, bridling my delighting and unseemly desires.

O most valiant Perseus, for this woman you would have fought more strenuously with the horrible monster, to win her sweetest love, than for your Andromeda. And then:

O Jason, if the lawful marriage of this woman had been set before you — with far greater peril (I swear by Jove) than was that of winning the golden fleece — I reasonably judge that, setting that aside, you would have contended fiercely for this one, judging her above all the jewels and precious treasures of the spacious world, and above even those of the richest Queen Eleuterylida, most precious, and of a greater worth and incomparable price.

Every hour and continually she appeared more shapely, more comely in aspect, with a cleanest adornment. Nor does plentiful gold show itself so welcome to Hippodamia, and to the ravening and anxious misers. Nor does the entrance of a quiet and safe harbour so offer itself to sailors, nor a cable or a mooring-post for their fastening when they are shaken in the winter storms. Nor was the falling rain so longed-for and timely at the pyre of Croesus, as the delicious Nymph offered herself, most acceptable to love. More joyful and dearer to me than the bloody battles to raging Mars; than to Dionysus the mysteries of great Crete.

And at once, the warm tears called up in my moist eyes, it seemed to me despicable and very hard to renew my wasted heart, and to bring in a new and unknown lord, and impiously to banish its ancient one.

RAGIONEVOLMENTE UNQUANTULO difficile ad gli superni Dei fare existimo, anci factibile facilmente si praesta qualunque effecto al suo volere, et in ciascuno loco, et sopra omni cosa creata. Il perché debitamente chiamati sono omnipotenti. Forsa chi alcuna fiata le miravegliose et stupende immo divine opere udirae narrare, supremamente miravegliarse potrebbe. Imperoché imitare, le cose naturale, l’arte aemula, quanto vale se sforza. Ma le divine sencia dubitare per qualunque creato ingegno et intellecto sencia sua ope, et spiramine non si pole aptamente simular né fingere. Dunque per sì facta ragione, niuno da dubio alcuno doverebbe lassarse occupare, ma quietamente animadvertendo pona nell’animo, ad gli superi possibile, ciascuna ad nui insueta factura, quale io cusì vidi. Reasonably, I judge it in no way difficult for the gods above to do; nay, any effect whatever readily shows itself easily to be done at their will, and in every place, and above everything created. For which cause they are duly called almighty. Perhaps whoever shall sometimes hear told the marvellous and stupendous — nay, divine — works, might marvel exceedingly. For art, the rival, strives as much as it can to imitate natural things. But divine things, without doubt, cannot aptly be feigned or copied by any created wit and intellect without their help and inspiration. So for such a reason no one ought to let himself be taken up by any doubt, but quietly taking note let him set in his mind that to the gods above every making unaccustomed to us is possible — such as I saw thus.

The description of the first triumph.

The first of the four wondrous and divine triumphs had its four swift wheels of finest stone of the greenest Scythian emerald, sparkling with atoms of a coppery colour. The rest, then, of the car I beheld, astonished, made all of tablets not of Arabian nor of Cyprian, but of iron-sparkling Indian diamond, defying the hard emery and the steel, victorious over active fire, its scorner and stubborn foe, but quiet and tameable to the warm blood of a goat, welcome to the magic arts. Which slabs, divinely worked with a sunken carving in relief, were carved and wonderfully set and enclosed in the cleanest gold.

In the right-hand tablet I beheld expressed a noble and royal Nymph with many of her own age in a meadow, crowning the victorious bulls with manifold garlands of flowers. And one clinging to her, made very particularly familiar with her.

EL TERTIO caeleste triumpho seguiva cum quatro vertibile rote di Chrysolitho aethiopico scintule d’oro flammigiante, traiecta per el quale la seta del Asello gli maligni daemonii fuga, alla leva mano grato, cum tutto quello che di sopra di rote è dicto. Daposcia le assule sue in ambito per el modo compacte sopra narrato, erano di virente Helitropia Cyprico, cum potere negli lumi caelesti, el suo gestante coela, et il divinare dona, di sanguinee guttule punctulato. Offeriva tale historiato insculpto la tabella dextra. Uno homo di regia maiestate insigne, orava in uno sacro templo el divo simulacro, quello che della formosissima fiola deveva seguire. Sentendo el patre la eiectione sua per ella del regno. Et né per alcuno fusse pregna, fece una munita structura di una excelsa torre, et in quella cum solemne custodia la fece inclaustrare. Nella quale ella cessabonda assedendo, cum excessivo solatio, nel virgineo sino gutte d’oro stillare vedeva. *

The third heavenly triumph followed, with four turning wheels of Ethiopian chrysolite, flaming with little sparks of gold — through which, being pierced, the bristle of a little ass puts malignant demons to flight; welcome to the left hand — with all that is said above of wheels.

The right-hand tablet offered this history carved. A man notable for royal majesty prayed in a sacred temple to the divine image, for what should follow from his most shapely daughter. The father, hearing of his own casting out of the kingdom by her, and that she should not be got with child by any man, made a fortified building of a lofty tower, and had her shut in it with a solemn guard. In which, sitting idle, with an excessive solace she saw drops of gold distil into her maiden lap.

Il residuo di tabulatura quadrangula, cum il modo antedicto, era di folgorante carbunculo tragoditano, non temendo le dense tenebre, di expolitissime caelature, longo di ragionamento distinctamente. The fourth triumph four wheels carried, of iron-like Arcadian asbestos, once kindled refusing to be put out. Now, with an excessive delight, while ignorant and astonished I carefully contemplated with an applied mind the heavenly troop and the divine triumphs hedged about with such dances, and the delicious fields — what they were was wholly unknown to me, save that they were amorous mysteries — the divine Nymph, my faithful companion and guide, taking note of my dullness, with an excellent face and adorned and sweetest little words (I not asking her) providently said:

"My Poliphilo, do you see that one?" (showing me who in the fleeting age they had been). "By high Jove she was ardently loved. And likewise that other beloved one. And this was such a one, and those godheads were taken with her sweet love." And in this manner besides making known to me her noble and royal lineage. And the name I did not know she affably, all solacing, told me, pointing.

Then she showed me a venerable crowd of young girls. To whom three holy matrons stood before with divine bearing, going ahead of so great a delight. Adding (changed somewhat in her angelic face), she said lovingly: "My Poliphilo, I would have you understand that no earth-born creature could enter here without a torch kindled — either by ardent love and with the utmost labour, such as you see me carry burning now, or by the safe company of those three matrons." And sighing from her heart she said: "The present torch it will behove me, for your love, to quench at the holy temple (as you shall see), offering it."

Such and so made a discourse pierced my inflamed heart, so most acceptable was it to me and delightful when she called me thus: "My Poliphilo." Because I was made wholly suspicious that without fail she was Polia. For which cause I felt myself, from head to foot, inwardly altered and refreshed with the highest sweetness, and my beaten heart flee to her alone. And of this vehement effect
