The Nymph, having fittingly declared to her Poliphilo the triumphal mysteries and the divine love, invites him to go on further from there, where with the utmost delight he saw countless other Nymphs with their most welcome lovers, delighting themselves in a thousand solaces among the flowers, and through the cool shades and clear streams and clearest fountains; and how Poliphilo, strongly stirred by love, raged there. But tempering himself with hope, he was quieted, gazing upon the sweet face of his fair Nymph.

Not only would he reckon himself happy, but he would be blessed above any other, to whom by a special favour it should continually be granted to see the divine pomps, the heavenly triumphs, and the glorious sports, and the kindly places, and such goddesses and demi-goddesses and adorned Nymphs, of incredible beauty and ornament. And to have a particular fellowship with them, and to look upon them unceasingly.

But above all to have beside him, as an equal companion, so renowned a Nymph of chief beauty, with an exquisite nymphlike and divine adornment, a guide and a sincere leader. And this I judged no small and scanty part of blessedness. Having really beheld these things, I stayed a great while in thought, and gladdened beyond esteeming, and marvelling beyond measure.

bent down, and, the fair flowers being plucked and their little swelling hands filled, with amorous semblances they scattered them upon their comely faces, solacing and sporting themselves with much delight.

All festive and cheerful, and all provoked to delights. With girlish gestures and movements and a maidenly simplicity, tangled in a sincere love without offence to honoured virtue. Free and exempt from any sad encounter, and from the rivalry of skin-changing fortune.

Beneath the tempered shades let down by the weeping sisters of wicked Phaethon, and by the undying Daphne, and by tufted pines, with fine and pointed fronds, and by the tree dyed again with the burning blood of the unhappy Babylonians, and by the straight cypresses and the greenest orange and cedar trees, and by other most notable and most leafy trees, most fruitful of flowers and fruits, with an eternal greenness, most beautiful beyond esteeming and fragrant. Which, set in order upon the gracious banks and dispensed through the plain, at a moderate distance and interval, took up the grassy earth, full and clothed with the green periwinkle with its sky-blue flowers.

Alas, then, what heart would be so cold and frozen that it should not be excitedly kindled, seeing present before it such real and delightful offices of an even and answering love? So I reasonably suspected that even Diana the huntress would wholly and easily have been set on fire. And the icy Helice pursued by her.

For which cause I should almost have dared to utter a foolishness: that the spirits below suffer no other torment than the envy they have of these. Who without end live happily in delights and triumph, with the utmost pleasure, with no weariness of things present nor any surfeit of them.

Whence more than once my heart, kindled through my eyes with an extreme sweetness, and greatly burning, my amorous soul went out as far as my hesitating mouth. And keeping my mind fixed upon those delightful pleasures, and the soft kisses, and the abundant rewards of winged Cupid, looking on with a curious gaze, it certainly seemed to me in that space to feel of that kindled soul that this was its passing, and that it was sweetly departing to the last and utmost bounds of blessedness.

And in this manner I found myself wavering beyond all measure, lifeless and astonished, so that I almost thought myself drugged. There offering itself to my tenacious memory the unguents of the mischievous

La quale acerbamente pativa, per non audere di interrogare, si essa fusse la mia diva et desideratissima Polia. Quivi volentieri essere io vorei connumerato municipe perpetuo, et si el se potesse, niuno affanno erumnoso, me potrebbe grave apparere, niuno imminente periculo me spagurirebbe. Quantunque la fallaciosa fortuna si opponesse, io allhora la cara et appretiabile vita, sencia altro pensare tutta la exponeria. Circe, the powerful herbs of Medea, the hurtful songs of Byrrhena, and the grave-verses of Pamphile. So that I lawfully doubted whether bodily eyes could see beyond humanity, and whether there could be there a most lowly, ignoble and heavy body, where the immortal blessed rest.

After I was drawn out of these long and anxious thoughts and fantastic imaginings, remembering exquisitely all the wondrous, holy and divine things seen by me until now nakedly and openly, at last I knew that they were not deceiving illusions, nor false magics, but truly things imperfectly grasped.

Looking intently, then, with these thoughts, the most excellent Nymph at my side and so close by, wounded my sad heart unceasingly, dying as I was, with her eyes packed with amorous and busy darts. By which she at once stirred up every wandering and straying thought of mine, and, all of them gathered and hardened into that one fixed object, she called back my deadened soul vigorously to renew itself in its first fires.

Which suffered bitterly for not daring to ask whether she were my divine and most desired Polia. Seeing that she had before given me a somewhat ambiguous and suspected knowledge; and doubting deservedly (since my rude and untilled speech would not have been fitting at all) that I should shamelessly offend her, my warm voice having come many times to my silent lips, for such a reason I pressed it down.

But whatever it was, being beset by a marvellous astonishment (like deceived Sosia by the counterfeited son of Atlas), I found myself greatly in suspense; above all, examining the heavenly workings with subtle glances and heartfelt weighings, invaded by an ardent desire — so that beyond measure I longed thus, saying within myself:

Here I would gladly be reckoned a perpetual citizen; and if it could be, no toilsome trouble could seem heavy to me, no threatening peril would frighten me. However deceitful fortune should set itself against me, I would then, without further thinking, lay out my dear and precious life entire. Not refusing to take up the laborious and heavy choice of the two doors shown to the son of Amphitryon, and to use up my sweet youth and my pleasant years through the mortal perils of the raging sea, and through the fearful places of Sicily, with greater and highest labours and terror than were borne by wandering Ulysses, being in the darkened and pathless cave of the horrible Cyclops Polyphemus, son of Neptune, and by the transformations of the company of Calypso; and not to spare my gracious life for any thing whatever, and to bear a harder and longer servitude than the loving Hebrew shepherd bore, and a more dreadful one than that of Androdus the slave — because there every labour is shut out where love burns — and to set myself to the

Il perché hora non valeo più simulare et fingere la accerbitate (per ocultare) lo infortito incendio, già mai io mi moro vivendo, et vivente non mi sento vita, io sum alacre tristantime, et non me tristo, et io vo poenando,io me consummo in flamma nutrientime, et la exuberante flamma augmenta, et ardendo quale Oro nel forte cemento trovome solido giacio. Heu me misero questo cusì grave amore tropo me molesta più che la grave Inarime Typhone, me dissipa più che gli rapaci Vulturi le glomerate viscere di Tityo, me implica più che labyrinthica obliquatione, me inquieta più che gli Nimbiferi venti il tranquillato mare, me urgie più che gli mordaci cani alla fuga Actaeone, et più che la horribile morte el dolce vivere, perturba gli spiriti mei. Et el mio crucioso core da gli sui mordenti ochii più noxiamente è deroso che dal Ichneumone le Crocodiline viscere perese. proving of the loving Milanion and Hylaeus, and for the fair Atalanta. And to strive in no other manner than the sinewy and strong Hercules, wrestling manfully for his beloved Deianira against the monstrous Achelous, conquered him; and I in no other way, to win so many delights, and to enter for long into the holy and most fruitful places, disposed with every delight and pleasure.

And above all to win the precious love, and to gain the long-desired good will of this woman: fairer beyond comparison than Cassiopeia, more shapely than Castiamira — alas for me, who carries my dying and my life in her will. And if by chance I appear unworthy of such fellowship and amorous commerce, at least that it might be eternally granted me by a special gift and privilege and favour to gaze upon her steadily and intently.

And then, speaking to myself, I said: O Poliphilo, if the burdensome and troublesome heaviness of this amorous weight should by chance frighten you, the sweetness of the fruit invites you, a lover of labour, to any sad toil; and if the toilsome perils frighten you, yet the hope of the patronage and help of such a Nymph ought to make you fierce and persuade you.

Then, my varied wavering having departed from here without delay, I said: O gods above and greatest, and you sovereign goddesses, powerful over mortals — if this is that most acceptable Polia whom at present I see, whom without interruption I have carried and keep most preciously stamped in my burnt and tenacious heart, cleaving with an everlasting glue, from the first years of love until now, I am content with everything, and beyond her I ask nothing else; but only this I beseech as a suppliant: bind her likewise to my fervent loves, and that she, with that same burning fire in which I so hardly feed myself for her and burn consuming, may burn equally, and both of us mailed together; or else loose me alone.

For which cause I can no longer feign and pretend the bitterness, to hide the strengthened burning. I am forever dying while living, and living I feel no life; I am cheerful while grieving, and I do not grieve, and I go on suffering; I consume myself, feeding in the flame, and the overflowing flame grows; and burning like gold in the strong crucible I find myself solid ice.

Alas, wretched me: this so heavy love troubles me more than heavy Inarime troubles Typhon; it scatters me more than the ravening vultures the coiled entrails of Tityus; it tangles me more than the labyrinth's winding; it disquiets me more than the storm-bearing winds the quieted sea; it presses me more than the biting hounds pressed Actaeon in flight, and more than horrible death troubles sweet living, it troubles my spirits.

And my tormented heart is more hurtfully gnawed by her biting eyes than the crocodile's entrails are eaten by the ichneumon. And beyond belief it is so taken up by them with unceasing strokes, as upon an anvil, more than the Ceraunian mountains often struck by the heavenly thunderbolts. And so much the more that I cannot, with all the power of my wit,

p. 187confidence: unstatedverified

pensiculare et intendere in quale parte del mundo me ritrovi. Si non di ricontro et pertinace obvio d’un suave foco de questa semidea, che sencia laesione corporale me consuma. Il cui ubero et flavo capillamento è a me uno nodoso Tendiculo circa alo septo core teso et parato, l’ampla et plegmatica fronte candicante lilii me contorque, quale virgula per ligatura in strophia, gli sagittanti risguardi della vita me sospendono, dolci suscitabuli ad affligerme, le rosee guance me invitano dolcemente ad exasperarme, la bucca Cinnamea uno suave cruciato mi fa appetere. Poscia el delitioso pecto come hyberna neve negli hiperborei monti albescente (el quale in sé essendo extrema dolcecia) a me è acerba et noxio flagello. Et gli sui non humani sembianti, et la venusta persona, ad uno imaginativo dilecto lo appetito mio trahendo me diramente strugeno. Et ad tutti questi insultanti martyrii et ad questo tanto discriminoso Agone, et al impio et insidioso Cupidine cum tutte queste insultante parte del Glabro corpusculo, el provocato core vigorosamente ingerentise Atleta strenuo, niente dimeno non poté unquanco resistere, ma quale Milone appresso costei, sopita omni virtute dilacerando me trovo, né d’indi divertire vaglio, come si incauto nel Babylonico palude intrato fusse. Dunque solo digno et rimedio complebile praesentaneo, et opportuno medicamento se offerirebbe, quantunque io me sentisse essere accepto, cum tutte queste mie asperrime et intollerabile poene, ad questa Dea essendo Polia, la quale caelatamente me ha accenso et sencia inducia perure, et delle flamme del rigido Cupidine per tutto me arde, né più né meno quale Minerva il figmento de Prometeo accense, rapito cum la leve ferula l’ardente foco dalle labile rote dello illuminoso Phoebo, o Tityo malamente mi suaderei che minore el mio tormento, che el tuo fusse, dummentre che gli framei Vulturi el tuo calido pecto sfindino, et d’indi senza dimorare el vivace core fumante evulso, et cum gli ungulati pedi rapientilo, et crudelmente cum gli adunci rostri membratamente lacerando el devorano, et in parva hora poscia ristorato a quella medesima laniena rapidi tornano. Similmente riserato el mio inflammato pecto, l’amoroso core da dui furacissimi ochii senza pietate duramente dissipando el straciano, et straciantilo aspramente mordicabondi el devorano. Poscia non sta guario de tempo, che el festivo et periocundo aspecto el risana, come si laesione non sentisse, et da poco instante reiterando, ad gli sui plagosi vulneri ritornano. Heu me poscia dicto questo tra me secretamente miseramente principiai di piangere, et sospirando a li lachrymabondi ochii le familiare lachryme uberrimamente provocare, et di ritrovare l’adito di appetere la exosissima morte, et per alquanto spatio, cusì da excessivo et funesto amore rabidamente istimulato, el quale fora el limite dolorosamente me agitava, et cum uno m ii

ponder and understand in what part of the world I find myself. Unless over against and stubbornly facing a sweet fire of this demi-goddess, which consumes me without bodily hurt.

Whose abundant and yellow hair is to me a knotted snare stretched and set about my hedged heart; her wide and smooth brow, whitening like lilies, twists me like a rod bound in a garland; the arrow-shooting glances of her life hang me up, sweet awakenings to afflict me; her rosy cheeks invite me sweetly to sharpen my pain; her cinnamon mouth makes me long for a sweet torment.

Then her delicious breast, white as winter snow on the northern mountains (which, being in itself an extreme sweetness), is to me a bitter and hurtful scourge. And her more than human semblances, and her comely person, drawing my appetite to an imagined delight, cruelly waste me.

And against all these insulting martyrdoms, and against this so perilous a contest, and against impious and treacherous Cupid, with all these insulting parts of that smooth little body, my provoked heart vigorously throwing itself in as a strenuous wrestler — nevertheless it could never resist, but, like Milo beside her, I find myself torn apart, every strength put to sleep, nor can I turn aside from there, as if I had entered incautiously into the Babylonian marsh.

So the only worthy and fulfilling present remedy and fitting medicine that would offer itself, however much I felt myself accepted, with all these harshest and intolerable pains of mine, would be that this goddess should be Polia — she who has secretly set me on fire and burns me without delay, and burns me all over with the flames of hard Cupid, neither more nor less than Minerva kindled the figure of Prometheus, the burning fire snatched with a light reed from the running wheels of shining Phoebus.

O Tityus, I should ill persuade myself that my torment were less than yours, while the sword-like vultures split your warm breast, and thence, without staying, your living heart, torn out and smoking, and seizing it with their taloned feet, and cruelly tearing it limb from limb with their hooked beaks, they devour it; and in a little while afterwards, it being restored, they return swiftly to that same butchery. And the sorrowful carnage begins again from the top.

Likewise, my inflamed breast being opened, two most thieving eyes without pity harshly scatter and tear my loving heart, and, tearing it, bitingly devour it. Then it is not long in time before her festive and most joyful aspect heals it again, as if it felt no hurt; and after a little instant, beginning again, they return to its stricken wounds.

Alas for me. Then, having said this to myself secretly, I began wretchedly to weep, and, sighing, to call up abundantly the familiar tears to my weeping eyes, and to find the way to long for most hateful death. And for some space, thus fiercely goaded by an excessive and deadly love, which sorrowfully stirred me beyond all bound, and with a

All’ultimo fora di tanta commotione del altercabondo animo evaso. burning heat with piteous sighs tormented me. Now, disordered with such anguish, many times I set this purpose in my mind: to cry out with the highest wailings and say: O more than most beautiful Nymph, my goddess, and chief and only hope, be moved to pity now, and helping me succour me, for at present I find myself at the point of dying.

But at once, dismayed, judging this deceitful, I rejected it as a false and light thought; and in an instant, moved by a raging and roaring spirit, confounding myself, I said: Why do you waver, Poliphilo? To die for love's sake is praiseworthy. And yet would it ever be, by my sad and malignant ill-luck, that my sorrowful happening, and my heavy kindlings, and my noble love of such a Nymph should be recited in the hollowed earth? And then that the fine and pliant reeds should sprout, which, sounding, should afterwards make plain my growing and hurtful loves?

Not shutting out such wickedness of my wandering thoughts, I said rightly: Perhaps this woman, as she shows, is a venerable goddess; and therefore talking Syrinx of Arcadia, in the reedy and marshy seats of the river Ladon, would not have been given, shaken, to the goading and forward east winds, and to the tumultuous and frost-bearing north wind, and to the blowing and cloud-bearing south, and to the troubled and rain-bringing wind, if her untimely and unseemly speech in the presence of the goddesses had been fitting. And answering Echo, by such a likeness, would not have been made into a last voice, if she had spoken seemly.

And therefore, the gods being of themselves most pious, such contempt and negligent daring makes them severe avengers. For which cause the companions of slow and searching Ulysses would deservedly have been kept safe without the mortal peril of shipwreck, if they had not shamelessly and wickedly stolen the fated herd of Apollo, watched over by the Nymphs Phaethusa and her sister Lampetie. And Orion likewise would not have known the horrible vengeance, if he had not rashly set himself against cold and chaste Diana. And the son of burning Phoebus was rashly struck by lightning from highest Olympus, and bound eternally in the Stygian waves, for using the peony herbs.

If, then, I should show by any sign any unseemliness towards this divine Nymph, might not the like, and worse, easily befall me? At last I came out of so great a stirring of my quarrelling mind.

Taking, then, the highest delight, I grew calm; and looking at her adorned elegance and contemplating the comely form of this noble and distinguished Nymph, I wholly comforted myself. Who held plentifully in herself all that can perfectly delight in love, and all that can be sweetly loved, dispensing so great a sweetness widely from her festive eyes that, the troubling and unbridled thoughts being driven out of my disquieted

Chapter XVII

The four Seasons and the Temple of Venus. Our translation opens with the four Seasons carved on an altar and the rustic rite of Priapus, then the round Temple of Venus Physizoa ("life-giving Venus") — its vine-cast bronze dome, its self-opening magnet-door inscribed Trahit sua quemque voluptas ("each is drawn by his own pleasure") — where, at the sacred well, Polia at last reveals herself and the lovers are joined.

LA NYMPHA PER ALTRI BELLI LOCHI, LO AMOROSO POLIPHILO CONDUCE, OVE VIDE INNUMERE NYMPHE SOLENNIGIANTE ET CUM IL TRIUMPHO DI VERTUNO ET DI POMONA D’INTORNO UNA SACRA ARA ALACREMENTE FESTIGIANTI. ET POSCIA CUM LA SACRIFICABONDA ANTISTETE, NEL SANCTO SACELLO INTRATA, DINANTI LA DIVINA ARA INVOCÒ LE TRE GRATIE.

Il quale era contermine della florigera et collinea convalle, ove terminavano a questo littore le ornate montagniole, et vitiferi colli, cum praeclusi aditi, questa aurea patria, piena di incredibile oblectamento circumclaustrando. Le quale erano di silvosi nemori di conspicua densitate, quanto si fusseron stati gli arbusculi ordinatamente locati amoene, quale il Taxo Cyrneo, et lo Arcado, il Pinastro infructuoso et resinaceo, alti Pini, driti Abieti, negligenti al pandare, et contumaci al pondo, arsibile Picee, il fungoso Larice, Tede aeree, et gli colli amanti, Celebrati et cultivati da festigiante Oreade, quivi ambidui m iii

mind, I tempered it somewhat. And I turned back my sounding sighs, and with flattering hope (O amorous food of lovers, and often enough joined with a tearful drink) I wheeled my stirred thoughts by another biting bridle, with so much considered and made pleasure, gazing with an extreme delight upon that most welcome and native body, upon those rosy cheeks, upon those bright and shining limbs, solacing myself. By which singular things I kindly comforted and softened my raging desires, redeemed from the furious angers of too great an ardour, and from the amorous fire so near that they were readily taking light.

The Nymph leads the loving Poliphilo through other fair places, where he saw countless Nymphs keeping solemn festival, and cheerfully keeping the feast about a sacred altar with the triumph of Vertumnus and Pomona. Then they came to a marvellous temple, which he in part describes, and its builder's art. And how in the said temple, at the warning of the priestess, the Nymph with much ceremony put out her torch, showing herself to Poliphilo to be his Polia. And afterwards, having entered with the sacrificing priestess into the holy shrine, before the divine altar she called upon the three Graces.

I could no longer contend against the heavenly and violent armour; and, the most elegant Nymph having lovingly gained an irrevocable lordship over wretched me, further on with her (I following her measured steps), driving me as her equal, she led me towards a spacious shore. Which bordered upon the flower-bearing and hilly valley, where the adorned little mountains ended at this shore, and the vine-bearing hills, with their ways shut, enclosing round about this golden country, full of incredible delight.

Which were of wooded groves of a notable thickness, as though the little trees had been pleasantly set in order: the yew of Corsica and of Arcady, the fruitless and resinous wild pine, tall pines, straight firs, careless of bending and stubborn under a weight, the burnable spruce, the spongy larch, airy torch-pines, and lovers of the hills, kept and tended by festive Oreads. Here we both,

We entered, then, where there were measured square spaces hedged about with the bounds of wide, straight, four-way roads, a pace high, of dog-thorn, or thorny grape, and of ground juniper, and most thickly bound to a wall-like level of most even box, enclosing the squares of the flowering and dewy meadows.

In the order of the said hedges I beheld planted symmetrically the lofty victorious palms, with their fruitful clusters of dates hanging out of their sheaths: some black, some crimson, many yellow, such as would not be found in dewy Egypt. And perhaps the Dabulan of the tent-dwelling Arabs is not so choice, and perhaps Jericho does not bring forth such. Which stood alternating with the greenest citrons and oranges, hawthorn-medlars, pistachios, pomegranates, quinces, tree-myrtles, and medlars, and service-trees, and many other noble fruit trees, most adorned with fruitfulness, in the fields as if newly come into the spring.

And the other carried a trophy of certain buds and green shoots joined together, and country instruments; leaping with an ancient rite and applause, solemnly circling, and going round a sacred four-cornered altar in the middle of the tufted and flower-bearing meadow, watered by the clearest springs, religiously set up. Sotto quello circumligamento poco sopra narrato, tra l’una et l’altra striata semiquadrangula nel primario pariete era una quadrangulata fenestra di uno quadrato et semi, come se richiede negli templi antiquarii. La apertione, o vero la luminatione delle quale occupava artificiosamente una speculare, o vero diaphana lamina de petra Sogobrina non temente la vetustate. Diqué in summa octo fenestre erano, perché una parte occupava la porta de esso templo, et per directo del Pronao in fronte un’altra parte della porta cum le valve auree del postico sacello, o veramente del sacro Adyto, la discriptione del quale in altro loco più accommodamente sarà tractata. All’incontro delle sopra recitate columne quadrangule, nel primo murale circuito infixe, gli pilli di fora prominevano, de tanta crassitudine dal muro exacti, quanta quella del muro, ad gli quali la sua latitudine davano le linee degli radii della divisione, dal centro alla circunferentia. La quale latitudine divisa, una portione era per la latitudine del pillastro. L’altra portione ancora in bina partitione deducta, una de qui et de lì l’altra dal Pillo collaterale attribuite, erano per uno arcuare nel solido del muro, o vero concamerato, tra uno et l’altro Pillastro, degli quali Pilli la proiectura, o vero exito, diviso per tertio, usurpava la prominentia del arcuato dal piano del muro scaffato, et gli dui tertii, eminevano gli Pilli, in uno solido muro arcuato et Pilli. Questa exquisita observantia laudavano gli eleganti Architecti, per non dare al muro rude crassitudine tanta, che le fenestre obtuse se accusasseron, cum perspicuo respecto del rude et superfluo solido, et per decoramento exteriore, gli quali arcuati in gyro se involtavano coniugato optimamente l’uno all’altro cum la medesima crassitudine, cum debito illigamento dagli Pilli circunferito sopra el muro per tutto bellamente concincto. Non altramente tra uno et l’altro contrastante arco opportunamente constava.

In the pier of the Arches, opposite, behind the Corinthian, a third of a fluted quadrangular (pilaster) stood forth, with the base upon the pavement, standing in the face of another (in the band under the arch that divided the vaults, fixed) wholly similar. The interval of these, from the one to the other, the radii drawn to the circumstance made, set upon the line of the outermost Piers. Upon the semi- capitals of which went round a circum-ligation of gracious workmanship.

The half-Tubes and half-Altars were of bright Alabaster, with curving ropes, or bundles, of manifold fronds and fruits — of lacterii (spurges), of medlars, and stalks of Poppy, growing heavy in their middle descent, of wavering shoots ensnared, suspended and knotted in certain rings comelily adorned.

Under that circum-ligation a little above narrated, between one and the other striated half-quadrangular (pilaster), in the primary wall was a quadrangular window of one square and a half, as is required in antiquarian temples. The opening, or lighting, of which artfully occupied a mirror-like, or diaphanous, plate of sogobrina stone, not fearing old age. Whence, in sum, eight windows there were — because one part the door of the temple occupied, and, directly opposite the Pronaos in front, another part (the door, with the golden valves, of the rear chapel, or the sacred Adytum, the description of which will, in another place, be more fittingly treated).

Over against the above-recited quadrangular columns, fixed in the first mural circuit, the piers projected outside, worked out from the wall of as much thickness as that of the wall — to which their breadth the lines of the radii of the division, from the centre to the circumference, gave. Which breadth divided: one portion was for the breadth of the pilaster; the other portion, again deduced into a twin partition (one here and one there, the other attributed to the collateral Pier), were for an arching in the solid of the wall, or vaulted, between one pilaster and the other. Of which Piers the projection, or outlet, divided by a third, usurped the prominence of the vault from the plane of the scarped wall; and the two thirds the Piers stood forth, in a solid arched wall-and-Piers. This exquisite observance the elegant Architects praised, so as not to give the wall a rude thickness so great that the windows should accuse themselves obtuse (deep-set), with conspicuous respect of the rude and superfluous solid; and for exterior adornment, which vaults in a ring turned themselves, conjoined most-excellently one to the other with the same thickness, with due binding, from the Piers, carried round upon the wall, throughout beautifully girt. Not otherwise, between one and the other contrasting arch, opportunely it stood.

Notes

Confidence: medium. The temple's wall-structure: fluted pilasters answering the columns, alabaster half-altar sub-bases with fruit-and-poppy festoons, eight windows glazed with translucent sogobrina stone (two bays taken by the door and the rear sanctuary), and the outer piers whose thickness is governed by the radial lines and lightened with wall-arches. All secure; a lucid (if dense) account of a buttressed, thin-walled rotunda.

In questo intervallato vacuo, tra uno et l’altro Pillone, o vero tra le fauce de questi archi prope dicti, sopra el relicto piano murale, excavato era la fenestra. Il quale arcuato tanto quanto egli era distante dal Pillo, tanto circinava sotto la coronice prima extrinseca, ambiente al primo tecto. Dece Pilli, o vero ossi del aedificio erano, et altratanti archi in solido, cum el muro extrinseco, exclusa la facia, ove appacto resideva el sacello. El dicto cornitione amplexando el rotundo sacello, el colligava cum el templo. Oltra questa ligatura ascendeva el suo tecto, che era una caeca cupula dalla maiore per sé distincta et libera. Retorniamo dunque hora allo illigamento interstitio de sopra la circumcolumnatione, o vero Peristylio del Trabe recto, fascia et coronice, porrecto sopra perpendicularemente delle Porphyrice columne, ove nascevano per ciascuna porrectione del illigamento, semicolumnelle de quadratura striate, di egregio Ophytes. Sopra el semicapitello delle quale, ambiva una coronice de liniamento conspicua. Dalla quale el convexo della excelsa cupula, el suo principio sopra incominciava. Infra una semiquadrangula et l’altra de proximo descripte, vidi una proportionata fenestra tempestivamente situata, et de lamina de Bononia de Galia obtusa, constituite in campo deaureato de artificioso Museo. Gli quali spatii cum commensa distributione et aequale partitione, mirai spectatissimamente depicto, de vermiculata tessellatura, la proprietate de ciascuno Mense del anno cum el suo effecto, et de sopra el Zodiaco occurrente cum el Sole operante, et a quello della Luna gli Schematismi, et essa è dita, tra gli menstrui nova cornicula, dividua et praetumida, et el suo circuito, per el quale gli mensi se includeno. Et gli anfracti del Sole indagante, le brume et el solstitio, circuiendo, et della nocte et del giorno la vicissitudine, et la quadrifaria commotione degli tempi, et la natura delle fixe et errante stelle, cum la sua efficacia, suspicai che tale arte fusse quivi ordinata dal nobilissimo mathematico Petosiris, o vero da Necepso. La inspectione delle quale cose, da trahere lo inspectore cum excessivo solacio ad una eximia et miranda speculatione. Non sencia egregio spectaculo, et elegante fictione, et venusta distributione de figure, cum diffinita pictura de coloramento et ombrature, per le quale la commodulatione degli corpi et requisiti lumi, ad complacentia rapraesentantise cum dignissima expressione degli effecti, cum laudabile et iocundo obstento agli sensi del animo. Opera sencia dubio de pensiculatione digna, quanto mai speculare se potesse. Dunque in una divisione el contento del significato delle antedicte operature, de notule antiquarie, elegantemente era inscripto. Gli spatii interpositi tra le semiquadrangule erano circumsepti di fascie, de venusto operamento inscalpte.

In this intervalled void, between one Pillar and the other — or between the jaws of these arches just- said — upon the left mural plane, excavated was the window. Which vault, as much as it was distant from the Pier, so much it circled under the first outer cornice, encompassing the first roof. Ten Piers, or bones, of the building there were, and as many arches in the solid, with the exterior wall — excepting the face where, set fast, resided the chapel (sacello).

The said cornice, embracing the round sacello, joined it with the temple. Beyond this binding ascended its roof, which was a blind cupola, distinct and free of the greater one by itself.

Let us return, then, now, to the interstitial binding above the circum-columnation, or Peristyle — of the straight architrave, fascia and cornice, stretched perpendicularly above the Porphyry columns — where there were born, for each stretch of the binding, little half-columns of quadrature, striated, of egregious Ophite. Upon the semi-capital of which went round a cornice of conspicuous lineament, from which the convex of the lofty cupola began its beginning above.

Between one and the other of the half-quadrangular (pilasters) just described, I saw a proportioned window, timely situated, and of a plate of Bononia (Bologna) of Gaul, opaque, constituted in a field gilt, of artful Mosaic. Which spaces, with commensurate distribution and equal partition, I beheld most- admiredly depicted, of wormwork tessellation: the property of each Month of the year, with its effect; and above, the Zodiac occurring, with the Sun operating; and, to that of the Moon, the phases — and she is called, among the monthly (states), the new little crescent, the halved, and the pre-swollen (full) — and her circuit, by which the months are included. And the windings of the investigating Sun, the solstices and the winter-turns, circling; and of night and of day the vicissitude; and the quadrifarious commotion of the seasons; and the nature of the fixed and wandering stars, with their efficacy. I suspected that such art was here ordained by the most-noble mathematician Petosiris, or by Necepso. The inspection of which things (was) enough to draw the inspector, with excessive solace, to a choice and wondrous speculation — not without egregious spectacle, and elegant fiction, and comely distribution of figures, with defined painting of colouring and shadings, by which the commodulation of the bodies and requisite lights, to complacency representing themselves with most-worthy expression of the effects, with laudable and joyous show to the senses of the soul. A work, without doubt, worthy of pondering, as much as ever one could contemplate. Then, in one division, the content of the meaning of the aforesaid works, of antiquarian letters, was elegantly inscribed. The spaces interposed between the half-quadrangulars were hedged round with bands, carved of comely workmanship.

Notes

Confidence: medium. The completion of the wall (ten piers, ten arches, the round sacello with its own blind cupola joined to the temple), and — the page's real subject — the upper windows glazed with mosaic depicting the twelve Months, the Zodiac, the Sun and Moon's phases, the solstices, and the seasons: a full calendar-astronomy programme in the clerestory, ascribed to the Egyptian astrologers Petosiris and Nechepso. All secure.

Gli reliqui parieti del templo, cum multiplice et variforme de Emblemature, erano operosamente, de pretiosi marmori incrustati, quanto meglio el multiscio Architecto, ad tanta magnificentia de structura imaginando sepe applicare, né forsa tale fue facto ad Ammone. Sopra l’ordine delle Corinthie, de perfectissima scalptura el facondo Apolline resideva lyrante. Et sopra ciascuna delle altre in circuito, sopra conveniente Arule, de tutto integro, una Musa de petra Pilates, ad li opportuni gesti et officio, cum summa laude del Statuario exquisitissimamente scalpte, sopralocate al pretenso dicto de sopra dell’ambiente illigamento. La ingente cupula monstrava maximo inditio, più praesto de divina operatione che de humana obstentatione. Ma se humana, non senza stupore et accusatione dell’ambitione de tanto tentato di arte fusoria dalo ingegno humano, perché considerando tanta vastitate, in una sola et solida conflatura, et iacto de metallo, como io arbitrava, io rimansi summopere mirabondo et allucinato, damnandola quasi alla impossibilitate, niente dimeno questo tale Aerificio, era tutto de Vite nascente fora de bellissimi vasi, della aenea materia, al perpendiculo et ordine stanti della columnatione, diffundendo et gli rami, palmite, o vero surculi, et Capreoli vertiginosamente intricantise, cum gratissimo coniugio, in observantia della formatione del convexo della dicta cupula, la una cum l’altra cum decente densitate, cum foglie, racemi, infantuli scandendo decerpenti, Avicule volitante, Lacerte serpente, ad aemulatione della natura, optimamente exacte, et tuto el residuo pervio. Le descripte operature tanto directamente conducte, che proportionate ne l’area quanto el naturale artificiosamente appariano. De perfectissimo oro tutto collustratamente inaurato. Le apertione, cioè lo intervacuo della fogliatione, fructi, et animali convenientissimamente se praestavano, obturati de crystalline plastre, de diverso coloramento tincte, quale perlustrabile gemme. Alla congruentia della structura opportuna è la integritate dela harmonia, imperoché omni cingibile ligamento intraneo, expostula el concincto extraneo. Gli pili externi continuavano el pedamento Areobato cum gli tre gradi impari, colligante tutto lo imo del tempio, tanto dall’area librato, quanto levato era l’interno pavimento, de sopra agli Areobati, o vero Stylobati, o vero Scabelli, in loco de Base, uno ornato, com Thori, Alvei, Fasce, Gule, et quarti di circulo circumiendo, et ancora d’intorno al sacello concinnamente circinava. Accepto lo infimo suo proiecto dal humano pede, et di sopra gli Pilastri. Gli quali in interstitio erano perterebrati, o vero fistulati, et pertusati, cioè lo imbricio, o vero el compluvio delle aque praecipite, per gli Tubuli fina al solo intromessi, se n

The remaining walls of the temple, with manifold and various-form Emblemature, were laboriously incrusted of precious marbles — as best the much-knowing Architect, imagining, could often apply to so great a magnificence of structure; nor, perhaps, was such made for Ammon. Above the order of the Corinthians, of most-perfect sculpture, the eloquent Apollo resided, lyring. And above each of the others, in circuit, upon a fit Altar, of the whole entire, a Muse of pilates stone — at the opportune gestures and office, with the utmost praise of the Statuary most-exquisitely carved — set above the aforesaid, above, of the encompassing binding.

The huge cupola showed the greatest token, rather of divine operation than of human ostentation. But if human, not without stupor and accusation of the ambition of so much attempted of the founder's-art by human wit — for, considering so great a vastness, in one sole and solid casting and pour of metal (as I judged), I remained most-highly marvelling and hallucinated, damning it almost to impossibility. Nonetheless, this such Bronze-work was all of Vine springing out of most-beautiful vases, of the bronze material, standing at the perpendicular and order of the columnation — diffusing the branches, vine- shoots, or twigs, and Tendrils, dizzily entangling themselves, with most-pleasing conjugation, in observance of the formation of the convex of the said cupola, one with the other with decent density; with leaves, clusters, little infants climbing and plucking, little Birds fluttering, Lizards creeping, in emulation of nature, most-excellently worked out, and all the rest passable (open).

The described works (were) so directly conducted, that, proportioned, in the area they artfully appeared as much as the natural. Of most-perfect gold, all shiningly gilt. The openings — that is, the void of the foliation, fruits, and animals — most-fittingly presented themselves stopped with crystalline plates, of diverse colouring tinged, like translucent gems.

To the congruity of the structure opportune is the integrity of the harmony; for every girdable inner binding demands the outer girdle. The external piers continued the areobate footing, with the three uneven steps, binding all the base of the temple — as much librated from the area as the inner pavement was raised — above the areobates, or stylobates, or Scabelli, in place of a Base: an ornament, with Tori, Alvei, Fasciae, Gulets, and quarter-circles circling round, and again round the sacello becomingly circled. Its lowest projection received (worn) from the human foot; and above, the Pilasters. Which, in the interstice, were pierced through, or tubed, and perforated — that is, the guttering, or compluvium of the precipitate waters, through the Tubes let down to the ground, were —

Notes

Confidence: medium. The temple's walls (incrusted in emblematic precious-marble panels), its sculpture programme (Apollo lyre-playing over the Corinthians, a Muse over each other column), and its crowning marvel — the great cupola cast as a single bronze vine, its foliage, clusters, climbing putti, birds and lizards gilt, and its openings glazed with coloured crystal like gems. All secure; the vine-dome is one of the book's supreme architectural inventions.

ingurgitavano, de optimo coagmento uno nel lingulato del altro coniuncti. Imperoché negli aedificii subdivo scale, compluvio, o vero gurgiti, non se debi locare. Primo, per el periculo del lapso. Secundo colui che minge proximo ad gli sui pedi, destruge et gli calciamenti sui spurca. Dunque debese tale inconveniente fugire. Lo imbricio discoperto, per inundante aqua l’area excava, et più enorme, si resistentia de subdita petra se oppone, che tanto più l’aqua al pedamento salisce et muri, quanto che dalle gutte, dalle stille resultante se defende. Non sencia grave iniuria, damno, et iactura, et per ventilare impeto, l’aqua per gli muri fundese, reddendoli poscia putri et terricosi, et per fenestre lacescente, exhausto, et evanido omni illimento. Per la expergine della quale, excresce nelle compacture herbacio, cotilidone, o vero cimbalaria Adianto, Digitello, Parietaria, et Polypodio, et a produre arbusculi et caprifici parata, exitio murale, cum populose et redivive fibre, o vero radice, reddendo gli parieti inconstanti et rituosi. Ritorniamo. Lo alamento del primo muro la sua altitudine derivava ad libramento della summitate, della crassitudine degli Trabi inflexi, o vero Archi sopra la columnatione, et quelli del testudinato dal muro a rimpecto della Corinthia columna. Sopra la superficie del quale muro, cioè dello illigamento della circunducta cornitione, era uno canaliolo excavato. Appresso el labro del quale verso el templo se terminava el squammato clivo del aeneo et inaurato tecto. Il supremo del quale culmo supra el camurato, aequalmente principiava, a ricontro della sublime linea della coronice, del Phrygio et Trabe interna. Nel dicto canaleolo sopra el muro nella plana del cornitione excapto, le aque che per piogia per el proclinato tecto scorreano, negli acceptabuli degli Pili infundevanse. Et per questa via gli rivuli della piogia concepta se imbricavano praecipitante al fondo, et per occulte fistule, o vero meati subterranei flueva nella Cisterna. La quale havea uno Voratore, per el quale el superfluo dell’aque se ne usciva, et a sufficientia delle cose sacre rimanea. Il fronte degli Pilastri, tra le undule de optimo liniamento de candelabri, foglie, fructi, fiori avicole et de varia altra eximia operatura, perfectamente se praestava ornata, oltra la fimbria del muro, continuavano dicti pilastri, tanto in altecia, quanto se ritrovava el residuo ascendente, dalla coronice, ove extava el suppedio, o vero Arula subiecta alle Muse, nel primario illigamento interiore, fina alla corona. Sopra la quale principiava la magna cupula a tuberare. Et da questa altitudine alla cima degli Pili

— engulfed, of excellent jointing, one conjoined in the tongued (socket) of the other. For in open-air buildings, stairs, compluvium, or gutters, ought not to be placed: first, for the peril of the slip; second, he who makes water next to his own feet destroys, and befouls his footwear. Therefore such inconvenience ought to be fled. The uncovered guttering, by inundating water, excavates the area — and more enormously, if a resistance of subjacent stone opposes — so that the water climbs so much the more to the footing and walls, as it defends itself from the drops, from the resulting drips.

Not without grave injury, damage and loss (and, by the ventilating impetus, the water pours through the walls, rendering them then putrid and earthy, and through the windows leaking, exhausted and vanished every rendering): by the sprinkling of which, there grows in the joints herbage — cotyledon, or cymbalaria, maidenhair, digitello, pellitory, and polypody — and, ready to produce little shrubs and wild figs, a mural ruin, with populous and reviving fibres, or roots, rendering the walls inconstant and rift.

Let us return. The band of the first wall derived its height to the level of the summit, of the thickness of the inflected Architraves, or Arches, above the columnation, and those of the vaulting, from the wall, opposite the Corinthian column. Above the surface of which wall — that is, of the binding of the circum-led cornice — was a little channel excavated. Near the lip of which, toward the temple, terminated the scaled slope of the bronze and gilt roof. The topmost of which summit, above the curved (dome), evenly began, opposite the sublime line of the cornice, of the Frieze and inner Architrave. In the said little channel, above the wall, in the flat of the cornice excavated, the waters that by rain ran down the sloped roof were poured into the receivers of the Piers. And by this way the rivulets of the conceived rain guttered, precipitating to the bottom; and by hidden pipes, or subterranean passages, flowed into the Cistern. Which had a Devourer (overflow-drain), by which the superfluous of the waters went out, and sufficiently for the sacred things remained.

Notes

Confidence: medium. A largely engineering page: the temple's rainwater system (roof-channel → piers-as-downpipes → subterranean pipes → cistern with an overflow), framed by a little essay on why open gutters and stairs are bad (slipping, fouling, and — the vivid part — water eroding foundations and weeds rooting in wet joints). All secure; Colonna the practical architect.

monstrava tanto discenso, o vero proclinato, quanto quello della tectura inscandulata squammea, et inaurata, che tale non fu quelle del Capitolio inaurato da Catulo, né tale squammeatura hebbe el Pantheon. Per questo modo tra la apertione del muro sotto la cupula, et tra questo adiuncto de Pillastro fundato a llibella sopra lo externo murale circuito, nasceva uno arco hiantemente aperto contrastante, cum liniamento de Trabe. Gli corni del quale pedavano d’ambidui gli lateri del muro et del Pillastro sopra el capitulo d’una semiquadrangula intrusa nel muro, excluso el tertio obvia della intranea de Ophytes et l’altra nel adiuncto del Pillastro. La facia del quale adiuncto de Pillastro dinanti era uno Nicholo, o vero Solio, et inanti questo Solio, o vero Nichio perpendicularmente sopra la piana dil Pillastro era situata per ciascuno una nobilissima statua, cum multiplici acti. Dal latere dextro et sinistro del quale, adiuncto se vedea tale scalptura, quale nel fronte del Pillastro subiecto. L’ultima superficie della crassitudine del arco exteriore ad aequamento era della plana del summo Pillastro. Il lapso dunque dal concincto innitiava, sopra el quale principio usurpava la cupula de fora, et cadeva sopra el Pilo, cum tutto quello liniamento colligantise, che era nel concincto circumacto sotto la cupula, et soto questo lapso resistentia facendo l’arco. Il quale concincto era una coronatione denticulata et echinata, o vero ovolata, cum el suggrundio gyrulato, o vero voragulato cum le pentafilete tra gli verticuli circunducto, cum le occurrente liniature perfecta. Nel plano della superficie de questo illigamento, o vero coronatione lo initio della cupula giaceva, nella proiectura della quale, era uno alveo excavato, nel quale le aque della cupula derivavano discurrendo, et giù per gli alveati lapsi ructuosamente se ingurgitavano negli Pilastri. Supra el lubrico dalla cupula terminando al Pilastro, cioè al suo cimatio, o vero plana, uno cortice, o vero chartella, cooperiendo faceva dui contrarii voluti. Lo uno achosta la cupula supino, et l’altro appresso el Pilo resupino, cum limacale linea facendo gli voluti. Negli inflexi del volume nascevano silique, o vero teche (pregne del suo parto) fabacee, o vero lupinacee. Il quale cortice era intecto de gratiose squamme. Et sopra el convolvulo resupino serpiva cadendo sopra la undiculatione squammea uno folio di Cynara. Il quale volucro cocleale facilmente a norma del circino acconciamente se involve, fermando il stabile et volvendo semicirculo. Ponendo poscia el stabile tra el ducto semicirculo, et el puncto, aperiendo el circino et lo instabile copulando cum lo extremo del semicirculo et vertendo, et cusì aperiendo, et el puncto movendo, quella n ii

— showed as much descent, or slope, as that of the scaled and gilt roof-covering — such as was not that of the Capitol gilt by Catulus, nor such scaling had the Pantheon. In this manner, between the opening of the wall under the cupola, and between this adjunct of Pilaster (founded, level, upon the external mural circuit), was born an arch, gapingly open, contrasting, with the lineament of an Architrave. The horns of which footed on both the sides of the wall and of the Pilaster, upon the capital of a half-quadrangular (pilaster) intruded in the wall (excepting the facing third of the inner Ophite), and the other in the adjunct of the Pilaster. The face of which adjunct of Pilaster, in front, was a Niche, or Solium; and before this Solium, or Niche, perpendicularly above the flat of the Pilaster, was situated, for each, a most-noble statue, with manifold acts. On the right and left side of which adjunct was seen such sculpture as on the front of the Pilaster beneath. The last surface of the thickness of the exterior arch was even with the flat of the topmost Pilaster.

Finalmente per absolutione di questa mirifica structura di Templo, resta a dire brevemente, che ello era compacto de quadrati de Augustea petra parte, et parte del supranarrato marmoro, in contignatione perfecta sencia ferro et lignatura, cum più subtile investigatione di scalptura, che unque al seculo nostro fare, né imaginare si potesse, né tale ad Api Deo, Sannitico aegyptio construsse. Sotto el suppedio delle columne, era circumacta quanta la sua crassitudine, una lista de Porphyrite, cum due collaterale di durissimo serpentino, cum l’ordine del Peristylio in circumductione. Il simile vedevasi l’orificio della cisterna cincto nel pavimento, una lista de Porphyro et un’altra di Ophytes. Il residuo dil spectatissimo pavimento tra l’orificio puteale et il peristylio, era di mirabile emblemature, di minutali, di tassellulato di fine petre circinantisi elegantemente includevano in partitione deducti, deci rotondi, per diametro pedali. Sotto el concamerato erano nel solistimo Asaroto di vermiculato emblemate, fogliamento, animali, et fiori tessellulati di minutissimi corpusculi, de recisamenti lapidei diligentemente tessellati depicto, et coaequatissimamente perfricati, o vero scalpturati. Quale arte non hebbe nel pavimentare Zenodoro in Pergamo, né tale fue il lithostrato in Praeneste nel delubro dilla Fortuna. — violated. And the vacillation of the light seemed to give motion to the sculpture.

Finally, for the absolution of this marvellous structure of Temple, it remains to say briefly that it was compacted of quadrates of Augustan stone in part, and part of the above-narrated marble, in perfect jointing, without iron and timber, with more subtle investigation of sculpture than ever in our century could be done, nor imagined — nor such did they construct for Apis, the Samnitic-Egyptian God.

Under the bases of the little Pilasters, or quadrangulars — which was the lowest and continuous binding, in the first band, or wall; and the upper girdle likewise, with the encompassing capitals — went round, in the most-even pavement, a strip, or band, of finest Porphyry, as much as was the projection of its square, and contiguous, almost without dispute, another of Ophite. Under the sub-base of the columns was circled, as much as its thickness, a strip of Porphyry, with two collateral of hardest serpentine, with the order of the Peristyle in circumduction. The like was seen of the orifice of the cistern, girt in the pavement — a strip of Porphyry and another of Ophite.

The remainder of the much-admired pavement, between the well-orifice and the peristyle, was of marvellous emblemature, of little-minutiae, of little tessellation of fine stones circling themselves, elegantly included, deduced in partition: ten roundels, a foot in diameter, of their colour and species, the one to the line of the other. There were two of reddening Jasper, most-pleasingly suffused with various spots; two of Litharmenon, of little sparks of gold, more minute, disseminated of rutilant atoms; two of green Jasper, variegated with chalcedonic veins, with reddening and yellow spots; two of Agate, confusedly undulated of milky threads; two, lastly, of most-limpid Chalcedony. And then, incontinently, an enucleated admiration succoured in the warm memory: that, it being natural that whiteness disgregates (scatters) the visual power, this (whiteness), with so much delectation, drew and congregated all the seeing into itself — not only not harming it, but, to the utmost solace and extreme pleasure, that so precious object, viscidly retaining it bound to itself, and taken, occupied it. Beyond this, reasonably I was stupefied that the valves, each by its very self, without any impulse, opened themselves. Et cusì dunque la sacra Antistite intrando el Templo cum la ingenua et praestante Nympha, et io pertinace sequentila, et cum tutte le altre sacre Damicelle, cum le uberrime capillature per gli lactei colli ornatissime cadente, vestite di electissima purpura, et di sopra riportate le tenuissime Gosapine più breve, o veramente curte del primo indumento. Al fatale orificio della mysteriosa cisterna divote et festive ne condusseron.

Nella quale, como dicto fue, altra aqua non intrava. Se non quella che per gli terebrati Pillastri dagli aquarii et compluvii dal fastigato Templo liberamente, senza pernicie della structura, intro se infundevano. La summa sacerdotessa quivi alle virgine fece nuto, et andorono in uno Adyto sacrario, nui tre soli rimasti.

In a tablet of Magnet, to the right of the ingress, was carved, of exquisite antiquarian Latin letters, that celebrated Virgilian saying:

TRAHIT SUA QUEMQUE VOLUPTAS — "Each is drawn by his own pleasure." (Virgil, Eclogue II.65)

On the left, the tablet I saw, of most-ancient Greek majuscules, elegantly inscribed:

ΠΑΝ ΔΕΙ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΦΥΣΙΝ — in Latin, "Each ought to do according to his own nature."

Raising then the eyes, curiously stimulated, to the magnificence of so great a Temple, and to the vastness of the noteworthy and sky-reaching cupola, with the other most-exact parts — of ambition, and of outstanding artifice, of divine device, and of superb workmanship, and wondrous lineaments, of stupendous ostentation, seasoned most-marvellously. And much more marvellous I judged the incredible beauty of the divine Nymph, which enticed my inspecting eyes, and held all my soul — insomuch that from the right disquisition of whatever considerable part of it (the temple) I might move, and she alone, drawing, coarcted (me) to contemplate her with stupor and marvel. Give pardon, then, reader, if I have not perscribed every fitting particular.

And so, then, the sacred Priestess entering the Temple, with the ingenuous and outstanding Nymph, and I pertinacious following her, and with all the other sacred Damsels — with their most-rich hair falling, most- ornate, over the milky necks, dressed in most-choice purple, and above, worn back, the most-tenuous cotton (robes) shorter, or curt, than the first garment — to the fateful orifice of the mysterious cistern, devout and festive, they conducted us.

Into which, as was said, no other water entered save that which, through the perforated Pilasters, from the water-channels and compluvia of the fastigiate Temple, freely, without harm to the structure, poured itself in. Sopra la mensula, overo piano dilla dicta Troclea, superastava un’altra rotonditate regulata, poscia alquanto gululata se contraheva verso la superficie plana et expedita. Nella parte mediana dilla quale promineva uno striato stilo, più porrecto nella inferiore parte sopra la piana cum proportionata crepidine. Diviso dunque il diametro dilla interna rotundatione di questo stilo. Partitione una era alla proiectura ambiente consignata. Il superno capo due portione havea cum tornatile gulule et lo imo ancora debitamente riservatose. Sopradicto stipite tegeva una inversa piana rotundata, tanto in proiecto gyrando, quanto l’extremo exito degli labri dilla subiecta Troclea Ornata nella superiore parte, nello extremo circuito in cliva dimonstratione cum una Sima di spectanda folliatura da una egregia coronetta perpollitamente nascendo. Nel circinato contento dunque dilla quale coronetta bellamente occupava la apertura di uno elegante fiore, in balaustico liniamento deformato, cum gli calicei labri sopra il piano lambenti, et quadripartito in periucundo foliamento acanthino fatiscente. The demonstration of which Altar, succinctly saying, I beheld a conspicuous device of unwonted make. The lowest of the said, upon the stepped and marble footing, was a round little slab. Upon which undulated an auricular foliage, most with polish jagged, and choicely cauliculate, ending its point at a little cord, or knot, or fillet, contained upon the little slab. And likewise, at the birth of the encompassing foliage, sat above another little cord; and between this and another was pressed a trochlea (pulley-moulding) moderately channelled, and then a little cornice. Upon the bracket, or plane, of the said Trochlea, over- stood another regulated rotundity; then, somewhat gulleted, it contracted itself toward the flat and unencumbered surface. In the middle part of which stood forth a striated stylus, more stretched in the lower part, upon the flat, with a proportioned base. The diameter, then, of the inner rotundity of this stylus divided: one partition was consigned to the encompassing projection; the upper head had two portions, with turned gulets, and the lowest also duly reserved.

The aforesaid stalk covered an inverted flat rotundity, turning in projection as much as the extreme outlet of the lips of the subjacent Trochlea, ornated in the upper part, in the extreme circuit, in a sloped demonstration, with a Sima of noteworthy foliage, from an egregious little cornice most-polishedly being born. In the circled content, then, of which little cornice, beautifully occupied the opening of an elegant flower, in balustered lineament fashioned, with the calyxed lips over the flat lambent, and quadripartite into most-pleasant acanthine foliage, gaping. Under which, in the jagged discrepancy, subsided another leaf, artfully carved. Upon the point of which, after the due lineaments, egregiously rounded a knot of exquisite expression. To which, fixed, set, dilatedly stood forth an antiquarian platter of purest gold, with the lips broadish, and a little lacunate (hollowed). In the flat rim of the lips, alternately, stood forth incomparable Diamonds and Carbuncles, with outstanding pyramidal fashioning, in the circuit marvellously disposed, of incredible thickness. Let yield here the Scyphus of most-strong Hercules, the Cantharus of pleasant Bacchus, and the Carchesium dedicated to immortal Jove.

Chapter XVIII

The sacrifice and the miraculous rose-bush. Polia, a temple-initiate, burns the incense of Venus and sacrifices the turtledoves; a winged spirit rises from the smoke; the priestess speaks the great prayer to Venus, and from the blood-quenched fire a rose-bush miraculously springs, whose fruit the lovers eat in communion. Then they come out to the ruined Polyandrion, the seaside tomb-temple of those who died of love.

IO NON POSSO UNQUANTULO LASCIarmi suadere, che tali riti, cerimonie, sacrificii, da Numa Pompilio, né a Cerite di Thuscia. Né unque in Hetruria né dal sancto Iudaeo fusseron ritrovati. Né cum tanta religiosa observantia et ordine litavano et adolevano li Memphitici Vati ad Api in Aegypto, nel Nilo la patera aurea immergendo. Né ancora cum tanto religiosissimo venerato in la citate di Rhamnis di Euboia fue culta Ramnusia. Né Iove Anxuro cum tale superstitione fue culto, né quelli che a Faronia afflati tali riti ritrovorono caminando sencia offensione sopra gli carboni accensi. Né tanto tresse furono le edonide clodane, né mymallone di numine aspirate. Quali nel praesente tressero. Meritamente arbitro (oltra questo che palesemente hoe riguardato) per le cose parate, et supersticiosamente disposite succedere dovesse. Imperò che degli capigli la isochrysia Polia Nympha, di cusì facto officio digna negli sacri imbuta et iniciata. Non più presto vide il nuto dilla sacraria monitrice, che dal mundissimo pavimento, sencia voce, indusio, et strepito (niun’altra moventise) promptissima religiosamente se levoe. Onde dalla sacratica monitrice ad una mira urnula hyacinthina da parte collocata nel sacello fue conducta, che di tale artificio mai Mentore non sepe fare. Et io attentissimo riguardantila in tuti acti scrutariamente observava. Et nello aspecto hora la vidi tale, quale il lucidissimo Phoebo cum il novo dì la fresca aurora colorabondo dipinge. Et quivi cerimoniosamente cum le prompte, et intemerate mano, uno odorante liquore fora exhauriva, et il suo lacteo et invermigliato volto spirante purpurante rose, cum le delicate mane madefacte tuto accortamente ella irrigoe. Diqué cusì divotamente purificata cum più sinceritate, quale forsa non hebbe la virgine Aemilia. Dinanti al grado dilla sanctissima Ara, ove extava uno mirando candelabro aureo. Il quale era di exactissimo expresso spectatissimo, et di crasse gemme elegantemente circumornato et glandulato. In questa dunque posito fue il suavissimo sperma degli ingenti ceti, mosco odorifico. La crystallina et fugitiva Camphora, olente Ladano, dilla magna Crete. Thimioma et Mastice, ambidui gli Stiraci lo amigdalato Beenzuì il ponderabile Zilaloè blactebisantis, overo ungule indice, et gli felici germini di Arabia. Le quale tute pretiose cose erano cum distributo pondo optimamente gradate. Alle quale la solicita Polia, et cum

I cannot in the least let myself be persuaded that such rites, ceremonies, sacrifices were found out by Numa Pompilius, nor at Caere of Tuscany, nor ever in Etruria, nor by the holy Jew; nor with so much religious observance and order did the Memphitic Seers sacrifice and burn-offerings to Apis in Egypt, immersing the golden patera in the Nile; nor yet with so most-religious a veneration, in the city of Rhamnus of Euboea, was Rhamnusia (Nemesis) worshipped; nor was Jupiter Anxur worshipped with such superstition; nor those who, at Feronia inspired, found such rites — walking without harm upon the kindled coals. Nor so entranced were the Edonian Clodones, nor the Mimallones, aspired by the numen, as in the present they were entranced. Deservedly I judge (beyond that which I have openly beheld) that, by the things prepared and superstitiously disposed, (a marvel) ought to succeed. For, of the hair, the golden Polia Nymph — of such-made office worthy, in the sacred things imbued and initiated — no sooner saw the nod of the sacristan monitress, than, from the most-clean pavement, without voice, delay, or noise (no other one moving), most-promptly, religiously, she rose. Whence, by the sacred monitress, to a wondrous hyacinthine little urn, set apart in the sacello, she was conducted — such as, of such artifice, Mentor never knew to make.

And I, most-attentive, regarding her, in all acts scrutinously observed. And in aspect now I saw her such as the most-lucid Phoebus, with the new day, colouring, paints the fresh aurora. And there, ceremoniously, with prompt and untouched hands, an odorous liquor she drew out; and her milky and vermilioned face, breathing purpling roses, with the delicate moistened hands, all shrewdly, she irrigated. Whence, thus devoutly purified, with more sincerity than perhaps had the virgin Aemilia — before the step of the most-holy Altar, where stood a wondrous golden candelabrum (which was of most-exact and much-admired expression, and elegantly circum-ornated and knobbed with thick gems; in its summit stood forth, exigently, a round opening of a little shell, or a platter, less than an arm's embrace) —

In this, then, was placed the sweetest sperm of the huge whales (ambergris); odoriferous musk; the crystalline and fugitive Camphor; odorous Ladanum of great Crete; Thymiama and Mastic; both the Storaxes; the almond- scented Benzoin; the ponderable Aloewood; blatte-bisantie, or Indian nails (onycha); and the happy germens of Arabia. Which all precious things were, with distributed weight, most-excellently graded. To which the solicitous Polia, and with —

And at the divine shoulder-blades a pair of arched little wings it had, with an unseen and unwonted light — which, not without some lesion of my eyes regarding it, most-avidly, the lost heart truly felt. Whence, full and surrounded by marvellous terror, and fearfully agitated, I invoked, silent, whatever divine subsidy and pity. And, scarce somewhat opening the frightened eyes, I looked to the smoking Altar. Out of which, purest smoke I saw miraculously issue, germinating, and successively multiplying itself into a verdant rose-bush — which, with multiplied little branches, a great part of the sacred sacello copiously occupied, to the raised altitude of the cupola, with a numerosity of vermilion and rubricating roses together, and with many round fruits, of wondrous odour fragrant, of colouring candid-and-vermilioned; which offered themselves more pleasing to the taste than, by chance, are not those which, to the famished mouth of Tantalus, present themselves. Upon this rosy bush, then, appeared three white little doves, with some little birds gregariously fluttering in the branches; and, festive, they leapt, colluding, and most-sweetly sang. Hora non più praesto che io degustai il miraculoso et suavissimo pomulo, che sencia mora in me sentivi ricentare et rinovare il rude et crasso intellecto, et lo affannoso et moerente core tuto ricrearse in amoroso gaudio delibuto, né più né meno, quale chi nel profundo mare obruto, et fin al fondo immerso cum obstrusi labri, sencia hausto di spirito, di sopra ritorna, le fresche et iucundissime aure avidissimo sumendo se vivifica. Per la quale cosa incontinente in me di ardere più amorose fiamme incomminciorono, et cum più suave cruciato di novelle qualitate d’amore transmutarme mi apparve. Et perciò principiai evidentemente di cognoscere, et effectuosamente di persentire, quale gratie sono le veneree, et di quanta efficacia ad gli terrigeni se praesta et quanto praemio loetamente conseguino, chi per gli delitiosi regni intrepidamente militando, et nelle amorose pugne pervicaci, ad quelli pervengono. Ultimamente dapoi la divota et sacra refectione degli fatali fructi sumpta sencia cunctatione, quel divino germe da gli ochii evanescente disparve. La libante Antistite dil sancto sacello fora ussitene, et Polia pare a llei, et io, et tute.

Cum tale et sì facto ordine terminati et diffiniti gli mystici sacrificii, et libamini et imolatione, et il divino culto, ambedue deposite le sacre veste, et exute, cum eximia veneratione, tuti quegli mysteriosi et pontificali instrumenti, cum domestici et templarii obsequii, nel sacrario riverentemente ripositorno.

Now, no sooner did I taste the miraculous and sweetest little apple, than without delay I felt in me refresh and renew the rude and gross intellect, and the anxious and mourning heart all recreate itself, anointed in amorous joy — neither more nor less than one who, overwhelmed in the deep sea, and to the bottom immersed with shut lips, without draught of breath, from above returns, most-avidly taking the fresh and most-pleasant airs, and vivifies himself. For which thing, incontinently, in me more amorous flames began to burn; and with a more sweet torment of new qualities of love it appeared to me to be transmuted. And therefore I began evidently to know, and effectually to feel, what the Venerean graces are, and of how much efficacy they present themselves to the earth-born, and how great a reward joyously they attain, who — through the delightful realms, intrepidly soldiering, and in the amorous, pertinacious battles — arrive at them. Ultimately, after the devout and sacred refection of the fatal fruits, taken without hesitation, that divine germ (bush), vanishing from the eyes, disappeared. The libant Priestess went out of the holy sacello, and Polia paired with her, and I, and all.

With such and so-made order, terminated and defined the mystic sacrifices, and libations, and immolations, and the divine cult — both, having deposed the sacred vestments, and stripped off, with choice veneration, all those mysterious and pontifical instruments, with domestic and templar obsequies, in the sacristy reverently they re-deposited.

Et quivi trutinatamente la summa Antistite cum praecipua maiestate, cusì familiarmente ne disse. Figlioli mei hora da me expiati, et benedicti al vostro amoroso incepto et viagio andate. Priego ancora la divina matre fausta et affabile se praesti, et ad gli vostri amorosi concepti, intenti, et casi, miserabile, favorevola, et propitia sia. Et nel praesente inclaustrate gli profundi, et crebri sospiri, gli lamentamenti postponete et lassate. Fugate omni moerore. Imperò che già cum la mia instantia questa praesente hora vi sarà salutare et secunda. Dunque a questi mei salubri moniti et proficui imperii l’animo vostro intenda, aciò che essa cum il suo pio et dolce affecto vi concedi foelice successo. Poscia che la sacraria monitrice cum blando affamine hebe dicto. Nui gratie immortale dicendo da tute licentia riverentemente impetrassemo, cum dulcissimi et mutui saluti, indicando il madido volto, che quasi gli molestava il nostro discesso. Tamen valedicendo, fora dil magnifico et superbo tempio uscissimo, et amonita la mia chrysocari Polia dilla via et itinere nostro, finalmente se partissemo. O desiderato cusì diutinamente gratissimo comitato, et foelice, et prospero exito dille transacte tristitie. Hora il mio core afflato d’interna dolcecia, et perfuso di caeleste rore il noxio foco, unquancho non me tituba, ma ferma et evidentemente questa è la mia tanto optatissima Polia. La mia tutelaria dea. Il genio dil mio core. Alla quale benemerente debita gratulatione, io debo di tanto suo famulato alla divina matre, et di tanta ostensione di amore in questo iucundissimo comitato. Queste et simigliante parole summissamente io dicendo, Polia in quel puncto avidutasi dil mio depresso parlare, me riguardoe cum dui festevoli ochii accesi d’amore. Più chiari che lucidissime stelle, sencia la cornuta Cynthia, nel sereno cielo corruscante, non altramente che lo ignito Calybe sopra l’incude malleato scintilla, cusì nel mio percito pecto quelli crebri scintillavano. Et nel parlare venusta cum angelici accenti, cum la purpurante bucca latibulo di omni fragrantia, apotheca di orientale perle, seminario uberrimo di enucleate et dulcicule parolete, tempestivamente mulcendo deliniva omni mia mentale inquietudine. Parlare, sencia dubio, da impiacevolire il terrifico aspecto di Medusa, et di mitigare la atrocitate horrenda dillo infiammato Marte, et dille sue cruentose armature spoliare. Di furare il bellissimo Ganymede dille adoncate granfie dilla suprema alite. Et da teneritudine di scopiare, et minutatamente scindere in parvissime fresule gli durissimi marmori, et cote, et caute, et saxi asperrimi, et abrupti di Persia, et dil invio et nubifero monte Athlante, nella parte di Oceano et acquietando mansuefare, overo cicurire le saevissime fere di Libya, et da vivificare omni pulvereo et cineroso morto, cusì disse. And there, weighingly, the high Priestess, with special majesty, thus familiarly said to us: "My children, now by me expiated and blessed, to your amorous undertaking and voyage go. I pray, again, that the divine mother show herself auspicious and affable, and to your amorous conceits, intents, and cases, be pitiful, favourable, and propitious. And, in the present, encloister the profound and frequent sighs; the lamentings postpone and leave; put to flight every mourning. For already, by my instance, this present hour will be to you salutary and favourable. Then, to these my salubrious admonitions and profitable commands let your soul attend, so that she, with her pious and sweet affect, grant you happy success."

After the sacred monitress with bland speech had said (this), we — immortal thanks saying — from all reverently took leave, with sweetest and mutual salutes, indicating (by) the wet face that our departure almost troubled them. Nonetheless, bidding farewell, out of the magnificent and superb temple we went; and, my chrysocari (golden-graced) Polia admonished of our way and itinerary, finally we departed.

O comitation so long desired, so most-pleasing, and happy, and prosperous exit of the transacted sadnesses! Now my heart, breathed-upon with internal sweetness, and the noxious fire perfused with celestial dew, no longer wavers me — but firmly and evidently this is my so most-desired Polia. My tutelary goddess. The genius of my heart. To whom, well-deserving, due gratulation I owe, of so great her service to the divine mother, and of so great a showing of love in this most-pleasant comitation. These and like words low-voiced saying, Polia, in that instant aware of my depressed speech, regarded me with two festive eyes kindled with love — more clear than most- lucid stars, without the horned Cynthia, in the serene sky coruscating; not otherwise than as the ignited steel upon the anvil, malleated, scintillates, so, in my smitten breast, those (eyes) frequently scintillated. And, in speaking, comely, with angelic accents, with the purpling mouth (hiding-place of every fragrance, apothecary of oriental pearls, most-rich seminary of enucleated and sweet little words), timely, soothing, she delineated (dissolved) all my mental inquietude. A speech, without doubt, to make pleasant the terrific aspect of Medusa, and to mitigate the horrendous atrocity of the inflamed Mars, and to despoil him of his bloody armours; to steal the most-beautiful Ganymede from the hooked talons of the supreme bird; and, from tenderness, to burst and minutely cleave into tiniest fragments the hardest marbles, and whetstones, and crags, and roughest rocks, and abrupt (cliffs) of Persia, and of the pathless and cloudy Mount Atlas in the Ocean-part; and, quieting, to tame, or make gentle, the most-savage beasts of Libya; and to vivify every dusty and ashen dead. Thus she said:

Circa al quale era uno religioso luco. Il quale era sopra aedificato al marisono et lavato litore dal refluo mare. Et quivi ancora restato era una vastitate magna di muri, o vero parieti, et di structure di marmoro albario, et uno fragmentato, et illiso mole di porto apresso. Nelle fracture dil quale et lassate compacture il salsiphilo et littoreo Critani germinava, et in alcuni lochi vidi il litorale Cachile, et molto Kali et lo odoroso Abscynthio marino, et per il Aggere sabulaceo Irringi, et Portulaca, et Eruca marina, et assai altri celebri simplici, il Caratia, et Mirsinytes et simigliante litoracole herbe dal quale porto per molti scalini dispari al suggesto dil propylaeo dil tempio si saliva. Alcune ancora mirai eree di mirabile arte, quale non erano nel gaditano tempio, ma omni cosa sub divo, di carie et vetustate offensa. La mia frugi et benemorata Polia quivi me disse. Poliphile dolcissimo mio mira quale digno monumento dille cose magne alla posteritate cusì in tale supinata ruina, et in tanto grumo di rupture di pietre aspero et camelloso relicte. Già nel primaevo fue uno egregio et mirando tempio, circa il quale già solemnissimamente si nundinava, et ingente de mortali multitudine eo omni anno convenivano spectaculi facendo, et per elegante structura, et per gli observati sacrificii diffusamente famoso, molto religiosamente dagli terrigeni celebrato. Which was built up above the sea-sounding and (wave-)washed shore, by the refluent sea. And there, again, was left a great vastness of walls, or partitions, and of structures of white marble, and a fragmented and battered mole of a harbour nearby. In the fractures of which, and left joints, the salt-loving and littoral crithmum (samphire) germinated; and in some places I saw the littoral cakile, and much kali (glasswort), and the odorous marine wormwood; and, by the sandy embankment, eryngo, and purslane, and marine rocket, and very many other celebrated simples — the caratia, and myrsinites, and like shore-dwelling herbs — from which harbour, by many uneven steps, one ascended to the suggestum of the propylaeum of the temple. Which building, by voracious time and by putrid antiquity, and by negligence, to the humid earth collapsed, here and there demolished, had left without capitals the shaft, or decapitated trunk, of some huge columns of Persian stone of red grain; some, with mutual alternation of Mygdonian marble; some had the contracture (fluting) broken — the hypothesis (base), nor the hypotrachelion, nor Astragal was seen; some, again, I beheld of bronze, of marvellous art (such as were not in the Gaditan temple) — but every thing under the open sky, of decay and old age offended.

My frugal and well-mannered Polia here said to me: "Poliphilo my sweetest, behold what worthy monument of the great things, to posterity thus, in such supine ruin, and in so great a heap of stone-breakages, rough and humpy, left. Already, in the primaeval (past), it was an egregious and marvellous temple, about which already most-solemnly they held market, and huge multitudes of mortals thereto, every year, convened, making spectacles; and, for its elegant structure and for the observed sacrifices, diffusely famous, most-religiously by the earth- born celebrated. But, because at present abolished is, and ignored, its dignity — thus, as thou seest it lie, disrupted and ruined, expressly destitute — it is denominated the Polyandrion temple. In which, Poliphilo, my little-heart, are many little tomb-pits, where were buried the pulverable bodies of those who, badly, for wicked, unlucky, and lugubrious love, to obscure death, miserable, ceded.
