Tuti quelli che ad amore affabile indulgendo davano opera, cusì homini, quale foemine. In questo loco ad gli celebri ferali et solemni panegyri da diverse regione et provincie contermine et remoti loci parentabondi convenivano, obsecrando et litando il nume di Plutone tricorpo. Che essi a tanta impietate non cespitasseno di essere conscii dilla propria et intempestiva morte. Diciò immolavano le furve hostie, overo nigricante pecore, non ancora cognita dal maschio supra una flagrante Ara aenea, gli masculi al deo, et le foemine alla dea, et gli lectisternii facendo trinoctio. Quella fiamma et foco daposcia cum spargiere di multitudine di rose, et cum arferia extingueano, como in questo loco grande roseto di qualunche maniera ancora relicto apertamente vedi. Le quale allhora racoglierle era cosa nepharia. Ma gli sacerdoti le commutavano. Daposcia cum multa divotione dava. Accepto il cinere catervatamente ussivano dil tempio cum observata veneratione ad gli iuncosi litori dil proximo mare come vedi. Poliphilo masters the temptation: recalling the disasters of forced love (Deianira, Lucretia — "the chaste Roman"), the resistance even the gods met, and the maxims of patience (the tamed lion, the ant wearing the flint), he resolves to win Polia "by suffering" not "by perilous improbity," remembering the sacrifices and the extinguished torch. Polia, seeing his face change colour "like the Tripolion," soothes him, and his soul burns on "like the phoenix" hoping to be renewed. This ends chapter XVIII; the argument previews chapter XIX (the epitaphs, the Rape of Proserpina, and the boat). All secure.

Chapter XIX

The Polyandrion and its epitaphs — the longest chapter. Poliphilo explores the ruined tomb-temple: the obelisk of Caesar with its ant-and-elephant concord-hieroglyph, the crypt with its fire-and-ice Hell-mosaic of lovers, and a great sequence of love-death epitaphs (Nevia, Leontia and Lollius, and Artemisia's Mausoleum). A Rape-of-Proserpina fresco frightens him back to Polia; Cupid then arrives by boat, and the marine gods do him homage as the crossing begins.

SOPRA TUTI GLI EXCOGITATI ET exquisiti cruciamenti d’amore non mediocremente obsesso vedendome, et alla praeoptata et salubre, et praesentanea medela, et mia architatrice propinquo essendo obstupefacto mirava che contra omni naturale ordine, quella me più morbidamente inficiava. Et qualunque suo praestante acto, ornato eloquio, morsicante risguardo da sì opportuna salute proximo ritrovantime me abdicavano, onde sempre più multiplicavasi una exhortabile suasione, di volere alla provocante commoditate (grato munusculo ad gli raptori) ingrato non me praestare et pusilanimo. Fremendo come furioso et ringibondo cane, gionta la insecuta fera negli alpestri salti. Cusì io né più né meno furibondo cupitore la propria desiderata praeda quivi gionta, al tuto satisfarmi. Assuefacto hogi mai ad una assidua et familiare morte d’amore, passione per questo non reputava la sua attrocitate, che d’indi ne fusse asseguita. Et peroe omni inconveniente quantunque damnosissimo licito mi suadeva. Diqué la mia eutrapela Polia solerte de l’improbe condictione dil coecuciente Amore, et accortasi per mortificare tanto importuno incendio, et alquanto sincoparlo, et come singulare sospitatrice mia succurrendo cusì benignamente me dice. Poliphile di tuti amantissimo mio già mai non son ignara, che le antiquarie opere ad te summamente piaceno di vedere. Adunche commodamente potes tu in questo intervallo, che nui il signore Cupidine aspetiamo ire licentemente, queste aede deserte, et dalla edace et exoleta vetustate collapse, o per incendio assumpte, o vero da annositate quassate, a tuo solacio mirare, et gli fragmenti nobili rimasti di venerato dignissimi speculare. Et io in questo loco sedendo contenta te aspeteroe, il signore nostro venturo vigile praestolante, che traiectare ne debi al sancto et concupito regno materno. Allhora io grandemente avidissimo, cum l’altre commendatissime opere vise, etiam queste accuratissimo et multivido di contemplare. Levatome dalla foelice sessione, di soto dille temprate umbre di lauro, et di myrto, et tra altiusculi cupressi, allhora circa il loco il periclimeno degli sui odorosi fiori dipingendo, ove, et uno volubile iosamino florente cum suave ombra opaculamente ne copriva disseminando sopra nui copiosamente gli sui bianchissimi fiori. In quel tempo suavissimo odoranti (sencia altro cogitare absorto) da chosta di Polia per quelli devii aggeri, di fastigiato et vasto cumulo et ruina, in la magiore parte occupate di chamaeciso, et di terrambula et di spini implicita solicito perveni. Ove pensiculatamente coniecturai questo essere stato magnifico, et meraveglioso templo di eximia, et soperba structura. Secundo che la proba et praeclara Nympha scitulamente ad me vaticinato havea. Quivi dunque apparia, che in gyro dil rotondo templo fusseron

Above all the excogitated and exquisite torments of love not mediocrely beset seeing myself — and to the pre- chosen and salubrious and present remedy, and my heart-healer, being near — stupefied I marvelled that, against every natural order, she more morbidly infected me. And whatever her outstanding act, ornate eloquence, biting regard, from so opportune a health, finding myself near, abdicated me (drove me off); whence ever more multiplied an exhortable suasion, of wishing, to the provoking commodity (a grateful little gift to ravishers), not to present myself ungrateful and pusillanimous. Fremishing like a furious and snarling dog, the pursued beast having reached, in the alpine leaps: so I, neither more nor less, a furious coveter, the very desired prey here reached, wholly to satisfy myself. Accustomed now to an assiduous and familiar death of love, I did not, for this, repute the atrocity a passion, that thence might be ensued. And therefore every inconvenience, however most-damaging, licit it suaded me. Whence my eutrapela (witty) Polia, shrewd of the improbe condition of blind Love, and aware — to mortify so importunate a burning, and somewhat to syncopate it, and, as my singular preserver, succouring — thus benignly says to me:

"Poliphilo, of all mine most-beloved, I am never unaware that antique works supremely please thee to see. So, conveniently thou canst, in this interval, while we await lord Cupid, go licitly to see these deserted temples, collapsed by devouring and obsolete old age — or by fire assumed, or by many years shaken — to thy solace to behold, and the noble fragments left, of veneration most-worthy, to speculate. And I, in this place sitting, content, will await thee, watchful, awaiting our lord to come, who must ferry us to the holy and coveted maternal realm."

Then I, greatly most-avid — with the other most-commendable works seen — also these, most-accurately and multividuously to contemplate, rose from the happy session, from under the tempered shades of laurel, and of myrtle, and among tallish cypresses (then, about the place, the honeysuckle painting its odorous flowers, where a voluble flowering jasmine, with soft shade, opaquely covered us, disseminating over us copiously its whitest flowers, at that time most-sweetly odorous). Absorbed, without other cogitating, from beside Polia, by those devious embankments of fastigiate and vast heap and ruin — in the greater part occupied with ground-ivy, and terrambula, and implicated with thorns — solicitous I came. Where, ponderingly, I conjectured this to have been a magnificent and marvellous temple, of choice and superb structure, according as the proven and illustrious Nymph had shrewdly vaticinated to me. Come then into the middle part of the temple, somewhat immune and unoccupied of rubble I found it. In circinatione di questo terreneo overo subterraneo loco, altra operatura non vidi si non appacti sedili dilla propria materia. Tute queste cose cum grande et smisurato piacere, et singular devotione diligentemente mirate di sopra ritornai. Ove mirabondo dilla integritate di questa insigne operatura di ciborio. Tra me confirmai il suspecto, che il cielo dil tempio aperto si fusse. Imperò che la ruina in circuito era aggerata, et questa parte trovai immune. Hora quivi inspectando mossi gli ochii, et vidi una tribuna alquanto integra. Disubito cum gli ochii comitanti gli pedi, ad quella festino andai. Nel cielo dilla quale una artificiosa pictura era ivi rimasta cum incredibile conato et efficientia dill’artifice di opera colorifica di museaco subtilmente expressa. Quivi cavernatamente picto era uno fornice di spissa caligine infuscato monstrante una ingente et trista, et terricula spelunca tuta cariosa quale uno multicavo overo fistuloso pumice. La quale dal lato sinistro verso la mediostima parte vicino ad una asperrima invia, et ferruginea et confragosa rupe terminava. Nella quale se videva uno hiato di concavatura dinanti, et nella facia verso il suo finire distante da uno tofineo saxeo monte scrupeo et chaimeno. Questo per il medesimo modo incavernato all’incontro et pervio. Nella mediata altecia tra l’uno et l’altro traiectava uno bipartito ponte di ferro candente fina al mediato et poscia apparea frigorissimo

— smoke of the sacrifices, ascending, sublimed itself through the passage of the porphyry cupola, and exhaled outside. And, by chance, I suspected that the tholos, or middle summit of the temple, was open, by the Egyptian rite, and (that) of the holy smoke the reek, or burning, without molesting the temple, went out. On the other side of the aforesaid Altar I found, of Roman letters exquisitely excavated, this title (I thought of the altar found by Valesius at Tarentum):

INFERNO PLUTONI TRICORPORI
ET CARAE UXORI PROSERPINAE
TRICIPITIQUE CERBERO

"To infernal Pluto three-bodied, and to his dear wife Proserpina, and to three-headed Cerberus."

In the circling of this earthy, or subterranean, place, other work I saw not, save fixed seats of the proper material. All these things, with great and unmeasured pleasure, and singular devotion, diligently beheld, I returned above; where, marvelling at the integrity of this notable work of the ciborium, within myself I confirmed the suspicion that the heaven (roof) of the temple was open — for the ruin, in circuit, was heaped up, and this part I found immune. Now, there inspecting, I moved the eyes, and saw a tribune somewhat entire. Of a sudden, with the eyes accompanying the feet, to it, hasting, I went. In the heaven (vault) of which an artful painting was there left, with incredible effort and efficiency of the artificer, of colorific work of mosaic subtly expressed.

There, cavern-wise, was painted a vault infuscated of thick gloom, showing a huge and sad, and frightful cavern, all carious, like a many-holed or fistulous pumice; which, on the left side toward the middle part, near a most- rough, pathless, ferruginous and craggy rock, terminated. In which was seen a gap of concavity in front; and in the face, toward its ending, distant from a tufaceous stony mountain, scrupulous and chasmy — this, in the same manner incaverned opposite, and pervious. In the middle height, between the one and the other, passed a bipartite bridge of iron, candent (white-hot) to the middle, and then it appeared most-frigid —

Oltra questi pendicei et putrei saxi, per quella divisione tra uno et l’altro, si dimonstrava intro essere tutto ardescente loco di foco pieno di ignite et volante scintille discurrente, et cane faville cadente (quali densissimi atomi negli radii solari) crepitanti per le fiamme fincto solertemente et uno ignito laco bulliente, et molti spiramenti extuarii per li saxi apparendo. Dalla parte antica uno scuro et cretamoso laco glaciale et rigidissimo dimonstrantise. Et dal lato dextro ancora uno crepidinoso et ruvido et muriceo monte era, et di colore sulphureo. Per il quale in diversi hiaticuli vomeva tetro et caliginoso fumo. Quale di materia repugnante al ingresso dill’activo foco, et immediate scaturiente una suppurata materia ignita. La quale vomitione dava vista di crepitare, o vero fare scloppo, quale vapore concreto diffusamente exalare coacto, et poscia negli fistulosi meati il ructo ritornare, et quella dimonstratione che uno loco non faceva l’altro loco ad indicare suppliva. In questo era una scabra ruptura cavamente inspeluncata cum crude grave et averne ombre. Nella quale fessura era impacto Tenaro cum una aenea porta ruvidamente exacta in questo arso et pumicoso saxo. Et quivi sotto questi cavernacei curvamini et crepidine trifauce Cerbero insomne sedente di pilatura nigerrimo et humecto, capitato di spaventosi serpi, di aspecto horrendo et terribile, cum grave afflato quelle metalline valve insopito explorabondo cum inconniva vigilia, in perpetua luce le pupule excubante. In questo horrendo et cuspidinoso littore et miserrimo sito dil algente et fetorifico laco, stava la saeviente Tesiphone efferata et crudele cum il viperino capillamento, in le meschine et miserrime anime, implacabilemente furibonda. Le quale cadevano catervamente nello aeternalmente rigidissimo laco giù dal ferreo ponte, et rotantise per le algente onde fugire properante il penoso et mortifero algore, pervenivano al frigidissimo littore. Et uscite infoelice et fugitive dala tartarea furia, per sopra una difficillima, laboriosa et salebricosa ripa, alla sinistra mano, fugivano citule cum le fauce aperte, et cum le ciglie depresse, et cum gli rubenti et lachrymosi ochii indicante clamori, stridore di fauce, et cum dolorosi pianti et guai. Le quale oppresse et di horrore una cum l’altra impulse, et inconculcantise giù nel frigidissimo averno et profundo, irruente praecipitavase. Et quelle che del praecipitio evadevano, nella scabra caverna se ricontravano in l’altra horribile furia di Megaera, et prohibiva che quelle in le volante fiamme non se praecipitasseron. Et coacte sopra lo incendioso ponte salivano. Tale penoso ordine iudicai essere da l’altra parte, perché la luctifica Alecto sorore dille due nominate di Acheronte filiole et dilla tetra Nocte, et essa era obstaculo et furialmente impediva, che l’alme deputate alle sempiterne flamme non obruesseron nel laco rigente. Ma ispaventate dalla horrenda furia salivano et esse, cum le altre obviantise, il biastemato ponte. Et cusì q

— metal. Beyond these pendent and rotten rocks, by that division between the one and the other, it showed within to be all a burning place of fire, full of ignited and flying sparks running, and white embers falling (like most- dense atoms in the solar rays), crackling through the flames, feigned shrewdly; and an ignited boiling lake; and many steam-vents, by the rocks, appearing.

On the front part, a dark and clay-muddy, glacial and most-rigid lake, showing itself. And on the right side, again, was a craggy and rough and murex-like mountain, of sulphurous colour; through which, in diverse little gaps, it vomited foul and caliginous smoke — as of matter repugnant to the ingress of the active fire — and immediately gushing a suppurated ignited matter; which vomition gave the appearance of crackling, or making a pop, like a concreted vapour compelled to exhale diffusely, and then, in the fistulous passages, the belch to return; and that demonstration which one place did not make, the other place supplied to indicate. In this was a scabrous rupture, cavernously in-caverned, with crude, grave and Avernal shades. In which fissure was fixed Taenarus, with a bronze door, roughly worked out in this burnt and pumiceous rock. And there, under these cavernous curvings and crags, three-throated Cerberus, sleepless, sitting — of blackest and humid coat, headed with frightful serpents, of horrend and terrible aspect — with grave breath, those metal valves, unlulled, exploring, with un-winking vigilance, in perpetual light the pupils keeping-watch.

In this horrend and cuspidate shore, and most-wretched site of the freezing and stench-bearing lake, stood the raging Tisiphone, ferocious and cruel, with the viperine hair, upon the poor and most-wretched souls implacably furious. Which fell in droves into the eternally most-rigid lake, down from the iron bridge; and, rolling through the freezing waves, hastening to flee the painful and death-bearing cold, came to the most-frigid shore. And, gone out, unhappy and fugitive, from the Tartarean fury, over a most-difficult, laborious and rugged bank, to the left hand, they fled headlong, with the jaws open, and with the brows depressed, and with the reddening and tearful eyes indicating clamours, stridor of jaws, and with dolorous weepings and woes. Which, oppressed, and by horror one against the other impelled, and treading each other down, into the most-frigid Avernus and deep, rushing, precipitated themselves. And those that escaped the precipice, in the scabrous cavern met the other horrible fury, Megaera, and (she) prohibited that they should not precipitate themselves into the flying flames; and, compelled, upon the incendious bridge they climbed. Such a painful order I judged to be on the other part, because the mournful Alecto — sister of the two named, daughters of Acheron and of black Night — she too was obstacle, and furially impeded, that the souls deputed to the everlasting flames should not overwhelm themselves in the freezing lake; but, frightened by the horrend fury, they climbed, they too, with the others meeting, the accursed bridge. And thus —

Notes

The Hell-mosaic in full: an iron bridge between a burning lake (sparks, boiling fire, sulphur-mountain, steam-vents) and a frozen lake (glacial, clay-muddy); Taenarus's bronze door guarded by three-headed Cerberus; and the three Furies — Tisiphone, Megaera, Alecto — driving the souls back and forth between fire and ice so neither the burning may reach the cold nor the frozen the flames. All secure; a vivid, Dante-adjacent infernal ekphrasis.

appareva ad me, che l’anime che all’ardente incendio, damnate erano, nel giacio demigrare optavano, et quelle che adiudicate furono al torpentissimo laco, molto più che ’l Styge palude frigidissimo, excessivamente desideravano nelle maledicte et calorifice flamme recentabonde intrare. Ma sforciate di salire il fallace traiecto. Il candescente passo, per fatale dispositione se divideva per tale modo, che l’anime proscripte allo inextinguibile foco, iterum cadevano nel suo aeternalmente constituito loco. Per il simigliante quelle che lo inevitabile algore perfuge tentavano di evadere, erano dal ponte nel rigentissimo profundo resummerse. Per virtute daposcia dilla divina iustitia il transito al suo pristino essere ritornava. Sencia intervallo altre dolorose alme questo proprio successivamente attentavano, cum vano et incompote voto, et per niuno modo consequire valevano il desiderato effecto. Quelle miserrime anime dunque che festinavano senza quiete fugire, da furioso horrore et rabie agitate, le incendiose flamme et per sollevamento venire et refrigerarse nel giacio non poteano. Et quelle similmente che davano assidua opera di fugire il durissimo fredo, et intrare nelle ardente flamme frustrate dil maximo disio non valevano. Et questa ad quelle gli era ineffugibile et poena indesinente, sempre più desiderose perdendo omni speranza. Le quale tanto più ardente aviditate accrescevano, quanto che sopra il ponte l’una et l’altra sentivano, quelle dil ardore il reflexo dil suo fredo, et quelle gelate, il calore, l’uno cum l’altro obviantise nel suo termine. Et questo nel affecto era maxima vegetatione di poena et di tormento. Per la quale cosa, cum tanta obstinata arte di coloramento et di simulati gesti et expressi conati, vidi tale pictura fabrefacta, et exquisitamente perfecta, quanto mai fare si potrebbe et dimonstrare. Et il titulo indicante era inscripto. Che nelle urente flamme erano condemnate le anime che per troppo foco d’amore, se medesime occidevano. Et nel horrido gelo, quelli erano demersi, che rigidi et fredolenti allo Amore et renuenti se havevano obstinatamente praestati. Finalmente cum tale dispositione mirai questo odioso, spaventevole et evitando Barathro, che dove gli lachi se ricontravano, cioè il frigorifico, cum l’ardentissimo, per la contrarietate fare dovevano cum aeterna controversia uno terribile tonare, perché poscia obvii se immergevano ambi dui in abrupto praecipitio effusi in scuro vasto et profundissimo meato et immenso abysso. Ove era la profunditate tanto artificiosamente dall’artifice ficta, che per la coloratione quelle dimonstratione essere vere mentivano, et di videre una absorbentissima voragine, cum mirifica aemulatione di gli coloramenti. Et di symmetria liniale di prospecto, et dille figure la elegantia, et copioso invento, et artifica designatione, et cum incredibile argutia, che Parrhasio Ephesio insigne pictore unque primo di simile excogitato non poté gloriarse.

— it appeared to me, that the souls that were damned to the ardent burning, into the ice desired to migrate; and those that were adjudicated to the most-torpid lake — much more frigid than the Stygian marsh — excessively desired to enter, refreshing themselves, into the maledict and heat-bearing flames. But, forced to climb the fallacious crossing (the candescent pass), by fatal disposition it divided itself in such manner, that the souls proscribed to the inextinguishable fire fell again into their eternally constituted place. By the like, those that attempted to evade the inevitable cold, refuged, were, from the bridge, re-submerged into the most-freezing deep. By virtue then of the divine justice, the transit returned to its pristine being.

Without interval, other dolorous souls attempted this same, successively, with vain and impotent wish, and by no means could they attain the desired effect. Those most-wretched souls, then, that hastened without quiet to flee, by furious horror and rabies agitated — the incendious flames — could not, by relieving, come and refresh themselves in the ice. And those likewise, that gave assiduous heed to fleeing the hardest cold, and entering into the ardent flames, frustrated of the greatest desire, could not. And this, to those, was inescapable, and a pain unceasing — ever more desirous, losing every hope. Which so much the more ardent avidity increased, as, upon the bridge, the one and the other felt — those (of the fire) the reflex of its cold, and those (frozen) the heat — the one with the other meeting at its term (the bridge's midpoint). And this, in the affect, was the greatest quickening of pain and of torment. For which thing, with so obstinate an art of colouring, and of simulated gestures and expressed efforts, I saw such a painting skilfully-made, and exquisitely perfect, as ever could be made and shown. And the title, indicating, was inscribed: that, in the burning flames, were condemned the souls that, for too much fire of love, killed their very selves; and, in the horrid ice, were immersed those who, rigid and chilly to Love and refusing, had obstinately shown themselves.

Finally, with such disposition I beheld this odious, frightful and to-be-avoided Barathrum (pit), that where the lakes met — that is, the frigorific with the most-ardent — by the contrariety they must make, with eternal controversy, a terrible thundering; because then, meeting, both immersed themselves in an abrupt precipice, effused into a dark, vast and most-deep passage and immense abyss. Where the profundity was so artfully feigned by the artificer, that, by the colouring, those demonstrations feigned (themselves) to be true, and (one seemed) to see a most-absorbing vortex, with wondrous emulation of the colourings, and of lineal symmetry of prospect, and of the figures the elegance, and copious invention, and artful designation, and with incredible sharpness — such that Parrhasius of Ephesus, notable painter, could never first glory himself of a like device.

Notes

Confidence: medium. The meaning of the Hell-mosaic, made explicit by its inscription: the fire punishes those who killed themselves for too much love; the ice punishes those who were cold and refused Love — and each is tormented by longing for the other's element, kept from it by "divine justice," feeling at the bridge's midpoint the very relief they cannot reach. The two lakes meet in a thundering abyss, painted with a trompe-l'oeil depth surpassing Parrhasius. All secure; the thematic key of the whole Polyandrion.

Whence, upon the limited bridge, in the diagonal compacture, meeting in droves, the one and the other of the first butted (against each other), and could not proceed, by the treading-down of those following. "To the shades. To my gladiator, by my love — for whom, burned to the utmost, I lay down in death's languor; but
by his blood (alas, wretched me!), unpurified, I recovered. Leaving a pious monument [to divine Faustus

day; and, the shades propitiated, they busy themselves about the sepulchre yearly, in perpetuity to be repeated.
By her testament she ordered it made." (Several abbreviations are conjecturally expanded.)

Then, when I had these two epitaphs accurately perused, and most-pleasingly seen, solicitous, inquiring, turning the eyes — lo, that I see a historiated sepulchre. To which, without tarrying, I went. On the anterior part of which, fixed, was a little altar, together with such (figures) expressed. Upon the flat of it, of wondrous artifice, was set a head of a sylvan goat, held by one of the horns by a little old man, with the head of hair, in the old manner, tormented (dressed), confused; who was clad, over the nude, in a pall thrown back over the right shoulder, coming under from the left, returning over the right, and at the back pendent; near, he was clothed in goat-skin — one (skin) in front and the other behind at the back, over the shoulders, the feet of both skins knotted, and the others hanging between the thighs with the rough hair turned to the flesh; and girt with a torque, or fillet, made of tanus, or black vine, with its leaves.

"To the shades. — Traveller, bring your eyes closer here; then make words with me. — 'I lived without love;
loving, alas, I die.' — *Say, I pray, I beg: my [body] I gave to this Polyandrion, dead by the fire of love for a
boy in the flower of his age, most beautiful. — 'Why art thou mad? Yet thou wast living, in love.' — Truly: when,
a young woman, I had begun (to my) harm to love, the gift of love spurned, he refused; I wasted away, snatched by
death, here I am. — 'What can I do for thee?' — Nevia the Roman, wretchedly dead of love for cruel Proculus,
through the whole city and world proclaim. This is enough. Farewell.'*"

Leaving this, which with the utmost gladness I saw, I entered into a tribune, broken and disrupted. Where, again, part of an egregious painting of most-lively mosaic I found. In which I saw a Matron, prostrate upon a kindled pyre, and raging upon her very self, killing herself. And there, no other than feet, womanly shod, appeared — some part with the calves, and little covered with drapes. All the rest was, by the unsated and voracious time, consumed, and by antiquity, and by winds, and rains, and ardent Sun destroyed. In this same place the Ark (tomb) was comminuted, and the greater fragment was this, reversed, which, righting it, I found with such writing. Next to this, lying on the floor, of alabaster stone, I found an antiquarian vase, high more than a pace and a half, with one of the handles broken, and part broken in its body; up to the opening, part superseated a half-cube, or Taxillus (die), high one foot, or —

HEUS VIATOR — (the epitaph of Leontia and Lollius; Poliphilo's Latin rendering of the Greek)

"Ho, traveller! Interpose thy hands a little (in prayer), being adjured; and, reading, much-groaning, give kisses
to the metal, adding: 'Ah, cruel monster of Fortune! They ought to have lived.'

"Leontia, a girl, the chief beloved of Lollius, a freeborn youth — when the intemperance of love pressed (her),
afflicted with paternal torments, she fled away. Lollius follows; but, amid embracing, taken by pirates, they sell
them to a certain trafficker. Both captive, they board a ship. When, by night, Lollius suspected Leontia to be
carried off from him, seizing a sword, he butchers all the sailors. The ship, the sea's savagery arisen, dashed on
the rocks near land, sinks. They climb a rock. By the impulse of hunger, seizing Leontia, I set her on my shoulders.
'Favour, be near, O father Neptune,' saying, 'us and our fortune I commit to thee.' Then, with a dolphin-like effort,
with my arms I cut the little waves. But Leontia, amid the swimming, speaks: 'Am I a trouble to thee, my life?'
'Lighter than a water-skater, Leontia, little heart.' And, oft asking, 'Hast thou strength, my hope, my little
soul?' 'I say (yes).' Those (words) thou rousest. Soon, embracing (my) neck, she sweetly kisses her bearer, solaces,
exhorts, gives spirit to the diver. I exult. To the shore at last we come, safe. Unhoped-for, a roaring lion attacks.
We embrace each other. The lion spares the dying. Terrified by the chance, a little boat cast up on the shore
together with a rowing-oar, we fugitives board. Each in turn, singing, we row. A day and a night — and a third —
wandering. Only the sky itself, on every side, lies open. By lethal hunger we are tormented; and, wasting with long
fasting, we rush into embraces. Leontia saying, 'I pray thee, dost thou perish of hunger?' 'It is enough to be with
thee, Lollius — I am fed.' But she, sighing: 'My Lollius, dost thou fail?' 'Not at all,' I say, 'in love, but in
body.' With only vibrating and mutual tongues we fed ourselves sweetly; and, more tightly, with gaping mouths, sweet
kisses cast, ivy-like we embraced. Both, without turning (breath), we die. By the surges — not (even) raging —
hither, by the breeze, we are carried; and, wretched, in the estuary-air, bound in those very embraces, among the
Plutonic shades here we are laid. And whom the piratical rapacity did not retain, nor the leonine maw devour, and
the sea's immensity refused to take — the narrowness of this little urn here holds them both. This unhappiness I
wished thee to know. Farewell."

Notes

Confidence: high (the epitaph is a continuous, secure Latin narrative). The epitaph of Leontia and Lollius — the longest and most novelistic inscription in the Polyandrion: a complete shipwreck-romance. The lovers flee her cruel father, are captured and sold by pirates, escape (Lollius killing the crew), are shipwrecked, swim to shore (Lollius bearing Leontia, praying to Neptune, their tender exchange mid-swim), are spared by a lion, drift three days in an open boat singing, and finally die of hunger in each other's arms, kissing — now both held in "the narrowness of this little urn." All secure; a masterpiece of the sepulchral-narrative genre.

  • the address to the traveller — like Nevia's (p. 256), it commands the passer-by to *pray, kiss the stone, and

From here departing, more avidly lustrating through the heaped ruins, I found another tetragonal altar, which on its flat had a base without plinth — that is, a gula (cyma), then a little fascia, and then a torus. Beyond this it was levelled. On which levelling sat a plinth, or little slab, that from angle to angle made a sinuous (curve), as one of its square figure incurving little by little; the projection of which angles did not exceed the circumference of the torus, or torus, subjacent. Upon which abacus-plinth lay a circular (base) of a vase; the circumstance of which did not pass the outlet of the angles of the subjacent plinth. Which vase dilated itself, in the opening, as much as was the extreme of the lowest of the underlying gula of the base. "To the shades. Death — contrary to life, and most swift — treads on all things, tramples, seizes, consumes, dissolves.
Mellifluously (sweetly) it has here joined two, who mutually, tightly and ardently loved each other, (now) extinguished."

Gladdened, with incredible solace, by so much variety of antiquarian and magnificent works, still, without doubt, my soul increased (in wishing), insatiably, more lustrating, to investigate other novelties. O LECTOR INFOELIX — (the epitaph of Lopidia and Chrysanthes)

"O unhappy reader, be present at this monument while it calls thee — and then, afterward, it asks that thou read
into what human pleasure falls. Here is the ash of two lovers, who, long since, mutually burning insolently with
itching love, by the wicked, unbridled impulse of pleasure, met in a deserted place among ruined rocks, where by
chance also stood the broken walls of sacred buildings and rough ruins. There we both were ardently urged to pay
Venus the desired gifts. Lying back, I, Lopidia, saw a snake, slipped down from on high, threatening. 'Ho! cease
from what thou hast begun,' I say; 'my Chrysanthes, rise, flee — lo, a serpent about to devour us!' — as I watch it
hurling itself from the wall. Soon he, terrified, looking up: 'O my Lopidia,' he says, 'I beg thee, go thy way, flee
thou the road, let me attack the dying dragon.' Scarcely had I risen — alas, sad, wretched me! — when I saw my
Chrysanthes, my life, entangled to destruction and tightly circled in the snake's coil, now anxiously breathing.
And suddenly it wounds the throat of my Chrysanthes with biting teeth; then I behold my Chrysanthes being
suffocated. 'Ah, ah, I perish, unhappy! I feel my Chrysanthes dying!' At once, furious, I rush at the serpent, and,
a club seized, I hasten to strike; but the serpent twists its wrangling neck, nor by force could I drive off the
entwined one. Striking at last, incautiously missing, I killed my Chrysanthes, most unhappy. Alas, I am undone!
What have I done? What shall I do? Shall the serpent and I, so wretched, survive? By no means! But with Herculean
daring — nay, with a ghostly, snarling fury — with that same club, the blow turned, upon the fallen corpse I strike
the coiled beast, and kill it. What then, a girl, was I to do — lost and dead? My Chrysanthes and the beast,
witnesses of my crime, thrown over my shoulders, I carry into the city, watering them again and again with sighs,
heart-grief and tears. I climb a certain platform in the public forum, and, sighing, I make the matter known. In a
crowd the citizens run together to the cruel and hateful spectacle; they pity the entangled chance, accuse Fortune,
damn Venus. I attest my crime, I invoke the infernal powers: 'Therefore,' saying, 'receive me to pay the penalty
together with my Chrysanthes; now let me transfer all the guilt upon myself.' Then, desperate, in the public sight
of all, a sword seized, I transfix my breast, and gave my most-wretched self to be buried here, in an eternal tomb,
with his corpse. Farewell."

Notes

Confidence: high (the epitaph is a continuous, secure Latin narrative). The harrowing epitaph of Lopidia and Chrysanthes: two lovers meeting secretly among the ruins to "pay Venus the desired gifts" are surprised by a serpent; it strangles Chrysanthes, and Lopidia, striking at it with a club, accidentally kills her own lover; she then kills the beast, carries both bodies to the forum, publicly confesses, and stabs herself to be buried with him. All secure; a small, complete tragedy.

  • the moral frame. The epitaph opens by asking the reader to "read into what human pleasure falls" — a memento
  • the serpent among the ruins — the snake striking from the broken wall while the lovers embrace is a vivid,
  • direct first-person voice — like Nevia (p. 256) and Leontia (p. 258), Lopidia speaks in her own voice from the

De qui ancora summe contento partitome, non molti passi facendo mi occorse una nobile tabula di marmoro tetragona, cum alquanto di fastigio, cum due columnelle una per lato. De disegno immune et expedite. Et per il capto di tutto il quadrangulo era quasi evulsa una foliata corona, o vero gioia, diligentemente conducta. Nella quale io legi tale inscriptione. La quale petra in terra deiecta iaceva. Ma cum la operatura supina. Le quale elegante varietate non poco piacere nel’animo mio iucundamente accumulavano.

Poi con voluti di venustissime fronde et fiori

And, to the compass of all the quadrangle, was, as if uprooted (in relief), a foliate crown, or jewel, diligently conducted; in which I read such an inscription. Which stone lay cast down on the earth, but with the workmanship supine (face up). Which elegant varieties not a little pleasure, in my soul, joyously accumulated.

More ardently invaded (I) found myself to the investigation of the most-worthy antiquarian works. There presented itself to me a disrupted tribune, with the right wall reserved, in which I saw, with excessive voluptuousness, a porphyry sepulchre, of most-worthy device, and of most-excellent workmanship, and of marvellous cost, and of incredible artifice of sculpture. Which stood — at the extreme sides raised by two quadrangular little columns (a third of them worked out, with regulated flutings, upon a footing with the base collocated) — and, perpendicularly subjacent, was a little altar, with three elegant mourning Nymphs, toward the middle turned, weeping together. By the like, on the other side, semi-detached from the solid, not without the corollary and requisite lineaments. Above both the capitals the epistyle, ornate, extended itself. investito, il Zophoro sopra resideva locato, di condecente coronula coperto. Tra l’una et l’altra quadrangula alquanto, uno solio, o vero nichio, cum regulata excavatura de stria promineva, ad libella dil piano, tra esse quadrangule. La prominentia dil quale faceva, da uno et l’altro lato dilla sua apertione uno pilastrello, cum capitelli et base. Sopra gli quali saliva una trabe inflexa. Tanto divulsi dal aequato, overo piano, che restava nella interiore parte, cioè ad gli labri dil solio, uno lingello. Ad libella degli capitelli, cingeva el solio, uno undulato illigamento, et di sopra la hemicupula. Gli quali pilastrelli egregiamente erano di scalptura ornati. Sotto gli pilastrelli iaceva una proiecta arula altiuscula, cum gli ornati degli sopra stanti pilastrelli. Tra una et l’altra proiectura dille dicte arule, overo subcolumnio, io vidi una inscriptione graeca, per la quale conobi essere questo il monumento dilla pia Regina di Caria. Cusì diceva. ARTEMISIDOS BASILIDOS SPODON. Cum sochi, et coronette, et sime, et gulule, optimamente il tuto cincto et sotiale. Nel piano inferiore dil nichio era uno plintho dilla narrata materia in aspecto bellissime deornato di scalptura, sopra la plana dil quale affixe stavano quatro aequilocate gramfie di leone di metallo inaurato. Gli quali premeva una antiquaria arcula, cum liniamenti di expresso insigne. Sopra il tectorio era uno scanno, per il capto dilla copertura, fincto di panno sericeo contecto, cum ambiente fimbriatura. Sedeva sopra una matrona Regina, cum regio culto, et maiestale indumento, nel pecto fibulato sopra una assettata vestitura. De qui cum laetissimo solatio partitome, cum curioso desiderio nove cose spectare percupido, ad una tribuna semiintegra properando, io mirai alcune reliquie exquisite, di pictura museaca, vermiculatamente facta. In questo loco sepulchro alcuno non trovai, ma nella vitricularia pictura ancora Proserpina cum Cyane et cum le Sirene, fiori colligente apresso l’ardente monte di Etna perfecto si cerniva. Ove Plutone reserando il cratere pyrivrizo dil flammispiro monte, al suo amore volupticamente la rapiva, et Cyane per non la potere soccorrere pietosamente illachrymante. Quivi trovai ingenti saxi dil putrescente muro patorato, et herbescente per le rime di Asterico et di urcelarea. Il quale era etiam implicito et distruso, quale da infixo cuneo di uno radichone di annosa caprifico, che per tuto le radice oborte serpendo, distructe havea le tessellature, et lo coito dille compacture diserto, grandi laxamenti de le parieti ne rendevano.

Diqué io solamente mirava parte de uno fluviolo, pareva vestigio di humana forma in quello tramutata, di arte incredibile fincto, et mirabilmente expresso. Quale simigliante unque nel delubro di Minerva in Capitolio nella tabula se vide il rapto dilla dicta, da Nicomacho depicto. Ove cum la mente applicata a tale piacevole respecto essendo, ecco che a spalle sento la casura d’alcune tessellature, et a mi solitario, in deserto, et silentioso loco trovantime, repente me alquanto pavefacto, et retro volventime mirando, vidi uno ascalabote, overo murilego, che era stato causa di tale ruina.

Per tanto non poca displicentia me invase, per non potere l’opera tuta integramente mirare, per essere in la magiore parte demolita, et rupta, et dalla subdivale relictione laesa. Considerando dunque il violentario modo, che repente surrepta fue Proserpina, uno subitaneo et tristo pensiero nel amante core diciò feramente me percosse dicendo. Omè meschino impudente, et infoelice. O importuna indagine, et effrena curiositate dille cose praeterite, et di saxi fresi disquirente, ad che son divoluto? Si per la mia mala isciagura la mia bellissima Polia da me fusse rapta, et per incuria di tanta cosa praesente, oltra tuti gli thesori dil mondo gratissima, mi fusse abacta. Et in momento una più acerba percossura me transfixe il tristo core, cum uno inseme vehemente et crebro pulso, presentantise già nella mente confusa, il piatoso et lachrymabile caso, che il fugitivo dill’ardente patria incautamente perdete la sua dilecta Creusa, et molto più excessivamente me conturboe invadendo tale terriculamento memorando, che ad gli harenosi litori, et solitarii, distracta dalla mia praesentia la amantissima mia Polia sola sedeva.

From here, with most-joyful solace, departing — with curious desire most-eager to behold new things — hastening to a semi-integral tribune, I beheld some exquisite relics of mosaic painting, wormwork-made. In this place I found no sepulchre; but in the glasswork painting, still, Proserpina, with Cyane and with the Sirens, gathering flowers near the burning mountain of Etna, was perfectly discerned. Where Pluto, unsealing the fire-rooted crater of the flame-breathing mountain, voluptuously ravished her to his love; and Cyane, for not being able to succour her, piteously weeping. There I found huge stones of the putrescent wall gaping, and grassy through the cracks with aster and pellitory; which was also entangled and destroyed, as by a wedge fixed of a big root of an aged wild-fig, whose roots, springing everywhere, creeping, had destroyed the tessellations, and, the coition of the joints deserted, rendered great looseness of the walls.

Whence I only beheld part of a little river, (that) seemed a vestige of human form transmuted into it (Cyane), of incredible art feigned, and marvellously expressed — such the like as once, in the shrine of Minerva on the Capitol, in the tablet was seen the rape of the said (Proserpina), painted by Nicomachus. Where, with the mind applied to such pleasant regard being — lo, at my back I hear the fall of some tessellations; and, finding myself solitary, in a deserted and silent place, suddenly somewhat frightened, and, turning back, looking, I saw a gecko, or wall-lizard, that had been the cause of such ruin.

Therefore no little displeasure invaded me, for not being able to see the whole work integrally, it being in the greater part demolished. Considering, then, the violent manner in which Proserpina was suddenly seized, a sudden and sad thought, in the loving heart, fiercely struck me, saying: "Alas, wretched, impudent and unhappy me! O importunate investigation, and unbridled curiosity of past things, and of broken stones inquiring — to what am I devolved? If, by my ill misfortune, my most-beautiful Polia were seized from me, and, by neglect of so great a present thing — above all the treasures of the world most-pleasing — were driven off from me!" And, in a moment, a more bitter blow transfixed the sad heart, presenting already in the confused mind the piteous and lamentable case: that the fugitive of the burning fatherland (Aeneas) incautiously lost his beloved Creusa. And much more excessively it disturbed me, invading, such a terror, remembering that, on the sandy and solitary shores, drawn away from my presence, my most- loving Polia sat alone.

Et che cusì ad ella il tridentifero Neptuno violentemente non facesse, quale ad Medusa. Omè che a questo puncto io certamente experimentai, che cosa è la afflictione di spirito, et la qualitate de gli veri amanti. Extremamente più tremefacto, perterrito, et stupefacto, et in magiore angustia trovantime, et in più misera trepidatione deducto. Che quando me vidi quasi absorbiculo putrescibile tra le hiante et horrende fauce dil venefico dracone al finitimo interito. Cum tanto terrore, che io poteva arbitrare essere per il sacerdote et simulachro amoto dil templo peleneo, discussa della mente omni serenitate, recrudescentise omni hora, più il formidoloso dolore nel fluctuante core.

Per la quale cosa impulso dalle coquente cure, et urgente angustie, sencia mora alcuna ocyssimamente aeripede, lasciando tanto incoepto nobile, et praeclara inquisitione et laudabunda lustratione, et virtuoso solacio, repente dunque per quelli amfracti et infesti cespugli, et asperi virgulti, et per il loco salebroso di petre et di spini coarctato, et per quelle prolapsione di marmori, et informe strue di rudimenti et fracticii inconcinna scrupulosa et tra caustiche urtiche et avie ruine propero, cum infenso curso, per vie asprete, et innumeri offendiculi cum prompta velocitate, non istimando dilla mia pannosa toga la laceratione, di qui et de lì, da spinose fronde ritenuta, et tuta piena di lappe et di lanugine, et papi di cardui et di barbula hircina, et di sonco, in alcuna parte complicata dalle rapace semence di Cynoglossa, fermamente tenendo di essere pervenuto nelle novissime erumne, et formidolosi discrimini, et ultima et exitiale privatione di omni mio sperato bene alla mia dulcissima et oculissima Polia, non tuto vivo ma semimortuo, quale asmatico trahendo il fiato, non per altra via, che si ’l grave odore dil babylonico hiato hausto havesse, cum gli ochii di rore lachrymabile madenti, ad essa vicino provolutome ispasimato, cum non credibile cordolio et tranguscito apena io gionsi.

Et lei cum l’animo molliculo commota, cum serena fronte, et propiciata facie commulcente cusì lurido et afflicto cum assiduo pulso nel mio doloroso pecto cum exangue pallore trepidante miserata dolentisi, cum amorosa pietate, se ne maraveglioe, sublevantime lepidula nel gli sui dolci amplexi, cum una genuina dulcedine, et cum uno tenuissimo velamine crociculo, la mia facia sucida, et rorefacta in uberrimo sudore cum amoroso obsequio levemente perfricata, me et officiosissima et cum blandicie assucava. Diqué la causa et l’accidente di tanta amara et turbabonda angoscia cupida siscitante, et me benignissimamente blandiendo,

And that thus, to her, the trident-bearing Neptune might not violently do (as to Medusa)! Alas, at this point I certainly experienced what is the affliction of spirit, and the quality of true lovers — extremely more trembling, terrified, and stupefied, and finding myself in greater anguish, and into more miserable trepidation deduced, than when I saw myself almost a putrescible little morsel among the gaping and horrend jaws of the venefic dragon, at the next-door demise. With so much terror that I could judge (myself), through the priest and the removed simulacrum of the Pellenean temple, to have every serenity struck from the mind, re-cruding every hour, the more, the formidable grief in the fluctuating heart.

For which thing, impelled by the coquent cares and urgent anguishes, without any delay, most-swiftly brazen-footed — leaving so noble an undertaking, and illustrious inquisition, and laudable lustration, and virtuous solace — suddenly, then, through those windings and infested bushes, and rough shrubs, and through the place made narrow of stones and of thorns, and through those prolapses of marbles, and formless heap of rudiments and fragments, uneven, scrupulous, and among caustic nettles and pathless ruins, I hasten, with hostile course, by rough ways and innumerable stumbling- blocks, with prompt velocity — not esteeming the laceration of my ragged toga, here and there held by thorny fronds, and all full of burs and down, and thistle-tufts, and goat's-beard, and sowthistle, in some part entangled by the rapacious seeds of hound's-tongue — firmly holding to have arrived at the newest troubles, and formidable perils, and ultimate and deadly privation of all my hoped good, to my sweetest and most-precious Polia: not wholly alive, but half- dead, like an asthmatic drawing the breath (not by other way than if the grave odour of the Babylonian gulf I had drawn), with the eyes wet with tearful dew, near her, having prostrated myself, spasming, with incredible heart-grief and swooning, scarce I arrived.

And she, with the soft soul moved, with serene forehead, and propitiated and soothing face — thus lurid and afflicted, with assiduous pulse in my dolorous breast, with bloodless pallor trembling — miserating, grieving, with amorous pity, marvelled at it; raising me, pretty, into her sweet embraces; and, with a genuine sweetness, and with a most-tenuous saffron veil, my dirty face, dewy in most-rich sweat, with amorous obsequy lightly rubbed, dried me — both most- officious and, with blandishment, sponging me. Whence, the cause and accident of so much bitter and troublous anguish eagerly inquiring, and most-benignly blandishing me —

Consoling me, then, my beauty Polia — on this pact, paired with her residing — the semi-fled life refreshed me; the boxwood pallor converted into its (natural) colouring, and the trembling invasion changed, I evaded into generous magnanimity. Iulio comparò per la cara Servilia. Et alcune haveano di rose et d’altri conspicui sertuli di flori implicati gli crispulabondi capegli, capreolatamente la lucida fronte inumbranti. Cum sumptuose collambie di turbinate petre di vario et consotiale coloramento pretiosissime, ambiente la lactea et drita gula. Daposcia strictamente erano nel transverso cincte sotto convicino alle dure mamillule, ad succumbere al tenuo indumento pectorale obstinato obstaculo. Le quale quantunque violentate, niente di manco al suo incolato, alquanto quassabonde, proterve ritornavano. Il quale pectorale nel circuito dil collare havea uno exornato, di soprafilo d’oro, contexto in maxima politura di expresso, di fili coartati, cum gli oroli di ordinate et pillulate margarite, et per il lungo di questo septo compositamente dispanse lucevano pretiosissime gemme. Replicare aptamente io non saperei, quello che ad me licentemente fue conceduto, et facto participe di speculare, omni cosa discussamente nell’animo versando, cum amoroso excogitato amplexabondo, nella memoria repetendo, nella mente uno dolce fruire repraesentando, et dulciculamente di tanta bellecia uno suave piacere verisimilmente usurpava. Due dunque di queste Aselgia, et Neolea erano di lascivo exornato pretiosamente indute attalicamente di panno chamochayno intramato di trama aurea, et di ordimento di seta cyanea. Quale il Re Attalo in Asia non valse trovare. Du’ altre similmente Chlidonia, et Olvolia, haveano il voluptico vestire Babylonico di pretioso Thalassio, cum variata textura. Le ultime Adea et Cypria, investite erano di nobilissimo Melledaro, cum vermiculata et aerea sutura, cum minutissime et pervie fracte plurifaria laciniate, nel fondo supposite bracthee d’oro nelle extreme phimbrie. Et al coniuncto degli brachii era latamente uno exito dil proprio vestito, donde ussivano li eburnei brachii nudati, per obstentatione di altra albencia, che il lacteo coagulamento, cum tutti gli ornati requisiti, et Nymphali additamenti. La fresca et lasciviente aura poscia secondo il moto suo, tale hora la forma dil rotondo, intacto et duro alvo reflando propalava, et il spectabile pube, talhora le polpose choxendice, alcuna fiata le tremule Nate. Poscia negli longiusculi petioli il calciamine a forcia (cum corniculario conducto) riportato, tali erano di Cyaneo sericii, et di verdigiante et punicea coloratione exquisitamente cerdati. Nel vertice dil pede cum sinuata apertura lunati, expolitissimamente conseptati, cum oroli et fibule d’oro politulamente corrigiati, et cum crepidule et cum socciculi obaurati. The divine Steersman I, with reverent and decent regards, willingly willing him, with every possible effort to contemplate — the disproportionate object, my feeble sight fittingly did not suffer. But, conniving with my cheeks (half-closing my eyes), in this manner somewhat the divine boy I manifoldly comprehended. Now the nautical Nymphs gave beginning — with a most-sweet note, and with a heavenly intonation, from the human wholly deviated, and beyond belief, with reasoned song-craft — to sing, and to trill a most-sweet concord, with consonant voice and melody. Insomuch that rightly I doubted I should shatter from excessive sweetness, because almost from its place removed I felt the resulting and wounded heart, and of sweetness it seemed to me, reasonably, that it should exile itself through my lips. And they, following, with vibrating little tongues, in the sonorous palate broke, crisping, doubling, and tripling into one the briefest little chromatics, or tailed notelets — and, first intercepted, two by two; then three and three; then by four; last, all six — the rosy little lips, tremulous, moderately opening them, and graciously joining them, they proffered the modulating spirits, with mosaic proportion, with mellifluous voice, in the warm heart syncopated, and with weary utterance of love. A voice sighing to the places, most-sweetly throating — enough to put into oblivion the natural need, and to neglect it — with stringed instruments they sang the sweetnesses and qualities of love: the facetious thefts of supernal Jove, the solacing warmths of most-holy Erothea (Venus), the lasciviousnesses of festive Bacchus, the fecundities of the foster-mother and golden Ceres, the savoury fruits of Hymenaeus — with versifying manner expressing, and rhythmically proffering, melos emmetron (metred song).

Et allhora la furente Tesiphone, cum le monstrifere sorore alle misere alme s’haveriano exposte placidissime, et benigne, né unque Parthenope cum le sorore, Leucosia, et Ligia, filiole di Acheloo, et di Calliope, alle Capree insule apresso Peloro cantante, se udirono cum tanta harmonia, cum voce, modo, Lyra, et forabile tibie, d’onde l’alma incendiosamente infiammata dal suo loco summota per gli foelici canti, et soni, effigie bellece, comitato, et maiestate redimere non la valeva né farla sua. Ma strectissimamente ligata il stato suo in le delicate brace commendava, et nel albicante sino di Polia obside perpetuo et dedititia la obligava. La quale poscia cogitando, per delectabile semite et voluptici conducti perveniva alle archane delitie. Et d’indi cum tute mie excitate virtute in me ristrecto non poteva altro reasumere, se non una solacievole imaginativa, et gloriosa.

— from the most-shady seats, from the eternal flames freed (Eurydice). Nor yet, with such a sound, did Hermes lull to sleep the eyed shepherd (Argus). Such (a sound), through the most-purged air scattering itself, breathed out of the precious and coral little lips; and through the white throat one saw the vocal spirits passing, with modulated sweetness diffusing itself. For that was celestial flesh, and a divine composite transparent — like crystalline, most-frigid, and refined camphor, tinged with crimson.

Whence Phoebus would have stayed from coming to bedew the wolf-light dawn with his coruscating rays, and would have forgotten to paint, and to make the colours for the flowers, and to renew a gracious day for the mortals. And by this, without doubt, the bow-bearing Diana would have forgotten the curved bows and the flying arrows, and the sedulous huntings, and the dense woods; and, warming the gelid fount, she would not have spurned the presence of the incautious hunter, and would not have turned the horned stag, to the biting dogs lacerable (i.e. she would have spared Actaeon). And the all-wandering Selene would have withdrawn from illustrating with her splendour the supernal heavens and the shadowed earth. And the frightful Proserpina, in her mournful realm, would not have racked the doleful subjects, had a like tone reached her ears. And the solacing Bacchus would have made resistance to the slippery lasciviousnesses, and would have neglected the Ogygian hills, Elis, Naxos, Chios, and Mount Massicus, and Mareotis, and would have made little of the must-sweet delights of the vintaging Autumn. And the fostering Ceres would have kept the ears of corn ever in green, postponing the abundant realms of Ausonia, nor would have exchanged the fat and four-grained ears with Chaonia. And the cloud-thundering bird (Jove's eagle), out of the hooked curvature of its inverted talons, would not have felt the ravished Phrygian cup-bearer (Ganymede) flee away — so most-sweetly the Nymphs sang, and concordantly sounded, and each of them, with my Polia singing along, dispensed celestial melodies to the open ears.

By which the black and multiform and lucubratory Cerberus would have been lulled; nor would he have kept watch, with unmoving eyes, the metallic valves of Taenarum. And then the raging Tisiphone, with the monster-bearing sisters, to the wretched souls would have shown themselves most-placid and benign. Nor ever were Parthenope, with her sisters Leucosia and Ligeia — daughters of Achelous and of Calliope — singing at the Capri isles near Pelorus, heard with so much harmony, of voice, mode, Lyre, and pierceable tibia; whence the soul, incendiarily inflamed, removed from its place by the happy songs, and sounds, effigies, beauties, retinue, and majesty, I could not redeem, nor make it my own. But, most-tightly bound, it commended its estate into the delicate arms, and in the whitening bosom of Polia, a perpetual and surrendered hostage, obliged it. Which then, cogitating, by delectable paths and voluptuous conduits, arrived at the arcane delights. And thence, with all my excited virtues drawn into myself, I could resume nothing else but a solacing imaginative, and glorious.

By which, of over-rich pondering, the anxious mind, with a refreshment of spirit, fed itself; and with little curious regards, and lewd appetites, the manifest and perfect shapelinesses (and rarely such a habit of appearance) of Polia most-avidly I beheld, refusing every other thing worth watching, avertible of protection. As much as ever the most-high Jupiter can imagine, to confer on the nature of it, and benignly to produce and skilfully-make — nor ever could Apelles have painted a like one, and much less Aristides, who feigned human souls with his little brush.

Of which sight I could not sate myself — neither more nor less than the murmuring bees do not sate themselves of the odorous thyme and amellus, and the wanton she-goats of the flowering cytisus, and of the tender fronds. The soul therefore interdicted, to vivify me fully availed not.

Use and exercise, therefore, toward me, pity; and consider, expert, the fragile quality of the cupidinous lovers; and temper somewhat your burning torches, and modify your noxious arms, and slacken your death- bringing bow — for of love I am all racked.

"For which I reasonably argue: that if, in your very self, savage and pitiless, you wounded yourself — what equability of soul persuades that I should not fear that, without pity, toward me, more harsh and unbridled and most-savage, you would not show yourself?" And so, exasperated, concitatedly I dared; and with diverse petitions, and prayers, and fabricated complaints, and feigned satisfactions, I somewhat softened the strong invasion, and the frequent impulse of the wicked and eyeless love. But for all this my enkindled heart was not condignly reconciled, nor really satisfied to my disjointed appetite. And that which then I prayed him: only that he put an end, at least, to my tormenting and long-lasting hoping, with the molesting expectation of a prison-like issue.

For, however much the coveted future be much more sweet of avidity than the acquired past delight, yet every hostile love contends toward the expected end. Chapter XXI

The gardens of Cythera. The circular island, ring within ring, is described from its own measured plan: the outer grove, the ring-river with its citrus pergola, the seven-step terraces and their jewelled knot-parterres (planted herb by herb), an aviary of the transformed, and the herb-set inscriptions dedicating the rings to Jupiter.

Having come most joyfully to the longed-for place, whose worthy loveliness Poliphilo affirms, fittingly describing its plants, herbs, birds and dwellers. But first the form of the little boat, and how, at the descent of the lord Cupid, many gift-bearing nymphs opportunely presented themselves to meet him.

The divine boy making sail with his spread wings — not from the wineskin of Ulysses, but urged by the obsequious and dew-bearing breezes, daughters of Astraeus and of rosy Aurora, of one unanimous consent — Polia and I, finding ourselves kindled and headlong with eagerness to reach the destined end, with the greatest delight of love that ever human sense could feel, nor foreconceive, nor much less divulge. Which, however excessive it was intimately in the heart, was nonetheless the more readily quickened by the deific presence, and by those most witty rowing nymphs, and by the sweetest singing, and by the mysterious form of the solid and unshaken little boat — a fit instrument organised of love — and by the precious material, and by the sweetness and pleasantness of the place; and much more by the near flame that Polia, with rare excellence, exuberantly breathed into my burnable heart. For her amorous and most refulgent eyes, gliding lightning-like through mine to my inmost heart, seditiously stirred up a most bitter conflagration; by which, heated through and prostrately wounded, frequent sobs gushed forth — not otherwise than the cook pours out over the burning and excessive fire through the lips. Just so, neither more nor less, the boiling gasps compelled from my fervent heart abundantly boiled up, showing themselves resounding; and the importunate fires I fittingly mitigated with the sole beauty of my lovely Polia, my guide. But how it was, I most abundantly experienced such pleasure that I was wholly absorbed and consumed — more than ever my most decent tongue could adapt itself to such expression.

Finally, most joyful, glad and triumphant, to the island extremely desired, with our proud and oar-wandering ship of six banks — not ballasted, but light — which was compacted of a form thus.

Cum questi amorosi triumphi, et euphonice voce dille nautice fanciulle, et oltra dagli marini numini completo era il sereno aere, et il ceruleo pelago di confusi clamori, et multitudine resultante le unde, et feste, et tripudii, et praecipua gesticulatione et festiva iucunditate, et divote veneratione al perameno loco allabenti applicassimo, tanto benigno et quam gratissimo, tanto delectevole et bello, di singulare ornamento arborario agli sensi se offerite, quanto mai cosa excellentissima et voluptuosa cum gli ochii mirare se potesse. Imperò che ciascuna fertile lingua di caritate et parca accusarebese. Et per tale similitudine troppo disconvenevole et abusiva comparatione sareberon gli anticommemorati ad questo. Imperoché sencia existima era quam solatiosissimo, et di delicie loco tuto consito et exornato horto olitorio, et herbario, et fertile pomario, et amoeno viridario, et gratioso arborario, et periucundo arbustario. Il quale era loco non di monti devii, et desueti, eliminata omni scabricie. Ma complanato et aequabile fina ad gli gyrati gradi verso il mirabile theatro exclusivo, gli arbori erano di odore suavissimo, di provento foecondissimi di expansione di rami latissimi. Horto di oblectamento incomparabile affluente, di largissima ubertate, di fiori iucundissimo, et referto, libero de impedimenti, et di insidie tuto ornato, di manali fonti, et freschi rivuli. Il cielo non rigido, ma temprato latissimo, perspicuo, et illustre, non di horrente umbre lochi averni, immune dil variabile, et incostante tempo, che cum insidie lacescente di venti infecti offendesse, non cum moleste et hybernale pruine. Né aestuatione di importuno sole, né invaso et torrido loco di aritudine di aesto. Né di gelatione horrida excocto. Ma tuto vernante et salubre che tale non è l’aere ad gli Aegyptii la Libya spectanti, di lunga salute, et salubritate, et destinato di aeternitate. Loco consito di vireti, di spectanda densitate di frondosi arbori, di gratissima ostentatione, cum venustissima praesentatione di virentia, et per tuto il liquido aere incredibile spiramento di florea ridolentia, cum tuta la area herbescente, et di frescho roramine perfusa, et floridanti prati, et oltra il pensitare di omni piacere faetoso et naturali beni, cum colorati fructi, tra il perenne foliamine virente, cum stabile cohaesione et consenso, cum itione diffinite per le piante, et di multiplici rose arcuatamente contecte, ceda quivi dunque lo irriguo et arborato Thermiscyra campo. Per la quale cosa più che arduo iudico, et difficile arbitro il volere, (et cum acre ingegnio) narrare. Ma, quanto la rapace retinente, et arida memoria nella lauda collocata mi sovenirae, tanto io brevemente me adapterò ad scrivere. Questo sancto loco alla faceta (ad gli mortali et miserabunda) natura dicato alumno degli dii et statione, et degli beati spiriti diversorio, circuiva (come rectamente coniectare valeva) tre miliarii, et da qualunche parte interfluxo di salse

With these amorous triumphs, and the euphonious voices of the sailor-girls, and beyond by the sea-deities, the serene air was filled, and the cerulean deep, with confused clamours, and a multitude resounding — the waves, and feasts, and dances, and especial gesticulation and festive gladness, and devout veneration — as, gliding to the most pleasant place, we put in. So kindly and most gratifying, so delightful and beautiful, offering itself to the senses with singular tree-set ornament, as ever the most excellent and voluptuous thing could be beheld with the eyes. For every fertile tongue would accuse itself of poverty of expression; and by such a likeness the things commemorated before would be too unbecoming and abusive a comparison to this. For beyond estimation it was a most solacing place, and of delights — all planted and adorned as a kitchen-garden and herb-garden, and a fertile orchard, and a pleasant pleasure-ground, and a gracious tree-plot, and a most delightful shrubbery. Which was a place not of trackless and disused mountains, every roughness done away, but flattened and even right up to the circling steps toward the marvellous theatre at its heart. The trees were of most sweet odour, most fertile of yield, of the widest spread of branches. A garden of incomparable delight, affluent, of the largest fruitfulness, of most delightful flowers, and stored, free of impediments, and of ambushes all adorned, of flowing fountains and fresh rivulets. The sky not rigid, but temperate, most wide, clear and bright; not of the horrid shades of infernal places; immune from variable and inconstant weather that might offend with the ambushes of tainted winds harassing, nor with troublesome and wintry frosts; nor the swelter of an importunate sun, nor an invaded and torrid place of the dryness of heat; nor scorched with horrid freezing. But all springlike and salubrious — such as the air is not to the Egyptians who look to Libya — of long health and salubrity, and destined for eternity. A place planted with green things, of admirable density of leafy trees, of most gratifying show, with most lovely presentation of greenery; and everywhere through the liquid air an incredible breathing of flowery fragrance, with all the grassy ground steeped in fresh dew, and flowering meadows; and beyond the imagining of every pleasure, teeming with natural goods — with coloured fruits among the perennial green foliage, in stable cohesion and consent, with paths marked out among the plants, and arched over with manifold roses. Let the watered and tree-set field of Themiscyra yield place here.

Wherefore I judge it more than arduous, and reckon it difficult, to wish — even with keen wit — to narrate it. But as much as my grasping, retentive, yet arid memory, set upon its praise, shall recall to me, so much briefly I will adapt myself to write.

— most limpid waters. Which was not heaped of tufa crags, gnawed by the obstinacy of the surging and foaming waves, full of cracks like rough Plotae; nor of shallow shores broken and eaten by the wave's harassing injury, nor by the clinging salt; nor was it composed of proud Niobe's rock, nor do her most sharp and hard children appear there. But all minerally of the most polished material — not brittle, nor friable, nor turning to mud, but translucent, whole and undefiled, like keen and artificial crystal.

Where with careful diligence I explored the little pebbly shores wiped clean by a kindly wash, of scattered gems of varied form and colouring, shining. There too, dispersedly, appeared an abundance of the fragrant issue of the monstrous whales, carried in by the fruitful tides. A most adorned island, then, of most gratifying and new and perennial covering of springlike greenery, admirable everywhere over the flat.

But first, upon the bare shore-banks close by, I beheld the coeval and tall cypresses with their close-set and cracked cones, persevering, and durable for weighty roofs — timbers not savoury to the gnawing woodworm — and the spacing between cypresses of three paces, one separated from the other. This regular order, turned round in a ring, was observed throughout the whole outer circle of the island. Then, in a circle, there went round a most delightful and flowery myrtle-grove, loving the talkative shores; which stands votive and dedicated to the divine mother of the amorous fires. Compacted and most densely reduced and shaped in the manner of a walled fence, a pace and a half tall, enclosing within it the trunk-stocks of the straightest cypresses, the beginning of its foliage rising two feet from the levelled top, or flat, of the myrtle-grove. Thus this greenery, so made, walled about the shore-banks, with fitting passages left and distributed at the seemly places. Which fence showed the least wood, but, protected by the delightful and flowery foliage — no top exceeding another, no leaf — kept its summit and its circling shorn with exceptional evenness.

Within this walled-about myrtle and green hedge (which might be, from it toward the centre of the island, about a semitertio of a mile), I saw, by the drawing of lines from the centre to the shore-circumference, in equal partition twenty, each of the immensity of a stadium, with a fifth part added — imitating the outer enclosure of the myrtle. In each division was a little grove of diverse meadows variously grassed, and of tree-plot the like; distributed specifically according to the required aspect of the kindly sky. Let Dodona's wood yield here. Which divisions, in a ten-angled figure, fittingly interposing a line for each interval, multiply into twenty. In the middle of the fence there opened, level, in each, a gate — seven feet in the opening, nine high up to the arching of its topmost curve. Which latticings were of such rhombs, and little squares, and such degenerate from the quadrangle, and by other most beautiful devices. Along these serpentined the periclymenon; others the jasmine; some of bindweed; some of hops; and some of black bryony, or black vine; others of convolvulus, with the lily-like half-azure bells; some all white; some of momordica — so each was varied. Some of Jove's flammula; of smilax, which for love of beautiful Crocus made itself Autophoros, adorned with a white fragrant lily-flower, with a thorny and ivy-like leaf; of bittersweet; of the little vine, with the three-cornered bladder-campion, its seed spotted with whiteness; and of many others which, serpentining on high, are unknown to me by name.

In the first partition the grove was a daphnon, or laurel-grove, of manifold laurels: here I saw the Delphic, the Cyprian, the Mustax with its greatest and whitening leaf, and the wild, the Cinos, and the Royal or Bacchalian, the Taxa, the Spadonic, and Chamaedaphne — such as never on Mount Parnassus, most admired and most pleasing to Apollo, most noble gift sent to the Romans. Nor did such laurel-bearing earth kiss Brutus, most pleasing to Tiberius; nor did Drusilla see such, borne by the white hen; nor were such born of the augur's command, planted in the villa of the Caesars, triumphal ornament — chiefly the Sterile. I saw also the Daphnoides, or Pelasgian, or Euthalos, fragrant with frankincense; nor did Peneus's daughter make such a perpetual green of so much beauty, with whose leaves Apollo was wont to adorn both his lyre and his quiver. Let the airy Sicilian mountains yield here, both as to their sweetest springs and as to their loveliness — however the most beautiful son of Mercury delighted himself there with Diana — which are not prescribed by the wrath of most high Jove, offering themselves so pleasing to cover the bald head of Caesar, mixed with many Comari in the most pleasant soil.

Foeconda alla sua magna Crete bella in Africa, et olente in Assyria, cum venusta intercalatura di vrate, overo savina di perenne virentia noxia ad Lucina deformate, et similmente variabile. Daposcia vidi et uno proceroso et comante pineto di nuce pinee, quivi la tarentina, overo silvestra pino, et la urbana et la pinea picra, overo Apina, et pinastro, et Zapina, et la lachrymante Resina, artificiosamente distribute. Ancora in uno altro claustro permaxime praestava uno copiosissimo buxeto, in marmorei busti rotundi, et quadruli plantati, tra odorabonde holuscule et floride, che simiglianti in Cytero monte Macedonico non se ritroverebeno, densissimi, cum venusta demigratura in acuminato, cum iusto modo et grado diminuentisi, et cum vaga scansione gracilavano, non sencia commertio di molti altri spectatissimi expressi bellissimamente riduti. Ma tute queste operature, una maravegliosa excedeva. Imperò che di questa specie di arbusculi, io vidi le virtute tute dil procero Hercule, industriosamente, et cum antiquaria deformatione composite, non sencia multifario expresso di innumere altre confictione di diversi animali, sempre virenti, cum non decisure fronde, regularmente collocate, et cum proporcionato et congruente intercapedine, per il prato herboso et florulento distribute. Similmente et uno altro era di multiplice arboramento concinnamente consiti. Et quivi il duro corno, cum gli fructi sanguinolenti, et alcune di candido fructo, era et il amarissimo taxo, ad gli instrumenti lethali di Cupidine grati et aptissimi. Daposcia inseme commixti vidi l’ulmo, tilii, et il tenuissimo Phylire, vitici, carpini, et fraxini, et la hasta di Romulo floribonda, et molti mespili, et asperi sorbi. Offerivase ancora, et uno di rectistirpio et sublimi abieti, quantunque

I beheld also another little grove, in which, with even placing, was a most pleasing oak-wood of tender leaves. And here I saw the broad-leaved, and the common oak, and the robur, and the hemeris producing the medicinal canchry, and the haliphloios with its salt bark, with plenty of Italian oaks, and Turkey oaks, and cork-oaks, and beeches, and holm-oak — or smilax, or holly — here leafy with leaves that do not fall, tended by the Querquetulan nymphs.

In another fence there followed, in equal order, another most gratifying little wood of fragrant wild cypresses, savin, romidascalo, or junipers, led topiary-wise into manifold figured devices, with minute and pricking leaves — the willing consort of the divine mother, preservable — and loftiest cedars of manifold use, weeping cedar-oil, of foliage like the cypress, of which at Ephesus stood the statue of Diana, in the most noble temples most highly prized for its eternal hardness; the aged Carie, and refusing the gnawing moth; fruitful to its great Crete, beautiful in Africa, and fragrant in Assyria; with a lovely interspersing of vrate, or savin, of perennial greenery, harmful to Lucina, shaped, and likewise variable.

Afterwards I saw also a tall and leafy pine-wood of pine-nuts: here the Tarentine, or wild pine, and the urban, and the bitter stone-pine, or Apine, and the pinaster, and the Zapina, and the weeping Resina, artfully distributed.

Again, in another cloister, there stood a most copious box-grove, planted in round and square marble tubs, among fragrant and flowering little pot-herbs — such as the like would not be found on the Macedonian mountain Cytorus — most dense, with a lovely tapering to a point, diminishing in just measure and degree, and thinning with a graceful gradation, not without commerce of many other most admirable devices most beautifully reduced. But one marvellous work exceeded all these. For of this kind of little tree I saw all the labours of tall Hercules industriously and with antique shaping composed [in topiary], not without manifold representation of innumerable other feignings of diverse animals, always green, with leaves that do not fall, regularly placed, and with a proportioned and congruent interval distributed through the grassy and flowery meadow.

Likewise there was another neatly planted with manifold trees. And here the hard cornel, with its blood-red fruits, and some of white fruit; and there was the most bitter yew, pleasing and most apt to the lethal instruments of Cupid. Afterwards, mixed together, I saw the elm, lindens, and the finest phylire, chaste-tree, hornbeams, and ashes, and the flowering spear of Romulus, and many medlars, and rough service-trees.

There offered itself also one of straight-stemmed and lofty firs, however —
