dill’amplo mare fugitivi se accusano, et il sito suo sia montano, niente dimeno, quivi proceri et in cielo abeunti inseme interpositi ordinatamente gli fungosi et agaricii larici, overo larigni il foco renuenti, et a questi simili cum opportuna et grata collocatione dispositi. Molto spectabile subsequendo se offeriva et uno altro, ove era la iuglande, prima dicta diuglande, quivi cum non infesta umbra, et la persica et la basilica, overo molusca, et la Tarentina, non sencia sociale composito di coryli. Ceda quivi Avellano, et Preneste, et le pontice. Consortiva et ancora cum questi la impatiente Phyllis arborescente, la quale dete il nome phylla alli foglii, prima denominate petale. Essa florulenta offerivase, quale nello advento dil pigritante Demophonte, chiamata, et nuce graeca, et amygdala, et thasia. Non sencia maxima voluptate mirai, et una silvecula di nuce castanee cum il fructo di pungente echinato calice armato, quale mai a gli Sardi primo saritrouorono. Diqué, et per graeco vocabulo Sardiani balani furono chiamati. Agli quali poscia Balano il Divo Tiberio poi gli dete nome. Pensai sinceramente che a queste la parthenia gli cedeva meritamente la tarentina di facillima mundatura et la più facile balaniti, et più rotunda. Queste praestano et alle pure salariane, et alle laudate coreliane, et le coctive, et le tarentine et neapolitane, ove era ancora il sparto, overo miryca, o vero Aspalato. Erano dunque quivi et silvule et di nobilissimi cotonei, overo cydonei, et uno siliqueto, quale Cypri simigliante non produce, et di lente palme se offeriva uno denso palmeto di utilissime fronde cum cultrato mucrone, resistente, et non inclinabile nella sua summitate onerata confertissimamente dil suo polposo fructo. Non squallidi et piccioli quali la Libyca, né quali la interiore Syria produce gli sui dulci carioti. Ma molto più excellenti di magnitudine ancora, et di dolcecia, che Arabia et Babylonia non rendeno, era et uno pervenusto di mali Punici nobilissimi di tute le specie, dolci, acri, mixti, acidi, et vinosi. Agli quali non se compari, né gli Aegyptii, né gli Samii, né gli Cretensi, né gli Cyprii, et Apyrini, et Erythrococomi, et Leucocomi foecundissimi di fructi et balusti. Daposcia vidi uno gratissimo boschetto di lotho, overo agrifolio, faba Syriaca, ciceraso, overo melli, overo celti, cum molto più suave provento, che le syrtice et nasamone, quivi in tuto la Africa superata consta. Non mancava ancora et uno di paliuro cum rubente fructo al vino aemula di suavitate. Ceda quivi la Cyrenaica, et la interiore Africa, et ancora quella che circa il delubro di Hammone nasce, et uno di ambi gli mori, lo uno exprime nel fructo il funesto amore, et l’altro nutrimento alle nostre delitie

— they show themselves fugitive from the ample sea, and its site is mountainous; nonetheless, here tall and reaching to heaven, set among them in order, the spongy and agaric larches, or larigni, that refuse the fire — and others like these, disposed with fitting and gracious placing.

Most notable, following, offered itself another, where was the walnut, first called diuglans: here with no hostile shade; and the peach, and the basilica, or molusca, and the Tarentine, not without the social company of hazels. Let Avella yield here, and Praeneste, and the Pontic nuts. Consorting also with these was the impatient Phyllis grown to a tree — she who gave the name phylla to the leaves, first called petala. She offered herself flowering, as at the coming of loitering Demophoon summoned; and the Greek nut, and the almond, and the Thasian.

Not without utmost pleasure I beheld also a little wood of chestnuts, with the fruit armed in a pricking bristly husk, such as first the Sardians found — whereby, by the Greek word, they were called Sardian acorns; to which afterwards the divine Tiberius gave the name Balanus. I sincerely thought that to these the parthenia rightly yielded, and the Tarentine of easiest shelling, and the more easily balanite, and rounder. These surpass both the pure Salarian and the praised Corelian, and the quick-boiling, and the Tarentine and Neapolitan; where too was the broom, or myrica, or Aspalathus.

There were then here also little woods of most noble quinces, or cydonians, and a carob-grove such as Cyprus does not produce the like; and of slow palms there offered itself a dense palm-grove of most useful fronds with knife-like point, resistant and not to be bent at its summit, laden most thickly with its pulpy fruit — not squalid and small like the Libyan, nor like the sweet dates the inner Syria produces, but far more excellent in magnitude too, and in sweetness, than Arabia and Babylon yield. There was also a most lovely one of most noble pomegranates of all the kinds — sweet, sharp, mixed, acid, and vinous — to which are not to be compared the Egyptian, nor the Samian, nor the Cretan, nor the Cyprian, both the seedless and the red-tufted and the white-tufted, most fecund of fruits and blossoms.

Afterwards I saw a most gratifying little wood of lotus, or nettle-tree, Syrian bean, ciceraso, or melli, or celtis, with a far sweeter yield than the Syrtic and Nasamonian — here in all Africa surpassed, it stands. Nor was there lacking one of Christ's-thorn with reddening fruit, a rival to wine in sweetness. Let Cyrenaica yield here, and inner Africa, and that too which is born about the shrine of Hammon; and one of both the mulberries — the one expresses in its fruit the mournful love, the other affords nourishment to our delights —

si praesta. Mirai et uno di foetosissimo oliveto, et uno ficulno di tute le specie cum copioso provento. Et uno iucundissimo populno, et similmente uno di hippomelides cum le silique aegyptie cum la lachrymante Metropo, quale all’oraculo di Ammone stillante gummo ammonaco non si troverebbe. Gli quali arbusculi cum elegantissimo et artificiosissimo distributo et ordine. Il quale l’aspecto dil coelo quivi non desiderava, ma sencia repugnantia dilla natura omni cosa optimamente locata constava. Diqué essa ingeniosa natura quivi sé manifestamente accusava tute le delicie, che sparsamente per l’universo havea solertemente producto. Quivi congesticiamente, et cum praecipuo studio coniecturare si pole tuto essere creato. Era et il solo herbido et floreo et da surgenti, et umbrati fonti, di vitreo latice perlucidi, madente di aque suavissime più che dil Salmacide fonte. Et quivi non pativano il rigifero Arcto, né il nubigeno Noto, ma l’aire saluberrimo purgatissimo, et quam purissimo, et longe lucidissimo, liberamente ad gli ochii pervio, levissimo et coaequabile, et invariabile cum grande amoenitate, et apricitate moderata dil loco et dil coelo, che mai non patisce turbulenta alteratione, ma dissipato, et omni nubilo dispulso, esso coelo liquido monstrantise exclusi gli procaci venti, gli crepitanti Euri, il sibilante Aquilo, et la malignitate, et la aspritudine cum magno fragore dilla saeviente procella, et qualunque iniquitate di tempi, non subditi agli tumultuosi mutamenti di aque né alla frigida Libra. Ma omni cosa luculente riguardare si pole, et la optabile luce, laeti et pululanti nella statione dil lanoso Ariete siccante le vellere nello illuminoso et heracleo Phoebo existente, cum non caduco, ma perpetuo virore, celebrato da multiplice canto di ucelli, quale volitante nell’aire la galericola, et inseme la cantante luscinia, l’aire tuto cantando personavano. Allo extremo termino di questo semitertio di milliario tuto in silvule distributo verso il centro, perché una circumferentia di circulare figura è di tanto commenso, quanto sono tre diametri sui. Et tanto più quanto che in undeci partitione, deducto uno diametro, sono due portione. Dunque il diametro di questa voluptuosa insula praestavasi uno milliario adiuncte dille undeci partitione due. Ambiva una egregia clausura, di altitudine passi .viii. et di crassitudine pedale tanto condensamente foliosa, che minimo stipite non apparia, cum binate fenestre pervie, et ordinatamente ad gli opportuni lochi, et itione, inarcuava patente porte, facta et compactamente conducta di meli rancii di limonii, et citri, cum illustre virentia nelle mature folie, et di novelle fronde, degli primi et maturi fructi, et degli odoratissimi fiori dispersamente ornate, tanto più all’aspecto grato et spectatissimo, quanto che rarissimamente è usitato di essere concesso agli humani intuiti videre aequivalente factura. [t]

I beheld also one of most teeming olive, and a fig-grove of all the kinds with copious yield. And a most delightful poplar-wood, and likewise one of hippomelides with the Egyptian pods, with the weeping metopon — such as, at the oracle of Ammon, dripping gum-ammoniac, would not be found.

Which little trees were of most elegant and most artful distribution and order — which the aspect of the sky there did not want, but without repugnance of nature everything stood best placed. Whereby that ingenious nature there manifestly avowed all the delights which, scattered through the universe, she had shrewdly produced. Here heaped together, and with especial study, one may conjecture all to be created. The ground too was grassy and flowery and with springing and shaded fountains, of glassy water most clear, moist with waters sweeter than the fountain of Salmacis. And there they suffered neither the frost-bearing Bear nor the cloud-born South Wind, but the air most salubrious, most purged, and most pure, and by far most lucid, freely pervious to the eyes, most light and even, and invariable, with great loveliness and a temperate sunniness of place and sky, that never suffers turbulent alteration; but dissipated, and every cloud driven off, that liquid sky shows itself, the bold winds shut out — the crackling east winds, the whistling north, and the malignity and asperity, with great crash, of the raging storm, and every iniquity of weather — not subject to the tumultuous changes of waters nor to the cold Balance. But everything may be regarded lustrous, and the desirable light, glad and pullulating in the station of the woolly Ram drying his fleece in the illuminating and Herculean Phoebus, with no falling but a perpetual green, celebrated by the manifold song of birds — as, flitting in the air, the little crested lark, and together the singing nightingale, made all the air resound with singing.

At the outermost boundary of this semitertio of a mile, all distributed into little woods toward the centre — because a circumference of circular figure is of as much measure as are three of its diameters, and so much the more that in eleven partitions, one diameter deducted, there are two portions; therefore the diameter of this voluptuous island stood at one mile, with two of the eleven partitions added — there went round an excellent enclosure, of a height of eight paces and of a foot's thickness, so densely leafy that the least stem did not appear, with paired pervious windows, and, in order at the fitting places and passages, arching open gates, made and compactly conducted of orange, lemon and citron trees, with lustrous greenery in the mature leaves, and of new fronds, of the first and mature fruits, and of the most fragrant flowers dispersedly adorned — so much the more pleasing and admirable to the aspect, as it is most rarely wont to be granted to human eyes to see an equivalent work.

Notes

Confidence: medium. The close of the bosco catalogue, the hymn to the island's perfect climate, and the citrus-hedge that bounds the middle zone are all secure. The pi-approximation embedded in the boundary sentence (below) is a literal rendering of Colonna's own arithmetic.

In questa iucunda et dilectosa clausura, tra il verdissimo mirteto, et tra questo florido naranceo septo ambiente, innumeri et promiscui animali inclusi vagamente discorrevano, quantunque la natura dissimile repugnasse innoxii et mansueti. Vagavano quivi cum mutua amicitia. Et prima gli caprigeni satyri cum gli pendenti et intorti spirili. Gli bicorni fauni, cum l’altro sexo. Dapoi gli semiferi Cervi, et Capree saxipete, et le pavide Dame, gli maculosi Hinnuli, gli saltanti Capreoli. Gli auriti Lepori. Gli timidi Cuniculi. Le Fele pullarie, candide et lutee Mustelle, et la mendace Gallante, Sciuri inquieti, et somnochiosi Glyri. Gli feroci Alicorni, et Tragope et Tragelaphi. Omni specie leonina sencia alcuna frammea, ma ludibondi. Gli collosi Gyraphi, celere Gavielle. Et infiniti altri animali, intenti ad gli solatii dilla natura. Ultra poscia di questo claustro verso il centro, trovai una magnificentia di uno eximio pomerio, overo delitioso viridario. Quali mai potreberon, non solamente gli humani ordinare, ma mi suado che né pensare. Facile è dunque, che le seconde operatrice faci secundo il primo operante. Et ancora io diciò consento, che né ingegnio tanto foecondo si ritrovasi, che singularmente valesse, di tante excellentissime operature di questo sacro loco dignamente di relato alquanto propalare. Cedano quivi gli pensili horti da Syro re constructi. Per la quale cosa rectamente iudicai, che non da altro, ma solo da divino artifice fue cusì exquisitissimo cogitamento ad contemplatione dill’alma dea dilla natura ad tale ordine, et effecto decentissimamente producto. Il quale spectatissimo giardino verso il centro porrecto, di passi .166. et semi in prati diviso. La quale divisione constava per itione di directo al centro, et circularmente transversarie. Late passi .V. Gli primarii prati nella prima linea dilla sua quadratura verso la clausura, cum le laterale erano passi .50. Ma la quarta linea verso il centro se decrementava, et da questa linea tolleva la dimensione, la prima linea dil secundo prato, et per il medesimo modo il tertio prato se quadrava. Perché la forcia dille linee al centro tendente causava il scambro. Et le angustie di essi prati et dille strate, et però era deformata la quadratura. Le transversarie nella sua integritate rimanente. Le quale strate erano pergulate, et in ciascuna grummia era tuberculato, sopra quatro columne ionice, il scapo overo la sua proceritate dille quale era di nove diametri dilla ima sua crassitudine. Et di qui et de lì dille itione, overo strate, erano altane busteate di finissimi marmori, cum liniamenti decentissimi. Et per omni quatro diametri extava una di sopradicte columne. Tale columnatione, et intercolumnio per tuto observato.

In this pleasant and delightful enclosure, between the greenest myrtle-grove and this flowery orange fence encircling, innumerable and mingled animals, shut in, roamed loosely — however nature, unlike, repugned — harmless and tame. They wandered there in mutual friendship. And first the goat-born satyrs with their pendent and twisted little horns; the two-horned fauns, with the other sex. Then the half-wild stags, and the rock-seeking roes, and the timid does, the spotted fawns, the leaping kids; the long-eared hares; the timid rabbits; the cat-kind, white and yellow weasels, and the lying gallante; restless squirrels, and drowsy dormice; the fierce unicorns, and tragopan and tragelaphus [goat-stag]; every leonine kind without any fierceness, but playful; the long-necked giraffes, swift gazelles; and infinite other animals, intent on the solaces of nature.

Beyond this cloister, then, toward the centre, I found the magnificence of an excellent orchard, or delightful pleasure-ground — such as never could humans, not only order, but, I persuade myself, so much as think. It is easy, then, that the second workers act according to the first worker. And I too consent to this, that no wit so fecund is found that could singly avail worthily to publish somewhat, by report, of so many most excellent works of this sacred place. Let the hanging gardens built by King Syrus yield here. Wherefore I rightly judged that by no other, but only by a divine artificer, was so most exquisite a conception, for the contemplation of the fostering goddess of nature, produced to such order and effect most becomingly.

Which most admirable garden, stretched toward the centre, of 166 paces and a half, divided into meadows. Which division stood by passages straight to the centre, and circularly transverse, five paces wide. The primary meadows, in the first line of their squaring toward the enclosure, with the lateral ones, were 50 paces. But the fourth line, toward the centre, decremented; and from this line took its dimension the first line of the second meadow, and in the same manner the third meadow was squared. Because the force of the lines tending to the centre caused the narrowing, and the straitness of these meadows and of the streets; and therefore the squaring was deformed, the transverse ones remaining in their integrity.

Which streets were pergola'd, and in each ridge was a little dome upon four Ionic columns, the shaft or their tallness being of nine diameters of their lowest thickness. And here and there of the passages, or streets, were tomb-shaped platforms of finest marbles, with most becoming lineaments. And every four diameters stood one of the aforesaid columns. Such columniation, and intercolumniation, was observed throughout.

Notes

Confidence: medium. The tame-beast catalogue is secure and vivid; the garden geometry that follows is technical and rendered literally, including Colonna's key admission about the shape of the compartments. This is the middle ring — the prati — with its measurement of 166½ paces, the semitertio Segre's whole reconstruction depends on.

Fora dille capsule, overo Altane sotto il socco dille columne solide pullulavano rosarii, non excedendo el passo l’altecia sua. Le quale tra una, et l’altra columna septo facevano delectabile, ad qualunque columna, et de qui, et de lì, perpendicularmente surrecto nel medio dilla columna interiore adhaeriva rectissima una virga di rosario. Le quale oltra il nobilissimo Epistylo extenso sopra la dicta columnatione, di petra russa quale praefulgido coralio sencia altro adminiculo de gli rosarii facevano il flexo topiario. Il fastigio dilla dicta pergula cum le capsule, columne, et trabe recta, di altura se praestava passi quini. Dal quale fastigio incohavano a ritondarse, overo tuberare le cupule in forma bullacea. Esse sole coperte di rose lutee. Le pergule per longo di tute specie di rose candide erano intecte. Et le transversale di vermiglie rose di omni conditione, cum perhenne fronde et floritura in summa multitudine, et spiramento di odore, germinavano et fora dille capsule, omni generatione di fiori et di aromatice herbe. La prima pergula circitora cum il claustro dill’aranceto continivase, il quale havea una fenestra dilla apertione dil circunflexo terminante al claustro dilla pergula al centro directa, meno aperta dal solo in su uno passo aequale al septo intercolumnato. Ciascuno prato havea quatro porte, nel mediano dilla sepiente columnatione. Le capsule pervie lassate. Le quale porte per tuti gli prati a llibella uniformamente se correspondevano. Nel mediano degli oliarii et florigeri prati, una elegante operatura di eximio distributo et praecipua politione, io vidi. Primo negli primi prati mirai una celeberrima fabricatura di scaturiente fontana, situata soto una specula di virentia buxea di solerte expresso. La quale uniforme se trovava per tuto il primario ordine, et in circuito degli prati per questo modo. In medio di ciascuno cum aequa distributione tre gradi torqueati in rotundatione iacti, erano extructi. Dil supremo nella coaequata superficie il diametro dui passi era et semisse, cum uno peristylio di octo columnelle sopra excitate cum le basule nel circinato gyro dil superiore grado, et cum gli capitelli. Le quale usurpavano sete diametri nella sua proceritate (doricamente dilla crassitudine ima) et ventriculate archi da una ad l’altra. Superambiva agli archi il trabe, fascia et coronice. Al perpendiculo dille supposite columnule per ciascuna superastructo uno antiquario vaso. Per diametro dilla sua dilatata corpulentia piedi tre, cum il rotundo fundo acuminato, et d’indi paulatinamente dilatantise, perveniva alla mediana prominentia, ornata di una exquisita zonula. Et de qui dal lymbo il moderato proclivo, ascendeva all’orificio, cum labii di grande politura circa lo hiato dilla sua apertione, et de qui al lymbo piedi uno et semisse, il residuo fina al t ii

Out of the little chests, or platforms, beneath the socle of the solid columns, sprouted rose-bushes, their height not exceeding a pace. Which between one column and the other made a delightful fence; to each column, on this side and on that, perpendicularly raised, in the middle of the inner column adhered, most straight, a rod of rose-bush. Which — beyond the most noble architrave extended over the said columniation, of red stone like most gleaming coral — without other support the rose-bushes made the topiary bend. The summit of the said pergola, with the little chests, columns, and straight beam, stood five paces in height. From which summit the little domes began to round, or swell, in bubble-form; these alone covered with yellow roses. The pergolas along their length were roofed with all kinds of white roses, and the transverse ones with vermilion roses of every condition, with perennial fronds and flowering in the utmost multitude, and a breathing of fragrance; and out of the little chests sprouted every generation of flowers and of aromatic herbs.

The first surrounding pergola continued with the cloister of the orange-grove, which had a window of the opening of the arch terminating at the cloister of the pergola, directed toward the centre, less open from the ground up by one pace, equal to the intercolumnar fence.

Each meadow had four gates, in the middle of the enclosing columniation, the little chests left pervious. Which gates, through all the meadows, uniformly corresponded to one another, level.

In the middle of the olive-set and flower-bearing meadows, an elegant work of excellent distribution and especial polish, I saw. In the middle intersit of the levelled, most solid inlay of the peristyle was a fountain, founded within a rounding somewhat shell-like hollowed, from the centre of which rose an inverted baluster, two feet. Above sat a platter, the gap of its opening having by diameter four feet; in the very middle of which, three straddling tails of three golden hydras, through the bottom outlandishly three-forked, then tightly intertwining in a most beautiful knot, divided by the belly one from the other in a bag-like form, with an arching discrepancy, and in their throats snake-wise knotted, with the head three-forked apart, vomiting the most fragrant water into the shell — equally sustained upright, two feet, a vase of ovate figure. Of which, in the part above the surface, were fixed eight little gold pipes, from which a most slender thread of water leapt forth. And through the gaps or intervals of the box columns it issued, dewily moistening the whole meadow. The interstice of which watch-tower was clear and pervious. The stone-work was all of finest jasper, reddening and lustrous, adulterated drop-wise with infinite spots of manifold colouring, with elegant and exquisite carving at the fitting places.

Now in each corner of the quadrangled meadow, with a proportioned distance from the little chests, was disposed a platform of four steps, in square form. The first step, most solid, in front appeared two feet; in the flat, or mouth, a side of a foot and a half; and they were hollow platforms. Then followed the other above, in graded order, tall as the open breadth of the first; and so the third, and so the fourth. In the first, fragrant herb germinated; so in the following. Here, then, were crisp and tiniest basils, citron-scented and chervils, which did not overpass the middle front of the step, the fronds kept even; the like stood uniform throughout. The other had fragrant and small thyme, gracious to the honey-making bees. In the third, the small and bitter glyciacon, or nectary, or southernwood, such as the Sicilian does not offer. In the topmost, Celtic spikenard, of pleasing odour.

This arrangement, in all four platforms placed at the corners of this first meadow, showed itself all clothed with flowering chamaedaphne. The opening of the topmost step was a foot in diameter, and in each was planted a most noble and fecund fruit-tree, led uniformly topiary-wise. And first they were apple-trees: in one corner I saw most fragrant Appian apples; in the other, Claudian apples; in the third, Paradise apples; in the fourth, the little Decian apples. But in each meadow of this first order the species of the said fruit varied. Trees here fecund with apple-bearing offspring, the fragrance diffusing everywhere — with such beauty of colour, and producing such sweetness of taste, as the tree of Hercules of Gades did not produce, nor such trees as Juno commanded to be grafted in her gardens; whereby they might be called pomarii aphyracori [orchards of golden apples].

The topiary shaping, and the circled thickness, was of a crown, with the winding toward the watch-tower. The parapets, or fences, of this stepped platform stood of most beautiful mirror-jasper, oversown with golden sparks, and mingled with yellow mottling, and with cyan veins serpentining, and reddish ones running, and confusedly dappled with a chalcedonic waving, squared off with most gratifying little wave- lines.

Beyond, then, from this described first order of greenery toward the island's centre — in the second order, in the middle of the area, in place of the watch- tower — I beheld a most admirable device of box, in artful topiary. Clothed in a rounding down to the cap of the knees, girt, with the arms spread on high, and to human stature the neck, head, breast, shaped with exacting harmony. Sequita ordinariamente, et ancora la descriptione dil tertio prato verso il centro, il quale nel suo mediano havea una capsa di contento circinato, tripedale levata, per diametro dui passi la apertione, cum gli accessori liniamenti. Fora se exaltava uno artificiato buxo, dil sequente topiario composito. La capsa era di litharmeno finissimo. Il stipite sesquipedale, sopra resideva una deformatura cepea, alquanto il circinao dilla capsa excedendo. La quale era vacua, et aperta nel supremo per diametro semi et uno passo. Sopra gli labri dilla quale apertura una columnatione di sei verdigianti stipiti gyrava cum arculi, pedi alti quatro. Poscia uno fastigio metale, overo deformato in caliceo pede ascendeva. In la summitate dil quale iaceva una iustissima pila, di pedi tre la sua crassitudine. Sopra l’extremo infernate dil metato fastigio, ad perpendiculo di ciascuno stipite se incocleava una cauda di uno serpente, cum el ventre repando, et pandante la spina, quanto era lo exito dilla proiectura dilla corpulentia cepale. Adhaerendo cum il collo alla supra existente pila, cum il capo porrecto et fauce aperte, et per occultissimi fistulacei meati saliva fundendo per la bucca odoratissima aqua, cum gli pedi extensi verso il capo, cum le ale panse, in numero sei. Fora dil vertice dilla pila prosilivano rami tre, trifaria divisi, et devexi bipedali sublevati. Ciascuno dunque degli quali nella sua cima sustentava una arula rotundata, overamente uno tubulo cum exquisita diligentia attributo di sopra la coronetta, et di sotto le gule opportune, cum aequatissima decimatura. L’altitudine sencia gli liniamenti pedi tre. Sopra la piana resideva una antiquaria hydria, quadrifaria ansata levata pedi tre. Dalle quale singularmente nasceva uno buxo cum dui gradi di rotundatura buxea. Lo inferno excedeva di circuito la corpulentia dilla subiecta hydria, levato dall’orificio sopra il stipite pedi uno, l’altro superno distava da questo alquanto minorato altrotanto. The waters then pouring headlong into the neighbouring sea. Moreover the water was copious with manifold fishes, of form beautiful, and various, and outstanding, with their scaling of golden and grey-green colour; nature, reluctant, opposed nothing here, so that they were secure and did not flee timid. Some of such bigness that, as bearers, they conveniently bore the girls, mounted, to the solacing battle — embracing with their snowy calves and comely little feet the scaled and yielding bodies, which without any fishy stink swam softly, and here and there twisting, and willing to do the women's bidding, one drawing the other. Heaped together were the white swans, with the voice sent forth with the tears poured out for beloved Phaethon; and otters and beavers, with other water-animals, all most joyously beneath the topiary covering made festival to voluptuous delight, without other pondering — so that nothing arose to cause molestation to their pleasure and solace, nor anything displeasing to oppose it — a silent desire sprouting again in my soul. In this happy place I would willingly still, with my goddess Polia, wish to dwell eternally. But then, every other roving desire extinguished and repudiated, without delay I fell back to my most firm intent, in the unique love of my most beloved Polia. Nonetheless I judged this without doubt a thing super-excellent, and super-delightful, above any delight, above every sweetness of pleasure.

Likewise, in the first circular and wooded enclosure of the groves, creatures of the one and the other sex, ever within that same hedge, dwelt with those animals appointed to pleasure. In the greening meadows within the peristyle, by another turning, I saw innumerable youths and outstanding girls, intent on solaces, on sounds, and songs, on dances, and delightful conversations, and pure and sincere embraces, given over to adornment and personal cultivation, to compose muse-songs, and to various works the studious and devoted damsels — where I judged virtue to be more affected than any other lascivious pleasure.

Beyond then this most clear and delightful river, with a continuous circling, was a grassy meadow as great as that which stretches from the peristyle to the river. Ove immediate incomminciavano altri septeni gradi a salire, cum la praefata operatura, mensuratione, et materia, et coloramento, et tuto questo negli sequenti era riservato integramente. Sopra il supremo era una capsea excavatura, pedi quatro in apertione. Il patore dilla quale a sufficientia era profundo, et cusì negli sequenti. Nella quale nasceva uno septo buxeo, quale vitrina illustratione gratissimamente virente. Et a llibella degli ponti, et strate, mirai una turre dilla dicta virentia, sublevata pedi nove, et lata cinque, cum una patente porta in hiato pedi tre, et alta sei, et cusì le sequente. Questo primo septo di crassitudine tripedale, et di sei alto, et cusì gli sequenti, vedevasi di foliamento densissimo, et era cusì disposito di pinnatura dilla propria arboratione. Tra una et l’altra turre vidi egregiamente facto uno triumpho cum caballi, una rheda trahenti, et praecedenti lo ovante alcuni militi macherophori, et cum haste triumphale artificiosamente compacti variando bellissime le opere. In uno altro interturrio promineva una navale enyo. Tra due altre turre clasica pugna terrestre. Tra due altre venatione et antiquarie fabule d’amore. Cum diligentissimo expresso, et exquisitissima deformatione. Tale ordine circumveniente variando le sequentie. Intro questo primario circumvallato, dapò una ambiente strata, quale quella inferiore tra il columnulato, et gli gradi di mirabile tessellatura offerivase di grande admiratione, et excessivamente delectabile artificio, sencia dubio di fatichare omni humana intuitione et senso. Il quale nel primo aspecto tapeti charaini dispositi et extensi stratamente alla planitie, facilmente arbitrai, cum tute maniere di coloratione, che a tale ostentatione meritamente expediva exprimere, in modo di gratiosa picturatione conducta in più variate et multiplice ingrupature et figure et signi cum la opportuna diversitate di coloramenti, di holuscule alla requisita distinctione dilla opera ficta. Alcune plene di colore, altre cum obscura coloratione, alcune mediocremente, tale più chiare et festichine, alcune prasine, altre di virore palide, alcune meno, et di subrubicundo coloramento, cum iucundissima conciliatione. Le figure principale continente in sé multiplice designature, era tra due rhombee, una circulare, et una rhomboida tra dui circuli, alternantise continuamente in gyro, exempta quella parte, ove le vie intercallavano providamente relicte. Le quale strate sempre tra due uniforme figuratione passavano.

And, level with the bridges and roads, I beheld a tower of the said greenery, raised nine feet, and five wide, with an open door gaping three feet, and six high, and so the following ones.

Between one tower and the other I saw excellently made a triumph, with horses drawing a chariot, and preceding the one who triumphs certain sword-bearing soldiers, and with triumphal spears artfully compacted, varying most beautifully the works. In another space between towers stood forth a naval Enyo. Between two other towers, a fleet-battle on land. Between two others, a hunt, and antique fables of love. With most diligent relief, and most exquisite fashioning. Such an order going round, varying in its sequences.

Within this first rampart, after an encompassing path — like the lower one, between the colonnade and the steps, of marvellous tessellation, which offered itself to great admiration, and an excessively delightful artifice, without doubt to weary all human sight and sense. Which, at first aspect, I readily judged to be charaine carpets laid out and spread flat upon the level, with all manners of colouring, which for such a show it fittingly served to express — in the manner of a gracious painting, conducted into more varied and manifold groupings and figures and signs, with the fit diversity of colourings, of little pot-herbs, to the required distinction of the feigned work. Some full of colour, others of dark colouring, some middling; some clearer and gayer, some leek-green, others of a pale verdure, some less so, and of a somewhat reddish colouring, with a most pleasant reconciling. The principal figures, containing in themselves manifold designs, were: between two rhombs, a circle; and a rhomboid between two circles, alternating continuously in a ring — except in that part where the ways were providently left to intercalate. Which paths always passed between two uniform figures.

THE SECOND kitchen-garden cloister follows immediately after the just-recited work. At the edge of which, in order, the other seven steps toward the centre began. Then the thick foliage began, fashioning itself into a moderate cypress. And so, in circuit through all, of two paces its height. Chapter XXII

The triumph of Cupid and the theatre of Venus. The landing, the trophies of the disarmed gods (Quis evadet? — Nemo, "Who escapes? — No one"), the masque of allegorical nymphs, and the serpent-drawn car that bears the lovers, bound in roses, to the great amphitheatre — an obsidian-floored theatre of planted tiers and perfumed pavements, where the lovers are unbound and Psyche restores Cupid's golden arrow.

Negli quali erano di pretiosissimi lapilli rosule, et altri mirabili expressi, in oro inclaustrati, et cum inchaustico operamento eximie deornati, et vermiculariamente depoliti. Gli labri dille quale thorace di miro efferato di syrmata textura aurea, gli phrygii iugimente ambivano, et nello infernate extremo alternatamente crassissime perle, et piruli cum moto inconstante ludibonde dependevano. Tra le quale cum partiario coloramento le circulare interposite lucevano et in campo aureo artificiosamente deputate. Cum tanta provocatione, che all’aspra morte lo homo ultroneamente se offerisca et volente. O contagioso artificio. O allectivo ministerio, o propugnante machine. Qualunque core sano tutissimo, valido et quieto, et libero, et renitente, di facilmente inficere, repente di subvertire et depopulare, sencia mora prosternere, sencia indusio perturbare, totalmente subiugare, et sencia relucto trahere. Di prostrare discussamente omni moderata, incredibile et pervicace continentia. Questi sono quegli veraci et infallibili sateliti dil operoso amore cum ampliabile numero di immanissimi carnifici, le immune remote, et disiuncte pensiculatione insidianti, et da tale inclinante subiectione exclusi di potere per alcuno modo, né cum audente animo prevalerse, et dalle praesentate inevitabile, et trahente dulcitudine, cum tanto solerte et diligente studio illaqueabile, et cum subtile ingegnio invento tanto exquisitissimo operamento et ad tanto bella et formosissima opera per sé dalla foecunda natura, artificio da distrugere ritrovato, et eximio adiuncto et accessorio di cruciare. Omè il quale ragionevolmente fingere se doverebbe, et usare per le marmoree statue, et non per gli humani et fragili cori. Imperoché ancora quel nobile et divo sexo, spoliato et denudato summamente contorque et infice periclitabondi, non che cum questo voluptico additamento di laquei pernitioso investigato. Ma solo questo accede, che elle non pensiculano essere assai il d’amore naturalmente perire, sencia tanto aucto incremento di excogitati modi adiungere gli miseri et molliculi amanti allo interito dil cordolio più facilmente di conducere, et continuamente excitare scintillule extremamente incendiose da vegetare alla consumptione le amorose et fervide flammule, divi obiecti di rimpire et confundere il caldo pecto di bullienti suspiruli, et di fermentare il core ad amore. Hora io non saperei debitamente exprimere per quale modo uno tanto fundamine iacto d’amore stabile et sincero fermamente in Polia collocato, che alquanto quassare il sentisse da queste inevitabile et parate insidie et impetuose violentie. Omè poscia tra me tacitamente replicava. O prophilea Pollia bellatula mia, custodi la tua adepta praeda. Imperoché grande periclitamento, è il transito per tante pyratice fallacie, et manifesti sicarii et praedonuli insidiarii. Gli quali contra omni sincera rectitudine sono dil suo amoroso offendimine commendati et laudabilmente approbati et dagli tristi offensi, tanto più desiderati et riverentemente più requisiti et più dolce amati. Hora nella sua laetissima fronte, sotto a due hemicycle, quale filo di seta subtile, et nigerrime ciglie più che illustrante electro, dui sagittabondi ochii festevolmente lucevano più che irradiantissime stelle nel lympidissimo coelo splendescente. Et nel aspecto suo più belle che incarnate, et ricente rose, et le gene non miltate, ma cum più gratissima et genuina rubedine, che degli

With such provocation that to bitter death a man would offer himself, of his own accord and willing. O contagious artifice! O alluring ministry, O assaulting siege-engines — which any heart, however sound, most safe, valid and quiet, and free, and resisting, you easily infect, suddenly subvert and depopulate, without delay prostrate, without respite perturb, totally subjugate, and without struggle drag away. To lay low, scatteringly, all moderate, incredible and stubborn continence. These are those true and infallible satellites of laborious Love, with an amplifiable number of most-monstrous executioners, ambushing the immune, remote and disjoined reflections, and excluding those inclined to such subjection from being able by any means, nor with a daring spirit, to prevail — and, by the presented, inevitable and drawing sweetness, with so shrewd and diligent study ensnaring, and with subtle wit invented so most-exquisite a working, and to so beautiful and most-shapely a work by fecund nature herself, an artifice found for destroying, and a choice adjunct and accessory of torment. Alas — which reasonably ought to be feigned, and used, for marble statues, and not for human and fragile hearts. For even that noble and divine sex, despoiled and denuded, supremely torments and infects the imperilled, let alone with this voluptuous addition of pernicious snares devised. But this alone accrues: that they do not consider it enough to perish of love naturally, without adding so much increased increment of excogitated modes, to conduct the wretched and soft lovers to the death of heart-grief more easily, and continually to excite little sparks extremely incendiary, to quicken the amorous and fervid little flames to consumption — divine objects, to refill and confound the warm breast with bubbling little sighs, and to ferment the heart to love. Now I would not know how duly to express by what means so great a foundation of love, stable and sincere, firmly placed in Polia, felt itself somewhat shaken by these inevitable and ready ambushes and impetuous violences. Alas, then, within myself I silently repeated: O my dear little beautiful Polia, guard your won prey! For a great peril is the passage through so many piratical fallacies, and manifest cut-throats, and little ambushing plunderers — which, against all sincere rectitude, are for their amorous offence commended and laudably approved, and by the sad, offended ones so much the more desired, and reverently the more sought, and the more sweetly loved.

Now, on her most-joyous forehead, under two half-circles like threads of subtle silk, and blackest brows more than shining amber, two arrow-shooting eyes festively shone, more than the most- irradiating stars resplendent in the most-limpid sky. And in her aspect more beautiful than incarnate and fresh roses; and the cheeks not rouged, but with a most-pleasing and genuine redness, than which —

Redimite di diademate di gioie di verno coronamine florente, tra gli variati flori bractee auree deornatamente intercalate, praecipuamente di amethystine viole, et di flori cumatili, et di purpurante amarantho, et holochryso et di cyclamino, et cum strophiole di mellilotho, cum viole luteole et candide, mensuratamente composite, et commixtamente inserte, et di altri coronarii flosculi, et cum candicante margarite et altre gemme, accessoriamente le ornate caesarie circundate et innexe, et alcune elegantissime callicridene tanta demulcente harmonia ad gli auditori communicando dispensavano, quanto forsa unque Apolline, immo sencia haesitare, la lyra pulsante alle helicone Muse non rende, né porge. Né tale et tanta suavitate di sono gli tyrreni navicularii sentirono. Né Arione tanto cum sono supra il delphino vectore ad Tenaro fece il traiecto. Le quale sonatrice, non in uno erano, ma in ordinato processo disposite, et divisione processionale al suo requisito, et constituto loco ad magna extollentia et triumphale adoria et victorine laude, in redundante turme. Per le quale dive cose fermamente mi suado inane praestarse omni foeconda et facunda lingua exprimere satagendo particula degli suavissimi soni, degli dulcissimi cantici, degli solemni et iocosi tripudii et feste, dille dive Nymphe et insigne puelle, dille sue singulare et incomparabile bellece. Dillo excellente et illustre et elegantissimo decoramento, da interrumpere et amputare la gratiosa vita, et da dissipare et distrahere omni duro et obstinato core laetante cum vario et triumphale gestamine et cum alacre

— and, with little cords of gold and silk twisted, hanging at the fleshy arms near the grasp of the hand. And then, with their turned and longish fingers, solicitously they forbade, and in time yielded, upon the pierced tibia, leaping — not such as was found by Mercury — the whistling voice which, among the most-purple lips, received composedly the sonorous breath. With gracious swelling, apple-rounding the coloured little cheeks. And then, with the little right hand, the drawn and stretched skin they beat with little beaters of whitest ivory, with measured and mosaic participation, with a soft and grateful murmur and raucousness, resounding in concord with the tibia's whistle.

Some with twin tibiae — to the invention of which let Marsyas yield, and the Phrygians likewise. Some lyring with garrulous lyres, and some citharising with citharas, exciting upon the trained brazen strings, with tender and delicate fingers, or with plectra, the brazen sound, striking it together; and again with other most-noble and marvellous and organed instruments, with golden and rattling sistra clattering with a sharp tinkle; and with steel triangles, with playful rings tinkling, soft and sharp, at the sweet stroke; and others conformably with hooked little horns, diffused an unheard harmony, with a crackling trumpet fore-singing.

Wreathed with diadems of jewels, flowering with a spring-crown, among the varied flowers gold foil becomingly intercalated — chiefly of amethystine violets, and of sky-blue flowers, and of purpling amaranth, and everlasting, and of cyclamen, and with little wreaths of melilot, with yellow and white violets, measuredly composed, and mixedly inserted, and of other coronary florets, and with whitening pearls and other gems, accessorily their ornate locks girdled round and woven in. And some, most-elegant, of beautiful voice, dispensed so much soothing harmony, communicating it to the hearers, as perhaps Apollo — nay, without hesitating — playing the lyre to the Heliconian Muses does not render, nor offer. Nor such and so great a sweetness of sound did the Tyrrhenian sailors hear; nor did Arion, with so much sound, upon the dolphin his conveyer, make the crossing to Taenarum. Which women musicians were not in one place, but disposed in ordered procession, and processional division at their requisite and constituted place, to great extolling and triumphal glory and victorine praise, in redundant troops.

Through which divine things, I firmly persuade myself, every fecund and eloquent tongue would prove vain, striving to express a particle of the sweetest sounds, of the sweetest canticles, of the solemn and playful dances and feasts, of the divine Nymphs and notable girls, of their singular and incomparable beauties. Of the excellent and illustrious and most-elegant adornment — enough to interrupt and amputate gracious life, and to dissipate and distract every hard and obstinate heart — rejoicing with various and triumphal insignia, and with alacrity —

Ciascuno gestava uno monstro rudemente exciso in ligno, et inaurato, effigiato humano vestito. Dal tricapo fina alla diaphragma solamente il residuo in quadrato acuminantise alla parte infernate, demigrava in una gulatura basiale, cum uno latastrello, cum una antiqua foliatura nel sito brachiale, cum uno pomo al pecto. Dinanti agli quali praecedeva immediate una politula Nympha, nel volto niveo dilla quale le gene porphyriace rubevano, cum la hederata fronte di corymbi, induta di segmentato palio, vibrati de qui et de lì da suavi reflati zephyrei, gli lacinii dil reflato sino, baiulava uno vasculo aureo, in modo di papila rotundato, lacte per angustissimo meato aspergendo libava. Similmente ancora due Nymphe praecedente redimite l’una di folii dilla foemina Linozoste, et l’altra di Hermopoane masculo, erano gestatrice. La una di uno integro puerulo inaurato nella dextra, et ne l’altra uno altro dil capo, brachioli, et dil collo mutilato. L’altra cum praecipuo honore et obstinata superstitione el simulachro dagli Aegyptii di Serapi venerato portava. El quale era uno capo di leone. Alla dextra prosiliva uno capo di cane blandiente. Et dalla laeva, uno capo di rapace lupo. La quale effigie era tuta in uno volumine di draco contenta et circundata, radii praeacuti emittente. Il quale draco cum la testa alla dextra parte del simulacro derivava faberrimamente deaurato.

— gesticulation advancing; and of so sumptuous and superb a triumph, and of so many delights and pleasantnesses, and immense amplitude of precious riches and greatest opulences — rather divine than of nature — to my eyes, by the Cytherean grace and cupidine privilege, openly to see, and clearly and really to behold, especially indulged.

In the last place, immediately, in front, next to the drawing serpents, two aegipans and wanton satyrs, with goatish beards, with goat-feet and cloven, proceeded. Each bore a monster, rudely cut in wood, and gilt, effigied human, clothed: from the three-heads to the diaphragm only; the rest, in a square, tapering to the lower part, passed off into a basal gullet-moulding, with a little slab, with an antique foliage at the arm-site, with an apple at the breast. And in the middle of the square, in the broadest part, appeared the ithyphallic sign.

Before whom, immediately, preceded a polished Nymph, on whose snowy face the porphyry cheeks reddened, with the ivy-crowned forehead of corymbs, clad in a segmented pall, quivered here and there by the soft zephyr-breaths, the lappets of the reflexed bosom; she bore a golden little vase, rounded in the manner of a nipple, from which, by the narrowest channel, sprinkling milk, she libated.

Likewise, again, two Nymphs preceding, wreathed the one of leaves of the female Mercury-plant, and the other of male Hermopoane, were bearers: the one, of a whole gilt little boy in the right hand, and in the other another, mutilated of the head, little arms, and neck. The other, with special honour and obstinate superstition, bore the simulacrum venerated by the Egyptians, of Serapis. Which was a head of a lion; to the right jutted a fawning dog's head; and to the left, a head of a rapacious wolf. Which effigy was all contained and surrounded in a coil of a dragon, emitting fore-sharpened rays; which dragon, with the head, derived to the right part of the simulacrum, most-excellently gilt.

Onde cum emusicata distantia, et cum longo et solemne progresso, comitato era il triumphante fanciullo, et ambidui Polia et io invinculati di florenti serticuli et viminali rosei festabondi. Whence, with mosaic distance, and with long and solemn progress, was accompanied the triumphant boy; and both, Polia and I, bound with flowering little wreaths and rosy withes, festive. The Nymphs, of facetious nature, most benignly active, gratifying us, made alluring amorous blandishments, with festive faces and genuine hilarity, and soothing amorous solace.

Finally, with this triumphal and mysterious discourse, and with the quiver-bearing pomps and amorous enticements, among fragrant flowers successively proceeding — the standard-bearing of the notable victory preceding, with the fore-singings of the most-joyous nymphal youth, with flowing gait and fore-dances, and with coruscating torches pre-shining, and with clear light pre-glittering, they went before — and among fragrant pot-herbs, sweet-smelling and living trees, odoriferous fruits, odorous air and clement and most-liquid sky. The road hedged, planted with every kind of shrubbery, and in every part covered with little herbs, and with green grass. Not lacking, step by step, the roses, and the plenty of flowers — every thing fragrant, and a place happy, blessed, delightful, and most- pleasant. And with so great and divine a following of the miscellaneous throng of Nymphs, with peculiar pomp, with religious progress — nay, triumphal — the one accompanied the other, with stature and determined distance, advancing under the rose-pergola of every manner, with new and spring fronds and leaves. Which, with sweet noises, whistled softly.

And there all the ground was fertilely overwhelmed and covered with strewn leaves of roses, and of orange-flower, of amethystine violets, and matronal yellow ones, and of white bells, and of purpling pulliphure, and of flowers of jasmine, of lilies, and other conspicuous and most-odorous florets. GIUNTI dunque cum solemnissimo gaudio, et incredibile laetitia, et solatioso dilecto per la triumphale via cum distributa aspergine indi et quindi per alcune strictissime auree fistulete, irrorante di odoratissime aquule gli processionarii, et tutta la triumphatrice turma rosidulamente perfusa alla porta dil ingresso, mirai che l’era stupendo artificio. Alcune cum aequa alteratione et distributo referte di signi et di imaguncule, quale in Epheso nunque furono vise. Ad gli anguli dille quale appacti pendevano dui ossi di capo di ariete, uno di qui, et l’altro di llì, cum gli rugosi corni incochleati, overo cum intorta vertigine, per le quale uscivano certe cymose inseme innodate, una frondea gioia cum suppresso foliamento, et di prominenti fructi retinente et illaqueante, nel contento dilla undulatione quadrata di l’arula. Beyond this first binding followed, ascending in order, a similar order of columns, in every thing conformable, and in no part discrepant. And although the building-art appetites that superposed columns ought to be shorter by a quarter than those set below — of which the perpendicular came, without the altar-work, above the centre of the columns beneath, with the sequence, and the third (order) a fifth (shorter) — nonetheless in this elegant and symmetrical building this was not observed, but of one height, the overstanding with the underlying. The third quadrangular ones obeyed in the third order. These superseated columns had also the encompassing binding, like the subjacent. Beyond this girdle, the quadrangular ones, or little pilasters, furrowed, rose. And between one and the other, a third of it emerging from the solid, in the evened intercapace gaped a window — not quadrangular in the temple- manner, but as is requisite in profane buildings, obliqued, or arched.

Supremely, in a turned orb above the square columns, the royal cornice, without projections, with every ornament and most-requisite lineament, and with the special due drip-moulding in it, with every harmonic proportion, went round. Beyond the said, raised, circled a clean and unencumbered band, a pace and a half high.

All this celebrated, illustrious, superb, and supremely-approved building, of finest Indian alabaster, of glassy sheen, artfully constructed, most-excellently decorated, and egregiously perfected — without any smearing of lime-paste, or cement, but with stable cohesion and contracted consent, perfect. Which pre- shining material was not disdained by staining smoke, nor paling by the anointment of oil smeared on, nor muddied by the infusion of vermilion wine, but in every part unliable, without any infection, kept in its superb, luculent brightness.

Ma la obvia resistentia mi restituite repente gli commoti, et territi spiriti cum laesione dil decepto pede. — so the upper as the lower, of most-beautiful stones, of varied colouring most-excellently, and with most-even cohesion, feigning one integrity, with mirror-like striation and most-comely polish, noteworthy. The soffits, with elegant work, the shrewd and beautiful-crafting architect had induced with histories of most-admired mosaic, most-highly adorned with most-elegant pigmentation. Out, then, of this marvellous entrance, or middle and Royal gate, all those officious Nymphs remained excluded. And the divine lord, and his most-pleasing Psyche, and we together — with those two who bound us — most-joyously, and with extreme voluptuousness, entered. Here in this entry-way only were not the loosened spaces, but walled, and hedged, and closedly boarded of the noble stone before insinuated. Thence we came, by under the vault, to another facing little door, the summit of which was conterminous, under an evening of a little pergola, which shall be told.

There arrived, being out of the interstitial opening of the vaulted entry, and into the levelled Area of the Theatre — most-highly worthy of admiration — entering, I, at the first aspect, saw a miracle greatly and grandly stupendous. For all the pavement of the space of the middle Area of the enclosed cavea of the Theatre, paved, I saw of a solid and integral Obsidian stone, of extreme blackness, and of indomitable hardness, polished and so lustrous, that I — abstracted upon it, at the first placing of my right foot — in that instant, into an Abyss inconsiderately (and I, all occupied with love and sweetness, truly moribund), feared to precipitate. But the facing resistance suddenly restored to me the shaken and terrified spirits, with the hurt of the deceived foot. Nel medio dilla quale Area nel centro, era il sanctissimo et delicioso fonte dilla divina Genitrice et domina di esso amore artificiosissimamente constituito. Dil quale sacratissimo fonte ante ch’io ne parli, primo tracterò dilla inaudita dispositione et foelicissimo intersito Theatrale. Il quale semota omni dubitatione, sopra il capto dil nostro imaginare fue composito, et miraculosamente definito, in forma (como ho dicto) di Theatro. La gradatione dil quale dall’area dilla lucidissima petra principiava. Non solidi, né massicii gradi, ma inani, cioè vacui, quatro cum il scalinato ascenso, uno sopra all’altro, quale et degli subsellii la gradatione. Ne l’altecia dil sedere palmi sei, et nella latitudine gemino pede, et semisse, o vero nell’apertura. Gli quali erano in ambito circundante capsule di diversi fiori constipate, gli quali la medietate dilla sequente bustula non excedevano. Il quarto et supremo grado coaequavasi la sua apertione cum li labri ad una interposita stratula, quini pedi lata. La quale intorniando era coperta d’una perguleta, alta semisse et uno passo. Ultra poscia il culmo dilla inflexura di tale pergula. L’altro ordine di altri tanti gradi ordinatamente sequiva. Il primo inferiore tanto più alto nell’alamento initiava, o vero pariete, circumvallatamente alla parte intrinseca, che la sublime incurvatura dilla pergula non occupava, il vedere dil fronte di esso primo grado. Tale Symmetria directamente era observabile agli subsequenti. Poscia la quarta gradatione, di questo secondo ordine, et cusì dilla tertia, quale la primaria, era di strata, et di pergula, et di commenso uniforme. Gli tabulati parieti, o vero dille dicte pergulature le sponde in circuito, di nigricante petra di nitore speculare erano. Il primo pariete dilla inferiore pergula, era coaxato di petra spartopolia. Il secondo di Hieratites, la tertia suprema di Cepionide. La nitella dille quale sotto le pergule, una apertura dil sereno aere, che in quella reluceva simulava, et non clausura. La quale petra in elevato sotto l’opera pergulare era tanto, quanto incominciava il flexo di essa pergulatura alla interna parte, ultra la nigra tabulatione, al primordio fina dil primo grado era parietato coassatamente dilla materia di esse capselle. Le quale tutte cose cum tanta solerte peritia, et speculato exquisito di arte, et contumace artificio incomprehensibile, et sapientia investigabile furono, cum divo invento, mirificamente conducte, extremamente contemplabile. — of the profound sky. And likewise all the things existing there in the ring reflected, much more than a most-clean mirror, and so the overstanding ones.

In the middle of which Area, at the centre, was the most-holy and delicious fount of the divine Genetrix and mistress of that Love, most-artificially constituted. Of which most-sacred fount, before I speak of it, I shall first treat of the unheard disposition and most-happy theatral interposition — which, setting aside every doubt, was composed above the grasp of our imagining, and miraculously defined, in the form (as I have said) of a Theatre.

The gradation of which began from the area of the most-lucid stone. Not solid, nor massy steps, but inane — that is, hollow — four, with the stepped ascent, one above the other, like the gradation of the benches. In the height of the seat, six palms; and in the breadth, two feet and a half, or in the opening. Which were, in their encompassing circuit, surrounded by boxes stuffed with diverse flowers, which did not exceed the middle of the following little box. The fourth and supreme step levelled its opening, with the lips, to an interposed little walkway, five feet wide. Which, encircling, was covered by a little pergola, a pace and a half high.

Beyond then the summit of the inflexure of such pergola, the other order of as many steps followed in order. The first, lower, began so much higher in the band, or wall, encompassingly at the inner part, that the sublime incurvature of the pergola did not occupy the seeing of the front of that first step. Such symmetry was directly observable in the subsequent. Then the fourth gradation of this second order, and so of the third — like the first — was of walkway, and of pergola, and of uniform commensuration.

The boarded walls, or the sides of the said pergolas in circuit, were of blackish stone of mirror sheen. The first wall of the lower pergola was boarded of spartopolia stone; the second of hieratites; the third, supreme, of cepionis. The sheen of which, under the pergolas, simulated an opening of the serene air, that shone within it, and not a closure.

Of all this discoursed fabric, the interior girdle — that is, the hollow steps — stood made of best jasper, ponderous, continuous, and oriental, and perhaps Cyprian, of confused colouring, with wavering little waves most-diverse. Here must perish the luxury of the golden vases of Bassus, and that of Antony; let yield also the glory of Nero, who gilded the Pompeian Theatre. The topmost trough, or box, led in a channel and filled and stuffed with earth, had planted cypresses, two and two, one next (but untouching) to the other, the pairing three paces distant. The two then of the middle: that on the right coupled with the fourth on the right order; and the left, by the like, joined itself with the fourth on the left side, alternating, one below and one above, knotting themselves, so much the better as could not be told. And between the neighbouring and curved cypresses, rose a straightest stalk of Juniper, in a most-just sphere, topiaried with spring foliage, which adorned the empty triangle of the cypress-arches. Then, after the reverent inclination, all together, departing from that middle, migrated to the other, with successive continuance. This delightful and choice disposition of the much-admired flowers succumbed here to no temporal change, nor order — nor such as in Memphis — but, ever irrigated and fresh, in one vernal being, and never deciduous, existing.

For which thing, contemplating such majesty of place, with so much grace astonishing, with this elegance ordered and allotted, and most-pleasant harmony of variation of the flowering colour — such as, in the dewy dawn, they present themselves fresh — with all the discoursed miracles, astonished and lifeless I wholly remained. My internal and external senses occupied, and surrounded with ineffable voluptuousness and delight — beyond the excessive love, which all the while in my lanced heart strongly burned, and the unceasing siege of the incomparable beauties of my most-comely Polia, my delight — insomuch that I did not know in what being I was. Finally, into this most-happy place, and most-blessed site, introduced — of a sudden the two Nymphs who bound us, there, again, unloosed us from the entangled little wreaths. And the venerable Psyche, most-honorifically, to her beloved Husband, laughing, restored the little golden arrow.

The Fountain of Venus. At the theatre's centre stands the most-holy fountain; the curtain before the goddess is torn away, and Venus is revealed in her majesty — the scene the whole island, and the whole 3-D world, is built to walk toward.

Dal quale appresentati fussimo dinanti al sacro sancto fonte cythereo.

POLIPHILO IL MIRABILE ARTIFICIO DIL VENEREO FONTE DESCRIVE NEL CENTRO DILLA THEATRALE AREA EXISTENTE, ET COME FRACTA FUE LA CORTINETTA. ET VIDE LA DIVINA MATRE IN SUA MAIESTATE, ET COME ESSA SILENTIO ALLE CANTANTE NYMPHE IMPOSE. DILLE QUALE TRE PER UNO A POLIA ET A LLUI GLI CONSIGNOE. DAPOSCIA CUPIDINE AMBI DUI GLI FERITE, ET LA DEA CUM L’AQUA DIL FONTE GLI IMBREFECE, ET POLIPHILO FUE REVESTITO. POSTREMO VENENDO MARTE IMPETRATA LA LICENTIA SE PARTIRONO.

CUM DECENTISSIME VENERATIONE ET summa honorificentia la Eutrapela Polia et io affectuosamente dinanti al mysterioso fonte dilla divina genitrice congenulati, io da una imperceptibile dulcedine diffusamente invadere vexabonda me sentiva, che in quel puncto che fare non sapeva. Imperò che per lo amoenissimo et incredibilmente delitioso sito, et ultra omni credito dilectoso di virentia et vernale decoramento. Et per le avicule per il purissimo aere discorrendo, et per le novelle fronde garriendo volante ad gli forinseci sensi, quam iucundissime, et cum le decorissime Nymphe cantante melode inseme cum gli sui insueti soni audiendo, et degli sui divi acti, et modestissime moventie videndo ardentemente impulso ad extrema voluptate, et de sì facta fabricatura di tanta dignitate di concepto, et dilla elegantissima dispositione solertemente et curioso pensiculando, et di tanta inexperta fragrantia avidamente hauriendo. Per lo immortale Iove rectamente ignorava ad quale sensitivo potere, lo intento obiecto mio da tanto diverso dilecto distracto, et excessivo et foelice solatio et voluptico placimine firma, et stabilmente applicare, et nescio me accusava. Le quale tutte belle, et dulcissime cose tanto più gratioso et desiderabile allectamento ad me allhora plenamente causando offerivano, quanto che io conosceva la Uranothia Polia participe placidamente delectarsene. In questo loco, at etiam di questo ammirando fonte la novitate et excellentia mirando.

(the last line of the preceding chapter) …by which we were brought before the holy and sacred Cytherean fountain.

Notes

Poliphilo describes the marvellous artifice of the Venerean fountain standing at the centre of the theatre's floor, and how the little curtain was torn away; and he saw the divine Mother in her majesty, and how she imposed silence upon the singing nymphs, of whom she assigned three apiece to Polia and to him. Afterwards Cupid wounded them both, and the goddess sprinkled them with the water of the fountain, and Poliphilo was clothed again. Last of all, Mars coming, they obtained leave and departed.

With the most fitting reverence and the highest honour, the graceful Polia and I knelt devotedly before the mysterious fountain of the divine mother, and I felt an imperceptible sweetness spreading through me and troubling me, so that in that moment I did not know what to do. For what with the delightful place, incredibly pleasing and beyond all belief lovely in its greenness and spring adornment; and the little birds coursing through the purest air and chattering as they flew among the new leaves, most joyfully, to the outward senses; and the hearing of those most beautiful nymphs singing their melodies together with their unfamiliar instruments; and the sight of their divine gestures and most modest movements, which drove me ardently toward the extremity of pleasure; and the careful, curious weighing of a fabric of such dignity of conception and such elegant arrangement; and the greedy drinking-in of a fragrance I had never known — by immortal Jove, I truly did not know to which of my senses I should firmly and steadily apply the object of my attention, distracted as it was by so many different delights, by so excessive and happy a solace and voluptuous pleasing; and I accused myself of not knowing.

And all these beautiful and most sweet things offered me an enticement so much the more gracious and desirable, in that I knew that Polia — heavenly Polia — was placidly taking her share of the delight in them.

In this place, then, and marvelling too at the novelty and excellence of this astonishing fountain.

Il quale nel mediostimo di questo inhumano aedificamento divinamente constructo et expresso per questo modo. Della nigerrima petra, che sola integramente era tutto il silicato, overamente il pavimento di l’area di essa propria nel mediano di uno murulo sublato pedale, cum egregia politura reducta cum omni ornato opportuno di forma extrinseca heptagono, et della interstitia rotunda. Cum l’ambiente cimasula et socco et arulette, et undiculatione fabrefacte et ordinariamente supposite alle base, sopra il mediano puncto degli anguli, dil quale per ciascuno era superastructa una enthesiata, overo ventriculata columna in numero septe, cum summa exquisitura turbinate. Dille quale due correspondevano aequale ex adverso dell’ingresso. In conspecto di questo ove stavamo proni geniculati. Una dille quale tornatile columne, alla dextera parte cyanava praefulgente di finissimo sapphyro, et dalla sinistra vernava virente smaragdo di praestantissimo colore più lucentissimo che gli affixi per gli ochii al Leone al tumulo di Hermia Regulo. Né tale fu donato da Ptolemaeo ad Lucullo. Né di tanta pretiositate fue il praesentato da Re di Babylonia al Re Aegyptico, né di tanto aestimamento furono quegli dil obelisco nel Tempio di Iove. Né di tanta miraveglia fue la statua nel templo di Hercule in Tyro, quale questo admirando se praestava. Which fountain, at the very middle of this more-than-human building, was divinely constructed and set out in this manner.

Of that blackest stone which alone, and entire, made the whole paving — that is, the floor of the area — there rose at its centre a little wall a foot high, brought to an excellent polish and furnished with every fitting ornament, heptagonal on the outside and round within. It had its running cymatium and socle, its small plinths and its wave-mouldings, wrought and set in due order beneath the bases; and over the middle point of each angle there was built up a column swelling in the shaft — that is, bellied — seven of them in all, turned with the utmost exquisiteness. Two of these stood answering one another, equally, opposite the entrance, in full view of where we knelt face down.

One of these lathe-turned columns, on the right hand, shone blue with the finest sapphire; and on the left one glowed spring-green with an emerald of a colour so surpassing, and more brilliant, than the stones set for eyes in the lion on the tomb of Hermias the prince. Nor was such a one given by Ptolemy to Lucullus; nor was that of so great price which the King of Babylon presented to the King of Egypt; nor were those of the obelisk in the Temple of Jove of such estimation; nor was the statue in the temple of Hercules at Tyre so great a marvel, as this one showed itself to be.

Next to this followed a column of turquoise stone, most beautifully coloured a lovely cerulean, endowed graciously with its virtue; and though it was an opaque stone, it was nonetheless most brilliant, and shone back like a mirror.

Touching the sapphire column there stood another precious one, opaque also, of a most delightful colour like melilot, and with a lustre like the translucent flower of the buttercup. Adjoining this was one of jasper of a glassy colour, and the other of topaz flashing with a golden colour. The seventh, alone and singularly, was hexagonal, of the most limpid Indian beryl with an oily sheen, giving back whatever stood before it reversed.

And this one answered to the midpoint between the first two — because every figure of an odd number of angles has one angle facing the middle of the interval between two others. So then: the circle drawn about its half-diameter, an equilateral triangle set up within it, and then a line from the centre, and in the middle of that line —

Il culmo poscia di questo mirabilissimo fonte et tectorio fulgeva di una insolente cupula di optimo et disvenato crystallo mundissimo et perspicuo. — drawn upon the adjacent circumference: such is the sevenfold division of the said circular figure.

In the middle of the shaft of the seventh, the beryl column, on the inner face, there was marvellously carved out of that same stone — as though wrenched free of the sculpture — a little Hermaphrodite child, held in a socket. The three shining columns of the right-hand order had likewise, each of them, an infant boy caught in a kind of receptacle; and so too on the shaft of each of the precious columns of the left there hung, set into it, the female sex. And this, by a mystical artifice, was expressed naturally at the middle of the columns, with such a scintillation of polish as neither the biting of whetstone nor emery with licking Tripoli chalk can give.

The bases, the capitals, the Phrygian architrave and the cornice stood out in the purest gold. The arches, and all the solid between one column and the next, were of the wrought stone of one of the columns of the surrounding order — that is, of sapphire toward the emerald, and of emerald toward the turquoise — and so on in sequence, the whole arcade was marvellously constructed.

At the angles of the crown, above the true central perpendicular of each column beneath, there stood a small altar, and rising from it projected the image of a planet with its proper attribute, its size exactly a third of the column below it, symmetrically, and of the purest gold. On the front face, at the right, sat scythe-bearing Saturn, and at the left the night-shining Cynthia; and beginning from the first and going round in order they ended at Selene. Beneath these, in the frieze running round, chased with the most exquisite artifice, were to be seen the twelve signs of the zodiac, with their governing impressions and characters, expressed in outstanding carving.

The crown then of this most marvellous fountain, and its roofing, blazed with an extraordinary cupola of the finest crystal, veinless, utterly pure and transparent. Xenocrates saw none such; none like it was found in Cyprus, nor produced in Asia, nor in Germany — without rust or roughness, without a clouded speck, no core of salt, nor any hairline flaw to be seen. Nor did Nero shatter such a one. But pure, surpassing, and unalloyed, it was girdled with a raised work, in a fitting and even binding of foliage issuing from certain little monsters, with small boys wonderfully interwoven playing among them; and it was of excellent bulk and convexity.

At the tapering of its topmost peak was fixed a miraculous show: in a golden and most cunningly wrought [?setting], a carbuncle flashing lightning on every side, egg-shaped, and of the thickness of an ostrich's.

Each face was three feet, and from the golden bases up to the architrave the height stood at seven feet. Of the artifice of this thing, marvellous and most highly finished, I judge that its dignity will be more fittingly preserved by my keeping silent than by my discoursing of it poorly and meagrely.

There, between the sapphire and the emerald column, hung on bent rings with knotted loops the most beautiful little veiling curtain that fertile nature could ever have devised to produce as a thing more pleasing to the gods — so beautiful a weaving, and of such a material, that I should never know how to describe it; but of a sandalwood colouring, woven with the loveliest flowering, and with four Greek letters of gold subtly embroidered over it, ΥΜΗΝ, stretched out most becomingly and heavenward. Let the marvellous curtain the Samians sent to Delphi rightly yield place here. This appeared to my Polia as a most precious treasure, and gracious; and it was this that veiled and hid the majestic and divine presence of the venerable mother.

And so, both of us — Polia and I — kneeling face down upon our bending knees, the divine lord Cupid gave the golden arrow to the nymph Synesia, and shrewdly made her a sign that she should offer it to Polia, and that Polia with that fearful arrow should rend and split the most noble curtain. But Polia, as though grieved at the command for such a cutting and breaking, however subject she was to that divine authority, seemed unpractised, and refused to consent. The lord in that same moment, smiling, charged the nymph Synesia that she should hand it to the nymph Philedia, and that she should then present it to me; and that what the honeyed and most upright Polia did not dare to do, I — [?spellbound], and most greedy to look upon the most holy mother — should carry out.

Whereupon no sooner had I taken hold of the divine instrument than, ringed about with a blind flame and not refusing, but rather with an urgent and headlong passion, I struck the little curtain. And as it split I saw that Polia was almost saddened by it; and the emerald column, cracking, seemed as though it must shatter entirely.

And behold, all at once I plainly see the divine form in the salt fountain, brought forth out of that venerable majesty from which all beauty deliciously flowed. Nor sooner had that unlooked-for sight —

Cum facteze et mirando composito tra gli humani né viduto né unque meditato. Nel ostento aemuli dil comoso Phoebo nel sudo Olympo, gli illuminanti radii irradiante. — that divine sight breathed upon my eyes and passed into them, but both of us, roused by an extreme sweetness and driven and harried by a new pleasure so long desired, remained together in a devout fear, almost in ecstasy.

And finding myself so, I began with some reason to be afraid, misdoubting the vision that the son of Aristaeus had in the vale of Gargaphie; and in a moment it put both wonder and terror into me.

In the midst, the divine Venus stood naked in the clear and most limpid little waters, up to her ample and divine flanks — waters which gave back the Cytherean body neither thickened nor doubled nor broken nor foreshortened, but wholly and simply, so that it was perfectly discerned in them just as it was. And round about, at the lowest level, there rose a foaming that gave off a fragrance of musk. With such divinity was that body transparent, with such particular clarity did that majesty and venerable aspect present itself, as a precious and coruscating carbuncle flashes in the rays of the sun — with features and a marvellous composition neither seen nor ever imagined among human kind.

She had — oh, with what loveliness — her golden hair pleasantly and delicately dressed, neatly curled and crisped above the milky whitening brow with wandering and restless whorls, which were hindered from spreading out like vine-tendrils; and from her rosy shoulders they were becomingly kept from falling free by the most beautiful little waves. The face rosy and snowing. The eyes starry and luminous, with an amorous and most holy regard. The honeyed cheeks purpled. The small narrow mouth most purple, of coral — the dwelling and the little estate of every fragrant bud. The breast more than snowy and treasured up, with two small swelling paps that resisted every inclination. The body most ivory and smooth. Divine semblances. Ambrosial — breathing, rather, a spirit of musk.

Her hair then, most beautiful, like the finest golden threads trailing, lay upon the purest waters, not sinking, but scattered in a gyre and floating out very long: in that show the rivals of long-haired Phoebus in the clear Olympus, radiating illuminating rays. And above the twisted little locks, over part of the loveliest brow, with a dense growth and an airy heaping, they shone out before her and covered her as with a little shade, down to the small ears. From these hung two ostentatious pearls, such as the divided Union did not hang for her in the Pantheon at Rome; nor did the island of Taprobane ever produce their like for conspicuous whiteness. And a circlet went about her, or rather a plaited band of vermilion-whitening and pleasant roses, springlike interwoven, and it flashed with little gems.

Notes

Confidence: medium. This is a blazon — a head-to-toe catalogue — and the sense of every clause is clear; the difficulty is that Colonna coins a diminutive or a compound in nearly every one (melule gene, eburissimamente glabello, torcularei crinuli), and English has to choose between keeping the strangeness and keeping the sentence readable. I have kept the strangeness where it carries meaning and let it go where it was only ornament, which is a judgement another translator could reasonably make differently. Nothing here is doubtful; a good deal is debatable.
