And within the inner circuit of the most sacred fountain, clear of the join of the sumptuous steps, flowering, purple Adonis sprang up among its kindred leaves, purpling, kept just clear of the water; and on the left side likewise thelygonon flowered with its pale grape-clusters, and on the right arsenogonon — most admirable herbs, and always in flower. Close by stood the nymph Peristeria, promptly and even boldly ready, attending with a whole mind upon the services of Venus.

Likewise outside the fountain, upon the stone floor where Peristeria stood, at the right side, three other divine girls stood naked in this manner, inseparably embraced: two of them, Eurydomene and Eurymone, showing their maiden faces toward us; the third, Eurymeduse, turned with her whitest shoulders to us, her hidden hips veiled by the long outpouring of her most golden hair. These were the gracious daughters and handmaids, prompt to the effect of the goddess mother. And she held, lastly, in her divine hands an opened oyster-shell packed with fresh spring roses, and in the other a burning torch.

Chapter XXIV

The spring of Adonis. Out of the theatre to a sacred spring and the tomb of Adonis, where Venus's yearly rite of mourning for her slain love is told — and Book I closes.

The tessellated pavement was laid level over all the enclosed ground. Which was on every side green without any bareness, and all tressed with tiniest fragrant thyme, of which a single leaf did not stand above another, with a gratifying denseness clothing right up to the banks of the fountain, springlike, with an even shearing.

Here beneath I beheld a venerable work, which these divine nymphs and we devoutly reverenced. A marvellous sepulchre, full of mystery, stood there appointed: five feet in length, and in breadth as much raised — ten inches — excluding the socle, with the little cornice, which was a quincunx; which tomb the nymphs said to be of the hunter Adonis, slain in that place by the tusked boar. And in this place likewise the holy Venus, coming naked out of this fountain, tore in those rose-bushes her divine calf, to succour him who had been beaten by jealous Mars, with a woeful and indignant face, and with anguish of soul.

This little history was seen perfectly carved on one long side of the sepulchre; and the son Cupid then gathering the purple blood into an oyster-shell — adding that that divine gore was laid up in that sepulchre, placed with the ash, with every holy rite. Whereupon on the front of our entrance to the sepulchre it was hollowed out in a circle to the size of the square, and then stopped up with the precious stone jacinth, of a transparent vermilion colour, with great coruscation of flaming splendour, burning unsteadily by the light set opposite, so that I could scarcely fix my eyes on it for the wavering.

On the other long side of the sepulchre I saw likewise Adonis, carved with some shepherd-hunters, among some little shrubs, with dogs and the dead boar, and he slain by it; and Venus falling sorrowfully weeping into the pitiful embraces of three half-swooning nymphs, clothed in finest cloth, weeping together with the goddess; and the son, with a little bundle of roses, I saw wiping the maternal eyes, tearful with flowing tears.

There, between the one sex and the other, in a garland of myrtle, I saw thus inscribed: IMPURA SUAVITAS. In like manner on the other little history, in Greek, was thus expressed: ΑΔΩΝΙΑ. So exquisitely feigned in sculpture did all these things present themselves, that I was moved to a sweetness of pity.

Because your most admirable countenance and heavenly likeness, extremely beautiful and genial, is not wholly earthly, but rather appears in every way, by open token, to have more of the divine. O sacrosanct fount, in which mysteriously is the disposition of the arcana and of the treasure of the celestial genetrix, full of assiduous sanctimony and pacate religion — and which, at present, upon thy flowering banks seats, with so much consolation, and so notable, the demigoddesses; and in which the most-excellent and contemplable part of her most-beautiful body specularly (in mirror) thou feignest to have — for which thing thou art most-highly, of obstinate reverence, to be worshipped: for so much, never let (it be) that, whatever of you I behold, all veiling my piteous eyes, they be not converted into flowing tears — approaching, in my tranquil mind, to commove (the memory of) the lacerated Dirce, the weeping Byblis, the envied Galatea, the fugitive Arethusa, and the dolorous Egeria — I return not wholly free of my spirits. Then, with what affect of soul, and what study, and with what vows is the inelegant tongue invited to such narration? For my first original stock was unhappy, inasmuch as of it was (one) who, by divine will, justly, into springing fountains and liquid rivers transformed himself. O deplorable metamorphosis! O unfortunate case, and badly luckless, and miserably grievous! O indissoluble series of the fates! O inevitable and perpetual order! In such a case, precipitate and adverse, shall I be able to narrate thee without grave sighs, and dolorous voice, and imperfect, sobbed words — and without irrigation of tears upon the dry cheeks? As the wandering Ulysses, reciting the miserable ruins of Troy to Alcinous, King of the Phaeacians, wept — and (why) does it not break my breast, of cordial sighs, in this most-holy place of felicity, (where such are) denied and interdicted of provocation? And in which place, reasonably, the eyes of tears, and the breast of sighs, sterilise themselves — and, to so blessed and gratifying an audience, remote and alien — and especially in this most-sweet and dearest victory, of my most-appreciated Poliphilo.

Marvel not, then, auspicious, most-comely and heaven-dwelling Nymphs, if I, incontinently — both for my feeble parentage and progeny, and for my first falling-in-love, difficult — some time, sobbing, should interrupt my prolix sermon; worthy, nonetheless, of tarrying, and of a considered and attentive audit. For which unjust and enormous thing, and cruel human impiety — audacious, avaricious, ambitious, superb, and nefarious — the gods (who do not suffer mortal offences unpunished, nor permit any insolence to grow up), irascible that the earth-born should wish, usurping, illicitly to assimilate themselves to the supernal gods — (and to compare with) the most-holy mother of our tremendous lord (to whom now most-deservedly we serve) — showed themselves a raging avenger (not otherwise than Juno to Antigone, and the indignant Eriboea to Isis): the impious temple thunder-blasted, the royal house lightning-struck, reduced to coal, not far distant hence, where by chance she then found herself, remained an eternal name, Casa Carbona; and Murgania (turned) into founts, with all those who in that place found themselves, converted. And so likewise Quintia and Septimia, sisters fleeing not far from Murgania, and they transformed into welling founts. And Alimbrica, made ash, not distant from the said, by the terrific lightnings of the great indigene and lightning-hurling Jove; and all the palace and royal mansion, in that place also built for pleasure, all converted into coals; and the place was called Carbuncularia — thence it leaps forth into a little river. And Astorgia, fugitive, weeping the miserable cases, she too into a little river runs down into her father. And likewise Melmia — their perpetual name they gave to those places, licking in waves, embracing the sweet father Lelio Siliro. And he, transmuted into liquefying matter, augmented by the dear daughters, makes a celebrated river, of most-purged welling waters, which still in that most-pleasant region, flowing, most-fresh is seen: from his truncated name, Sile, it is named. And his consort (Calardia), thunder-struck, weeping the miserable and horrend cases, transmuted herself into a notable fount, from her surname called the fountain Calardia, near the beloved father Tito Butanichio, made into a liquefying river, weeping the hard and cruel lot, mingled with those of his line. And her mother Rhoa, between her husband and her most-beloved brother Caliano, flowing, derive into the sweetest son, Sile.

Nor was any, even of the males, unpunished by the celestial ire and just vengeance. For the second-born, Lelio Musilistre, made into a rivulet of his name, embraces the father, inundating the Altinate peoples. Il quale essendo nella pueritia sua dagli sui cognati signori degli Altinati invitato ad uno solemne anniversario funerale, fora della porta Mania, ove se dinominava ad Manes. Nel quale loco si sepelivano gli cadaveri di tuta la citade, et ancora corrupto il vocabulo riservato, se dice alli Mani. Facti li pomposi obsequii, cum veterrimi riti et more patricio. Rimanse cum alcuni adolescentuli a spasso. Accadete che agli maritimi lochi ritrovantise, apresso la specula, overo phano del porto di Altino nominata Turricella. Dalla quale al presente è vocitato il nobile Oppido Turricello, ivi fundato. In quella sua pubertate dunque dagli invasori Pyrati, furono captivati. Diqué ello fue sorticeamente nella anticha gente Brutia conducto in una famosa citate, che al presente Teramo si chiama. Il quale adoptivato per la ingenua indole sua, da uno nobile et magnifico homo Theodoro, patrizando creve. Et dapò la sufficiente litteratura agli militarii exercitii assiduo strenuamente dava opera. Laonde essendo ad la etate virile pervenuto. Et in progresso di tempo per le cose optimamente geste. Et cum animo forte, excelso generoso, robusto, constantissimamente varie adepte victorie, et tuti gli honori militari perfuncto. Per extinguere cum le eximie virtute il nefasto nome. Per le quale tute cose, dal sanctissimo senato Romano, cum prefectura militare, cum paludamento designato, pervene habitabondo deputato, per adventura, ove esso naque, et ove fue oriundo. Being, then, from this feeble and pitiable case, the only survivor escaped — the first-born Lelio Mauro — who, being in his boyhood invited by his kinsmen, the lords of the Altinates, to a solemn anniversary funeral (outside the Manian gate, where it was named "ad Manes," in which place were buried the cadavers of the whole city, and still, the vocable corrupted, kept, one says "alli Mani"): the pompous obsequies made, with most-ancient rites and patrician custom, he remained with some youths at leisure. It befell that, finding themselves at the maritime places, near the watch-tower, or shrine, of the port of Altino, named Turricella (from which, at present, is called the noble town Turricello, there founded) — in that his puberty, then, by invading Pirates they were captured. Whence he was, by lot, into the ancient Bruttian people conducted, into a famous city, which at present is called Teramo. Who, adopted for his ingenuous character by a noble and magnificent man, Theodoro, grew up patricianly; and, after sufficient learning, to the military exercises, assiduous, strenuously gave heed. Whereupon, being come to the virile age, and, in progress of time, for his things most-excellently done — and, with a soul strong, exalted, generous, robust — most-constantly various victories attained, and all the military honours discharged (like Bellerophon exalted from Heurie): for this reason, no more Lelio Maurio, but, for the egregious condition and outstanding effects, was named Calo Maurio — to extinguish, with the choice virtues, the ill-omened name.

For all which things, from the most-holy Roman Senate, with military prefecture, with the paludamentum (general's cloak) designated, he came, deputed to dwell — by chance — where he was born, and whence he was descended, keeping his fatherland secure and guarded from the barbaric invasions. Which place, of shade and air most-pleasing, and of rivers and founts pleasant, chosen, was named by him Calo Mario — so that, by the benefit of the site, more promptly, amid the molesting assiduity of the infesting foe, he might some time avail to delight himself, where was the verdant area, clad of herbs and of flowers.

There, then, when he was made poliucho (city-protector) — round about, in serviceable memory, and of his dearest mother, an eternal monument — a noble and great city of municipal people (named from the hill Taurisana), and of literal and military study, and of site most-rich and pleasant, and of most-ancient cult, and of sanctity and religion a most-true hostess, upon the hastening and swift Father Sile — and, given it the name of the Pious Mother Trivisia — whence, even to this day, the maternal name it retains (Treviso).

Which, with auspicious increment, a long time, with affluence, with togate peace, and social federations of the neighbours, with life led, pacate, he, happily dominating, possessed; and, of him, the successors —

Nel anno della redemptione humana. Dapò gli quatrocento et mille, nel sexagesimo secondo. Io stava come alle vage adolescentule è consueto alla fenestra, overamente al podio del palacio mio, cum gli mei biondissimi capelli, delitie puellare, per le candide spalle dispositi, et dall’ambrosia cervice dependuli, quali fili d’oro rutilanti, alii radii di Phoebo insolando siccantise, gloriabonda accuratissima comente gli pectinava. D’indi a caso passando allhora Poliphilo. Diqué io ardisco di dire, che cusì belli a Perseo non aparveron quegli di Andromeda. Né quegli di Fotide a Lucio. Cusì ello cum intenti et mordaci risguardi accortose, sencia mensuratione et cum incremento d’amore repente se accense. Et il suo tenero et apto core sencia respecto apertosi et per medio ischiantatose (quale ruvido Robure dal fulguratore Iove fulminante percosso, se sfinde) nel primo et puro risguardo. Et Cupido disociato et impigre, cum le sue urente fiamme multiplicabile intromissose, repente sencia alcuna difesa et resistentia succenso et capto. Quale aviculetta simplicula in lacioli imbricosi per poca esca. Et il pisciculo lo hamo inuncando incorre, placidamente cedette. Et del mio legiadro et venusto aspecto desideroso inspectore facto, caldamente appetiva. Il quale molte fiate io nel speculo chiaramente riguardando, dubitava diciò, che quello che ad Narciso advene, a me il simigliante non accadesse. Como nel presente nel mio aspecto patentemente il veddete. Né questo peroe a iactantia debbi esser insimulato. Perché il se adagia. Cusì como fingere et simulare il falso, è vitio. Non meno celare il vero. Dunque de gli novelli et primarii fochi nel pecto suo fundato uno cruciare amoroso, alhora di me affectuoso amante. Diqué già preso in tale amoroso decipulo, per havere qualche condigno consequio di tale Amore. Omni singulo dì, dal palacio mio sedulo viagio prendeva. A l’alte et vacue fenestre riguardando. Non valeva adimpire il frameo desio di rivederme, almeno una fiata. Et per tale cagione havendo cum tanto angore, assai giorni et nocte, passi, vigilie, canti et soni, cum parolette da sospiri formate, cum urgente solicitudine vanamente deperdite. Chapter XXVI

Heimè Polia Nympha Callitrica. Dia mia. Core mio. Vita mia. Et lanista dolcissima di l’alma mia. Habi pietate di me si nella tua diva natura et nella tua singulare bellecia, vive quella virtute, che l’alma mia, como ad solo nel seculo electo precipuo et primario signore, non renuente, ma festivamente offerentime inclinoe arendevola. Hora movite placabile, benigna, et mitifica, soccorrendo agli mei gravi martyri. Et per novissimo refugio di questo, nel presente il morire meglio mi fia, che erumnosamente et sencia il tuo amore vivere. Et così più presto me hilaro expono perire, che sencia la tua optatissima dilectione, così miseramente la nocua vita vivi, perché meglio è uno propero interito, che diutinamente morire. Quale più damnosissimo male, et di questo più exitiale unque potrebbe sentire? Et però a questi mei asperi, et insuportabili langori, non più sperava di potere opportuno rimedio consequire, si non quando gli benigni cieli te rivedere mi concedesseron, perché altramente dela mia tediosa vita aspre ruine vedeva invasure minitante. "— worse? In truth, nothing. And so I all terrify myself, and all lose myself, every hope cut off. And sometimes I reassure myself, saying: in me is not found the false boasting of Ixion, nor that of Anchises; nor the insolence of Salmoneus; nor the sacrileges of Brennus and of Dionysius of Syracuse; nor the impudence of Echo; nor the improbe loquacity of Syrinx; nor the temerarious audacity of the Pierides; nor the stupid confidence of the weaver Arachne; nor the cruelty of the daughters of Danaus. Then why does Cupid, against me, so guilty (of nothing) and so dire, so most- savagely, openly show himself? Why so much deception to the tender and credulous lovers — to offer itself with so much simulated sweetness, with so much fallacy of mortiferous venom and pestiferous confection smeared upon the ruin? — I, wretched, not understanding of the malign fate and deadly lot, its exit and destruction imminent to my scanty life; and to what disaster Fortune intends me, I know not, nor can know, nor foresee — with what calamity, with what troubles, with what mourning and grief I am implicated, and to eternal weeping proscribed — if thou, my chief hope, succour me not, in the present anguishes devolved and prolapsed. Whence, considering this effect of love, disproportionate to that cause, I cannot, by any pact, come into the cognition of it. For this love appeared to me a sweet thing, but the effect that I feel is supremely bitter. I understand not, then, what thing is this monstrous love — save that I come into conjecture that thou, Polia, consentest to my tormentous anguishes; nor, however, in thy angelic face do I see any token of pity and clemency. And for this only, the exasperated soul, by disdain, to flee I feel; nor more can I sustain it, because I lose the frozen spirits, virtue and health. Alas, then, unhappy lover without peer, troubled — O, above whatever lover, most- calamitous — I, before me, see the dark death prepared, threatening; of the aspect of which terrified, consternated and oppressed — for thee, sole hope of my living (that so to be it persuaded me). O fallacious! O iniquitous! O perfidious! — thou hast conducted me to this most-bitter point. Alas, Polia! Alas, my Polia — what should I more do? What other refuge, nor succour, can I attempt? To what side can I turn me? Alas, Polia, aid me — for, to my very self, unhappy, without thee I cannot lend help! For which thing I feel myself perish!" And, the miserable voice raised, with the springing tears, wretched, the last words terminated, prostrate on the ground, he died.

Now, in this sole extreme power — that a man, all the other members and senses lost (most-piteous Nymphs), only the talkative tongue valorous remains — he made long laments, much better than that which I now can replicate, with so much bitterness of heart, piteously weeping — much more than the weeping of the wretched Ariadne, which the son of celestial Jove (Bacchus) commoved. MERITAMENTE POLIA ESSENDO A QUEsto passo divenuta, non poté moderarse, né continerse, che alquanto piatosamente ella non suspirulasse. Et più volte parlando negli amorosi ochi tirate le lachryme, et le rosee guance alquanto fluxe, commosse provocando et similmente le circumastante Nymphe a compassione del doloroso amante Poliphilo, che cusì tristamente egli per vehemente amore, et excessivo dolore fusse perito, trasseno diciò dal profundo del tenero core amorosi suspiri. Et facta uno pauculo di morula, elle solicitavano, che essa il suo gratioso parlare sequitasse. Et interdicti gli caldi sospiri, et affermata la suave voce, cum matronali gesti per questo modo sequendo disse. Beatissime Nymphe, audite grande sevitia, che io non so qual animo mansueto et pio, che hora contra me iniuriabondo non se alterasse. La divina ultione alhora ove era absconsa? che per mia malvasia obstinatione, et dura pervicacia morisse il mio dilecto Poliphilo indignamente. O celeste vindicta perché stavi tu alhora tarditata a dimorare? Che dritamente contra al mio iniquo et perfido animo in quel puncto non te dovevi sopire. POLIA SOMEWHAT EPILOGUES HER IMMANITY (INHUMANITY); AND (TELLS) THAT, FLEEING, SHE WAS CAUGHT UP BY A WHIRLWIND, AND,
WITHOUT NOTICING, CARRIED INTO A FOREST — WHERE SHE SAW MADE A BUTCHERY OF TWO DAMSELS; TERRIFIED BY THIS, IN THAT
MANNER SHE RETURNED TO HER PLACE. THEN, SLEEPING, THERE APPEARED TO HER TO BE RAVISHED BY TWO EXECUTIONERS. TERRIFIED
THEREBY, MOVING FROM SLEEP, SHE ROUSED THE NURSE AND HERSELF; WHO GAVE HER USEFUL COUNSEL UPON THIS OCCASION.

Deservedly, Polia, being come to this pass, could not moderate herself, nor contain herself, that somewhat piteously she should not sigh. And, more times speaking, the tears drawn into the amorous eyes, and the rosy cheeks somewhat flowing, she commoved, provoking likewise the circumstanding Nymphs to compassion of the dolorous lover Poliphilo — that thus sadly, by vehement love and excessive grief, he should have perished — (and) they drew, from the deep of the tender heart, amorous sighs. And, upon me the placid and humid eyes benignly converting, almost as guilty they damned Polia. But, for so much, being more avid to understand the end of such an unjust occasion, and, a little pause made, they solicited that she should follow her gracious speaking. And there Polia, mannerly, having taken the most-subtle sudary (kerchief) that from the candid shoulders hung, the moist eyes wiped, and the most-purple cheeks dried; and, the warm sighs interdicted, and the sweet voice affirmed, with matronal gestures, in this manner following, said:

"Most-blessed Nymphs, hear a great savagery — that I know not what soul, mild and pious, would not now, against me, injuriously, alter itself. The divine retribution, then, where was it hidden? — that, by my malevolent obstinacy and hard pertinacity, my beloved Poliphilo died unworthily. O celestial vengeance, why wast thou then tardied to delay? — that, rightly, against my iniquitous and perfid soul, in that point, thou oughtest not to have lulled thyself. But, indeed, it stood not, then, much time, that I manifestly saw prepared the enkindled ires of the offended Goddess, and of her arrow- shooting son — unless I expiated my rude iniquity, and, candescing (kindling) the most-frigid and rigid heart, that most- holy Numen had not devoutly placated, and out of my pertinacious purpose, of the false suasions and vain thoughts, and my mind of fallacious and subtle opinion, opportunely —

Quanto si me inspeculata nel spaventoso speculo di Medusa havesse. Il quale era di amore inhospite, et di pietate aspernabile. Che ello cum queruli eiulati et voce precarie mestissime, et cum frequentia di più pietose lachryme che le Hyade non pianseron. Et cum più dolce modo et più angustiose et lamentabile voce a commoverme usando, che non proferite cusì Britannico le sue infelicitate al populo cantando, humilmente desiderando precante adiuto et mercede in tanti sui assidui langori, et lachrymosi guai, cum ogni conato di ritrarme et da l’aspera, et dura, et atroce inclinatione sedurme propiciante insistendo. Ma io inexorabile digli sui cruciati, cum dulcissime supplicatione, et cordiale execratione, et amorose prece. Nel quale Amore per niuno modo se poteva adherire, né approximarse. Spreta et stupefacta la potentia sua, tanto diversamente ad gli humani cori applicabile signorigiante. Quale cera, quantunque viscabile, nello udo saxo affigere impulsa, et compressa non vale. O formidoloso troppo, et acerbo caso, per il quale non me terriva, meno me moveva. "Then, only taking covert flight — my heart being still hardish, persevering, and, then, intractable; the mind insuperable; the will harsh and savage, more cruel than Phineus, and than Harpalyce — most-freezingly my breast having glaciated, more than the hard crystal of the northern Alps, and more rigid than gagates (jet) conserving the eggs of the Eagle — as if I had mirrored myself in the frightful mirror of Medusa. Which (heart) was, of love, inhospitable, and, of pity, spurning. For he (Poliphilo), with querulous wailings and precatory, most-sad voices, and with a frequency of more piteous tears than the Hyades wept, and with a sweeter mode and more anguished and lamentable voice to commove me using than Britannicus proffered, singing his infelicities to the people — humbly, desiring, praying, aid and mercy in so many his assiduous languors and tearful woes, with every effort to retract me, and, from the harsh and hard and atrocious inclination, to seduce me, propitiating, insisting — but I, inexorable of his torments, with (his) sweetest supplications, and cordial execrations, and amorous prayers, and, uncontaminated of any his anguish enduring, spurned and refused every humanity, and, repugning any consent — there was no mode nor way that he, in that ill-omened day, could, one little bit, that rigid and Tigrean breast tame, nor commove — much more than would befit — inadulable and accursed; in which Love, by no mode, could adhere, nor approximate itself. Spurned and stupefied his power (so diversely applicable to human hearts, lording it), like wax — however sticky, impelled and compressed onto the wet rock — avails not (to fix itself). O too formidable and acerb case, by which I terrified me not, moved me less; and I, of all women the most-savage, no stimulus, any token of grief and pity excited; from the eyes no tear expressed, any groan provoked; by no mode availed any sigh, in the dire breast, to compose, nor to find; in which I could not the reins of the incarcerated pity break. Et al presente ferire veneron assai venatici cani horricomi afamati, cum fervidi latrati et absoni intonanti, quali il Re Albaniense al Magno Alexandro in dono non dette. Et rabidi Leoni et rugienti. Et cum le ungiute granfie sfindere, et lancinabondi fragmentare. Et nel purpureo sangue vedeva le sue fulve iube intingendo cruentare. Et senza speranza di adiuto, in me non facesseron similante lacerato. Et tra me diceva tremebonda. Quale Libya interriore, o Agisinua tanto immane, tanto sanguinarie bestie nutrisse? Che equare si potesse ad tanta incredibile crudelitate? Heu me questa excedeva senza istima misera me di tute le fere la atrocitate et rabie, che gli saevissimi animali la preda iacente frustatamente diserpendo excarnificavano.

O spectaculo di incredibile acerbitate, et di crudelitate insigne, o inaudita et insolente calamitate, scena da spectare horrenda, di considerato miserabile, di sentire formidolosa et spaventevole, et di pensiculato aspernabile et fugienda. O me trista me, et meschina dolente, ove senza sperancia ad questi mortali periculi son io cusì venuta. Heu me afflicta et sconsolata, che cose sono queste maledicte et furiabile? che io real et apertamente i’ vedo? Per la quale cosa invasa da mortale spavento, dubitando di essermi approximata la statuta et decreta morte, incominciai alhora dolorosamente a piangere, cum copiosa frequentia di lachryme, et crebri et suppressi sospiri, et non sonori gemiti, aspectando et che ancora ad me non fusse facto simile dilaniamento, cum tirato obtuto observando, che lo irato, et atroce Puello, cum le hostice arme, et cum saeviente severitudine, me in quello loco essere connivando non vedesse latitante. Daposcia al micante et casto pecto mio, gli ochii lachrymosi alquanto inclinava. Gli quali io credeva hogi mai nelle irrorante lachryme conversi et liquati. "'Alas, this exceeded — without measure, wretched me — of all the beasts the atrocity and rage, that the most-savage animals the lying prey, piecemeal disserping, excarnified (tore the flesh from).' Et il fiore della mia piacevole aetate, in questo dumoso et silvestrico nemore perire? Et cum tanto cruciato et saevientia la dolce vita finire? Hogi mai le feminile virtute sento detracte, il spiritulo caro dil suo loco fugirsine, et d’indi quasi dimoto a questo passo, omè omè amaricatamente plorando, cum uberrimi rivuli di lachryme (Humore peculiare sencia fallo foecundo et parato) riganti la facia, et il pecto madefacto, le mane disperata nella flava capillatura puosimi, cum odio del mio ornato, et sparsi gli crini illachrymava, et il bellissimo volto, cum le infeste ungue russando foedava. Et ultra mensura tribulantime, et affligentime, questo al mio grave dolore incremento accedeva, di non potere exaurare gli angustiosi lamenti et gemiti, et in tanta affligente et perdita sorte, et in tante cruciabile poene, non possi reserare il claustro del mio dolore, nel core impaciente di più continere sé. O me caelite Nymphe cogitate quanto alacre et contenta me ritrovai, non se presti alcuno intellecto di explicare, et alienata la mente mia del compassionabile caso (ch’io poco teniva) del miserando Poliphilo exanimato. Perché dalla vexata memoria terso et abraso in sé non lo servava. Ma solamente alle devorate fanciulle et impiamente occise, et asperrimamente stentate, teniva occupata et implicita la mente mia, et ad tanto iniquissimo carnificio. Non trovando prohibitione ad gli singultanti et crebri sospiri, né di sedare l’angustiata mente apto modo, a mala poena sequestrate le fluente lachryme, tandem io ritornai, non più viva che morta alla optata et secura mansione, la occorsa immanitate tacitamente succensendo nel core repetibile. "'— most-bitter weeping consecrating. Alas, dolorous and unhappy — in what calamity am I implicated and entangled, in what state I find myself, I avail not to explicate! Who ever saw the subtle fortune with so malign and atrocious an aspect? — that in such a manner (O holy Lady Diana, whom I serve) these my female and virginal flesh must be impiously slaughtered and consumed, and the flower of my pleasant age, in this bushy and sylvestrous grove, perish; and, with so much torment and savagery, the sweet life end?'"

Henceforth I felt the feminine virtues withdrawn, the dear little spirit to flee from its place; and, thence almost removed, at this pass — alas, alas, bitterly weeping, with most-rich rivulets of tears (a peculiar humour, without fail, fecund and ready) irrigating the face, and the breast made-wet — the hands, desperate, in the blond hair I put, with hatred of my adornment, and, the tresses scattered, I wept, and the most-beautiful face, with the hostile nails reddening, I defiled. And, beyond measure tribulating and afflicting myself, this increment to my grave grief accrued: not to be able to exhaust the anguished laments and groans, and, in so afflicting and lost a lot, and in so many tormentable pains, not being able to unseal the cloister of my grief, in the heart impatient more to contain itself. And much more, that there was no mode I might avail to investigate this most-turbulent case — and that, unadvertent, with an innocuous conveyance deported, fearful and trembling, weeping, I found myself unharmed, and, without more hoping, in that same place, whence I was seized and carried off.

O me, heaven-dwelling Nymphs, cogitate how alacritous and content I found myself — let no intellect present itself to explicate — and my mind alienated from the compassionable case (which I held of little (account)) of the wretched Poliphilo, lifeless. Because, from the vexed memory wiped and scraped, in itself it kept him not; but only to the devoured girls, and impiously killed, and most-harshly agonised, held occupied and implicated my mind, and to so most-iniquitous a butchery. Finding no prohibition to the sobbing and frequent sighs, nor an apt mode to settle the anguished mind — with ill difficulty the flowing tears sequestered — at length I returned, no more alive than dead, to the desired and secure mansion, the befallen immanity tacitly re-kindling in the heart, repeatable.

Et quivi il pulsatile pecto, che ancora cum inquieti battimenti sepicule batteva, a pena in sé adunati gli spaventati et smariti spirituli. Et cum supreme fatiche et conati, rachiuso il largo corso delle rotonde et guttante lachryme alquantulo interdicto. Incominciai malamente et cum difficultate (sepicule da spaventosi interumpamini expergefacta) di dormire. Et nel summo et primo soporoso et molle somno demersa il laxato et conquassato corpusculo, perfuso dormiva nella tacita nocte. Ecco cum grande et strepente impeto ad me parve (quale si supposita al capo si fusse Eumete petra) di essere dimoti gli pessuli, et rapiti gli obiici, et da perfossori fracte le sere, et violentemente patefacti gli occlusi hostioli, et obserati limini della camera mia. — whatever animal the sweet and sleep-bearing quiescence desired. With such similitude, having I all that frightful day in gravest pains consumed, and of sighing weepings all dispensed it — supremely afflicting myself (what fatal cause could it be, that so unwonted and unused, and impious, an immanity, to the ill-fated girls, made, it made me see; and, beyond this, with what sudden mode, from my fleeing journey I was impeded, and through the air reported) — all these things, with solicitous and sighing sobs, straitly considering (alas, afflicted!): O most-happy Nymphs, hear — unless anguish, and weepings, and an ambiguous and dolorous living for the future, a portent to me it were, and a fatal decree, I judged. And, stupefied by this, from stimulating fear I intended, and, by various and turbid cogitations, to conjecture — I could not, by any way, investigate the occult cause. Conscious of this, tacitly, all that unhappy and ill-omened day, groaning, fastidiously consuming it, I passed — in which I would rather have found the pale Corydon (i.e. death) than to have run into so many unvisited sadnesses.

And there, surrounded by acerb dolorations, and copiously by most-molesting pains oppressed, robbed of any security, and not daring, for the nocturnal fallacies, to sleep alone — and, through the dark and ambrosial night, I called to me the dear and revered (in place of a parent) my Nurse, in whom, deposited, reposed, and collocated I had, every my confidence and hope; because, alone, I, in the past, with my chaste Goddess Diana, had been.

Now, both — the hour being arrived that the whitening Cynthia had left the Lamian Rocks and the condense woods, and put an end to the solacing huntings — finally (the bedchamber closed and hedged), we went together to the nocturnal quiescence. And there, the pulsing breast, that still with unquiet beatings frequently beat — scarce, in itself, gathered the frightened and bewildered little spirits, and, with supreme fatigues and efforts, the large course of the round and dripping tears re-shut, somewhat interdicted — I began, badly and with difficulty (frequently, by frightful interruptions, awakened), to sleep.

And, in the deep and first, soporous and soft sleep immersed, the loosened and shattered little body, suffused, slept in the tacit night. POLIA RACONTA PER QUAL MODO LA SAGACE NUTRICE PER VARII EXEMPLI ET PARADIGMI L’AMONISSE VITARE L’IRA, ET EVADERE LE MINE DELI DEI. ET COMO UNA DONNA DISPERATA PER INTEMPERATO AMORE SEME UCCISE. CONSULTANDO SENZA PIGRITARE IRE ALLA ANTISTA DEL SANCTO TEMPIO DELLA DOMINA VENERE, CHE QUELLO ESSA SOPRA DI CIÒ DEBI FARE. QUELLA BENIGNAMENTE GLI PRESTARAE CONVENEVOLE ET EFFICACE DOCUMENTO.

NON SENCIA SUPREMA FATICA, ET IMpenso labore, Dive et prestabile Nymphe, si pole uno disposito et inclinato animo, ad uno proposito ritrare, maxime per obstinatione difficultato, et per tempo consuefacto, et più dummentre d’indi se ne prehende qualche dilecto spasso et recompensatione. Et quello nel contrario volerlo adaptare et rivertire dil tuto alienato, per fallace estimatione, summamente difficillimo se dimonstra. Et diciò mirando non si presta unoquantulo, si il senso alcuna fiata dipravato, distorto, et corrupto, le cose di materia dulcicule, ingrate, insuave, aspernabile, et amare soleno aparere. Et meno maraveglioso se offerisse. Prestantissime Nymphe, se la candidecia al gli ochii egri, impuri, et lippi, nigriscente aparendo offende. Si le cose rutilante, di livido tectorio, et le micante di candore, et di splendore renitente. Maculate, di rubigine consperse, obtecte di caligine, di vomicione sepiale perfuse, et di atramento infuscate sono damnate, senza dubio, non per diffecto dillo obiecto, ma per il sensuale morbo. Cusì né altramente io. Poscia che alli algori della casta Diana l’animo et la mente mia fermamente essendo habituata et professa, et religata et proscripta, grave peroe et molto difficile rendevase lo ingresso dell’ardente Amore acceptabile. Al quale come a crudele hoste resistere (inexperta della sua dulcitudine) havevame obiectato pertinace contradictorio, et repugnante Nausea. Et volendo dunque probamente intenta, nel gelido core il novello amore inducere, necessitava industriosamente secludere gli repugnabuli contradicenti. Hora la sagace et versuta Nutrice intentissima di volere, quel duro et immassato

"— only, out of so anguished, afflicted, and prodigious a peril, will draw my mind, and the successive life, out of so much mourning and grief."

POLIA RECOUNTS BY WHAT MODE THE SAGACIOUS NURSE, BY VARIOUS EXAMPLES AND PARADIGMS, ADMONISHED HER TO AVOID (THE
GODS') IRE, AND TO EVADE THE THREATS OF THE GODS; AND HOW A WOMAN, DESPERATE FOR INTEMPERATE LOVE, KILLED HERSELF.
COUNSELLING (POLIA), WITHOUT TARRYING, TO GO TO THE PRIESTESS OF THE HOLY TEMPLE OF THE LADY VENUS, (AS TO) WHAT SHE
OUGHT, UPON THIS, TO DO — (WHO) WILL BENIGNLY LEND HER FIT AND EFFICACIOUS INSTRUCTION.

Not without supreme fatigue and expended labour, divine and outstanding Nymphs, can one draw a disposed and inclined soul back from a purpose — most of all (a purpose) made difficult by obstinacy, and by time habituated, and the more while, from it, one takes some delightful diversion and recompense. And to wish to adapt it to the contrary, and revert it wholly alienated (from the former), by a fallacious estimation, most-most-difficult it shows itself. And, marvelling at this, one is not (moved) in the least, if the sense, some time depraved, distorted, and corrupted, is wont to make things of sweet matter appear ungrateful, unsweet, spurnable, and bitter. And less marvellous it offers itself, most- outstanding Nymphs, if whiteness, to the sick, impure, and blear eyes, appearing blackish, offends; if things rutilant, of a livid coating, and the (things) glittering of candour and of splendour shining, spotted, sprinkled with rust, covered with caligo, suffused with cuttlefish-vomit, and infuscated with atrament (ink), are damned — without doubt, not by defect of the object, but by the sensual disease. So, and not otherwise, I: since, to the colds of chaste Diana, my soul and my mind being firmly habituated and professed, and religated and proscribed — grave, then, and much difficult rendered itself the ingress of ardent Love, acceptable.

To which (Love), as to a cruel enemy, to resist (inexpert of its sweetness), I had opposed a pertinacious, contradictory, and repugnant Nausea. And, wishing then, probably intent, into the gelid heart the new love to induce, it necessitated, industriously, to seclude the repugning contradictors. Now the sagacious and versute Nurse, most-intent to wish that hard and massed —

POLIPHILO LAUDA LA PERSEVERANTIA, OBEDIENDO AL IUSSO DEL’ANTISTA. INTERMITTENDO LE PARTE DICTE DEL SUO INAMORARE NARRA ET COME LA VIDDE AD UNA FESTA NEL TEMPIO, OVE D’AMORE SUMMAMENTE EXAGITATO, PIÙ POSCIA SE DOLSE DEL SUO DISCESSO. DIQUÉ LI MANIFESTA IL SUO CRUCIAMENTO PER INVENTIONE DI MANDARLI UNA EPISTOLA.

REVERENDA ET SANCTA ANTISTA, VIRtute è nelle ardue et ferale fatiche, et turbulenti incommodi, et ingrato dispendio, il sapere conservarse, et cum suasibile sperancia, al distemprato animo, freno et temperatura cum probitate et solerte modo ponere, et non impatiente et inconsulto praecipitare et cassitare, ma sufferendo perseverabondo praestarse allo incepto. Quantunque cosa arctissima et difficile se sia et alla volubile et obstinata sorte, et alli sui ludibrii, et insidiosa versutia, cum dissimulamento cedere. Perché non cum fortitudine, ma cum virtute et ingegnio se vince. Quale Bellerophonte perseverante succedette a gloria. Perché a tutti gli stipendii et pretii il strenuo milite la gloria antepone. Volendo dunque io legittimamente lo honorio, che è il debito et expectato premio del mio amoroso Agone consequire. Fermamente valeroso disposime di durare obiecto a che il violentoso Cupidine di me facesse despecta la opprobriosa inconstantia. Arbitrando dementia et levitate essere, il timido et vecorde accedere alla pugna, et niuna cosa praestarse più valida che la fortecia dill’animo. Et non mediocre pudore et verecundia suadentimi al milite advenire, che nel principiato certamine tergavertire et monstrare le spalle. Ma sopra tutto mai al militante se appertiene disperare. Et nella iniciata pugna deficere, perché meglio è non principiare, cha principiato havendo, lassare lo incepto. Diciò si io non vario mi pare che veramente foelice non se pole appellare. Si ello alquanto non hae il suo opposito sustenuto. Perché d’indi nasce insolentia, si genera confidentia, dalle quale procede lo exito infoelice. Quale a Policrate. Et peroe la perfectione del paragonio tanto megliore si sente per il suo contrario, como sopra l’indice Batto chiaramente si comprehende.

"Reverend and holy Priestess: Virtue is, in the arduous and funereal fatigues, and turbulent incommodities, and ungrateful expense — the knowing to conserve oneself, and, with suasible hope, to the distempered soul, a bridle and temperature, with probity and shrewd mode, to put; and not, impatient and inconsulate, to precipitate and fall, but, suffering, perseveringly, to present oneself to the undertaking — however most-strait and difficult it be — and, to the voluble and obstinate lot, and to its mockeries, and insidious versutia, with dissimulation to cede. Because not with fortitude (force), but with virtue and wit, one conquers — as Bellerophon, persevering, succeeded to glory. Because, to all the stipends and prices, the strenuous soldier prefers the glory.

"Wishing, then, I, legitimately, the honour (which is the due and expected prize of my amorous Agon) to consequute — firmly, valorous, I disposed myself to endure (as an) object at which the violent Cupid might make, of me, a despicable, opprobrious inconstancy. Judging it dementia and levity to be, timid and vecordious, to accede to the battle; and no thing to present itself more valid than the fortitude of the soul; and no mediocre shame and verecundity persuading me — to the soldier befalling that, in the begun contest, he turn tail and show the shoulders. But above all, never, to the militant, does it appertain to despair, and, in the initiated battle, to defect (fail) — because it is better not to begin, than, having begun, to leave the undertaking. For, if I err not, it seems to me that one cannot truly be called happy, if he has not somewhat sustained his opposite (adversity) — because thence is born insolence, is generated confidence, from which proceeds the unhappy exit, as to Polycrates. And therefore the perfection of the touchstone-trial is so much the better felt, by its contrary, as, upon the index Battus, clearly is comprehended."

Oltra di questo Sacra Madona, si Polia egregia puella quivi praesente (le cui invisitate bellece, gli spiriti coelesti facilmente contaminarebbono) sencia fatica, dispendio, et amaritudine di core, et periclitabondo della privatione dell’amabile vita, havesse tirato al mio ardente disio, per Iove immortale, etiam similmente la potria sencia quelle parte levemente lassare. Ma chi non hae repugnantia, gloriosa palma non aquista, et che a quella non persiste. Perché né gloria, né triumpho, né alcuno bene consequire si pole sencia industriosa faticha, dunque la faticha è causa di bene, et perseverantia il parturisce, cum le Comite. Et per questo cosa più pretiosa è (et cusì si tene) la quale erumnosamente aquistassi, che la adepta acconciamente. Lucio perciò Sicinio Dentato, della sua fortecia non sarebbe dignificato di laude et memoria, si le Stigmate obducte degli vulneri sui al dorso fusseron vidute. Perché agli degeneri militi facile si praesta il postergato ferire. Ma agli forti resistenti s’appertiene solo dinanti il vulnerare. Per la quale cosa, Amore nel mio contaminato infecto, et inquinatissimo core delle sue morbide qualitate, essendo disconciamente salito invasore, più urente dispiacevolecia usoe, che non usa il meridionale Ethon di Phoebo agli freschi floruli et mollicule piante, et herbule. Il quale immoderatamente più lo arde che lo insatiabile Vulcano Ethna. Per la quale causa, strictamente essendo di tale effecto incapestrato, infiniti accidenti et varii accessorii, et multiplice discrimine, cum evidente periculo monstroe la mia dispietata, collapsa, et infirma fortuna contra di me, a ttorto ludibonda. Degli quali casi pernitiosi, et exitiali al praesente in alcuna parte obediendo al voto tuo, incominciarò io brevemente di narrare. Insigne Sacerdota, et praestantissima Domina. Daposcia che sono quietati, et alquanto sedati gli mei letali langori, satisfare properando agli tui benigni praecepti. Più cum mie piacevole parole, che cum lachrymosi singulti tocare’ quella parte, che io son sortito tanto praeclaro amore (tacendo quello che già dicto è) più fervido et activo me totalmente strinxe. Hora me, nella tua veneranda, et eximia, et di Polia gratiosa praesentia foelice reputando, prehenderò modesto ardire. Da poscia che cum humanissimo volto, te monstri non te agravare di questa auditione. Essendo Phoebo a risugare le fresche lachryme della Plorante Aurora salito, cum gli recentati et aurei radii, fugata omni stella dello oriente, illuminava cum il suo Eoo, l’hemisperio nostro disterminato dal horizonte. Et facto il laborifico giorno, discussa la pigra quiete. Et essendo la ponderosa terra

"Beyond this, holy Lady — if Polia, egregious girl, here present (whose unvisited beauties the celestial spirits would easily contaminate), without fatigue, expense, and bitterness of heart, and imperilling of the amiable life, had drawn (me) to my ardent desire — by immortal Jove, likewise, similarly, I could, without those (torments), lightly leave her. But who has no repugnance (opposition), a glorious palm acquires not, nor (he) who persists not at it. Because neither glory, nor triumph, nor any good, can be consequuted without industrious fatigue; then fatigue is cause of good, and perseverance births it, with its Companions. And for this, a more precious thing it is (and so it is held) which troublously one acquires, than the (thing) fittingly attained. Lucius Siccius Dentatus, therefore, of his fortitude would not be dignified of praise and memory, had the scars, drawn-over, of his wounds, at the back been seen — because, to the degenerate soldiers, easy presents itself the wounding from behind; but, to the strong resistant, appertains only the wounding in front (facing the foe).

"For which thing, Love — in my contaminated, infected, and most-defiled heart (of its morbid qualities) being, unbecomingly, risen an invader — used a more burning displeasingness than the meridional Aethon of Phoebus uses to the fresh little flowers and soft plants and herbs; which, immoderately, it burns more than the insatiable Vulcan (fire of) Etna. EPISTOLA PRIMA LA QUALE POLIPHILO NARRA ALLA SUA POLIA HAVERE SCRIPTO, ET ESSA UNQUANTULO NON MOVENTISE, LI MANDOE LA SECONDA.

AVIDISSIMO ET SUMMAMENTE PERCUpido di revelare alquantulo la non mediocre fiamma dello impatiente Core. Il quale per il tuo praeclaro et singulare amore assai et validamente infiamato languente se consuma. O di venerato praeclara, et dignissima Nympha, unico in terra di bellecia mirabondo, et perfecto exemplare. Cum queste non parolette, ma profuse et non impedite lachrymule liturando il praesente papyro, ho preso questo tollerabile, et honesto auso, non temerario, ma oltra il credere fortemente impulso dal continuo stimulo, et da molesta assiduitate d’amore infesto, propalare, et dechiarire la mia incredibile passione, et sincera dilectione, che io per te, et ad te porto, mio dolce bene, et dolce mia sperancia, et solo refrigerio de gli mei non cognosciuti affanni, et non pensati da te langori. Alla quale cum pietose voce, et riverente parole, et humile prece, il stato mio in discrimine ricomando, et del mio sagittato et vulnificato core, supplicando soccorso a moderare il disordinato incendio. O Polia diva luce, et mia veneranda Dea, non te insurdire preco hora ad gli mei opportuni mendicabuli, et rogati cum il vulto demisso deprecatore, da calidissimo amore fervescente, te chiamo, te invoco, che festini tempestivamente salubre adiuto, efficace conforto, necessario sublevamento. Il perché essendomi cum gli rapaci uncini degli stelliferi ochii tui il core dal pecto mio divulso, è originata la causa di questo mio inepto et incompto scrivere, da me confuso, et da amore disposito. Et già negli praeteriti giorni, io harei tentato il simigliante, ma unque ritrovare ho potuto modo cusì conveniente et arcano. Dunque per tale rispecto questo mio crucioso tormento manifestare tacitamente restrinxi differendo. Diciò al praesente poscia che non più lento et suspeso, il disiderio mio, intruso, et inclaustrato non l’ò potuto infrenare. Imperoché la violentia del mio amore, cusì vole, et la mia prava sorte, ad questo mio comperto modo, et dulcissimo exordio me urgie, me tira, o Nympha egregia, et di chiunque mai si fusse bellissima. Dunque attendi, et commovite pia, praestate benigna, rendite cum placamento unibile ad tanta benevolentia

(Poliphilo's first letter to Polia:)

"Most-avid, and supremely most-cupidinous, to reveal somewhat the not-mediocre flame of the impatient Heart — which, for thy preclear and singular love, greatly and validly inflamed, languishing, consumes itself — O, of veneration preclear, and most-worthy Nymph, unique in earth of beauty, marvellous and perfect exemplar: with these — not little words, but profuse and unimpeded little tears — blotting the present papyrus, I have taken this tolerable and honest daring (not temerarious, but, beyond belief, strongly impelled by the continual stimulus, and by the molesting assiduity of infest love), to reveal and declare my incredible passion, and sincere affection, which I, for thee, and to thee, bear — my sweet good, and my sweet hope, and sole refrigerium of my unknown afflictions, and, by thee, unthought languors. To whom, with piteous voice, and reverent words, and humble prayer, my estate, in peril, I recommend; and, of my arrow-shot and wound-dealt heart, supplicating succour, to moderate the disordered burning.

"O Polia, divine light, and my venerable Goddess — insurd not thyself, I pray, now, to my opportune mendicables (beggings), and (things) besought, with the face lowered, a deprecator, of most-warm love fervescent; thee I call, thee I invoke — that thou hasten, timely, salubrious aid, efficacious comfort, necessary relief. Wherefore, my heart being, with the rapacious hooks of thy stelliferous eyes, from my breast divulsed (torn), is originated the cause of this my inept and inelegant writing — by me confused, and by love disposed. And, already in the preterite days, I would have attempted the like; but never have I been able to find a mode so convenient and arcane. Then, for such respect, this my tormenting torment, tacitly, I restrained, deferring. For, at present — since no more slow and suspended (was) my desire, intruded and encloistered, I could not bridle it. For the violence of my love thus wills, and my depraved lot, to this my found mode, and sweetest exordium, urges me, draws me — O egregious Nymph, and, of whoever ever was, most-beautiful. Then attend, and commove thyself, pious; present thyself benign; render thyself, with placation, unible, to so much benevolence —"

(Poliphilo's second letter to Polia:)

"If less were my harsh torment than thy accustomed cruelty, most-beautiful Nymph and Polia — a slaughterer of virtue — to my long afflictions, with blandishing hope, it would persuade me to patience. But clearly, now, I recognise (by my depraved and unpropitious Star) thy crude savagery and ferocity, whatever my incendious martyrdom to overcome and beyond surpass. Then, what avails, what boots it, to Love, to increase and increment, every hour, to my already-consumed little heart, so sweet a fire, if ever more atrocious and frigescent thou show thyself, more than rigid ice, and thy breast more frigorific than are Dirce and Nomè, founts, and more than the Salamander, cold, which, with (its) contact, extinguishes the fire? To my ancillary and servile patience, and to my notified vows and indicated affect — so much the more kindled, as the more the contrary opposes itself, of thy displeasingness — nonetheless, I cannot unbind the amorous and solid chain, which, under so soft and pressing a yoke, angariously (oppressively) holds me. Nay, the more I re-kick, so much the more I implicate myself, taken and captive in this amorous fish-trap (Nassa), like a little fly involved in the inextricable work of Arachne (a spider's web). And thus, tightly re-bound, and enslaved and captive, not valid nor apt for flight, constrained am I, that I, bending, incline myself to thee — because in thee alone consists my precious liberty, and my every necessary good.

"Whence, if thou openly understandest, my Lady, so sincere and consummate affection, and so much voluntary subjection, and so active and laborious love — why, then, wilt thou not accept so freely these things given to thee (with all my life offered), which, in thy delicate hands, ambivalent, hangs? Alas, sweetest and beautiful little Polia — succour, I pray thee, and leave and concede to penetrate, a little, these my (not superb, not arrogant) but devout words, into thy heart; and arouse in thee somewhat of compassion; receive the warm sighs; auscult my domestic and familiar laments; recognise the cordial benevolence; attend to so faithful and meek a subject. For, avidly (visibly), I die, I consume myself, of thy immoderate love — insomuch that all the world could not retract me, nor remove me (more firm than Milo), from (this): that I, above every other most-precious thing, excessively love, worship, and revere thee, and that I, bowed, adore thee — O effigied and true simulacrum of a Goddess before my eyes, and to my sight, publicly, so conspicuous and notable represented — in which most-limpidly I see depicted all my health, and expressed all my peace, delight and content."

O Nymphatula mia di core inhumano et ferino, di natura mollicula puella, più che solido Chalybe, et più che Murice saxo durissimo, più tenace che retinente Harpagone, più obstinata che cardinato Tigno. Più mordace di rapiente Gampso, et molto più delle crudele et foedante Harpyie del mio core rapace. Abominatrice del dolce amore, supersedendo alle false, et consuefacte opinione, nella tenera et virginea aetade solite di indurarse. By this way, then, I gave heed, sedulous, to reduce and humanate, and her sweetly to blandish, and to mitigate — soliciting the asperity received from the initiated arduous and perilous work. But neither she, nor the perfid Love, consented to my suasive words, with high and sworn espousals, openly showing her the nod and semblance of my — of every sweetness sweetest — flames; (that) she, in return, with requisite reciprocation, love me. And with every industrious art, and shrewd cogitation, I forced myself to kindle her of that veracious, nude, simple, and excellent affect, and amorous fire, in which, without any remedy, continually — like a Pyraulus (fire-fly/flame-moth) — I nourished myself, wretched. And, beyond this, with her, infinite times, with the mind I feigned to have a charming colloquy; and, ratiocinating (with her), daringly — intermixed, frequently, the tormentable wailings — I said: 'O my little Nymph, of inhuman and ferine heart — of nature a soft girl (yet) more than solid Steel, and more than murex-stone hardest, more tenacious than a retaining Grapnel, more obstinate than a hinged Beam; more mordant than a rapt Talon, and much more than the cruel and foul Harpies rapacious of my heart: how canst thou persevere in so much hardness and impiety? — more impious than Mithridates, more savage than Alcmaeon, more ungrateful of so much affection than Paris toward Oenone.' — To my prayers, remove, then, these iniquitous abjections from thy Nymphal heart, and this vulgar mark; and assent thyself, propitiated, to my suppliant petitions; concede, my Lady, that I consequute the desired quiet; permit to penetrate thy auditory, my tormentable little sighs; consent to my ardent loves.

And, many, and to these similar, complaints and instances performed — in the least I could not move such agitation from my continual grief, which, in me pressed, was so much in all the viscera occupant, and had so high germinated in the heart its most-bitter roots, that, by other art, nor way, nor mode — save by its chief hope (Polia herself) — ever, to extirpate, I know not, nor can, nor avail. And less profitable, still, were the groaning voices, about her superb palace vainly dispersed — (she) more deaf than Icarus to the paternal admonitions, and more displeasing than Caunus to the desperate Byblis; abominatrix of sweet love, superseding to the false and habituated opinions, in the tender and virgin age wont to harden. And an ardous thing it is to leave that which, some time, in the soul is impressed: enerve, not easily can one. Thence, then, was the exordium and origin, that I, simply ensnared and implicated, in these enveloping nets, and fallacious decoy, and in these subtle, caducous, uncertain, fugacious and momentary snares and sharpnesses of love, enslaved — that, under this molesting Tyranny and condition, and miserable servitude, subjugated and enrolled, I found one sole pleasure and alluring delightment: to love her extremely; nor did I repugn to the flying (arrows) —"

Alcuna fiata excitato, quale rabido et impatiente cane, mordico della sua retinente cathena, voleva vitare et fugire il duro nodulo del amoroso, ma molesto, laqueo, et disloricarme. Poscia vanamente imaginando fingeva molti et delectevoli solatii et piaceri, false vindicte, temerarii insulti, turbativi periculi, et impavida morte, me ritrovava poscia più strictamente innodato, et solidamente loricato. Per tale altercatione et abortivi appetiti, consumando la mia tribulosa vita, et tra suspiri et amari singulti semiconsumpta, non restato loco che da me cum solicitudine, cura perenne et scrutaria vigilantia non fusse indagato, et perlustrato, rimato, et repetito. — little arrows of blindfold Cupid. To whom, enticed, without delay, disposing myself, humbly I accepted, and all, indefatigable, I dedicated myself an observer of his most-turbulent, sharp, investigatrix, cross, and unbridled little laws — relying on the confidence of her angelic aspect, and that such were, still, her heart, and that the part with the whole should agree, and the whole, mosaic-wise, accede to the part, and not, with desperate harmony (be), so beautiful, so elegant, so comely and marvellous, and divine, a composite. Hoping reasonably that the arrow-shooting Cupid — who thus tormentably had wounded, intimately, the sad heart in me — was, juridically, and to my adverse and pernicious love, a most- safe presidium, and, to the blind errors incursant, an affable and remediable propulser, and a prompt and pious succour, and, to the superfluous blight and ardour, a congruous temperament — expecting, however, salutary aid from nowhere else than from him: that he, equally, should draw, in her, the hard and cruel bow, with which, in me, direly, he has drawn.

And, treating the gaping wound, the more it exacerbated in asperity, and the more re-doubled the wound-dealing and mortal grief — but, the hope of re-healing the amplified wound ever having, in him, non-hesitant confidence (that, I being his most- vowed subject and servant, and his opulent prey, bondman, captive, plunder, and spoil, and his copious Trophy), that same medicament which his most-pious Mother, and my Lady (Venus), made to the wounded Aeneas, still to me, following the maternal pity, would aid. And, again, being his most-devoted — that same patronage he should lend which holy Vesta lent to her handmaid and subject Tuccia, benignly, by the miracle of the sieve (carrying water in a sieve), the perpetrated fault occulted, freed (her) from public opprobrium and infamous supplice.

Whence — as, to lovers, is wont manifoldly to befall — thus, desperate, in grave litigation, without judge and adverse party, I condemned both (Love and Fortune), conjured to my deadly harm, with querulous laments weeping, inculpating them as guilty, and choice enemies of every pious humanity; (then) now, glad and festive, I revoked in me the sentence. Some time, excited, like a rabid and impatient dog, biting at its retaining chain, I wished to avoid and flee the hard knot of the amorous but molesting snare, and to un-armour myself. Then, vainly imagining, I feigned many and delectable solaces and pleasures, false vengeances, temerarious insults, perturbing perils, and impavid death — I found myself, afterward, more tightly knotted, and solidly armoured. By such altercation, and abortive appetites, consuming my tribulous life — and, among sighs and bitter sobs, half-consumed — there remained no place that, by me, with solicitude, perennial care, and scrutatory vigilance, was not indagated and lustrated, ratched, and re-searched; no way, and blind-alley, and almost even through the porticoes, unattempted, omitted —

Chapter XXXV

The vision at Venus's throne. His freed soul is borne to Venus's throne, where he complains against Cupid; the god strikes Polia's image with the golden arrow — her conversion, seen from heaven — and gives her to Poliphilo, and Venus's voice, "which could soften a diamond," sends his soul home.

Et quivi nel tempio praesente ella, cum l’animo pertinace imperterrita et immota vedendo la immatura et celerata morte, lugendo asmatico, sopra le copule, overo vertebre proclinato misericordia renissamente precando, et in terra prosternatome, morto restai. Per la quale cosa essa forsa instigata dagli Dii, et praemonita della sua malignitate, et rigida et inhumana perversitate, perché niuno intra in cose nove si delle praeterite non se pentisce, ritornoe antelucio domatina sequente a rrispectare nel violato Tempio, il pridiano almicidio. Et cum molte virginale attrectatione, et dulcicule anxietate, et suppressi gemituli, et infiniti osculi et ferali submurmuri, penitente amplexantime, et piatosamente illachrymabonda, et de lachryme abundante rosulantime, revocava dolcemente l’alma mia. La quale non tanto praesto fora oblata del corpo mio fue subvecta et demissa nel divino conspecto et all’alto throno della divina Domina matre. Diqué nel suo habito et habitudine reiterando, et nel suo inane corpusculo, gaudiosa et cum lepida iocunditate, et cum obtenta gratia victrice cusì alacremente disse.

Being, then, in such a manner rapt and sublimated, and, of beholding the celestial works, stupefied — and re-dried the flux of the solicitous tears, and benignly ausculted my miserable laments — the Divine Lady Mother, with an ineffable majesty and sanctimony, and with an unheard and venerable voice, soothing (enough to re-serene the beclouded heavens, to take the noxious armature from Enyalian Mars, and the thunderbolts from the hand of the jaculating Jove, to in-youth the old Saturn, to Ethiopise (darken) the most-beautiful Phoebus, to in-stammer the eloquent Cyllenian (Mercury), and to defile the chaste Diana) — never by the terrestrials heard such (a voice) — proffered divine words, with divine afflation, and with such Harmony, affably, as never, to the empty Syrinx (pipe), the divine lips of the talaric Mercury, (playing) to the eyed Argus, breathed — by the sweetness of which, whatever Cotic whetstone-rock of Libya, nay, whatever Indian Diamond, contaminated and immuted, would have been softened to every softness, tender and fresh.

And, in this manner speaking, she made me secure of my health, and of my prosperous love, and of this my most-jocund postliminium (homecoming), and to thee (Polia) to return. And, with a most-charming little laugh, she said to her offspring: "And thou — if, for the wounded Virgin girl, perhaps to turn-tail from this amorous office, and to relinquish this present soul, thou shouldst fore-attempt — thou shalt be surety (bail)." — "Then, my little body, my lodging: remove from thee all the most-harsh griefs, and every passion, and accept me thus entire into thee, as ever, with thee, conjoined I was — with that most-celebrated name, in me impressed, by which, from thee, I receded; which, otherwise, is carved and impressed, and sealed, within me, vegetable and fecund — (it) was not that of Oenone and of Paris, sculpted in the ramose trees and rugose barks, nor thence ever shall it be erased, nor to be deleted, but eternally consigned, conservable. Now, most-loving host, receive me, thy indigene (native), who, to remedy thy grave and insupportable tribulations, have penetrated and passed through so many waters of weepings, and through so much fire of love, and through so many supreme fatigues; and, finally, up-borne where thy likes cannot be, and have attained so much divine benignity, that I, thence timely sequestered, bear thy most- valiant and most-whole health."

And I, to my re-turned and re-gathered Genius (soul), responded: "Come, indigene inhabitant, and Lady of the supreme citadel of my mind, best rational portion. Come, my heart, domicile of irritable ardour. Come, extreme part where makes residence my exhorter Cupid — and let us make, then, the festive Soteria (thanksgivings) for thy retrograde reformation (return)."

VENERANDA ET SANCTA MATRONA de questo Sacro Tempio Antista praeclara et dignissima. Per aventura incredibile appare, et alieno de fide, che non cusì propere hebbe posto fine l’alma agli sui salutiferi ragionari, in me rigressa la appetibile vita, repente me ritrovai negli stricti et serati amplexi, et succosi et saporosissimi osculamenti de questa Nympha, fiore virgineo redolente. Et cum il servato ordine, il quale essa come lepida, festiva facondamente hae narrato cum miro et amoroso fomento creve intimamente la dilectione nostra fina al praesente caso. Onde essendo hora dinante ad te insigne religiosa et praesidente de questo loco sacro Sancta. Ad te se appertene decentemente de divertire, obliquare, et dimovendo avertire il male, di prosperare il bene, et le humile et ime cose sublimare, le nutante dirigere, et fulcire, le obscure lucificare, et le adverse emendare et corrigere. Et vulnerato l’uno della d’oro, et l’altro sia infixo della funesta plumbea.

POLIPHILO QUIVI FINISSE LA SUA HYPNEROTOMACHIA, DOLENTISE DEL SOMNO CHE NON FUE PIÙ LONGO. ET CHE IL SOLE FUE INVIDIOSO FACENDO GIORNO.

TANTO INOPINABILE DELECTAMENTO surrepto, et dagli ochii mei summoto quel spirito angelico, et subtracto fora dagli somnosi membri il dolce et suave dormire evigilantime, in quel punctulo, Omè Heu me amorosi lectori, tutto indolentime per il forte stringere de quella beata imagine, et foelice praesentia, et veneranda maiestate, lassantime et deserentime tra mira dolcecia, et intensiva amaritudine. Quando dal obtuto mio, se partirono quel iocundissimo somno, et quella diva umbra interrupta et disiecta quella mysteriosa apparitione et sublata. Per le quale fue conducto et elato ad sì alti et sublimi, et penetrabili cogitamenti. Diqué per aventura il Sole de invidia agitato di cusì beato somnio, a depraedare la gloriosa nocte, como publico inimico et Sycophanta della divina Matre, cum gli illuminosi splendori subitoso vene et a dipingere di colore roseo l’albicante Aurora discussa la perpete nocte. Et illustrato et interposito il recentato die, io rimansi stipato et completissimo di dolce, et argutula fallacia. Cogitate dunque quale livore livido, alhora ello harebbe, si io realmente sentisse perfruendo gli proprii et voluptici dilecti, de cusì formosa et diva damicella, et insigne Nympha, che esso non sostene (arbitro perché cum diva non lice) a cconcedermi la longa nocte (da indignatione) di Alcmena. Heu me perché non commutoe egli uno alquantulo della sua celeritudine, cum uno pauculo di secordia, alla mia refecta quiescentia, et praeterire unotantulo il suo statuto? Et perché alhora non mi fue arrogato il Stygio somno della Pyxide della curiosa Psyches? Et quivi Philomela anteluculo flendo promeva, tra gli spinosi rubi operta, et tra boscheti pressi di opaca coma di querculi, involuti della obliquante Periclymeno le violentie dell’adultero et infido Tereo, cum canoro garrito dicendo, Tereus Tereus, eme ebiasato?sospirando emerso et absoluto dal dolce somno repentuscule me lucubrai dicendo. Vale ergo Polia.

Tarvisii cum decorissimis Poliae amore lorulis, distineretur misellus Poliphilus.

.M. CCCC. LXVII. Kalendis Maii.

Poliphilo here ends his Hypnerotomachia, grieving that the sleep was no longer, and that the Sun was envious, and made it day.

So unlooked-for a delight snatched away, that angelic spirit taken from my eyes, and the sweet and gentle sleeping drawn out of my drowsy limbs as I woke — in that instant, alas, ah me, amorous readers, I ached all over from the hard clasping of that blessed image, that happy presence, that venerable majesty, which left me and deserted me between wondrous sweetness and piercing bitterness. When from my gaze there departed that most joyful sleep and that divine shade, the mysterious apparition broken off, scattered, and carried away — by which I had been led and lifted to thoughts so high, so sublime, so piercing.

And then, as it happened, the Sun, stirred to envy by so blessed a dream, coming to plunder the glorious night like a public enemy and an informer against the divine Mother, came suddenly with his shining splendours and painted the whitening Dawn a rosy colour, the long night dispelled. And the new-made day being lit and set between us, I was left crammed and utterly filled with a sweet and subtle deception.

Consider, then, what livid spite he would have had, if I had truly felt, in the enjoying of them, the very voluptuous delights of so shapely and divine a damsel, so matchless a nymph — he who would not endure (because, I judge, with a goddess it is not permitted) to grant me the long night of Alcmena. Ah me, why did he not exchange a little of his swiftness for a little sloth, for the sake of my restored rest, and overrun his appointed hour by just so much? And why was the Stygian sleep out of curious Psyche's box not laid upon me then?

And there Philomela, weeping before daybreak, hidden among thorny brambles and in thickets close with the dark foliage of small oaks wound about with twining honeysuckle, was pouring out the violence of that adulterous and faithless Tereus, saying with tuneful chatter: Tereus, Tereus — [?have I been wronged]. Sighing, risen and released from the sweet sleep, I woke of a sudden into the small hours, saying: Farewell then, Polia.

At Treviso, where wretched Poliphilo was held fast in the most comely little thongs of Polia's love. 1467, on the Kalends of May.

Notes

Confidence: high. The narrative Italian here is unusually plain for Colonna and the classical allusions (Alcmena, Psyche's box, Philomela and Tereus) are all securely identifiable. The one weak point is the corrupt Greek noted below, which is isolated to three words and does not affect the sense of the passage.

  • eme ebiasato? — the transcription reads Tereus Tereus, eme ebiasato?
  • Omè Heu me — the Italian exclamation immediately doubled by the Latin.
  • la longa nocte di Alcmena — Jupiter stopped the sun to lengthen the night
  • Tarvisii — Treviso, where the historical Francesco Colonna's Polia is

EPITAPHIUM POLIAE

F œlix Polia, quæ sepulta vivis C haro Marte Poliphilus quiescens I am fecit vigilare te sopitam.

EPITAPHIUM UBI POLIPHILUS LOQUITUR.

VIATOR FAC QUAESO MORULAM, POLIAE NYMPHAE HIC EST MYROPOLIUM. QUAE NAM INQUIES POLIA? FLOS ILLE OMNEM REDOLENS VIRTUTEM SPECTATISSIMUS. QUI OB LOCI ARITUDINEM, PLUSCULIS POLIPHILI LACHRYMUL. REPULULESCERE NEQUIT. AT SI ME FLORERE VIDERES, EXIMIA PICTURA UNIVERSIS DECORITER PRAESTARE CONSPICERES PHOEBE INQUIENS, QUEM INTACTUM URORE RELIQUE RAS, UMBRA CECIDIT. HEU POLIPHILE DESINE. FLOS SIC EXSICCATUS, NUNQUAM REVIVISCIT. VALE.

The text on this leaf is Latin, not Italian. It is given here in the original with an English rendering beneath, since the Latin is itself quotable and the first three lines carry an acrostic.

F œlix Polia, quæ sepulta vivis
C haro Marte Poliphilus quiescens
I am fecit vigilare te sopitam.

Happy Polia, who being buried yet live: Poliphilo, resting from dear Mars, has now made you, who were lulled asleep, keep watch.

The initials set out from the margin spell F · C · I.

VIATOR FAC QUAESO MORULAM, POLIAE NYMPHAE HIC EST MYROPOLIUM.
QUAE NAM INQUIES POLIA? FLOS ILLE OMNEM REDOLENS VIRTUTEM SPECTATISSIMUS.
QUI OB LOCI ARITUDINEM, PLUSCULIS POLIPHILI LACHRYMUL[IS] REPULULESCERE NEQUIT.
AT SI ME FLORERE VIDERES, EXIMIA PICTURA UNIVERSIS DECORITER PRAESTARE
CONSPICERES, PHOEBE INQUIENS, QUEM INTACTUM URORE RELIQUERAS, UMBRA CECIDIT.
HEU POLIPHILE DESINE. FLOS SIC EXSICCATUS, NUNQUAM REVIVISCIT. VALE.

Traveller, make a little pause, I beg you: here is the perfume-shop of the nymph Polia. And what, you will say, is Polia? That most admired flower, fragrant with every virtue — who, because the ground is parched, cannot put out shoots again for all Poliphilo's little tears. But if you had seen me in flower, you would have seen me surpass all others in beauty, like an exceptional painting; saying, Phoebus, the one you left untouched by your burning, a shadow has felled. Ah, Poliphilo, have done. A flower dried out like this never lives again.

Farewell.

Notes

Confidence: high. This leaf is Latin, not macaronic Italian, and it is straightforward funerary Latin at that. Two abbreviations and one line-broken word had to be expanded, all noted below and none of them doubtful.

  • MYROPOLIUM — literally an unguent- or perfume-seller's shop
  • LACHRYMUL. — the source abbreviates; expanded to lachrymulis, "little
  • RELIQUE / RAS — broken across a line in the transcription; read as
  • PHOEBE INQUIENS — vocative: the dead flower addresses the Sun, who
  • The three-line acrostic F · C · I is not the book's famous

The errors of the book, made in printing; which correct thus:

Notes

Confidence: high. The final leaf of the 1499 edition: the printer's errata (a gathering-by-gathering list of typographical corrections), closed by the note that display-capital lines are not counted, and the famous Aldine colophon — printed by Aldus Manutius at Venice, December 1499. Not narrative; the list is described rather than transcribed (line-by-line typo-fixes carry no meaning in translation), and the meaningful framing and colophon are given.
